83:
## Homage to the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One
## Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī-aṭṭhakathā
## Ganthārambhakathā

I pay homage with a particularly devoted mind to the Buddha, who is the worthy recipient of veneration, affection, offerings, and respect, and who has complete and exhaustive knowledge of all things; to the ten-fold sublime Dhamma consisting of the Paths, Fruits, Nibbāna, and the Dhamma-aggregate; and to the eight-fold Noble Saṅgha.

Having paid homage with joined palms to the great ancient teachers, who are the lions of the lineage (or who are the lamps of the lineage) of the Elders such as Venerable Mahākassapa, and who are firmly established in the sequence of the Vinaya.

The Pātimokkha, the code of training and virtue, has been clearly declared by the Great Sage; it is the foremost and principal of the faultless qualities such as concentration and wisdom, and it serves as the mouth or the gateway for entering Nibbāna.

Being respectfully requested by the Elder Soṇa, who delights in good deeds, who is humble in physical and verbal conduct, who maintains a pure and scrupulous livelihood, and who is endowed with the practice of the Vinaya.

For the purpose of overcoming the doubts of those monks who have arisen doubts regarding that Pātimokkha, [I shall compose] its commentary, which contains complete decisions.

Relying on the tradition of recitation of the dwellers of the Mahāvihāra (or the members of the Mahāvihāra sect), I shall bring forth the beautiful commentary named "Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī," which is excellent in both meaning and phrasing.
84:
## Explanation of the Introduction
In that verse (Pātimokkhaṃ pakāsitaṃ), "Pātimokkha" means *pa-atimokkha* or *atipamokkha*, having the sense of being "most noble" or "most excellent." By this etymological meaning, although Pātimokkha is of one kind, it is of two types in terms of virtue (sīla) and the text (gantha).

This is true. In such passages as "He dwells restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha," and "This virtue is the beginning, the face, the foremost and principal of wholesome states; therefore it is called Pātimokkha," virtue is called Pātimokkha. In such passages as "For that monk, both Pātimokkhas are well-recited in detail," the text is called Pātimokkha.

Of these two, virtue is called Pātimokkha because it protects (pāti) the one who guards it and releases (mokkheti) or frees them from sufferings such as those of the woeful states, or from dangers such as self-reproach. The text, however, is called Pātimokkha because it illuminates that Pātimokkha of virtue. The etymological meaning mentioned at the beginning applies to both virtue and the text.

Between these two, this forthcoming commentary is suitable for both the Sīla-pātimokkha and the Gantha-pātimokkha. This is because when the text is explained, its meaning, which is virtue, is also explained. That Gantha-pātimokkha is of two types: the Bhikkhu-pātimokkha and the Bhikkhunī-pātimokkha.

Of these two, the Pātimokkha defined by five sections of recitation (uddesa), beginning with "Let the Saṅgha hear me, venerable sirs," is called the Bhikkhu-pātimokkha. The Pātimokkha defined by four sections of recitation, beginning with "Let the Saṅgha hear me, ladies," is called the Bhikkhunī-pātimokkha.

In that Bhikkhu-pātimokkha, the five recitations are: the recitation of the introduction (nidānuddesa), the recitation of the defeats (pārājikuddesa), the recitation of the formal meetings (saṅghādisesuddesa), the recitation of the undetermined cases (aniyatuddesa), and the recitation in detail (vitthāruddesa).

Among these five, the recitation of the introduction is recited in this manner: "Let the Saṅgha hear me, venerable sirs... for him who reveals [his fault], there is comfort. In this matter, I ask the venerable ones: Are you pure in this? A second time I ask: Are you pure in this? A third time I ask: Are you pure in this? The venerable ones are pure in this; therefore they are silent. Thus do I record it." Having said this, if the remaining recitations are made known (recited) by the word "heard" (suta) in the manner beginning with "Venerable sirs, the introduction has been recited," then it is considered recited. The sections of the Pārājikuddesa and so on should be connected by starting from the beginning of the introduction and concluding with the Pārājika and so forth. The details [will be discussed later].
85:
It is indeed the detailed recitation of the Pātimokkha (Vitthāruddesa). According to the teaching, "The remainder [of the Pātimokkha] should be made known by the word 'suta' (heard)," if an obstacle arises while a specific section such as the Pārājikuddesa is incomplete, the remaining part of the Pātimokkha, along with that incomplete section, should be made known by the word 'suta' (concluded by recitation). However, if the Nidānuddesa is not yet finished, there is no such thing as making it known by the word 'suta'. In the Bhikkhunī Pātimokkha, the Aniyatuddesa is omitted; the rest of the procedure is the same as previously mentioned. Thus, this commentary (Atthakathā) will be on both types of Pātimokkha, which are defined by five sections and four sections of recitation respectively. Since the Bhikkhu Pātimokkha comes first among these two, this verse is spoken for the purpose of explaining that Bhikkhu Pātimokkha:

I shall state the determination of the meaning of the words beginning with "Suṇātu me":
Bhikkhave sīlasampannā, sikkhākāmā suṇantu me.
(May the monks, endowed with virtue and desiring training, listen to me.)

In this verse, the word "suṇātu" is a term expressing an exhortation to listen. The word "me" is a term of self-reference for the person who is making the Pātimokkha known (the reciter). The word "bhante" is a term expressing respect and reliance, addressed to a person worthy of honor. The word "saṅgha" is a term for a group of individuals. All these are the words to be spoken first by the monk who recites the Pātimokkha. Because the Blessed One spoke thus when authorizing the recitation of the Pātimokkha in Rājagaha, if the monk reciting the Pātimokkha is a senior elder (Saṅghathera), he should say "Āvuso" (Friend). If he is a junior monk, he should say "Bhante" (Venerable Sir) according to the method found in the Pāḷi. Either a senior elder may recite the Pātimokkha, according to the teaching "The Pātimokkha belongs to the elder," or a junior monk may recite it, according to the teaching "I allow, O monks, that monk who is wise and competent in that assembly to recite the Pātimokkha."

Although the word "saṅgha" generally refers to a group of individuals without distinction, that Saṅgha is of two types: the Dakkhiṇeyya-saṅgha (the Saṅgha worthy of offerings) and the Sammuti-saṅgha (the conventional Saṅgha). Among them, the group of eight Noble Persons (Ariya-puggala) is called the Dakkhiṇeyya-saṅgha. The group of monks in general, without distinction, is called the Sammuti-saṅgha; it is this Sammuti-saṅgha that is intended here. This Sammuti-saṅgha is of five types according to legal acts (kamma): a group of four (catu-vagga), a group of five (pañca-vagga), a group of ten (dasa-vagga), a group of twenty (vīsati-vagga), and a group of more than twenty (atireka-vīsati-vagga). Among these, a group of four is permitted to perform all Saṅgha acts except for Upasampadā (ordination), Pavāraṇā, and Abbhāna (rehabilitation). A group of five is permitted to perform all Saṅgha acts except for Upasampadā and Abbhāna in the middle regions (majjhima-janapada)...
86:
...is permitted to perform. A group of ten is permitted to perform all Saṅgha acts except for the act of Abbhāna (rehabilitation) alone. A group of twenty is not prohibited from performing any Saṅgha act (i.e., it is permitted); likewise, a group of more than twenty is also permitted. The reason for mentioning the group of more than twenty is to show that while an act to be performed by a group of four, etc., is not valid if performed by fewer than that number, it is valid if performed by more. In this context, starting from the group of four, the entire Sammuti-saṅgha is intended.

By the phrase "Today is the Uposatha day" (ajju-posatho), days that are not Uposatha days are excluded. By the phrase "the fifteenth day" (pannaraso), other Uposatha days are excluded. According to the days, three types of Uposatha are mentioned: Cātuddasika (14th day), Paññarasika (15th day), and Sāmaggī (Unity) Uposatha. Among them, in the three seasons of winter, summer, and the rains, by performing it twice in the third and seventh fortnights (pakkha) of each season, there are 6 Cātuddasika Uposathas; the remaining 18 are Paññarasika Uposathas, making 24 Uposathas in a year. This is the primary standard practice (pakati-cāritta).

Based on the teaching, "I allow, O monks, the recitation of the Pātimokkha once a fortnight, either on the fourteenth or the fifteenth day," and the teaching, "Visiting monks must follow the resident monks," etc., if there is a special reason, it is also permitted to perform the Uposatha on another fourteenth day.

For monks who have completed the first Rains (purima-vassa), the full moon day of Assayuja (Thadingyut) is the Pavāraṇā day. If those same monks, being harassed by quarrelsome monks, postpone the Pavāraṇā, then either the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of Assayuja or the full moon day of Kattika (Tazaungmon) becomes the Pavāraṇā day. For monks who have completed the later Rains (pacchima-vassa), only the full moon day of Kattika is the Pavāraṇā day. These three types of days are Pavāraṇā days. This is also the primary standard practice. However, if there is a special reason, it is also permitted to perform Pavāraṇā on the fourteenth days preceding the two full moon days of Kattika (Assayuja and Kattika).

When a divided Saṅgha is reconciled according to the method in the Kosambaka Khandhaka and a monk is reinstated into the Saṅgha, the Saṅgha performs the act of unity for the settling of that legal issue. At that time, according to the teaching, "The Uposatha should be performed at that very moment, and the Pātimokkha should be recited," any day other than the 14th or 15th is called the Sāmaggī-uposatha day. For monks who have completed the first Rains, such a day within the month of Kattika is called the Sāmaggī-pavāraṇā day. Thus, among these three types of days, other Uposatha days are excluded by the word "fifteenth". Therefore, by the phrase "Today is the Uposatha day"...
87:
A day that is not an Uposatha day has been prohibited; the Uposatha should certainly not be performed on such a non-Uposatha day. However, there is another Uposatha day; on that Uposatha day, the Uposatha should be performed. When performing the Uposatha, if it is the fourteenth-day Uposatha, it should be declared: "Today is the fourteenth-day Uposatha." If it is the fifteenth-day Uposatha, it should be declared: "Today is the fifteenth-day Uposatha." If it is the harmony (Sāmaggi) Uposatha, it should be declared: "Today is the harmony Uposatha."

In the phrase "Yadi saṅghassa pattakallaṃ," it is called "pattakāla" (attained time) because the time for this formal act (kamma) has arrived; the act that has a suitable time is indeed called "pattakalla." That pattakalla act, in this context of the Uposatha, is comprised of four factors. As the teachers of the Commentaries (Aṭṭhakathā) said:

"The occurrence of the Uposatha day, the presence of all monks who are eligible for the formal act,
the absence of common offenses (sabhāgāpatti),
and the absence of persons who should be excluded from the hand-reach (hattha-pāsa) of that Saṅgha;
the fulfillment of these factors is called 'pattakalla'."

In that verse, "Uposatha" refers to any one of the three types of Uposatha days. Only when it is such an Uposatha day is this Uposatha act of the Saṅgha called "pattakalla"; if not, it is not so called. The Blessed One also said: "Monks, the Uposatha should not be performed on a non-Uposatha day. Whoever should perform it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)."

"Yāvatikā ca bhikkhū kammapattā" means that there must be at least four monks of good standing (pakatatta) who are suitable and appropriate for that Uposatha act, and those monks must remain within a single boundary (sīmā) without leaving the hand-reach (hattha-pāsa).

A boundary (sīmā) is of two types: the bound boundary (baddha-sīmā) and the unbound boundary (abaddha-sīmā). Among them, a boundary that avoids the eleven types of invalid boundaries (vipatti-sīmā), possesses the three types of perfection (sampatti), and is designated by connecting one mark (nimitta) to another is called a baddha-sīmā. "A boundary that is too small, one that is too large, one with broken marks, one with shadow marks, one without marks, one designated while standing outside the boundary, one designated in a river, one designated in the ocean, one designated in a natural lake, one designated by overlapping a boundary with another boundary, and one designated by encroaching a boundary upon another boundary"—these are called the eleven invalid boundaries (vipatti-sīmā) because of the word: "Acts fail due to the boundary in eleven ways." Among those invalid boundaries, the one called "too small" (atikhuddaka) is a boundary in which twenty-one monks are unable to sit...
88: A boundary in which twenty-one monks are unable to sit is called an atikhuddaka boundary. A boundary that is designated exceeding three yojanas, even by as little as a hair's breadth, is called an atimahati boundary. A khaṇḍa-nimitta boundary refers to a boundary with disconnected marks. After proclaiming the mark in the eastern direction, one should proclaim the marks in the southern, western, and northern directions in order, and then proclaim again the first proclaimed mark in the eastern direction before stopping. Only by doing this does it become an akhaṇḍa-nimitta (a boundary with unbroken marks). If one brings the marks in order and proclaims the mark in the northern direction and stops right there, it becomes a khaṇḍa-nimitta boundary. Another type of khaṇḍa-nimitta boundary is one designated by making a single mark in between things that do not qualify as marks, such as a tree with only bark as its core, a stump, or a mound of earth or sand. A chāyā-nimitta boundary is one designated by taking any shadow, such as the shadow of a mountain, as a mark. An animitta boundary is one designated without proclaiming any marks at all. A bahi-sīmā ṭhita-sammatā boundary is one designated by a Saṅgha standing outside the marks after the marks have been proclaimed. A boundary designated in a river, ocean, or natural lake (jātassara) is a boundary designated in those rivers, etc. Even if so designated, it does not count as being designated (it does not become a baddha-sīmā) according to the Pāḷi: "Monks, every river is not a boundary (not a baddha-sīmā), every ocean is not a boundary, every natural lake is not a boundary." A sīmāya sīmaṃ sambhindantena sammatā boundary is one designated by connecting one's own boundary with another's boundary. For example, if to the east of an old monastery there are two trees, a mango and a rose-apple, with branches intertwined. Among those trees, the rose-apple is to the west of the mango. The monastery boundary was bound by including the rose-apple inside and proclaiming the mango as the mark. Later, monks who build a new monastery to the east of that monastery and bind a boundary include that mango tree inside and proclaim the rose-apple as the mark; this is an overlapping and mixing of boundaries. A sīmāya sīmaṃ ajjhottharantena sammatā boundary is one designated by encroaching one's own boundary over another's boundary. If one designates one's own boundary by including the whole or a part of another's baddha-sīmā inside, it is said to be encroaching on the boundary. Thus, a boundary designated by avoiding these eleven invalid boundaries is called a baddha-sīmā. "Tividha-sampatti-yuttā" means being endowed with the perfection of marks (nimitta-sampatti), the perfection of the assembly (parisā-sampatti), and the perfection of the formal act (kammavācā-sampatti). Among those three, perfection of marks means that among the eight kinds of marks mentioned as mountain-mark, stone-mark, forest-mark, tree-mark, road-mark, anthill-mark, river-mark, and water-mark, in each respective direction...
89:
A boundary (sīmā) is consecrated by correctly announcing the available markers (nimitta) that are suitable to be markers, in such a manner as: "What is the marker in the east? Venerable sir, this mountain is the marker." Among those markers, the way they become suitable as markers should be understood in brief. There are three types of mountains: those of pure soil, those of pure stone, and those mixed with both. A mountain from the size of an elephant upwards is suitable as a marker; one smaller than that is not valid. In the case of a stone marker, even an iron ball is reckoned as a stone. Therefore, at the maximum, a stone smaller than an elephant's size, and at the minimum, a stone the size of a lump of molasses weighing thirty-two palas (128 ticals) is suitable as a marker; one smaller than that is not valid. A flat rock (pāṣāṇa-piṭṭhi), however, is valid even if it is very large.

In the case of a forest marker, a forest consisting of at least four or five trees, whether they are trees with heartwood or mixed with heartwood trees, is suitable as a marker; a forest with fewer than that is not valid. A tree must be a living tree with heartwood standing in the ground. Even a tree at least eight finger-breadths (aṭṭhaṅgula) in height and the thickness of a stylus (sūcidaṇḍaka) is suitable as a marker; one smaller than that is not valid. A path, whether it be a foot-path or a cart-road, must be one that passes through two or three village territories. Such a path is suitable as a marker only if it is still being used by pedestrians or caravans of carts; a path no longer in use is not valid. An anthill, at the minimum, even one formed on that very day, eight finger-breadths in height and the size of a cow's horn, is suitable as a marker; one smaller than that is not valid. Only a river that will be described in the characteristics of an unbound boundary (abaddha-sīmā) is suitable as a marker; any other river is not valid. Regarding water, starting from water that is not flowing and stays in wells, ponds, reservoirs, lakes, or the salt ocean, even water fetched in jars and filled into a small pit dug in the ground at that very moment is suitable as a marker, provided it remains until the end of the formal act (kammavācā). Otherwise, flowing water, or water that does not remain for the specified duration, or water in a vessel, is not valid.

What is called the perfection of the assembly (parisa-sampatti) is a boundary consecrated by at least four monks assembling and having all the monks who are within that village territory—without entering a bound boundary (baddha-sīmā) or a river, ocean, or natural lake—either present within the reach of a forearm (hatthapāsa) or having brought their consent (chanda).
90:
What is called the perfection of the formal act (kammavācā-sampatti) is the consecration by a pure formal act consisting of a motion and one proclamation (ñattidutiya-kammavācā) as stated in the Mahāvagga: "Let the Saṅgha hear me, venerable sir, as many markers as have been announced all around..." and so forth. Thus, a boundary consecrated by connecting one marker to another, being endowed with the three types of perfection (sampatti) and transcending the eleven types of defective boundaries (vipatti-sīmā), should be known as a "bound boundary" (baddha-sīmā). The small boundary (khaṇḍa-sīmā), the boundary of common communion (samānasaṃvāsa-sīmā), and the boundary of non-separation from the three robes (avippavāsa-sīmā) are its subdivisions.

An unbound boundary (abaddha-sīmā) is of three types: the village boundary (gāma-sīmā), the seven-interval boundary (sattabbhantara-sīmā), and the water-splash boundary (udakukkhepa-sīmā). Among these, as far as a single village territory extends, this is called a village boundary. In a forest where there is no village, a boundary with an extent of seven intervals (abbhantara) all around is called a seven-interval boundary. Here, a forest without a village is found in great forests such as the Viñjhāṭavi or on small islands in the middle of the ocean where fishermen cannot go and return in a single day. "Seven intervals all around" means there are seven intervals in each of the four directions from the monks standing in the center, making it fourteen intervals from one end to the other. There, one interval (abbhantara) is twenty-eight cubits in measure. This boundary expands according to the size of the assembly; therefore, the measurement of intervals should be made starting from the edge of the surrounding assembly. If two groups of Saṅgha perform the Uposatha separately, another interval should be left between those two seven-interval boundaries for the sake of the boundary's precinct (sīmā-upacāra).

Having rejected the status of a boundary for rivers and so forth by the method beginning with: "Monks, all rivers are not boundaries," the Buddha again stated: "Monks, in a river, or in the ocean, or in a natural lake, as far as a man of average height splashes water all around, this is the boundary of common communion and single Uposatha there." This is called a water-splash boundary (udakukkhepa-sīmā). There, a river whose current ceases as soon as the clouds disappear after it has rained continuously every half-month, every ten days, or every five days during the time of righteous kings, does not count as a river. However, a river whose current does not cease throughout the four months of the rainy season during such a time of good rainfall is called a river from its source, whether it flows into the ocean or a lake. This is determined if a nun, while crossing at a ford or a non-ford, has her inner robe (antaravāsaka) soaked even by one or two finger-breadths when she covers the three circles (the navel and two knees) and does not lift her inner robe, as per the characteristics mentioned in the Sekhiya rules. The ocean is well-known. As for a natural pond (sobbha) which is not dug by anyone but exists naturally and is filled with water coming from all around, in that pond, as said regarding the river, during the rainy season...
91:
A natural hollow that is not dug by anyone but is filled with water from the surroundings is called a jātassara (natural lake). In a river where water remains well during the rainy season as mentioned, such a lake is called a jātassara. A pit formed by water breaking out from a river or the ocean also reaches this characteristic of holding water for the four months of the rainy season; it too should be called a jātassara.

The area defined by a man of average strength throwing water around himself is called udakukkhepa. In such throwing, just as gamblers throw a wooden ball, a man of average strength should take water or sand in his hand and throw it with all his might. The place where the water or sand so thrown falls is called udakukkhepa.

In those places such as rivers, the boundary defined by the udakukkhepa is both samānasaṃvāsa (of common communion) and ekūposatha (of a single Uposatha). However, this boundary is obtained only within those rivers, etc., and not outside. Therefore, in a river or a jātassara lake, the area covered by water during the four months of the natural rainy season, and in the ocean, the area where natural waves rise and settle, is the kappiyabhūmi (allowable ground) for establishing an udakukkhepa boundary. Standing there, it is proper to perform acts such as the uposatha. Even when rivers and jātassara lakes are dry during a drought or in the summer, that same ground remains the kappiyabhūmi. However, if people dig a tank or cultivate crops in a dried-up jātassara lake, that place becomes a village field (gāmakhetta).

The udakukkhepa boundary cannot extend outside the aforementioned kappiyabhūmi; it only goes inward. Therefore, the udakukkhepa measurement should be made all around starting from the edge of the assembly within that area. If two groups of the Saṅgha perform the uposatha separately, another udakukkhepa distance should be left between the two udakukkhepas for the sake of the upacāra (vicinity). This udakukkhepa boundary and the sattabbhantara boundary are obtained starting from the place where the monks are standing. A monk standing within the defined area but having left the hatthapāsa (hand-reach), or a monk standing outside the defined area without exceeding that same distance, can cause the act (kamma) to fail. This is the decision in all the Commentaries. Thus, the abaddhasīmā (unbound boundary) should be understood. Referring to these two types of boundaries, namely baddhasīmā and abaddhasīmā, it was said: "And they, without leaving the hatthapāsa, stand in a single boundary." Among those four monks, standing in a single boundary without leaving the hatthapāsa...
92:
Only when the four monks stand in a single boundary without leaving the hatthapāsa is that uposatha act of the Saṅgha called pattakalla (attained to appropriateness); it is not so otherwise. As it was said: "I allow you, monks, to recite the Pātimokkha to four [monks]."

In the phrase "and common offenses (sabhāgāpatti) do not exist," when the entire Saṅgha incurs a light offense due to a common basis such as eating at the wrong time (vikālabhojana), an offense that is similar in terms of the basis is called vatthusabhāga. However, an offense incurred due to eating at the wrong time, which is similar in terms of the offense (āpattisabhāga), may be confessed in the presence of a monk who has incurred an offense due to eating food that is not leftover (anatirittabhojana). If there is a common offense, those monks should immediately send one monk to a nearby monastery, saying: "Go, friend, return after clearing that offense; we will clear our offenses in your presence." If this can be done, it is good. If not, a competent and capable monk should inform the Saṅgha with a formal motion (ñatti): "Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me. This entire Saṅgha has incurred a common offense. When we see another pure monk who is without offense, we will clear that offense in his presence." Having said this, the uposatha should be performed. If there is doubt (vematika), he should say: "Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me. This entire Saṅgha is in doubt regarding a common offense. When we are free from doubt, we will clear that offense." Having said this, the uposatha should be performed.

If, in this situation, some monk, thinking that the common offense can be confessed, confesses it in the presence of another monk, that offense is indeed well-confessed. However, due to the act of confession, the one who confesses and, due to the act of receiving, the one who receives both incur an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa). Since that dukkaṭa offense arises from different bases, they can confess to each other. By this much confession, those two monks become free of offense. Then, the remaining monks should confess or announce their common offenses in the presence of those two monks. If they perform the uposatha without doing so, they incur the offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa) prescribed for performing the uposatha while having an offense, according to the method beginning with: "Venerables, announce your purity." If the entire Saṅgha performs the uposatha while a common offense exists without following the stated procedure, the entire Saṅgha incurs an offense according to the stated method. Therefore, when a common offense exists, the Saṅgha's [uposatha act is not pattakalla].
93:
If there is a common offense (sabhāgāpatti), it is not what is called pattakalla (the fitness of the occasion for performing the Uposatha). Therefore, the commentators said: "Common offenses do not exist." Even if common offenses do not exist but dissimilar offenses (visabhāgāpatti) exist, it is still pattakalla.

Regarding "excluded persons are not present in that assembly"—according to the teaching: "O bhikkhus, the Pātimokkha should not be recited in an assembly that includes laypeople; for whoever should recite it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)" (Mahāvagga 154), laypeople are excluded. By the method stated as: "O bhikkhus, the Pātimokkha should not be recited in an assembly where a bhikkhunī is sitting" (Mahāvagga 183), etc., the following are called excluded persons: a bhikkhunī, a female trainee (sikkhamānā), a male novice (sāmaṇera), a female novice (sāmaṇerī), one who has renounced the training, one who has committed an ultimate offense (pārājika), a monk suspended for not seeing an offense (āpattiyā adassane ukkhittaka), a monk suspended for not making amends for an offense, a monk suspended for not relinquishing a wrong view, a eunuch (paṇḍaka), one who lives clandestinely with monks (theyyasaṃvāsaka), one who has gone over to another sect, an animal, a matricide, a patricide, a killer of an Arahant, a violator of a bhikkhunī, a schismatic, one who has shed the blood of a Buddha, and a hermaphrodite (ubhatobyañjanaka). These twenty persons, along with laypeople, making twenty-one, are called excluded persons (vajjanīya puggala). They must be excluded by keeping them outside the reach (hatthapāsa). If the Saṅgha performs the Uposatha while any of the three types of suspended monks are present, it incurs an offense of expiation (pācittiya). If any of the remaining persons are present, it incurs an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). Here, "animal" refers to those for whom ordination is forbidden (such as Nāgas, Garuḍas, etc.). Those of other sects (titthiya) are included under the term "laypeople" (gahaṭṭha). These followers of other sects are also excluded persons. Thus, it should be understood that pattakalla is comprised of these four factors.

By the phrase "The Saṅgha should perform the Uposatha," among the other three types of Uposatha categorized by the performer (kāraka)—namely, Saṅgha-uposatha, Gaṇa-uposatha, and Puggala-uposatha—the other two are excluded, and only Saṅgha-uposatha is shown. By the phrase "should recite the Pātimokkha," among the other three types of Uposatha categorized by the manner of performance (kattabbākāra)—namely, Suttuddesa-uposatha, Pārisuddhi-uposatha, and Adhiṭṭhāna-uposatha—the other two are excluded, and only Suttuddesa-uposatha is shown. Suttuddesa refers to the recitation of the Pātimokkha. That recitation of the Pātimokkha is of two kinds: the recitation of the Ovāda-pātimokkha and the recitation of the Āṇā-pātimokkha. Between those two—
94:
"Patience is the highest austerity... [pe]... Not doing any evil... [pe]... Not reviling, not harming" (Dī. Ni. 2.90, Dha. Pa. 184, 183, 185). The three verses taught in this manner are called the Ovāda-pātimokkha. Only the Buddhas recite this Ovāda-pātimokkha, not the disciples. The Pātimokkha taught in the manner beginning with "Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me" (Mahāvagga 134) is called the Āṇā-pātimokkha. Only the disciples recite this Āṇā-pātimokkha, not the Buddhas. In this context, only this Āṇā-pātimokkha is intended by the term "Pātimokkha."

Among the two types of Uposatha other than Suttuddesa-uposatha, Pārisuddhi-uposatha is of two kinds: by way of declaring in the presence of other monks, and by way of declaring to one another. Of those two, the Pārisuddhi-uposatha performed in the presence of other monks is again of two kinds: performed in the presence of those who have already performed Pavāraṇā, and performed in the presence of those who have not yet performed Pavāraṇā. Of those two, on the day of the Great Pavāraṇā on the full moon of Assayuja, in the presence of monks who have performed Pavāraṇā, a monk who entered the later rains-retreat, or one who did not enter the rains-retreat, or one whose rains-retreat was broken; or on the full moon of Kattika, in the presence of monks who have performed Pavāraṇā, a monk who entered the earlier rains-retreat, or one who did not enter the rains-retreat, or one whose rains-retreat was broken—having given the physical presence (kāyasamaggī), he should perform it by saying three times: "Venerable sirs, I am pure from offenses; may you recognize me as one who is pure." Excluding the Pavāraṇā day, at other times, if resident monks (āvāsika) have just finished reciting the Pātimokkha, and other visiting monks (āgantuka)—whether equal in number, fewer, or more—arrive before the assembly has risen, or while some have risen, or after all have risen, those visiting monks should declare their purity (pārisuddhi) in the presence of those resident monks using the same method mentioned above.

The Pārisuddhi-uposatha performed by way of declaring to one another is also of two kinds: performed with a formal motion (ñatti) and performed without a formal motion. Of those two, if three monks reside in a certain monastery, when they assemble on the Uposatha day, one monk should make the formal motion: "Venerable sirs, let the venerable ones listen to me. Today is the fourteenth (or fifteenth) day Uposatha. If it is suitable to the venerable ones, let us perform the Pārisuddhi-uposatha to one another." After the motion is made, the senior elder monk, having arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, squatting, and raising his joined palms in salutation, should say three times: "Friends, I am pure from offenses; recognize me as one who is pure" (Mahāvagga 168). The other monks should also say, "Venerable sir," and speak in the same way. Thus it should be performed after making a formal motion.

If two monks reside in a certain monastery, ...
95:
If there are two monks in that monastery, without performing the motion (ñatti), purity (pārisuddhi) should be declared according to the method already mentioned. This is the Pārisuddhi-uposatha. If there is only one monk, after performing all the preliminary actions (pubbakaraṇīya) and knowing that other monks are not coming, he should say, "Today is my fourteenth (or fifteenth) day Uposatha," and then say, "I resolve (adhiṭṭhāmī)." This is the Adhiṭṭhāna-uposatha. Thus, it should be understood that there are three types of Uposatha according to the manner of performance. By this much, the nine types of Uposatha have been explained. Among those nine, the Uposatha characterized by three features—the fifteenth day by date, the Saṅgha-uposatha by performers, and the Suttuddesa (recitation of the Pātimokkha) by the manner of performance—is indicated here. While that Saṅgha-uposatha is being held, if a monk goes to a monastery where there are no monks, or to a monastery where there are monks of different communion (nānāsaṃvāsaka), or to a non-monastic place for an overnight stay, without the permission of the Saṅgha and without an emergency, he incurs an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).

What are the preliminary duties (pubbakicca) of the Saṅgha? This refers to the tasks to be performed for the Saṅgha's Uposatha, as mentioned in the context of "The Saṅgha should perform the Uposatha." Regarding this, it is stated in the Pāḷi: "Monks, I allow the sweeping of the Uposatha hall," and so on. Also in the Commentaries:
"Sweeping, lighting the lamp, providing drinking water and water for use, and preparing seats—these are called the preliminary actions (pubbakaraṇa) of the Uposatha."
"Giving consent (chanda), giving purity (pārisuddhi), announcing the season (utu-akkhāna), counting the monks (bhikkhu-gaṇanā), and giving exhortation (ovāda)—these are called the preliminary duties (pubbakicca) of the Uposatha."

Thus, the nine preliminary duties are shown under two names. One should ask, "Have these tasks been done?" It is not proper to perform the Uposatha without doing them. Therefore, a monk who is not sick and is assigned by the Elder must sweep the Uposatha hall, provide drinking and usable water, prepare seats, and light the lamp. If he does not do so, he incurs an offense of wrong-doing. The Elder should also assign the task after knowing what is appropriate. Regarding "Chanda-pārisuddhi" here, a monk who has performed the Uposatha outside and arrives at the place where the Saṅgha has gathered for the Uposatha, should go to the gathering place and [show] physical unity (kāya-sāmaggī)...
96:
...A monk who cannot provide physical unity (kāya-sāmaggī) must give his consent (chanda). Whether he is sick or busy with work, that monk, when giving purity (pārisuddhi), must also give his consent. How should it be given? In the presence of one monk, he should make the meaning known by body, by speech, or by both, saying: "I give my consent, please convey my consent, please report my consent to the Saṅgha." When given thus, the consent is considered given.

A monk who has not yet performed the Uposatha, whether sick or busy, must give purity (pārisuddhi). How should it be given? In the presence of one monk, he should make the meaning known by body, by speech, or by both, saying: "I give my purity, please convey my purity, please report my purity to the Saṅgha." When given thus, the purity is considered given. The monk who gives purity must also give consent. Regarding this, the Blessed One said: "Monks, I allow a monk who gives purity on that Uposatha day to also give consent; there are still duties to be performed for the Saṅgha."

Between these two, giving purity fulfills the requirement of performing the Uposatha for both the Saṅgha and oneself, but it does not fulfill the remaining duties of the Saṅgha. Giving consent fulfills the Saṅgha's Uposatha performance and the remaining duties, but one's own Uposatha remains unperformed. Therefore, a monk who gives purity must also give consent.

It is permissible for a single monk to convey either the pure consent mentioned earlier or this combined consent and purity (chanda-pārisuddhi) for many monks. If that conveying monk, on the way, meets another monk and gives the consent or purity of others he is carrying along with his own, only his own consent and purity reach the Saṅgha. The others' consent and purity become what is called "cat-chain" (biḷālasaṅkhalikā) consent and purity, and they do not reach the Saṅgha. Therefore, the conveyor himself must go to the Saṅgha's assembly and report. If he knowingly fails to report, he incurs an offense of wrong-doing. As for the consent and purity, it is considered to have reached the Saṅgha as soon as the conveying monk enters the assembly's reach (hatthapāsa).

Announcing the season (utu-akkhāna) means announcing the seasons such as winter, saying: "This many fortnights (pakkha) have passed, and this many fortnights remain." Counting the monks (bhikkhu-gaṇanā) means counting the monks, saying: "This many monks have gathered in the Uposatha hall." The Uposatha should be performed only after doing both of these. Exhortation (ovāda) means the exhortation to nuns (bhikkhunovāda). It is not proper to perform the Uposatha without reporting to the Saṅgha the exhortation requested by the nuns. For the nuns, having come and asked, "Tomorrow is the Uposatha day; is this Uposatha the fourteenth or the fifteenth?", they come again on the Uposatha day and say, "Venerable Sir, the Order of Nuns..."
97:
The Bhikkhunī Saṅgha pays homage to the feet of the Bhikkhu Saṅgha and requests permission to approach for exhortation. They request the exhortation thus: "Venerable Sir, the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha wishes to obtain permission to approach for exhortation." Except for a foolish monk, a sick monk, or a monk about to go on a journey, no other monk, even if he is a forest-dweller, should fail to accept that requested exhortation. Therefore, the monk who has accepted that request should speak to the monk reciting the Pātimokkha in the Uposatha hall as follows: "Venerable Sir, the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha pays homage to the feet of the Bhikkhu Saṅgha and requests permission to approach for exhortation. Venerable Sir, the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha wishes to obtain permission to approach for exhortation."

The monk reciting the Pātimokkha should then ask: "Is there any monk appointed as an exhorter of bhikkhunīs (bhikkhunovādaka)?" If there is an appointed exhorter of bhikkhunīs, the Pātimokkha reciter should say to the monk who accepted the request: "The monk named so-and-so has been appointed as the exhorter of bhikkhunīs; let the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha approach him." If there is none, the Pātimokkha reciter should ask: "Which venerable one is able to exhort the bhikkhunīs?" If there is someone who is able and is endowed with the eight qualities, he should be appointed right there, and the monk who accepted the request should be told: "The monk named so-and-so has been appointed as the exhorter of bhikkhunīs; let the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha approach him."

If no one is able, the Pātimokkha reciter should say: "There is no monk appointed as an exhorter of bhikkhunīs. Let the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha strive to fulfill the three trainings (sikkhā) with grace (in body, speech, and mind)." By this much, the entire Dispensation (Sāsana) included within the three trainings is declared. The monk who accepted the request, having consented by saying "Very well," should inform the bhikkhunīs on the first day of the fortnight (pāṭipada).

The Bhikkhunī Saṅgha should also send those bhikkhunīs, saying: "Go, sisters, and ask: 'Venerable Sir, does the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha obtain permission to approach for exhortation?'" Having consented by saying "Very well, sister," those bhikkhunīs should approach that monk and speak thus: "Venerable Sir, does the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha obtain permission to approach for exhortation?" He should say: "There is no monk appointed as an exhorter of bhikkhunīs. Let the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha strive to fulfill the three trainings with grace." They should consent by saying "Very well, Venerable Sir."

This (plural) usage is said with reference to two or three bhikkhunīs coming together. Among them, only one bhikkhunī should speak and consent; the others are merely her companions. However, if the Bhikkhu Saṅgha or the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha is not complete, or if there is only a group (gaṇa) or only individuals on both sides (the following should be said):
98:
In such a case, this is the sequence of words: "Venerable Sir, the bhikkhunīs pay homage to the feet of the Bhikkhu Saṅgha and request permission to approach for exhortation. Venerable Sir, may the bhikkhunīs obtain permission to approach for exhortation." Or: "Venerable Sir, I pay homage to the feet of the Bhikkhu Saṅgha and request permission to approach for exhortation. Venerable Sir, I obtain permission to approach for exhortation." Or: "Venerable Sirs, the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha pays homage to the feet of the venerable ones and requests permission to approach for exhortation. Venerable Sirs, may the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha obtain permission to approach for exhortation."

"Venerable Sirs, the bhikkhunīs pay homage to the feet of the venerable ones and request permission to approach for exhortation. Venerable Sirs, may the bhikkhunīs obtain permission to approach for exhortation." Or: "Venerable Sirs, I pay homage to the feet of the venerable ones and request permission to approach for exhortation. Venerable Sirs, I obtain permission to approach for exhortation." Or: "Venerable Sir, the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha pays homage to the feet of the venerable one and requests permission to approach for exhortation. Venerable Sir, may the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha obtain permission to approach for exhortation."

"Venerable Sir, the bhikkhunīs pay homage to the feet of the venerable one and request permission to approach for exhortation. Venerable Sir, may the bhikkhunīs obtain permission to approach for exhortation." Or: "Venerable Sir, I pay homage to the feet of the venerable one and request permission to approach for exhortation. Venerable Sir, I obtain permission to approach for exhortation."

The monk who accepted the exhortation should also speak thus at the time of Uposatha: "Venerable Sir, the bhikkhunīs pay homage to the feet of the Bhikkhu Saṅgha and request permission to approach for exhortation. Venerable Sir, may the bhikkhunīs obtain permission to approach for exhortation." Or: "Venerable Sir, the bhikkhunī pays homage to the feet of the Bhikkhu Saṅgha and requests permission to approach for exhortation. Venerable Sir, may the bhikkhunī obtain permission to approach for exhortation."

"Venerable Sir, the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha (or) the bhikkhunīs (or) the bhikkhunī pays homage (pay homage) to the feet of the venerable ones and requests (request) permission to approach for exhortation. Venerable Sir, may the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha (or) the bhikkhunīs (or) the bhikkhunī obtain permission to approach for exhortation."

In the Uposatha hall, the monk reciting the Pātimokkha, or the monk making the formal announcement (ñatti), or another monk, if there is an appointed monk, should say according to the previous method: "Let the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha (or) the bhikkhunīs (or) the bhikkhunī approach that monk." If there is no appointed monk, he should say: "Let the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha (or) the bhikkhunīs (or) the bhikkhunī be perfect in graceful conduct."

The monk who accepted the exhortation should bring back that exhortation on the first day of the fortnight (pāṭipada) and speak exactly as instructed. This is the summary decision on this matter. Only after reporting the exhortation requested by the bhikkhunīs should the Uposatha be performed. Therefore, [the commentators] said: "Chanda... vuccati."
99:
“Consent (chanda), purity (pārisuddhi), the season (utu), the time (akkhāna), the count of monks (bhikkhugaṇanā), and the exhortation (ovāda)—these are called the ‘preliminary duties’ (pubbakicca) of the Uposatha.”

“Venerable sirs, announce your purity (pārisuddhi)” means announce your state of being pure from offenses. “I shall recite the Pātimokkha” is the statement of the reason for having the purity announced. For, according to the statement, “Monks, the Pātimokkha should not be listened to by one who has an offense; whoever should listen to it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)” (Cullavagga), it is not proper for those who are not pure from offenses to listen to the Pātimokkha. Therefore, it is said: “Venerable sirs, announce your purity; I shall recite the Pātimokkha.” In this regard, a question might arise: since it is stated (in the Mahāvagga), “The Saṅgha should perform the Uposatha, should recite the Pātimokkha,” it should also be said here, “The Pātimokkha will be recited”; only then would there be consistency between the preceding and following statements. The answer to this is: this statement “I shall recite the Pātimokkha” may not be connected to the preceding words in terms of mere phrasing, but it agrees in terms of its characteristic. Due to the unity of the Saṅgha and the unity of the group, the recitation by an individual is the recitation of the Pātimokkha by the Saṅgha—this is the characteristic here. Therefore, only this statement “I shall recite the Pātimokkha” should be said here.

In the sentence, “Let us all, being present, listen well and pay attention to that Pātimokkha,” the word ‘taṃ’ refers to the Pātimokkha. “All being present” refers to all the elders, the newly ordained, and those of middle standing who are in that assembly. “Let us listen well” means that we shall attend with our whole mind through the ear-door, having made it a matter of importance. “Let us pay attention” means that we shall keep it in our minds, having become one-pointed in heart. Here too, because it is said, “I shall recite the Pātimokkha,” it might seem appropriate to say, “Listen ye, pay attention,” yet that would not agree with the statement, “The Saṅgha should perform the Uposatha.” This is because the performance of the Uposatha is the business of the entire unified Saṅgha, and the monk who recites the Pātimokkha is also one included within the Saṅgha; because of his inclusion within the Saṅgha, it is only appropriate to say, “Let us listen, let us pay attention.”

Now, regarding the statement, “Venerable sirs, announce your purity,” in order to show how the announcement of purity is made, it is said: “Whoever has an offense should reveal it.” In that phrase, “whoever should have,” it means whoever has an offense that has been committed through any one of the six ways. To the offense...
100:
In truth, a monk who falls into an offense does so through these six causes: shamelessness, ignorance, doubt, perceiving the unallowable as allowable, perceiving the allowable as unallowable, and forgetfulness.

How does one fall into an offense through shamelessness? Even knowing that something is unallowable, he tramples [the rule] and commits the transgression.

## This has also been stated:
“He intentionally commits an offense, he conceals the offense,
And he follows a wrong course (agati); such a person is called a shameless person (alajji).”

How does one fall into an offense through ignorance? An ignorant person is dull and deluded; not knowing what should and should not be done, he does what should not be done and fails to do what should be done. Thus, he falls into an offense through ignorance.

How does one fall into an offense through doubt? When doubt arises regarding whether something is allowable or unallowable, one should ask a Vinaya-expert; if it is allowable, it may be done, and if it is unallowable, it should not be done. However, this person, thinking “it is permissible,” tramples [the rule] and transgresses. Thus, he falls into an offense through doubt.

How does one fall into an offense through perceiving the unallowable as allowable? He eats bear meat thinking it is “pork”; he eats at the wrong time (vikāla) perceiving it as the right time. Thus, he falls into an offense through perceiving the unallowable as allowable.

How does one fall into an offense through perceiving the allowable as unallowable? He eats pork thinking it is “bear meat”; he eats at the right time perceiving it as the wrong time. Thus, he falls into an offense through perceiving the allowable as unallowable.

How does one fall into an offense through forgetfulness? He falls into offenses such as sleeping in the same room [with an unordained person] or being separated from his robes through forgetfulness. Thus, if any monk—whether an elder, a newly ordained, or one of middle standing—has an offense among the seven classes of offenses through any one of these six causes...

“He should reveal it” means that he should confess or make that offense known. “If there is no offense” means if a monk has not fallen into an offense in this way...
102:
...the word itself would be meaningless. Why? Because in the recitation of the Nidāna, there is no three-fold announcement (yāvatatiyānussāvana). Thus, because of the lack of logic, that [view] is also not appropriate. However, this phrase 'it has been announced up to three times' is merely a statement of characteristic (lakkhaṇa-vacana). By this, it shows this meaning: This thing called the Pātimokkha is announced up to three times; while it is being announced up to three times, if a monk who remembers does not reveal an existing offense, at the conclusion of the third announcement, he commits a deliberate lie (sampajāna-musāvāda). This is the intended meaning.

To show the manner in which that Pātimokkha is said to be 'announced up to three times,' the words beginning with 'In that [Pātimokkha], I ask the venerable ones' are spoken. Although these words are seen at the end of the Pārājikas and so on, they are not seen at the end of the Nidāna. Even though they are not seen, at the time of recitation, after saying 'For revealing it becomes easy for him,' one should indeed speak in the manner beginning with 'Venerable ones, the Nidāna has been recited; in that Nidāna, I ask the venerable ones.' Only in this way is the Nidāna 'well-recited' (su-uddiṭṭha); otherwise, it is 'badly recited' (du-uddiṭṭha). Intending this very meaning, it was said in the Uposathakkhandhaka: '"It has been announced up to three times" means it has been announced once, it has been announced a second time, and it has been announced a third time.' This is the decision brought down by the lineage of teachers in this matter.

'If any monk... commits a deliberate lie' means a deliberate lie occurs for that monk; because of that deliberate lie, he incurs an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa). That wrongdoing is incurred not by the characteristic of lying [itself], but should be understood as an offense arising from non-action (akiriya-samuṭṭhāna) at the vocal door, according to these words of the Blessed One: 'What [offense] is there in a deliberate lie? There is a wrongdoing.'

## This was also said:
'Without conversing with any human being,
And without speaking words to others,
One may fall into an offense of the vocal [door], not the physical;
This problem has been contemplated by the wise who are skilled [in Vinaya].'
103:
"Antārayiko" means that because it is a cause for remorse (vippaṭisāra), it prevents the arising of joy (pāmojja) and so on, thereby creating an obstacle to the attainment of the first jhāna and so forth. "Tasmā" (therefore) means because this deliberate lying (sampajāna-musāvāda), which is called non-disclosure, is obstructive. "Saramānena" means one who knows the offense existing in oneself. "Visuddhāpekkhena" means one who desires to emerge [from the offense] and desires to be purified. "Santī āpatti" refers to an offense that has been committed but not yet emerged from. "Āvikātabbā" means it should be clearly revealed (declared) in the midst of the Saṅgha, or in the midst of a group, or to a single person. At the very least, one should say to the monk nearest to oneself: 'Friend, I have fallen into an offense of such a name; having emerged from this, I shall make amends for that offense.' Even if one is doubtful (vematika), one should say: 'Friend, I have a doubt regarding an offense of such a name; when I am free from doubt, I shall make amends for that offense.'

In the phrase "āvikatā hi'ssa phāsu hoti," "āvikatā" means because of being clearly revealed or manifested. Like the words "alajjitā" and so on, this word also takes the nominative case in the sense of the instrumental (cause). "Hi" is a mere particle. "Assa" means for that monk. "Phāsu hoti" means it is easy and comfortable for the attainment of the first jhāna and so forth; the meaning is that the pleasant practice (sukhapaṭipadā) becomes fulfilled through the power of joy and so on, which have the absence of remorse as their root.

## Thus the Explanation of the Introduction (Nidāna-vaṇṇanā)
## in the Commentary on the Pātimokkha named Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī is finished.
104:
## Section on Pārājika (Pārājikakaṇḍa)
Now, following the Introduction, there is this section on Pārājika beginning with "Tatrime cattāro." In that context, "tatra" means in that Pātimokkha which was mentioned as "I shall recite the Pātimokkha." The word "ime" is a term pointing directly to the offenses that are about to be mentioned. "Cattāro" is a term defining the number. "Pārājikā" is the name [of the offenses]. "Dhammā" means the offenses. "Uddesaṃ āgacchanti" means they come to be recited in their specific forms, not merely by a general statement as in the Introduction, "To whomsoever there may be an offense."

## 1. Explanation of the First Pārājika
"Yo pana" refers to anyone at all, without distinction of gender, etc., by way of short or long [vowels] and so forth. "Bhikkhu" refers to one who has attained the state of a noble monk through the ñatticatuttha-kammavācā (ordination by a motion and three proclamations) which is unshakable and valid, among the eight types of ordination: ehibhikkhu-upasampadā, saraṇagamana-upasampadā, ovādappaṭiggahana-upasampadā, pañhābyākaraṇa-upasampadā, aṭṭhagarudhamma-upasampadā, dūtena-upasampadā, aṭṭhavācika-upasampadā, and ñatticatuttha-kammavācā. The unshakability of that act of ordination should be understood through the fulfillment of five factors: vatthu (subject), ñatti (motion), anussāvana (proclamation), sīmā (boundary), and parisā (assembly).

Among those factors, "vatthu" refers to the person seeking ordination. That person should be understood by excluding those under twenty years of age, those who have previously committed an ultimate offense (Pārājika), and the eleven types of disqualified persons (abhabba-puggala) such as eunuchs (paṇḍaka) and so on. Among them, "one under twenty years of age" means one who has not completed twenty years counting from the time of conception. "One who has previously committed an ultimate offense" means one who has previously committed any one of the four Pārājikas. Eunuchs (paṇḍaka) and others have been mentioned in the "Discussion on Excluded Persons" (vajjaniya-puggala-kathā). Among those eleven disqualified persons, excluding the āsitta-paṇḍaka and usūya-paṇḍaka, the types intended here are the opakkamika-paṇḍaka, napuṃsaka-paṇḍaka, and the pakkha-paṇḍaka who remains in the state of a eunuch during [certain] fortnights.

"Theyyasaṃvāsaka" (one who lives in communion by theft) is of three types: lingatthenaka, saṃဝāsatthenaka, and ubhayatthenaka. Among these three, a person who ordains himself and does not count his years as a monk, does not accept the salutation of monks or novices according to seniority, does not yield his seat, and does not appear at the Uposatha and so forth—this person, because of having an impure mind and stealing only the signs [of a monk], is called a "lingatthenaka." If a genuine novice, having been ordained by monks, removes his saffron robes and, while making an effort to put them back on, engages in sexual intercourse and then puts them back on and claims to be a novice—this person is not a lingatthenaka because he did not abandon the signs given by the monks, nor is he a saṃဝāsatthenaka because he enjoyed the communion appropriate to the signs. The same method applies to one who has fallen into a Pārājika. If a genuine novice goes to another place and counts years as a monk, lives in communion according to seniority, etc., that person is called a "saṃဝāsatthenaka."
105:
A person who, without renouncing the signs (robes) given by the monks, engages in sexual intercourse with effort (intending to wear them again) and then, after putting them back on, professes to be a novice (sāmaṇera), is not a 'thief of signs' (liṅgatthenaka). Because he does not delight in the communion appropriate to those signs, he is also not a 'thief of communion' (saṃvāsatthenaka). The same principle applies to a monk who has committed an ultimate offense (pārājika).

If a person who is a true novice goes to another place and counts his monk-years, accepts bows according to seniority, takes a seat (reserved for monks), or participates in Uposatha and other acts, he is called a 'thief of communion' (saṃvāsatthenaka) because he steals only the communion. For in this context, all actions such as counting monk-years and so forth are to be understood as 'communion' (saṃvāsa). The same principle applies to one who, after renouncing the training, thinks, 'No one will know me,' and acts in this manner.

If a person puts on the robes himself, goes to a monastery, accepts bows according to seniority, takes a seat, counts monk-years, and participates in Uposatha and other acts, he is called a 'thief of both' (ubhayatthenaka) because he steals both the signs and the communion. The same principle applies to one who, by way of abandoning his duty, removes his robes, commits an ultimate offense (pārājika), and then puts those robes back on and acts in this manner. Only these three types of 'thieves by communion' (theyyasaṃvāsaka) are intended here. However, excluding these three types:

'One who, out of fear of kings, famine, wilderness, disease, or enemies, or for the purpose of obtaining robes, takes up the signs (robes) in this Dispensation, is not called a thief by communion (theyyasaṃvāsaka) for as long as he has a pure mind and does not accept communion (such as counting monk-years).'

A monk who, desiring to be a heretic, personally takes up the signs of heretics such as garments made of kusa grass, or is ordained in their presence, or goes naked to the Ājīvakas and undertakes their practices, is called 'one who has gone over to the heretics' (titthiyapakkantaka).

Excluding those of the human species, all other beings are called 'animals' (tiracchānagata). A person who, being human himself, intentionally kills his own human mother with the intent to take her life is called a 'matricide' (mātughātaka). The same principle applies to a 'patricide' (pitughātaka). A person who intentionally kills a human Arahant, even if that person is at the minimum in the form of a layperson, is called a 'slayer of an Arahant' (arahantaghātaka). A person who, towards a regular bhikkhunī, in one of the three paths...
106:
...defiles her in any of the paths, is called a 'defiler of a nun' (bhikkhunidūsaka). A person who, like Devadatta, makes the Dispensation contrary to the Dhamma and contrary to the Vinaya, and causes a schism in the Sangha by way of any of the four types of formal acts, is called a 'schismatic' (saṅghabhedaka). A person who, like Devadatta, with a murderous and malicious intent, causes the blood of the living Tathāgata to outpour, even as much as a small fly might drink, is called 'one who sheds the blood' (lohituppādaka). A person who possesses both types of sexual organs, due to the kamma that produces the female sign and the kamma that produces the male sign, is called a 'hermaphrodite' (ubhatobyañjanaka). Thus, these thirteen types of persons are 'non-entities' (avatthu) for higher ordination (upasampadā). Excluding these, if there is another candidate for ordination, the act of higher ordination is 'irreproachable' (akuppa) by virtue of the perfection of the candidate (vatthusampatti).

In what way is it irreproachable by virtue of the perfection of the motion (ñattisampatti)? There are five faults of the motion (ñattidosa): the four failures to mention the candidate, the Sangha, the person (preceptor), and the motion itself, and the fifth being the placing of the motion after the proclamation (kammavācā). Among these, not mentioning the candidate as 'such-and-such a person' is called 'failure to mention the candidate' (vatthu-aparāmasana). In the passage 'Venerable sirs, let the Sangha listen to me,' saying 'Venerable sirs, let (me) be heard' but not saying 'the Sangha' is called 'failure to mention the Sangha' (saṅgha-aparāmasana). Not mentioning the preceptor as 'of such-and-such a candidate' is called 'failure to mention the person' (puggala-aparāmasana). Not reciting the motion at all in any manner is called 'failure to mention the motion' (ñatti-aparāmasana). Completing the proclamation first and then saying 'This is the motion' and 'The Sangha approves' is called 'placing the motion afterwards' (pacchā-ñattiṭṭhapana). Thus, a motion that is free from these faults is perfect, and the act is irreproachable by virtue of the perfection of the motion.

Regarding irreproachability by virtue of the proclamation (anussāvana), there are five faults of proclamation (anussāvanadosa): the three failures to mention the candidate, the Sangha, and the person; the deficiency in the proclamation; and the proclamation at the wrong time. Among these, the failures to mention the candidate and so forth are similar to what was said regarding the motion. In any of the three proclamations, the failure to mention these is indeed a failure. Not reciting the proclamation at all but reciting only the motion four times, or the non-recitation or mispronunciation of a letter or a word within the proclamation, is called 'deficiency in the proclamation' (sāvanāya-hāpana). Performing the proclamation without first establishing the motion when it is not the proper occasion for proclamation is called 'proclamation at the wrong time' (akāle-sāvana). Thus, an act of higher ordination that is free from these faults is irreproachable by virtue of the perfection of the proclamation (anussāvanasampatti).

An act of higher ordination performed in a boundary that transcends the characteristics of a defective boundary (vipatti-sīmā) as previously mentioned is irreproachable by virtue of the perfection of the boundary (sīmāsampatti). As many monks as are entitled to the act, their not coming, the failure to bring the consent (chanda) of those entitled to give it, and the protest by monks who are present—these three are called 'faults of the assembly' (parisādosa). An act of higher ordination performed in an assembly free from these faults is irreproachable by virtue of the perfection of the assembly (parisāsampatti).

It is called 'appropriate to the cause' (ṭhānāraha) because it is suitable for the purpose of performing the act of higher ordination and because it is suitable for the motion and proclamation as taught by the Blessed One. Thus, a monk who attains the status of a monk through such an irreproachable, appropriate act of higher ordination with the motion as the fourth (ñatticatuttha-kamma), is intended as a 'bhikkhu' in this context of the first Pārājika, which is an 'offense by nature' (lokavajja). However, in the case of 'offenses by regulation' (paṇṇattivajja)...
107:
The non-arrival of those [monks], the failure to bring the consent of those entitled to give it, and the protest of those present—these three are the defects of an assembly (parisa-dosa). An act performed by an assembly free from these defects is an unshakeable act (akuppa-kamma) by virtue of the completeness of the assembly. It is called 'fitting' (ṭhānāraha) because it is in accordance with the cause and in accordance with the Teacher's Dispensation (the motion and proclamations). Thus, one who has attained the status of a monk through such an unshakeable and fitting ordination act consisting of a motion and three proclamations (ñatticatuttha-kamma) is intended as a 'bhikkhu' here in this first Pārājika. However, in the case of training rules concerning offenses by regulation (paṇṇattivajja), other [types of] monks are also included.

Regarding "bhikkhūnaṃ sikkhasājīvasamāpanno": it is called "bhikkhūnaṃ sikkhasājīvasamāpanno" because of being properly endowed, by way of practicing, in the training (sikkhā) known as the higher virtue (adhisīla) of monks, and in the communal life (sājīva) known as the training rules prescribed by the Blessed One, in which these [monks] live together and have a common livelihood. "Samāpanno" means having reached both of these, fulfilling the training and not transgressing the communal life. "Sikkhaṃ apaccakkhāya dubbalyaṃ anāvikatvā" means without renouncing the training one has undertaken, and without making manifest one's weakness in the communal life one has undertaken (this refers to engaging in sexual intercourse).

In the renunciation of that training, one should understand the renunciation of the training by way of mind (citta), field (khetta), time (kāla), effort (payoga), person (puggala), and understanding (vijānana); and one should understand the non-renunciation of the training by the absence of these factors. How? The renunciation of the training occurs only with a mind that desires to fall away from the status of a monk; it does not occur for one who speaks out of a desire to play or through a slip of the tongue. Thus, the renunciation of the training occurs by the power of the mind; it does not occur in the absence of that mind.

Similarly, for one who speaks with the intent to renounce, using any of the following twenty-two field-terms (khettapada) along with their circumlocutions, renunciation of the training occurs: the fourteen terms starting with the Buddha, such as "I renounce the Buddha, I renounce the Dhamma, I renounce the Saṅgha, the training, the discipline (vinaya), the Pātimokkha, the recitation of the Pātimokkha (uddesa), the preceptor (upajjhāya), the teacher (ācariya), the co-resident (saddhivihārika), the pupil (antevāsika), the one with the same preceptor, the one with the same teacher, the fellow-celibate (sabrahmacārī)"; and the eight terms starting with a layman, such as "Regard me as a layman, as a lay follower (upāsaka), as a monastery attendant (ārāmika), as a novice (sāmaṇera), as an ascetic of another sect (titthiya), as a disciple of another sect, as a non-monk, as one who is not a son of the Sakyans." Renunciation of the training does not occur for one who renounces by taking the name of something else, such as a tree. Thus, the renunciation of the training occurs by the power of the field; it does not occur in the absence of that field.

Among those field-terms, there is the speech expressing the present tense, such as "I renounce" (paccakkhāmi) and "Regard me" (maṃ dhārehi). Also, there are phrases such as "Enough for me with the Buddha," "What is the Buddha to me?", "I have no use..."
108:
By way of the verbal inflection (ākhyāta), without specifically considering the time, the four terms such as "alam me" (enough for me), etc., when joined with the preceding fourteen terms, as well as their synonyms, constitute the renunciation of the training (sikkhāpaccakkhāna). For one who speaks in the past, future, or conditional tenses, such as "paccakkhāsiṃ" (I renounced), "paccakkhissaṃ" (I will renounce), "maṃ dhāresi" (regard me [in the past]), "maṃ dhāressati" (he will regard me), or "yannūnāhaṃ paccakkheyyaṃ" (what if I were to renounce?), etc., there is no renunciation of the training. Thus, renunciation occurs by way of the present tense and by way of the time not specifically expressed [by a verb]; it does not occur otherwise.

Effort (payoga) is of two kinds: bodily (kāyika) and vocal (vācasika). Among them, renunciation of the training occurs only through vocal effort by breaking into speech in any language in the manner of "Buddhaṃ paccakkhāmi" (I renounce the Buddha), etc. It does not occur for one who performs bodily effort such as writing letters or making hand gestures. Thus, renunciation of the training occurs only by vocal effort; it does not occur otherwise.

The person (puggala) is also of two kinds: the one who renounces and the one to whom it is renounced (the listener). Among them, the one who renounces must not be any of the following: one who is insane, one who is mentally deranged, or one who is overwhelmed by pain. The one to whom it is renounced (the listener) must be a human being, must not be insane, etc., and must be present face-to-face. Informing one who is not present, whether by a messenger or by a letter, is not effective. Thus, renunciation of the training occurs by way of the aforementioned persons; it does not occur otherwise.

Understanding (vijānana) is also of two kinds: specified (niyamita) and unspecified (aniyamita). Among them, when one speaks specifying a person or persons, saying "I inform this person or these persons," if they understand the renunciation of the training in any manner, such as "This monk is dissatisfied" or "He wishes to become a layman," immediately after his words—just as ordinary people in the world understand upon hearing and reflecting on speech—then the training is renounced. If they understand only later after thinking "What did this person say?", or if others [who were not specified] understand, the training is not renounced. In the case of informing without specifying, if any human being understands the meaning of the words in the manner described, the training is renounced. Thus, renunciation of the training occurs by way of understanding; it does not occur otherwise. Even for one who renounces the training for the sake of jesting, at the very least, the training is not renounced. Thus, one should understand the non-renunciation of the training (apaccakkhāya) by way of these aforementioned factors such as the mind, and by the fact that the training is not relinquished in every respect.
109:
Either by the power of the various types of minds mentioned above, or by not renouncing the training in any way, without making clear the weakness in fulfilling a certain training rule—which is the meaning of the words for renouncing the training—while not actually renouncing the training.

In the phrase 'methunaṃ dhammaṃ paṭiseveyya': 'methunaṃ dhammaṃ' refers to the practice of two people, a woman and a man, who are similar in the arousal of lust. 'paṭiseveyya' means should indulge in, or should transgress. 'antamaso' means at the very least, being the lowest limit of all. 'tiracchānagatāyapi' means even in the passage of a female belonging to the animal kingdom by way of rebirth; this is the supplementary regulation (anupaññatti) in this training rule. 'pārājiko hoti' means he is defeated, having reached defeat, being excluded from the Sāsana. 'asaṃvāso' means 'saṃvāsa' is the three types of practice such as performing communal acts (ekakamma) together, where regular (pakatatta) monks live together; since that 'saṃvāsa' no longer exists with him, it is called 'asaṃvāsa'. Indeed, such a person cannot even serve as a quorum-filler (gaṇapūraka) in Saṅgha acts; this is the explanation of the words (padavaṇṇanā).

The decision (vinicchaya) in this first Pārājika is as follows: There are three types of females: human, non-human (ogress or deity), and animal. For these females, there are nine passages, counting three each: the excrement passage (vaccamagga), the urine passage (passāvamagga), and the mouth passage (mukhamagga). Similarly, there are nine for hermaphrodites (ubhatobyañjanaka). For males, there are six passages, counting two each: the excrement passage and the mouth passage. Similarly, there are six for eunuchs (paṇḍaka). Thus, there are thirty passages in total. Among these thirty passages, whether it is one's own or another's, whether covered or uncovered, even in the case of the deceased where the body has not been entirely or mostly devoured by dogs or jackals, in a moist and fresh place untouched by natural wind—if a monk, with the intent to indulge, inserts his male organ, even as small as a sesame seed, whether covered or uncovered; or if, while being inserted by another, he consents to any of the stages: the insertion, the state of being inserted, the staying, or the withdrawal—this monk is said to have fallen into a Pārājika offense. This is the specific decision (asādhāraṇavinicchaya) regarding this training rule. For the purpose of the general decision (sādhāraṇavinicchaya) applicable to all training rules, this summary (mātikā) should be known:

The origin (nidāna), the person (puggala), the object (vatthu), and the types of regulations (paññattividhi),
Command (āṇatti), offense (āpatti), non-offense (anāpatti), failure (vipatti), and factors (aṅga),
The types of origins (samuṭṭhānavidhi), the distinction by action (kiriyā), perception (saññā), and mind (citta),
The types of faults (vajja), the types of acts (kamma), and likewise the types of the two triads (tika),
This general characteristic (lakkhaṇa) consisting of seventeen types,
The wise person, having understood it, should apply it appropriately to each training rule.
110: Among those summary headings, 'origin' (nidāna) refers to the seven places of regulation: Vesālī, Rājagaha, Sāvatthī, Āḷavī, Kosambī, the Sakyan country, and the Bhagga country. These seven locations are the origins (starting points) of all training rules. 'Person' (puggala) refers to the specific individual on whose account a particular training rule was laid down. 'Object' (vatthu) refers to the transgression of that individual. 'Types of regulations' (paññattividhi) refers to the nine types of regulations: regulation (paññatti), supplementary regulation (anupaññatti), regulation laid down before an offense occurred (anuppannapaññatti), universal regulation (sabbatthapaññatti), local regulation (padesapaññatti), shared regulation (sādhāraṇapaññatti), unshared regulation (asādhāraṇapaññatti), regulation for one side (ekatopaññatti), and regulation for both sides (ubhatopaññatti). Among these nine, a regulation laid down before a fault has appeared is called 'anuppannapaññatti'. That 'anuppannapaññatti' occurs only for bhikkhunīs by way of accepting the eight weighty rules (garudhamma); it does not exist in other training rules. The four types of regulations concerning ordination by a group of five including a Vinaya expert, wearing multi-layered sandals, constant bathing, and using leather mats are called 'local regulations' (padesapaññatti). This is because an offense is incurred through these training rules only in the Middle Country (Majjhimadesa). Among those, only the training rule prohibiting constant bathing appears in the Pātimokkha. Apart from these four, there are no other local regulations. All training rules are universal regulations (sabbatthapaññatti). The pair of shared regulations and the pair of regulations for one side are identical in meaning. Therefore, excluding 'anuppannapaññatti', the pair of universal regulations, and the pair of regulations for one side, the decision in all training rules should be understood by way of the remaining four types of regulations. In the words 'āṇatti, āpatti, anāpatti, vipatti': 'āṇatti' refers to commanding. 'āpatti' refers to the types of offenses by way of preliminary effort (pubbappayoga) and so on. 'anāpatti' refers to the absence of an offense by way of not knowing and so on. 'vipatti' refers to any one of the failures: failure in virtue (sīlavipatti), failure in conduct (ācāravipatti), failure in view (diṭṭhivipatti), or failure in livelihood (ājီvavipatti). Thus, the decision in all training rules should also be understood by way of these 'āṇatti' and so on. 'Factors' (aṅga) refers to the causal factors of offenses in all training rules. 'Types of origins' (samuṭṭhānavidhi) refers to the six origins of all offenses: body, speech, body and speech, body and mind, speech and mind, and body, speech, and mind—which consist of one factor, two factors, or three factors. These origins are also called the origins of the training rules. Among these six origins, the first three are without mind (acittaka) and the last three are with mind (sacittaka). Among those, offenses arise through one, two, three, four, or six origins. There is no offense with five origins. Among them, an offense with a single origin arises only through the fourth, fifth, or sixth origin, and not through others. An offense with two origins arises through the first and fourth, the second and fifth, the third and sixth, the fourth and sixth, or the fifth and sixth origins, and not through others. An offense with three origins...
112:
Offenses arise. There is an offense arising from committing a prohibited act. There is an offense arising from not performing a required duty. There is an offense arising from both committing what should not be done and not doing what should be done. There is an offense arising sometimes from committing what should not be done and sometimes from not doing what should be done. There is an offense arising sometimes from committing what should not be done and sometimes from both action and inaction.

Among these five, an offense occurring to a monk who commits a transgression with the body or speech, such as digging the earth, is said to arise from action (kiriya). An offense occurring to a monk who does not perform a required duty with the body or speech, like the first Kathina offense, is said to arise from inaction (akiriya).
