An offense occurring to a monk who commits what should not be done or does not do what should be done, like the offense incurred by receiving a robe from the hand of an unrelated nun, is said to arise from action-inaction (kiriya-akiriya). An offense that arises sometimes from action and sometimes from inaction, like the offense incurred by receiving gold and silver, is said to arise sometimes from action and sometimes from inaction. An offense that arises sometimes from action and sometimes from both action and inaction, like the Kuṭikāra offense, is said to arise sometimes from action and sometimes from both.

All offenses are also of two types by way of perception: offenses released by perception (saññā-vimokkha) and offenses not released by perception (no-saññā-vimokkha). Among these two, the offense from which one is released due to the absence of the perception of transgression is called saññā-vimokkha. The other is called no-saññā-vimokkha. Furthermore, all offenses are of two types by way of consciousness: those with consciousness (sacittaka) and those without consciousness (acittaka). Among these two, an offense that arises only by way of an origin accompanied by consciousness is called sacittaka. An offense that arises either through an origin without consciousness or through an origin mixed with consciousness is called acittaka.

Regarding the phrase "classification of faults and actions" (vajjaka-mma-ppabhedaṃ), all offenses are of two types by way of fault: worldly faults (lokavajja) and faults by regulation (paṇṇattivajja). Among these two, an offense where the mind is exclusively unwholesome in its conscious aspect is called a worldly fault (lokavajja). The remaining are faults by regulation (paṇṇattivajja). All offenses are also of three types by way of bodily action, verbal action, and both. Among these three, an offense to be committed at the body-door is called bodily action (kāyakamma). An offense to be committed at the speech-door is called verbal action (vacīkamma). An offense to be committed at both doors is called bodily and verbal action. There is no such thing as an offense at the mind-door (manodvāra). Thus, the decision in all cases should be understood by way of this classification of faults and actions.

"The method of the two triads" (tikadvayavidhiṃ) refers to the classification of the wholesome triad (kusalattika) and the feeling triad (vedanāttika). A monk who commits an offense does so either with an unwholesome mind, or with a wholesome or indeterminate mind. Likewise...
113:
Whether one is possessed of painful feeling (dukkha-vedanā) or the other two feelings (pleasant and neutral), an offense is incurred. Even so, in all training rules, there is one type of consciousness by way of unwholesome consciousness (akusala-citta), two types by way of wholesome and indeterminate consciousness, and three types by way of all consciousnesses. There is one type of feeling by way of painful feeling, two types by way of pleasant and neutral feelings, and three types by way of all feelings. Only this classification is obtained, and no other.

Knowing this characteristic which has seventeen divisions and is generally common, a wise person should apply it. This means that a wise monk, having known the seventeen-fold characteristic beginning with the Introduction (Nidāna) and ending with the Triad of Feeling (Vedanā-ttika), should apply it accordingly. A wise monk should apply this characteristic in each training rule as appropriate. Without such application, it is difficult to understand. Therefore, at the end of the specific (asādhāraṇa) decision of all training rules, I shall demonstrate it by applying it without extracting this summary (mātikā).

The application in this first Pārājika is as follows: This training rule was laid down in Vesālī concerning the Elder Sudinna in the case of committing sexual intercourse. "One should engage in sexual intercourse" is the original rule (paññatti) here. "Without renouncing the training" and "even with a female animal" are the two supplementary rules (anupaññatti). A supplementary rule may be one that creates an offense, as in the training rule on speaking of another's offense and so forth; it may be one that creates no offense, as in "except in a dream" and so forth; or it may be one that supports an offense, as in the training rule on taking what is not given and so forth. Here, it should be understood as a supplementary rule that supports the offense. Henceforth, where there is a supplementary rule, I shall only indicate, "This is a supplementary rule." It should be understood in the decision of all training rules that, excluding the supplementary rule, the rest is the original rule itself.

Since it was laid down for bhikkhunīs as well, even in the case arising concerning a bhikkhu, in this way: "Whatever bhikkhunī should consensually engage in sexual intercourse," it is a common rule (sādhāraṇa-paññatti). It is a non-command rule (anāṇattika) because an offense is not incurred by commanding another. However, a bhikkhu who commands another bhikkhu is not exempt from the dukkaṭa offense of undertaking what is improper (akappiya-samādāna). If there is bodily contact with lust for sexual intercourse, a dukkaṭa offense is incurred. In the aforementioned path (orifice) of a living body, even if the skin and so forth are completely removed so that only the appearance of the sign (genital form) remains, if a bhikkhu with the intent to engage in intercourse inserts even a pimple or a skin-peg (wart) that has arisen on his own member and whose physical sensitivity (kāyaprasāda) is not yet destroyed, he incurs a Pārājika. If he inserts a dry pimple, dead skin, or hair whose physical sensitivity is destroyed, he incurs a dukkaṭa. If the path is completely uprooted without leaving even the appearance of the sign, then by the effort...
114:
By the power of inserting into a wound, a grave offense (thullaccaya) is incurred. Likewise, if one inserts into the eye-socket, nostril, ear-hole, or the sheath (prepuce) of humans, or into a wound made by a small knife, a grave offense is incurred. If one inserts into the sheath or the nostrils of animals such as elephants, horses, and so forth, a grave offense is also incurred. If one inserts into the eye, ear, or nose-wound of animals, or into the tiny sign (genital) of snakes, fish, and so forth which lacks the size for insertion, or into the remaining parts of the body such as the armpits of all beings, a dukkaṭa offense is incurred.

In the sign (genital) of a corpse, from the time it has been half-eaten by dogs or jackals until it has not yet become putrid and bloated, a grave offense is incurred. If it has become putrid, a dukkaṭa offense is incurred. Likewise, for one who inserts the member into a mouth opened wide without touching the sides, a dukkaṭa offense is incurred. If one inserts into the tongue protruding outside the lips or into the teeth, a grave offense is incurred. If one inserts into a piece of flesh fallen outside the sign, a dukkaṭa offense is incurred. This is the classification of offenses in this Pārājika.

There is no offense for one who does not know, one who does not consent, one who is insane, one who is distracted, one who is oppressed by pain, and the first offender. Here, one who does not know the effort made by another because of being asleep is "one who does not know" (ajānanta). One who knows but does not consent is "one who does not consent" (asādiyanta). One who has reached incurable insanity due to bile is "the insane" (ummattaka). One whose mind is distracted by yakkhas is "the distracted" (khittacitta). For both of these, the standard (for determining insanity) is the state of not knowing due to having an equal attitude towards fire and gold, or excrement and sandalwood. One who knows nothing because of being afflicted by extreme pain is "one oppressed by pain" (vedanāṭṭa). One who is the first to commit the act in each case is "the first offender" (ādikammika). These are the instances of no offense.

Among the four failures (vipatti), it is a failure in virtue (sīla-vipatti). The factors of that Pārājika offense are two: the intent to engage in intercourse and the insertion of the path into a path. In terms of its origin (samuṭṭhāna) and so forth, this training rule has the origin of the first Pārājika; it is an act (kiriya); it has release through perception (saññāvimokkha); it is with consciousness (sacittaka); it is a worldly fault (lokavajja); it is a bodily action (kāyakamma); it has unwholesome consciousness (akusala-citta); and it has two feelings. These origins and so forth are factors of the offense, not of the training rule. However, for the sake of ease in expression, in all commentaries, the teaching is presented under the heading of the training rule. Therefore, in other such places as well, one should not be overly concerned with the letter (expression) but should grasp the intended meaning.

For the Lord, the Great Sage who sought the welfare of the world, declared the meaning as the refuge, not the letter. Therefore, a wise person, not taking delight in the syllables, should establish his intellect in the meaning alone.

## The Explanation of the First Pārājika is Finished.
115:
## 2. Commentary on the Second Pārājika

In the second Pārājika training rule, the meaning of the phrase “gāmā vā araññā vā” (from a village or from the wilderness) should be understood as follows: A “village” (gāma) includes a single-house village and other types, whether fenced or unfenced, inhabited or uninhabited, and even any caravan (or the site of a caravan) that has stayed for more than four months. Excluding the village and its precincts, the remaining area is called “wilderness” (arañña).

To avoid confusion regarding the village and the wilderness, one should understand the distinction between a house, house precincts, a village, and village precincts. The area within the drip-line where water falls from the eaves is called a “house” (ghara). The “house precincts” (gharūpacāra) include: the place where a woman standing at the door throws water from washing vessels; the place where a winnowing basket or a broom lands when thrown naturally by a woman standing inside the house; and the entire enclosure made at the two front corners of the house, connected with a wooden bolt-gate in the middle to prevent cattle from entering.

For the outermost house, the area within the range of a stone thrown by a man of average strength standing in such house precincts—as young men might stretch their arms to show their strength and throw a stone—is called the “village” (gāma). The area within the range of a second stone’s throw from where the first stone fell is called the “village precincts” (gāmūpacāra). However, the place where the stone rolls after falling should not be included.

In a fenced village, the fence itself is the boundary of the village. If there are two threshold posts (indakhila), the area within a stone’s throw from the inner threshold post is called the “village precincts”. The meaning should be understood in the same way in the Word-for-Word Analysis (Padabhājanī). Among those village precincts, according to the description of the precincts of an unfenced village, the offenses in training rules such as entering a village at the wrong time (vikāla) should be determined. Thus, excluding this village and the village precincts, the remaining area in this training rule is called “wilderness”. The phrase “gāmā vā araññā vā” is merely a way of teaching (desanā). A monk who steals a Pārājika object even from those places mentioned to show the boundaries—the house, house precincts, and village precincts—indeed commits a Pārājika offense.

“Adinnaṃ” (what is not given) refers to the property of others of the human race. In the term “theyyasaṅkhātaṃ”, “thena” means a thief; the state of a thief is “theyya”, which is a name for the intention to steal. The terms “saṅkhā” and “saṅkhāta” are identical in meaning, signifying an “aggregate” or “group”.
116:
As in the Pali passages such as “Papanca-concepts having perception as their source” (saññānidānā hi papañcasaṅkhā), it is called “theyyasaṅkhāta” because it is both the intent to steal and an aggregate. It means an aggregate of the intention to steal. Here, the nominative case is used in the sense of the instrumental; therefore, it should be understood as “by an aggregate of the intention to steal”. If a monk takes something with an aggregate of the intention to steal, because he has the intent to steal, the Word-for-Word Analysis (Padabhājanī) of that term is taught as “one with the intent to steal, one with the mind of taking away” (theyyacitto avaharaṇacitto) to show the meaning without emphasizing the literal word.

“Should take” (ādiyeyya) means taking by way of any one of the twenty-five modes of theft. These modes of theft should be carefully noted by combining the five pentads (pañcaka). The five pentads are: the pentad on various goods (nānābhaṇḍapañcaka), the pentad on a single good (ekabhaṇḍapañcaka), the pentad on taking with one’s own hand (sāhatthikapañcaka), the pentad on prior effort (pubbappayogapañcaka), and the pentad on theft by stealth (theyyāvahārapañcaka). Among these five, the first two pentads are obtained by way of these terms: “should take, should carry, should steal, should disturb the posture, should move from its place”. Therein, the pentad on various goods should be understood by way of animate (saviññāṇaka) and inanimate (aviññāṇaka) goods, while the other, the pentad on a single good, should be understood by way of animate beings only.

How? “Should take” means if one makes an effort (files a lawsuit) to claim a park as one’s own, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). If one causes doubt in the owner, there is a grave offense (thullaccaya). If the owner gives up the burden (relinquishes ownership), saying “It will not be mine,” there is an offense involving defeat (pārājika). “Should carry” means while carrying another’s goods, if one touches the load on the head with the intent to steal, it is a dukkaṭa. If one makes it shake, it is a thullaccaya. If one lowers it to the shoulder, it is a pārājika. “Should steal” means when asked to return a deposited good, “Give me my goods,” if one says “I did not take it,” it is a dukkaṭa. If one causes doubt in the owner, it is a thullaccaya. If the owner gives up the burden, it is a pārājika. “Should disturb the posture” means intending to “carry it away along with the person carrying the goods,” if one makes him take the first step, it is a thullaccaya. If the second step, it is a pārājika. “Should move from its place” means if one touches goods on the ground with the intent to steal, it is a dukkaṭa. If one makes them shake, it is a thullaccaya. If one moves them from their place, it is a pārājika. Thus should the pentad on various goods be understood. The pentad on a single good should be understood by way of taking, carrying, stealing, disturbing the posture, and moving from the place of a slave or an animal belonging to an owner, using the same method of lawsuit, etc., as mentioned before.

What is the pentad on taking with one’s own hand (sāhatthikapañcaka)? It consists of: taking with one’s own hand (sāhatthika), by command (āṇattika), by throwing/dropping (nissaggiya), by accomplishing the purpose (atthasādhaka), and by laying down the burden (dhuranikkhepa). Among these five, “taking with one’s own hand” means another’s...
118:
Taking by force is known as *pasahyāvahāra*. Taking by reflection is called *parikappāvahāra*. This *parikappāvahāra* is of two types: reflection on the object (*bhaṇḍaparikappa*) and reflection on the place (*okāsaparikappa*). Among these two, reflection on the object is as follows: A monk desiring a robe enters a room and reflects, "If it is a robe, I will take it; if it is thread, I will not," and then picks up a bag in the dark. If there is a robe inside, he incurs a *pārājika* at the moment of lifting it. If it is thread, he is safe from *pārājika*. Even if he takes it outside, opens it, and upon realizing "it is thread," brings it back and leaves it, he remains safe. However, if after realizing "it is thread," he thinks, "I will take whatever I have obtained," and goes away, he must be dealt with according to each step taken. If he sets it on the ground and then picks it up again, he incurs a *pārājika* at the moment of lifting. If he is pursued by people shouting "Thief! Thief!" and he drops it and flees, he is safe. If the owners find it and take it back, he is also safe. But if someone else picks it up, he is liable to replace the property. When the owners have turned back, if he sees it himself and takes it with the perception of it being ownerless cloth (*paṃsukūla*), thinking, "I had already taken this earlier; it is now mine," he is still liable to replace the property. Such reflection occurring in the manner of "If it is a robe, I will take it," etc., is called *bhaṇḍaparikappa*.

Reflection on the place (*okāsaparikappa*) should be understood thus: A certain monk enters another's compound or similar place, sees a desirable object, and sets a boundary such as the door of a room, a porch, the ground floor of a palace, a gateway, or the foot of a tree, reflecting: "If they see me within this space, I will act as if I am holding it out of curiosity; if they do not see me, I will take it away." As soon as he takes that object and crosses the predetermined boundary, the act of theft is completed. Reflection occurring in this stated manner is called *okāsaparikappa*. Theft committed by taking an object through the power of these two types of reflection is known as *parikappāvahāra*.

Stealing by concealment is called *paṭicchannāvahāra*. It should be understood thus: A monk in a garden or similar place sees a ring or other item that someone has taken off and left behind, and thinking "I will take it later," he covers it with dust or leaves. By merely covering it, since there is no lifting from its place, the act of theft is not yet completed.
119:
If the owners search but do not find it and go back still having attachment, thinking "We will find out tomorrow," then for the monk who lifts that [hidden] property, it is theft (avahāra) at the moment of lifting. Even while it is hidden, if he takes it with the perception of it being his own, thinking "This property has become mine," or with the perception of it being refuse-rag (paṃsukūla), thinking "They have gone now, this is abandoned property," it is only restitution of goods (bhaṇḍadeyya) for that monk. Even if those owners come to search on the second or third day and, not finding it, give up hope (relinquish ownership) and leave, the property taken is still only restitution of goods. If he is later known [to have taken it] and does not give it back when asked, it becomes theft (avahāra) when the owners give up hope. Why? Because they did not find it due to his action [of hiding it]. If a monk, without hiding such property where it is, but with the intent to steal, steps on it and sinks it into mud or sand, it is theft (avahāra) for that monk as soon as it is sunk.

Theft by moving a lot (marker) is called kusāvahāra. This kusāvahāra should also be understood thus: when distributing robes by casting any marked lot made of bamboo strips or palm leaves, if a monk, desiring to take another's portion—whether of lesser value, greater value, or equal value—which is near his own portion, lifts the lot that fell to his own portion with the intent to make it fall into another's portion, he is still protected [from pārājika] while lifting. He is still protected even when it is made to fall into another's portion. But when that lot has fallen, if he lifts another's lot from another's portion, it is theft (avahāra) as soon as it is lifted. If he first lifts another's lot from another's portion with the intent to make it fall into his own portion, he is still protected while lifting and while making it fall. For a monk who lifts his own lot from his own portion, he is protected only while lifting; but when he lifts it and lets go of it from his hand to make it fall into another's portion, it is theft (avahāra) as soon as it is released. This is kusāvahāra. Thus, the meaning of the statement "'He should take' (ādiyeyya) means he should take by way of any of the twenty-five types of theft" has been clarified.

## Yathārūpe means "of such a nature." Adinnādāne means "in the taking of what is not given, belonging to another." The word "Kings" (Rājāno) is said with reference only to King Bimbisāra; as for other kings, they may or may not act accordingly, so they are not the standard. "They might kill" (haneyyuṃ vā) means they might beat with hands etc., or cut with a weapon. "They might bind" (bandheyyuṃ vā) means...
120:
...they might bind with ropes etc. "They might banish" (pabbājeyyuṃ vā) means they might drive out. They might rebuke with these words: "You are a thief, you are a fool, you are deluded, you are a thief." For taking what kind of ungiven property do kings act thus? It is a pāda or property worth a pāda. "A monk taking such ungiven property" means a monk who, by any of the aforementioned twenty-five types of theft, steals property belonging to another that is not given, whether living or non-living, situated anywhere such as on the ground, which is a pāda of an ancient kahāpaṇa or property worth a pāda, becomes a pārājika. What need is there to say more regarding [theft of] more than that?

This training rule was laid down in Rājagaha concerning Venerable Dhaniya, because of the incident of taking the king's wood without it being given. "From a village or from a forest" is a subsequent regulation (anupaññatti) in this context. It is a common regulation (sādhāraṇapaññatti) [for both monks and nuns]. It is a rule involving a command (sāṇattika). Due to the preliminary effort (pubbappayoga) such as going to steal, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). Due to touching, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). Due to making the object of pārājika move, there is a grave offense (thullaccaya). For the monk who takes, if it is a māsaka or property worth less than a māsaka, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). If it is more than a māsaka but less than five māsakas, there is a grave offense (thullaccaya). If it is five māsakas (one pāda) or property worth more than five māsakas, there is a pārājika offense. In all thefts, the decision should be known by way of the time of taking, the place of taking, and whether the value decreases or not due to use or changing containers, etc. There is no offense for one who perceives it as his own, one who takes on trust, one who takes temporarily, property possessed by petas, property possessed by animals, one who perceives it as refuse-rag (paṃsukūla), and for the insane, etc. The five factors here are: the failure of virtue (sīlavipatti), property possessed by another human being, the perception of it being possessed by another, it being a heavy requisite worth a pāda or more, the intent to steal, and stealing by way of the aforementioned types of theft. This training rule has the origin of adinnādāna; it is an action (kiriya); it has release through perception (saññāvimokkha); it is with intention (sacittaka); it is a worldly fault (lokavajja); it is associated with bodily action, verbal action, unwholesome consciousness, and the three feelings.

## The Commentary on the Second Pārājika is finished.

## 3. Commentary on the Third Pārājika

In the third [Pārājika], "intentionally" (sañcicca) means having intended, having fully purposed. It means having purposed and planned with the perception of "a living being" and with the murderous intent "I shall kill him." "Human being" (manussaviggaha) means the body of a living human being from the stage of the kalala (embryo) onwards.
122:
...(Efforts by fixed means include) digging a pit, arranging a support [to cause a fall], placing a sword or similar weapon nearby, poisoning a pond or similar place, or presenting a visual form [to cause shock/death], and so on. In this effort by fixed means as well, the distinction between specific and non-specific should be understood in the same way as previously mentioned. 'Effort by magic' (vijjāmaya) is the recitation of mantras or spells for the purpose of killing. 'Effort by psychic power' (iddhimaya) is the use of psychic power born of kamma-result.

In the phrase "or should seek a weapon-bringer (sattha-hāraka) for him," it is called 'hāraka' because it takes away life. What does it take away? It takes away life. Alternatively, it is called 'hāraka' because it is something to be brought or placed nearby. Since it is both a weapon and a taker of life, it is called 'sattha-hāraka.' "For him" (assa) refers to a human being. "Should seek" (pariyeseyya) means to act in a way that it is obtained, or to place it nearby. This phrase illustrates 'effort by fixed means.' Otherwise, if one were to incur a defeat (pārājika) merely by seeking, it would not be appropriate. In the word-by-word commentary (padabhājanī), without following the literal sequence of words, the text says "or a sword" (asiṃ vā) etc., to show only the weapons included in 'effort by fixed means.'

"Or should praise the beauty of death" (maraṇavaṇṇaṃ vā saṃvaṇṇeyya) means to manifest the virtues of death, either verbally or by writing on palm leaves etc., in such a way as: "One who dies thus gains wealth," and so on. By this, it should be understood that while in the rule on taking what is not given (adinnādāna) one might be free from an offense through indirect speech because it says "should take" (ādiyeyya), in this rule, one is not free from an offense even through indirect speech because the word used is "should praise" (saṃvaṇṇeyya).

"Or should incite to death" (maraṇāya vā samādapeyya) means to make someone adopt a method for the sake of death, such as by saying, "Bring a weapon," etc. This illustrates 'effort by command' (āṇattika-payoga). "O man" (ambho purisa) is merely a form of address. "What is the use of this [life] to you" etc., are examples of the manner of praising death.

"With such a mind and thought" (iti cittamano) means having such a mind, having such a mind. It means having a mind focused on death as expressed in the phrase, "Death is better for you than life." Here, the word 'mano' is used to clarify the meaning of 'citta.' Therefore, in the word-by-word commentary, it says, "That which is mind (citta) is thought (mano)."

"Thought-conception" (cittasaṅkappo) refers to having various intentions. Here too, the word 'iti' should be applied. 'Saṅkappa' is a name for the mere act of arrangement or planning (saṃvidahana), and not only for initial thought (vitakka). That arrangement, in this context, is comprised of perception (saññā), intention (cetanā), and purpose (adhippāya). Therefore, "with such a thought-conception" (iti cittasaṅkappo) should be understood here as having the perception of death, the intention for death, and the purpose for death as expressed in the phrase, "Death is better for you than life." This same method is shown in the word-by-word commentary.
124:
## 4. Explanation of the Fourth Pārājika

In the commentary on the fourth Pārājika training rule, "anabhijānaṃ" means not knowing that [those states] exist in oneself because they have not yet arisen in one's own continuity. "Uttarimanussadhamma" refers to the Dhamma of those who have attained jhānas and the Noble Ones, who are superior men.

"Attūpanāyika" means applying that Dhamma to oneself by saying "It exists in me," or applying oneself to that Dhamma by saying "I will be known in this Dhamma." It should be connected as "one should communicate by doing so."

In the term "alamariyañāṇadassana," sublime and supramundane wisdom is called "knowledge" (ñāṇa) in the sense of knowing. It is called "vision" (dassana) in the sense of seeing, because of making the Dhamma manifest as if seen with the eye. Therefore, the vision of knowledge is called "ñāṇadassana." Because it is pure and noble knowledge and vision, it is called "ariyañāṇadassana." Among the superhuman states such as jhānas, the pure knowledge and vision capable of destroying defilements is "alamariyañāṇadassana." Alternatively, it is called "alamariyañāṇadassana" because one possesses the pure knowledge and vision capable of destroying defilements, and it refers to that Dhamma.

"Samudācareyya" means communicating this superhuman state of the aforementioned variety to a human being who understands, by applying it to oneself through body, speech, or both. "Thus I know, thus I see" is a demonstration of the manner of communication. This is because when one communicates by applying it to oneself without using other pretexts, one communicates in this way. Therefore, it should be understood that all the varieties mentioned in the word-analysis (padabhājana) such as "I attained the first jhāna, I am attaining, I have attained," etc., are included right here.

A monk who says "Thus I know, thus I see" does not merely say these words, but rather shows the meaning: "This Dhamma exists in me because of this and that reason." By saying "I attained," etc., the existence of that Dhamma is shown through reasons such as the ability to attain. Therefore, it is said, "All the varieties shown in the word-analysis are included right here."

"At a later time" means at a time other than the time of communication. This shows the time of confessing the offense, but in reality, the offense is committed at the very moment of communication. Since a monk who has committed an offense might confess whether he is reproved by others or not, it is said "whether reproved or not reproved." "Āpanno" means having reached the Pārājika offense at the very moment of communication.
125:
"Visuddhāpekkho" refers to one who expects or desires his own purity, such as the state of being a layman. This is because, since this person has already committed a pārājika offense, he is no longer fit to remain in the state of a monk and attain jhāna and so forth; thus, his state as a monk is not called "purity." However, by becoming any one of the following—a layman, an upāsaka, an ārāmika, or a sāmaṇera—he is still capable of achieving the path to heaven through acts like giving (dāna) or the path to liberation through jhāna and so forth. Therefore, his state as a layman and so on is called "purity." With this intention, it is said, "expecting purity such as the state of being a layman."

"Should speak thus" means speaking in such a way as, "Friend, I spoke this without knowing," and so on. In that text, "ajānaṃ" means not knowing; "apassaṃ" means not seeing. "I have spoken empty lies in a rambling manner" means "I have spoken empty words because they are devoid of the meaning of the terms, and I have spoken lies because of the intention to deceive."

"Except for overestimation (adhimāna)" refers to the overestimation known as the perception of attainment in what has not yet been attained—such as jhāna, magga, or phala—which arises in a monk who has undertaken insight (vipassanā), contemplating conditioned formations (saṅkhāra) by applying the three characteristics (tilakkhaṇa). The meaning is that, setting aside such overestimation, if one speaks merely out of boastfulness due to evil desire, he also becomes a pārājika.

This training rule was laid down in the story regarding the monks on the banks of the Vaggumudā river in Vesālī, concerning their reporting of superior human states (uttarimanussadhamma). "Except for overestimation" is the supplementary regulation (anupaññatti) here. This is a general regulation (sādhāraṇapaññatti) and a regulation not involving a command (anāṇattika). A monk who reports non-existent states such as jhāna in the manner already described, such as "I have attained the first jhāna," if he reports it to anyone who is a human being, and if that person understands the meaning in any way immediately after the report, such as "This person is an attainer of jhāna" or "He is an Ariya," it is a pārājika. If the person does not understand, it is a thullaccaya (grave offense).

If he reports by referring to another person, such as "That monk who lived in your monastery attained the first jhāna," and if it is understood, it is a thullaccaya. If it is not understood, it is a dukkhaṭa (wrongdoing). There is no offense for a monk who speaks out of overestimation, for a monk who has no intention to boast, or for those who are insane, etc. There are five factors in this training rule: failure in virtue (sīlavipatti), the non-existence of superior human states in oneself, reporting it out of evil desire, direct reporting without referring to another, the recipient being a human being, and understanding at that moment. The origins (samuṭṭhāna) and so forth are the same as those stated in the Adinnādāna training rule.

## The Commentary on the Fourth Pārājika is finished.
126:
"Venerable sirs, the four Pārājika rules have been recited." This statement merely clarifies the Pārājikas that have been specifically set forth in this Bhikkhu Pātimokkha. However, when taken together, it should be understood that there are twenty-four Pārājikas in total. What are these twenty-four? First, there are eight: the four Pārājikas of monks and the four unique Pārājikas of nuns mentioned in the Pāḷi. These eight, together with the eleven Pārājikas consisting of the unfitness for ordination of the eleven types of persons such as the paṇḍaka, make nineteen. Together with the Pārājika of a nun returning to lay life because she desires the state of a layperson, there are twenty. Furthermore, there are four called "Anuloma Pārājikas" (derivative Pārājikas) based on these four: a monk with a long sexual organ, a monk with a flexible back, one who takes another's sexual organ with the mouth, and one who sits down on another's sexual organ. Thus, these four and the previously mentioned twenty should be understood as totaling twenty-four Pārājikas.

"He does not receive communion with the monks" means he no longer shares in communion such as the Uposatha and so forth with the monks. "As before, so after" means that just as he did not have communion before, during the time he was a layman or a novice, so too after having committed a Pārājika offense, he becomes one without communion; for him, there is no communion such as the Uposatha and so forth with the monks.

Regarding those Pārājikas, "I ask the venerable sirs" means asking the venerable sirs concerning those four Pārājikas, "Are you pure in this?" "Kaccittha" is analyzed as "kacci ettha," meaning "In these four Pārājikas, are you pure?" Alternatively, "kaccittha parisuddhā" means "Are you those who are pure?" The remaining groups of words are clear in all places.

## In the Explanation of the Pātimokkha called Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī,
## The Explanation of the Pārājikas is finished.
127:
## Saṅghādisesa Section
The phrase 'Ime kho pana' refers to bringing the offenses that are about to be spoken of into presence (making them manifest). 'Āyasmanto' is an address to the assembled monks using affectionate words. 'Terasa' is the delimitation of the number. 'Saṅghādisesā' is the name of such [offenses]; 'Dhammā' refers to the offenses. 'Uddesaṃ āgacchanti' means they come to be recited in their specific form, not merely as a general statement like 'whoever may have an offense' as in the Nidāna (Introduction).

## 1. Explanation of the Training Rule on the Emission of Semen
In that [rule] regarding the emission of semen, it is called 'sañcetanā' because there is a distinct intention; the emission of semen with intention is itself 'sañcetanikā'; or it is called 'sañcetanikā' because there is a distinct intention in that emission of semen. 'Sukkavissaṭṭhi' means the emission of semen. Among causes such as the stiffness of the male organ due to lust, when the male organ reaches a state capable of emitting semen due to any cause, and a monk makes an effort regarding the male organ with the intention of enjoying the release of semen in any part of his own body or elsewhere, citing some reason such as health, it means the displacement from its place of any of the ten types of semen, such as the blue-colored one, due to the diversity of the physical elements (āsayadhātu). 'Aññatra supinantā' means except for the emission of semen that occurs in a dream. 'Saṅghādiseso' means that the intentional emission of semen, other than in a dream, is the category of offense called Saṅghādisesa.

Regarding the word-meaning (etymology) here: It is called 'Saṅghādisesa' because the Saṅgha is required (iicchitabba) at the beginning (ādi) and in the remainder (sesa). What does this mean? For a monk who has fallen into this offense and wishes to be rehabilitated, the Saṅgha is required at the beginning of the process of rehabilitation for the purpose of granting probation (parivāsa); in the middle, which is the remainder after the beginning, for the purpose of granting penance (mānatta), or for the purpose of granting penance along with the sending back to the beginning (mūlāyapaṭikassana); and at the end, for the purpose of rehabilitation (abbhāna). In these matters, not a single act can be performed without the Saṅgha. Thus, because the Saṅgha is required at the beginning and in the remainder, it is called 'Saṅghādisesa'.

It was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning the monk Seyyasaka on the matter of emitting semen. 'Aññatra supinantā' is the supplementary regulation (anupaññatti) here. It is an uncommon regulation (asādhāraṇapaññatti) and a training rule that does not involve a command (anāṇattika). If one causes another to make an effort on one's own male organ and causes semen to be emitted, one still falls into an offense. For a monk who makes an effort regarding the male organ with intention, even by at least moving the waist in the air, if semen is not emitted, it is a grave offense (thullaccaya). If, however...
128:
...at least as much as a small fly would drink is released from its place, even if it has not yet descended into the urinary tract, it is a Saṅghādisesa offense. Semen that has been displaced from its place inevitably descends into the urinary tract; therefore, it is stated in the Commentaries: "Whether it has just descended into the urinary tract, or has come out, or has not come out, it is a Saṅghādisesa."

There is no offense (anāpatti) for one who does not make an effort, for one who has no intention to emit, for one who is dreaming, and for those who are insane, etc., even if semen is emitted. In this training rule, there are these three factors: failure in virtue (sīlavipatti), intention (cetanā), effort (upakkama), and emission (muccana). The origins (samuṭṭhāna) and so forth are just as stated in the first Pārājika.

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on the Emission of Semen is finished.

## 2. Explanation of the Training Rule on Physical Contact
In the second training rule, 'otiṇṇo' means overcome by lust that has arisen within, just as beings are possessed by yakkhas and so forth; or it means oneself descending into the pit of lust, being lustful towards a lust-inducing object without reflecting on the true nature, just as beings fall into wells and so forth. This is a designation for one who is possessed of lust for physical contact.

'Vipariṇatena cittena' means with a mind that has arisen in a different way, having abandoned its natural state known as the pure subconscious (bhavaṅga) continuum; or it means with a mind that has changed into a perverted state. The meaning is: with a mind that has changed and persists through the power of the aforementioned lust, such that when it changes, it becomes perverted.

'Mātugāmena saddhiṃ' means together with a human female who is still alive, even if she is a girl born on that very day. 'Kāyasaṃsaggaṃ samāpajjeyya' means should enter into physical contact or bodily intermingling, such as holding the hand. 'Hattha-ggāhaṃ vā' and so forth are the detailed explanations of the meaning of that physical contact.

Among those [acts of touching], 'hand' (hattha) refers to the part from the elbow to the tips of the fingernails. 'Braid' (veṇī) is a designation for a mass of hair made by braiding or not braiding, with hair alone, or mixed with any of the following: blue-colored threads, flowers, coin-garlands, gold strings, strings of pearls, and so forth. In this training rule, by the mention of holding the braid, the hair and body hair are also included. Holding the hand as defined is called 'hattha-ggāha'; holding the braid is called 'veṇi-ggāha'. Touching the rest of the body or touching any limb, large or small, is called 'parāmasana'. If a monk should enter into holding the hand, or holding the braid, or touching any limb, there is for that monk the category of offense called Saṅghādisesa.
129:
At Sāvatthī, on account of the Elder Udāyī, this training rule was laid down regarding the matter of physical contact (kāyasaṃsagga). This training rule is an uncommon prescription (asādhāraṇa-paññatti) and is non-commandable (anāṇattika - an offense is not incurred through ordering another). For a monk who, perceiving a woman as a woman, touches even a woman's hair with his own hair at the minimum, or for a monk who, being touched by a woman, makes an effort with the desire to indulge and acknowledges the contact with pleasure, a Saṅghādisesa offense is incurred. If he holds with one hand and touches various places with the second hand all day long, there is only one offense. For a monk who touches without holding, if he touches from the head down to the feet without removing his hand from the body, there is only one offense. Even in grasping five fingers at once, there is only one offense. However, if he grasps the five fingers of five different women at once, five offenses are incurred.

For a monk who has doubt about the woman, or who perceives her as a eunuch, a man, or an animal, a Thullaccaya (grave) offense is incurred. Similarly, in touching a woman with an object connected to his body, or in physical contact with a female non-human (ogress/goddess) or a eunuch, a Thullaccaya offense is incurred. In touching objects connected to a human woman's body with an object connected to his own body, or in touching a man's body, etc., a Dukkaṭa (wrongdoing) offense is incurred.

There is no offense for: a monk who, though being touched by a woman and having the desire to indulge, does not make a physical effort but merely perceives the contact; a monk who touches a woman with the desire to be free; one who touches unintentionally; one who touches unmindfully; one who touches without knowing; one who knows but does not take pleasure; and for those who are insane, etc. These five are the factors here: breach of virtue (sīlavipatti), a human woman, perception of her as a woman, lust for physical contact, effort made with that lust, and reaching the state of grasping hands, etc. The origins (samuṭṭhāna), etc., are the same as those stated in the first Pārājika.

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on Physical Contact is finished.

## 3. Explanation of the Training Rule on Lewd Speech

In the third training rule, 'being overcome' (otiṇṇatā) and 'having a corrupted mind' (vipariṇataciittatā) should be understood by the power of lustful pleasure in lewd speech. 'A woman' (mātugāma) refers to a human woman capable of distinguishing between lewd and non-lewd speech. 'With lewd words' (duṭṭhullāhi vācāhi) means with words connected to the excrement passage, the urine passage, and the act of sexual intercourse. 'Should address' (obhāseyya) means he should speak to her in various ways with unwholesome words through praising, disparaging, begging, longing, questioning, counter-questioning, explaining when asked, instructing without being asked, or reviling. In the phrase "yathā taṃ", "taṃ" is merely a particle; it means "just as a young man speaks to a young woman". By this, it shows the state of having no hesitation in addressing her.
130:
"With words associated with sexual intercourse" (methunupasaṃhitāhi) is a demonstration of the characteristic of lewd speech reaching its peak. "Saṅghādisesa" means: for a monk who addresses a woman lewdly by means of the two passages, whether through praise or disparagement, or through begging for sex, etc., or by any of these three insulting words: "You are a woman with protruding flesh (sikharaṇī)", "You are a woman with passages joined (sambhinnā)", "You are a hermaphrodite (ubhatobyañjanakā)", an assembly of offenses called Saṅghādisesa occurs.

At Sāvatthī, on account of the Elder Udāyī, it was laid down regarding the matter of addressing with lewd words. This training rule is an uncommon prescription and is not by command (anāṇattika). For a monk who perceives a woman as a woman and addresses her lewdly in the manner stated, even by hand gestures (bending fingers), if that woman understands that meaning at that very moment, a Saṅghādisesa offense is incurred. For a eunuch, a Thullaccaya offense is incurred. For that same eunuch, if he perceives him as a woman and speaks, a Dukkaṭa offense is incurred. For a monk who addresses lewdly repeatedly, or for a monk who addresses many women with a single utterance, offenses are incurred according to the number of utterances and the number of women. If the woman addressed does not understand, a Thullaccaya offense is incurred. Even in speaking praise, etc., referring to the area below the collarbone and above the kneecaps, a Thullaccaya offense is incurred. For a eunuch, a Dukkaṭa offense is incurred. In speaking praise, etc., referring to the area above the collarbone, below the kneecaps, or objects connected to the body, a Dukkaṭa offense is incurred in all instances. There is no offense for monks who are focused on the meaning, the Dhamma, or instruction, or for those who are insane, etc. These five are the factors here: breach of virtue, a human woman, perception of her as a woman, lustful pleasure in lewd speech, addressing with that lust, and understanding at that moment. This training rule has the origin of theft (adinnādāna-samuṭṭhāna), is an action (kiriyā), is released by perception (saññāvimokkha), is intentional (sacittaka), is a worldly fault (lokavajja), is a bodily action, a verbal action, an unwholesome mind, and has two feelings (joy and equanimity).

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on Lewd Speech is finished.

## 4. Explanation of the Training Rule on Self-service

In the fourth training rule, 'being overcome' (otiṇṇatā) and 'having a corrupted mind' (vipariṇataciittatā) should be understood by the power of lust for self-service (attakāmapāricariyā). "In the presence of a woman" (mātugāmassa santike) means near a woman of the type stated in the training rule on lewd speech. "For self-service" (attakāmapāricariyāya) means service with desire (kāma) known as sexual intercourse (kāmapāricariyā), service with the sensual pleasure of sexual intercourse for one's own benefit (attakāmapāricariyā). Or, it means service desired or wished for by oneself through the power of sexual lust. Because it is both desired by oneself and is a form of service, it is called "attakāmapāricariyā".
131:
Pāricariyā means ministering or serving through sexual intercourse for one's own benefit (attakāmapāricariyā). In speaking of the virtues of that attakāmapāricariyā, vaṇṇam bhāseyya means clearly declaring the virtues and benefits. The phrase beginning with Etadaggaṃ indicates the manner of speaking about the virtues of that attakāmapāricariyā. In that context, the summary meaning by way of word-connection is: 'If a woman were to serve and delight a noble person like me—who is virtuous because of being free from taking life and the like, who is a celibate (brahmacārī) because of being free from sexual intercourse, and who possesses good conduct because of both—with this sexual intercourse, then such service of that woman who serves a person like me is the best among all forms of service.' Methunupasaṃhitena saṅghādiseso means that even when speaking of the virtues of attakāmapāricariyā in this way, if a monk speaks only with words connected to sexual intercourse, such as 'You are worthy of giving me sexual intercourse,' he commits a saṅghādisesa offense.

This training rule was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning the Elder Udāyi on the occasion of speaking about the virtues of attakāmapāricariyā. It is an uncommon regulation (asādhāraṇapaññatti) and is not an offense committed by command (anāṇattika). For a monk who perceives a woman as a woman, if he speaks of the virtues of attakāmapāricariyā even by a mere gesture of the hands or feet in the manner already described, and if that woman understands the meaning at that very moment, he commits a saṅghādisesa offense. If she does not understand, he commits a thullaccaya offense. If he speaks to a paṇḍaka (eunuch) perceiving them as a paṇḍaka, he commits a thullaccaya offense. If he speaks to that same paṇḍaka perceiving them as a woman, he commits a dukkaṭa offense. There is no offense for a monk who speaks of the virtues of service with requisites such as robes, nor for one who is insane and the like. These five are the factors of this training rule: being a moral failure (sīlavipatti), the object being a human woman, the perception of her as a woman, having lust for attakāmapāricariyā, speaking praise with that lust, and her understanding at that very moment. The origins (samuṭṭhāna) and other details are the same as those stated in the Duṭṭhullabhāsana training rule.

## The Explanation of the Attakāma Training Rule is finished.

## 5. Sañcarittasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

In the fifth training rule, sañcaritta means the state of acting as a go-between (matchmaking) between a woman and a man. Samāpajjeyya means he would commit the offense while performing the acts of accepting the commission, inquiring, and reporting back. The phrase beginning with itthiyā vā shows the manner of committing the offense. In that phrase, itthiyā vā purisamatiṃ means that being sent by a man or by his parents and the like, he informs the woman of the man's mind or intention. Purisassa vā itthimatiṃ means that being sent by a woman or by her parents and the like, he informs the man of the woman's mind or intention...
132:
...means he should inform the man. As a wife (jāyattane) or as a paramour (jārattene) means in the status of a wife or in the status of a paramour. Indeed, when informing a woman of a man's intention, he informs her for the status of a wife; when informing a man of a woman's intention, he informs him for the status of a paramour. Furthermore, when informing a woman of only a man's intention, he informs her either for the status of a permanent wife (nibaddhabhariyābhāva) or for the status of a temporary wife in misconduct (micchācārabhāva). Therefore, in the word-analysis (padabhājanī) of that term, it is said: 'As a wife means you will be a wife; as a paramour means you will be a mistress.' By this same method, it should be understood that when informing a man of a woman's intention, it should be said: 'You will be a husband, you will be a lover.' Regarding the phrase 'even for a momentary woman' (antamaso taṅkhaṇikāyapi), by the ultimate limit, one who is to be associated with for just a moment or a brief duration is called 'taṅkhaṇikā,' meaning a momentary woman. For a monk who informs such a woman of a man's intention, saying 'You will be a momentary wife,' he commits a saṅghādisesa; by this same method, it should be understood that one who informs a man of a woman's intention, saying 'You will be a momentary husband,' also commits a saṅghādisesa.

This was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning the Elder Udāyi on the occasion of committing an act of go-between (sañcaritta). The phrase 'even for a momentary woman' is a supplementary regulation (anupaññatti) here. It is a common regulation (sādhāraṇapaññatti). By the method of 'he accepts, he inquires, he causes the disciple to report back,' it is a training rule involving a command (sāṇattika). To any woman other than one to whom it is not fit to speak, even to one's own mother, if he wishes to say 'Please be a wife bought with wealth' and informs her by any one of the ten types of wives such as a 'willing resident' (chandavāsinī), whether she accepts saying 'Very well' or does not accept, if he returns to the sender and reports that matter, he commits a saṅghādisesa. Whether she actually becomes that man's wife or not is irrelevant. Even if he does not see the woman to whom he was sent, but tells someone else who will certainly inform her, 'Please inform her,' and then returns to report back, he still commits the offense. If he is sent to 'Speak to the woman guarded by her mother' but goes and speaks to another, such as one guarded by her father, it is a case of miscommunication (viśaṅketa). Having accepted the word of either the man or the woman by body, by speech, or by both, and having informed or caused another to inform that woman or that man, for a monk who himself reports that matter back to the sender or causes another to report it back...
133:
...he incurs a Saṅghādisesa offense. Indeed, by this much—merely by telling back or causing to tell—the three factors of accepting, inquiring, and reporting are fulfilled. For any two of these three factors, or for all three factors regarding a paṇḍaka, a Thullaccaya offense is incurred. For one factor, a Dukkaṭa offense is incurred. There is no offense for a monk going on business for the Saṅgha, for a Cetiya, or for a sick person, nor for those who are insane and so forth.

## Failure in Virtue (Sīlavipatti), the state of being a human being of those for whom one acts as a matchmaker, being one fit to be spoken to,

Accepting, inquiring, and reporting—these five are the factors here. This training rule has six origins (samuṭṭhāna). For a monk who, not knowing the regulation or the state of the person being fit to be spoken to, takes a message by bodily gesture, inquires in the same way, and reports in the same way, the origin is from the body. When someone says, "A woman of such-and-name will come; please find out her mind," and he agrees saying "Very well," then speaks when that woman arrives, and later reports when that man arrives—since he did nothing with his body, the origin is from speech. Having accepted the message by speech saying "Very well," and having gone to that woman's house for some other business, or seeing her while going elsewhere, he inquires by breaking into speech, and then having departed from there for some other reason, he later sees that man and reports—for him too, the origin is from speech. Even for an Arahant who does not know the regulation, if he goes at his father's word and says to his mother, who is fit to be spoken to, "Come, attend to my father," and then reports back, the origin is from both body and speech. These three are origins without intention (acittaka). However, for a monk who knows both and falls into an offense by these three methods, those same three become origins with intention (sacittaka) due to the mind knowing both. This training rule is an action (kiriya), not released by perception (nosaññāvimokkha), without intention (acittaka), a violation of a regulation (paṇṇattivajja), a bodily act (kāyakamma), and a verbal act (vacīkamma). Herein, by way of wholesome states and so forth, there are three types of consciousness; by way of pleasant states and so forth, there are three types of feeling.

## The Explanation of the Sañcaritta Training Rule is finished.

## 6. Explanation of the Kuṭikāra Training Rule

In the sixth training rule, regarding the phrase "saññācikāya pana," saññācikā means a request initiated by oneself. Therefore, "saññācikāya" means by one's own request. It means with materials such as billhooks, axes, etc., requested by oneself. Here also, any...
134: It is not proper to request property possessed by others with the intention of taking permanent ownership, but it is proper to request it for temporary use. It is proper to say 'Give me a man' for the sake of companionship or for doing work. It is also proper to request purisattakara (labor performed by men). Purisattakara refers to manual labor to be performed by men such as carpenters. It is proper to request it by saying 'Give me purisattakara' or 'Give me manual labor.' Manual labor is not a physical object. Therefore, whether asked 'Venerable sir, for what purpose have you come?' or not asked, it is proper to request it. There is no fault due to the request. However, one should not request hunters and the like for their own work (killing). A hut (kuṭi) is one of the types such as ullitta. Therein, ullitta means a hut where, excluding the pillars, beams, rafters, door frames, windows, and smoke holes which are not to be plastered, the remaining plasterable areas together with the walls and the inside of the roof are plastered with mortar or fine clay. Avalitta means a hut where the outside of the roof is plastered in the same manner as mentioned. Ullittāvalitta means a hut where both the inside and outside of the roof are plastered. In the phrase 'one who is causing to be built,' it includes both doing it oneself or commanding others to do it. 'Asāmika' means without an owner or a donor who is causing it to be built. 'Attuddesa' means referring to oneself, as in 'This is my dwelling place.' A hut referred to for oneself in this way must be built according to the measurement. The measurement of that hut is as follows: In length, it should be twelve Sugata spans. Here, a Sugata span is equal to three spans of a medium-sized man of today, which is one and a half cubits by a carpenter's cubit. When measuring, one should not take the end of the first layer of fine clay plastered on the outside of the hut's wall, but should measure twelve spans to the end of the clay mixed with husks. If one does not use clay mixed with husks but finishes with only fine clay, then that fine clay itself is the limit of the measurement. In width, it should be seven spans. This means that seven Sugata spans from the inner edge, not taking the outer edge of the wall, is the measurement. Here, it is not proper to decrease even a hair's breadth from the length to increase the width, or to decrease from the width to increase the length. What need is there to mention increasing both? However, if a building is sixty cubits long but its width is only three cubits or less than four cubits, such that a standard-sized couch cannot be turned around this way or that, and it is not four cubits wide at the final edge, this does not fall under the category of a 'hut' and thus it is proper to build it. After a monk has cleared the site where he wishes to build a hut, he must request the Saṅgha three times as stated in the Padabhājanī and invite either the whole Saṅgha or two or three monks appointed by the Saṅgha to point out the site. Those monks must point out a site that is free from dangers, such as the thirteen types of habitats of creatures like ants and the sixteen types of sites associated with crops, and which is not oppressive.
135:
Monks should be invited to designate the site for a hut. This means that if one wishes to build a hut in a certain place, after clearing that area, one should request the Saᅉgha three times according to the method stated in the Padabhājanĩ. Then, either all the monks belonging to the Saᅉgha or two or three monks appointed by the Saᅉgha should be invited to designate the site.

Those monks should designate a site that is without danger (anārambha) and has an open perimeter (saparikkamana). Those monks should note that 'anārambha' means being free from the thirteen types of habitats of creatures such as ants and the sixteen types of dangers associated with crops. 'Saparikkamana' means having enough space to circle a cart drawn by two or four oxen, with one wheel placed at the drip-line and the other wheel outside. If the whole Saᅉgha is able to go, the designation should be done right there; if not, the monk building the hut should go to the midst of the Saᅉgha and the site should be designated by a formal act consisting of a motion and a second (attidutiyakamma). The phrase 'sārambhe ce' and so on should be understood by the opposite method.

This training rule was laid down in Āጹavĩ concerning the Āጹavaka monks building huts by their own begging. It is an uncommon regulation (asādhāraᅇa-paatti) and contains a command. From the moment one goes to the forest for materials with the intention, 'I will build a hut on an undesignated site or one that exceeds the measurements,' there is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaᅡa) for every effort. When one says, 'Now it will be finished with two lumps of clay,' a grave offense (thullaccaya) is committed upon giving the first of those two lumps. When the second lump is given and the plastering is joined, if the site is indeed undesignated or if it exceeds the measurements, there is one saᅉghādisesa and two dukkaᅡas. If it fails in both respects, there are two saᅉghādisesas and two dukkaᅡas.

If one applies the clay without having yet installed the door frame or window, or if they are installed but the clay has not yet joined them, one is free from offense for that duration. The saᅉghādisesa is incurred only when further plastering causes them to join. If, while installing the door frame etc., it becomes continuous with the previously applied clay, the saᅉghādisesa is incurred from the very beginning. There is a dukkaᅡa simply for building on a site with danger; likewise, there is a dukkaᅡa for building on a site without an open perimeter.

There is no offense for: a monk who gives an unfinished hut to another; a monk who destroys it to level the ground; a monk who builds any of the types of dwellings such as a cave, a grotto, a grass-roofed hut, or a leaf-roofed hut; a monk who builds even a hut for another's residence; a monk who, excluding a residence, builds for other purposes such as an uposatha hall; and for those who are insane, etc. These six or seven factors are: the occurrence of a failure in virtue (sĩlavipatti), being one of the types of huts such as those plastered (ullitta), having the minimum measurement, the site being undesignated, exceeding the measurement, being intended for oneself, being a residence, and the joining of the plaster. This training rule arises from the action (kiriya) of a monk who, having had the site designated, builds a hut exceeding the measurement. It also arises from the act of building without having the site designated.
136:
In this training rule, these six or seven factors, such as being a residence and the joining of the plaster, are the constituent factors. There are six origins (samuᅡᅡhāna), and it arises due to action (kiriya) and action-inaction (kiriyākiriya). This is because this training rule arises from action (kiriya) for a monk who, having had the site designated, builds a dwelling exceeding the measurement. It arises from action-inaction (kiriyākiriya) for a monk who builds without having the site designated. The remaining procedures here are the same as those stated in the Sacaritta training rule.

## The Explanation of the Kuᅡikāra Training Rule is Finished.

## 7. Vihārakāra-sikkhāpada-vaᅇᅇanā

In the seventh training rule, 'mahallaka' (large) is so called because it has the nature of being larger than a hut built by one's own begging (saācika-kuᅡi) due to having an owner. Alternatively, it is called 'mahallaka' because of its large size, as it is permissible to build it exceeding the measurement after having the site designated. Since that large size is only obtainable because of having an owner, it is stated in the Padabhājana to show this meaning: "A dwelling called mahallaka means a dwelling that has an owner." All the remaining procedures are the same as those stated in the Kuᅡikāra training rule. The only distinction is the state of having an owner (sassāmika-bhāva).

The distinctions of this training rule are: it was laid down in Kosambĩ concerning Elder Channa for causing a sacred tree (cetiya-rukkha) to be cut down; the origin is due to mere inaction (akiriya); and it involves a single saᅉghādisesa.

## The Explanation of the Vihārakāra Training Rule is Finished.

## 8. Duᅡᅡhadosa-sikkhāpada-vaᅇᅇanā

In the eighth training rule, 'duᅡᅡho doso' (malicious anger) means both 'corrupted' and 'corrupting'. This is because when anger arises, the person is corrupted by that anger and is made to abandon their natural state; therefore, it is called 'duᅡᅡha' (corrupted). It also causes others to be ruined; therefore, it is called 'dosa' (anger/fault). Thus, 'duᅡᅡho doso' is a description of a single person through different aspects. 'Appatĩto' means being displeased, being devoid of joy (pĩti) and happiness (sukha), etc., and it means not being pervaded in the heart. 'Amũlakena' means that the accuser...
137:
In the case of a person being accused, if this Pārājika is unseen, unheard, and unsuspected, it is called 'amūlaka' (groundless) because of the absence of the roots known as seeing, hearing, and suspecting. Whether the accused person has actually committed that Pārājika offense or not is not the main point in this training rule. In this context, 'unseen' (adiṭṭha) refers to an object not seen with one's own physical eye or with the divine eye. 'Unheard' (assuta) similarly refers to not having heard it being spoken by anyone. 'Unsuspected' (aparisaṅkita) refers to not having suspected in one's mind through the power of seeing, hearing, or sensing (diṭṭha, suta, muta) by oneself or by another. It means accusing with such a groundless charge.

'Pārājikena' (with a Pārājika) means accusing with any one of the nineteen Pārājikas suitable for a monk. However, in the Padabhājanī, only those Pārājikas directly mentioned in the Pārājika section of the Pātimokkha are taken, and it is stated as "with any one of the four."

'Anuddhaṃseyya' means should destroy, should overwhelm, or should harass. Since this act of accusing and destroying can be done by oneself or by causing another to accuse, it is stated in the Padabhājanī as "whether he accuses himself or causes another to accuse."

Briefly, there are four types of such accusations: vatthusandassanā (pointing out the grounds/incident), āpattisandassanā (pointing out the offense), saṃvāsappaṭikkhepa (rejection of communion), and sāmīcippaṭikkhepa (rejection of proper duties).

Among these four, 'vatthusandassanā' is an accusation made in such a way as "You have indulged in sexual intercourse," etc. 'Āpattisandassanā' is an accusation made in such a way as "You have committed the Pārājika offense of sexual intercourse," etc. 'Saṃvāsappaṭikkhepa' is an accusation made in such a way as "There is no longer any Uposatha, Pavāraṇā, or legal act of the Saṅgha with you." However, the matter does not reach its completion (the Saṅghādisesa offense) by this much alone; it only reaches completion when combined with words such as "You are no longer a monk."

'Sāmīcippaṭikkhepa' refers to not performing duties such as bowing, rising to greet, saluting with joined palms, performing proper respect, and fanning. This non-performance should be understood when, while performing bowing and so on in sequence, one omits one monk while performing them for the rest. Although this much constitutes an accusation, the offense does not yet reach completion. Only when asked, "Why do you not perform bowing and so on to me?" and one replies with words such as "You are no longer a monk," does it reach completion. Therefore, if a monk stands near another monk and accuses him himself with words such as "You have indulged in sexual intercourse" or "You are no longer a monk," or even by indicating this meaning through hand gestures (hatthamuddā) alone, or causes any one among laypeople or monastics to accuse him, this is called defaming (anuddhaṃseti).

"Perhaps he may be made to fall away from this holy life (brahmacariya)" means the desire to remove that person from this excellent practice. It means he defames with the intention: "It would indeed be good if I could cause this person to fall away from this holy life."
138:
By this phrase "Perhaps... he may be made to fall away," the single intention of wanting someone to fall away from the Dispensation is taken, and the other seven intentions—the intention to insult, the intention to perform a legal act, the intention to make one rise from an offense, the intention to suspend the Uposatha, the intention to suspend the Pavāraṇā, the intention to cross-examine, and the intention to give a Dhamma talk—are excluded.

"Tato aparena samayena" (at a later time) means at a time other than the time when the accusation was made. "Samanuggāhīyamāno vā" means being cross-examined or interrogated by a Vinaya expert (Vinayadhara) in such a way as "What did you see?" etc. "Asamanuggāhīyamāno vā" means not being spoken to (not being interrogated) regarding any of the grounds such as seeing, etc., or by any person such as a Vinaya expert.

These phrases should be connected with the subsequent phrase "bhikkhu ca dosaṃ patiṭṭhāti" (and the monk admits to malice). The meaning is: whether being thus interrogated or not interrogated, the monk admits to the fault, stands by that fault, and confesses it, then it is a Saṅghādisesa. This phrase "bhikkhu ca... saṅghādiseso" is stated to show the time when the groundless nature of the charge becomes clear. As for the offense, he has already incurred it at the very moment of defaming.

In the phrase "amūlakañceva taṃ adhikaraṇaṃ hoti," it is called 'amūlaka' (groundless) because of the absence of roots such as seeing (diṭṭhamūla). It is called 'adhikaraṇa' (legal issue) because it is a matter to be settled by formal procedures (samatha). That matter, concerning which, starting from which, and depending on which the formal procedures proceed, is called an 'adhikaraṇa'. In this training rule, only the 'āpattādhikaraṇa' (legal issue concerning an offense) known as Pārājika is intended. If that legal issue is groundless due to the absence of roots such as seeing, etc., and this monk who came to accuse admits to the malice and stands by that fault, confessing by saying such things as "I have spoken falsely," then for that monk, at the very moment of defaming, it is a Saṅghādisesa. This is the meaning according to the sequence of words in the training rule.

This was laid down in Rājagaha concerning the monks Mettiya and Bhummajaka in the case of defaming with a groundless Pārājika charge. It is a common regulation (sādhāraṇapaññatti). It is with an authoritative command (sāṇattika). When one accuses a person who has received the higher ordination, whether pure or impure, with a Pārājika, knowing "This person has not committed it," and with the intention of making him fall away from the Dispensation, if he accuses without asking for permission (okāsa) by saying, "May the venerable one give me the opportunity, I wish to speak to you," and if the accused monk understands at that moment, "He is accusing me," then for every word spoken, there is both a Saṅghādisesa and a Dukkaṭa. For a monk who accuses after asking for permission, there is only a Saṅghādisesa. The same method applies to a monk who accuses in the presence of the other using hand gestures. However, for a monk who accuses behind the other's back, the accusation does not reach completion. Standing near him and [accusing] another monk...
139:
If a monk, standing nearby, commands another monk [to accuse someone], and that commanded monk accuses that person based on the words of the commander, the offenses occur only to the commanding monk in the manner already described. However, if that commanded monk also accuses, saying, "I have something seen or something heard," then the offenses occur to both of them who are aware [of the situation] in the same manner. For a monk who speaks without asking permission with the intention of insulting, there is a Pācittiya offense and a Dukkaṭa offense in the manner already described. For a monk who speaks after asking permission, there is only a Pācittiya offense. For a monk who performs the seven types of legal acts (kamma) behind someone's back with the intention of carrying out a legal act, there is only a Dukkaṭa offense.

For a monk who speaks with the intention of making someone rise from an offense, saying, "You have fallen into such-and-such an offense, rehabilitate that offense," or for a monk who suspends the Uposatha or Pavāraṇā, there is no need to ask permission; however, the proper time (khetta) for suspension must be known. Also, for a Vinaya expert (vinayadhara) who, when a case arises, speaks with the intention of investigating, saying, "Is this matter present in you?", there is no need to ask permission. For a Dhamma preacher who preaches the Dhamma in a general way without specifying a person, saying, "Whoever does such-and-such, he is not a true monk (asamaṇa)," etc., there is no need to ask permission. If, however, he speaks by specifying and designating a person, saying, "Such-and-such a person is not a monk, not a lay follower (upāsaka)," he must descend from the seat, confess his offense, and then depart.

There is no offense for those who are insane and so forth. (1) Accusing personally or commanding another to accuse regarding a breach of virtue (sīlavipatti), (2) perceiving the accused as a fully ordained monk (upasampanna), (3) having the perception of purity in that person, (4) the groundlessness of the Pārājika with which one accuses in terms of seeing, etc., (5) accusing face-to-face with the intention of causing a fall [from monkhood], and the understanding [by the accused] at that moment—these five are the factors [of the offense] here. The origins (samuṭṭhāna) and so forth are similar to the Adinnādāna Sikkhāpada. The feeling (vedanā) here is only painful (dukkha).

## The Explanation of the Duṭṭhadosa Sikkhāpada is Finished.

## 9. Explanation of the Aññabhāgiya Sikkhāpada

In the explanation of the ninth, the Aññabhāgiya Sikkhāpada, regarding the words "aññabhāgiyassa" and so forth: it is called "aññabhāgiya" because it belongs to another part (aññabhāga) or because it has another part. "Adhikaraṇa" should be understood as the basis; it means the ground or foundation of the matter (vatthu-adhiṭṭhāna). In the arising of the story, a certain he-goat was called "Dabba Mallaputta" (by the monks Mettiya and Bhummajaka). That he-goat has a part, a portion, a side, which is the human birth and the state of being a monk of the Venerable Dabba Mallaputta; [but in reality] it belongs to another part, portion, and side (which is the animal birth).
140:
Because of being of the animal species and being a he-goat, or because that he-goat has a part different [from the monk Dabba], it receives the name "aññabhāgiya" (belonging to another part). And because it is the basis, the object, and the foundation for the perception of those monks who, in naming it, said, "We shall make this [creature] named Dabba Mallaputta," it should be understood as "adhikaraṇa" (basis). Referring to that basis, it was said [in the Pārājika Pāḷi]: "Is it true, monks, that you [accused] Dabba Mallaputta with an adhikaraṇa belonging to another part (aññabhāgiya)?" etc. It does not refer to any one of the four types of legal issues (vivādādhikaraṇa, etc.). Why? Because it is impossible. Indeed, Mettiya and Bhummajaka did not produce even a slight trace (lesamatta) or a portion of any groundless legal issue (aññabhāgiya adhikaraṇa) among the four types of legal issues; nor is there such a thing as a "trace" (lesa) of the four types of legal issues. For the traces such as birth (jātilesa), etc., were spoken of [by the Buddha] only as traces of persons, not as traces of vivādādhikaraṇa and so forth.

And that name "Dabba Mallaputta" becomes a slight pretext (lesamatta), a portion of that he-goat which stands as the basis of another part (aññabhāgiyādhikaraṇa), for the purpose of harassing the Elder with a Pārājika offense. Here, it is called "desa" (aspect/part) because it is shown, pointed out, and expressed as "this is his." This is a designation for one of the portions such as birth (jāti), etc. It is called "lesa" (pretext) because it slightly adheres to another matter merely by way of verbal expression. This also is a designation for one of the portions such as birth, etc.

In the Word Analysis (Padabhājanī), however, regarding the harassment with a Pārājika offense by taking a mere pretext (lesamatta) or a certain aspect (desa) of an aññabhāgiya adhikaraṇa: because that aññabhāgiya adhikaraṇa is evident only by way of the origin story (atṭhuppatti), the four types of legal issues—which arise by way of extracting the meaning from the common term "adhikaraṇa" without distinguishing it—are presented. Since the state of being aññabhāgiya (belonging to another part) or tabbhāgiya (belonging to the same part) of those four legal issues is not obvious and must be known by Vinaya experts, and in order to clarify the accusation by way of an offense belonging to another part (āpattanyabhāgiya) at the end, it was said: "aññabhāgiyassa adhikaraṇassāti āpattanyabhāgiyaṃ vā hoti adhikaraṇanyabhāgiyaṃ vā" (of an adhikaraṇa belonging to another part means it is either an offense belonging to another part or a legal issue belonging to another part), etc. The remaining explanatory discussions are similar to what was said in the eighth training rule (Duṭṭhadosa).

However, this is the distinction: this rule was laid down regarding the matter of harassing with a Pārājika offense by taking a mere pretext or a certain aspect of an aññabhāgiya adhikaraṇa. In this rule, there is no offense even for one who has such a perception when accusing with an āpattanyabhāgiya (an offense of another category). Among the factors, the taking of a mere pretext or a certain aspect of an aññabhāgiya adhikaraṇa is the additional factor.

## The Explanation of the Aññabhāgiya Sikkhāpada is Finished.
141:
## 10. Saṅghabhedasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

10. In the commentary on the Saṅghabheda training rule, 'a concordant Saṅgha' (samagga saṅgha) refers to the community of bhikkhus who are united, being inseparable both in mind and in body. For this very reason, it is stated in the word-for-word analysis (Padabhājana) of that term: 'A concordant Saṅgha means those of the same communion (samānasaṃvāsaka) and staying within the same boundary (samānasīmā).' Indeed, a Saṅgha of the same communion is inseparable in mind because of having a common mind. A Saṅgha staying within the same boundary is inseparable in body because of giving bodily concord.

'Should strive for a schism' means making an effort for the purpose of causing a division, thinking, 'How indeed might this Saṅgha be divided?' 'A legal issue (adhikaraṇa) conducive to a schism' means a cause that leads to the objective of dividing the Saṅgha. In this context, 'adhikaraṇa' is intended as 'cause' (kāraṇa), as in the passages 'kāmahetu kāmanidānaṃ kāma-adhikaraṇaṃ' (due to sensual pleasures, having sensual pleasures as the source, on account of sensual pleasures), etc. That cause is of eighteen kinds based on the grounds for causing a schism. 'Having taken up' (samādāya) means having grasped. 'Should persist in supporting' means having grasped that cause which is conducive to a schism and capable of producing a schism in the Saṅgha, one explains it and does not abandon it.
