Desiring to conceal, there are three factors here: concealing one matter with another, or remaining silent. The origins and so forth are similar to the Adinnādāna Sikkhāpada. This training rule may be an action (kiriya) or an inaction (akiriya), and it involves painful feeling (dukkhavedanā).

## The Explanation of the Aññavādaka Sikkhāpada is finished.

## 3. Ujjhāpanaka Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā

In the third training rule, the words 'This named monk performs such an act out of favoritism (chandāgati),' and so forth, are used to disparage a monk who has been appointed by the Saṅgha as a distributor of lodgings (senāsanapaññāpaka) or similar roles. When one, desiring to bring disrepute to him, makes other monks look down on him or think of him as inferior, that speech is called 'inciting complaints' (ujjhāpanaka). Similarly, when one speaks and grumbles, making his faults known everywhere, that is called 'grumbling' (khiyanaka). In the phrase 'there is a pācittiya in inciting complaints and grumbling,' it means two pācittiya offenses are incurred due to the two instances. Therefore, if a monk, desiring to bring disrepute to an appointed monk, speaks to another monk to incite complaints or grumbles, he commits a pācittiya offense.

This was laid down in Rājagaha concerning the monks Mettiya and Bhummajaka in the matter of inciting complaints and grumbling. It is a common regulation (sādhāraṇa-paññatti) and is non-commandable (anāṇattika—offense only if done by oneself). If the formal act of authorization (sammuti-kamma) performed by the Saṅgha for that monk is a valid act (dhamma-kamma), there are three pācittiyas (tika-pācittiya). If it is an invalid act (adhamma-kamma), there are three dukkaṭas (tika-dukkaṭa). However, speaking thus in the presence of a non-ordained person, or speaking ill of an unappointed monk in the presence of anyone, or speaking ill of an unappointed person (whether unordained or ordained) in the presence of anyone, results only in a dukkaṭa offense. There is no offense (anāpatti) for one who incites complaints or grumbles against a monk who is naturally acting out of favoritism (chanda) etc., nor for those who are insane (ummattaka) and so forth. There are six factors here: being appointed by a valid act, being ordained, not following the wrong paths (agati), the desire to disparage him, the person to whom one speaks being ordained, and the act of inciting complaints or grumbling. The origins and so forth are similar to the Adinnādāna Sikkhāpada. This training rule involves only painful feeling.

## The Explanation of the Ujjhāpanaka Sikkhāpada is finished.
201:
## 4. Pathamasenāsana Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā

In the fourth training rule, 'saṅghika' means property belonging to the Saṅgha. Among couches (mañca) and so forth, anything made in the form of a couch is considered a couch; the same applies to chairs (pīṭha). A bolster (bhisi) is a lodging accessory made by creating an outer covering of cloth or allowable skin, excluding human hair and clean palmyra leaves, and stuffing it with any of the following: animal hair, leaves, grass, fiber, or cloth scraps. It is permissible to sit or lie down on such a bolster, and there is no restriction on its size. A stool (koccha) must be made from one of the following: fiber, usīra-grass, muñja-grass, or pabbaja-grass. It is bound by being well-wrapped inside, resulting in a drum-like shape that is narrow in the middle and wide at the top and bottom. The middle is often bordered with lion skin or similar materials. There is no such thing as unallowable skin for this stool, because even if a lodging accessory is made of gold, it is allowable.

In the phrase 'in the open air' (ajjhokāse), excluding the eight months designated as the non-rainy season when it is understood that it will not rain, during the remaining four months of the rainy season, even if it does not rain, it is not permissible to spread [bedding] in the natural open air or in a leaky pavilion. If it is a region where it rains in the winter, it is also not permissible during the four months of winter. In the summer, however, since the sky is clear and free of clouds everywhere, one may go about one's business [without putting it away]; it is allowable. But it is never permissible to leave it under a tree where birds like crows habitually roost. Thus, one should understand where and when it is not permissible to spread [bedding]. All such instances are considered 'in the open air' (ajjhokāse) in this training rule.

'Having spread' (santharitvā) means having spread it for oneself or for another in such a place. Even if spread for another, as long as that person has not yet sat there or has not said 'you may go,' the responsibility remains with the one who spread it. 'Having caused to be spread' (santharāpetvā) means having an unordained person or a novice spread it. This becomes the responsibility (palibodha) of the monk who gave the command. If one monk has another monk spread it, the responsibility lies with the one who spread it, provided the one who gave the command has not yet sat there or has not said 'you may go.' Whether one has caused it to be spread or it was already spread, if an ordained monk comes and sits on it, the responsibility lies solely with the monk who is sitting; thus it is still reckoned as 'caused to be spread.' 'When departing, neither removing it himself nor causing it to be removed' means not removing it oneself to place it in a suitable (dry) place, or not having another do so. 'Should depart without asking' means if a monk, or a novice, or a monastery attendant...
202:
A monk who is conscientious, fearing that the equipment might be damaged, regards it as his own responsibility. If he departs without informing such a person (a monk, novice, or monastery attendant), without handing over that monastery equipment to him, and without any concern for returning to put it away: if he crosses the distance of a stone's throw of a man of average strength, for the first step beyond that distance, he incurs an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa); for the second step, an offense of expiation (pācittiya). If, while standing in the dining hall, he gives an order saying, "Go and spread [the bedding] at such-and-such a place for the day-rest," and then leaves the dining hall for another place, the offense is determined by the lifting of his feet.

This training rule was laid down in Sāvatthī on account of many monks who departed without putting away their spreads and without asking permission. This is a common regulation (sādhāraṇapaññatti), an anāṇattika (not involving an offense through command) training rule, and involves a triad of expiation (tikapācittiya). Regarding another person's bedstead, etc., there is a triad of wrongdoing (tikadukkaṭa). If he leaves a coarse cloth, a coverlet, a floor mat, a reed mat, a piece of leather, a foot-wiper, a wooden bench, or any other wooden or clay article, even down to a bowl-stand, in the open air as described and departs, he incurs only an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa). A forest-dwelling monk, if there is no place sheltered from rain, should hang everything on a tree or arrange it so that termites cannot eat it before going. A monk living in the open air (abbhokāsika) should protect it by making a small hut with his robes.

There is no offense: if it is his own property; if it is the property of a friend; if he departs after putting it away; if he goes while sunning it with the thought, "I will return and put it away"; if seniors make him get up; if non-humans sit there; if powerful people take it; if lions and so forth come and stay there (thus the lodging is obstructed); or if the lodging is thus obstructed; or if he goes due to dangers to life or to the holy life; or in the case of one who is insane, etc. The six factors here are: the communal nature (saṅghika) of the bedstead, etc.; spreading it or having it spread in the described area; the lack of obstruction; the absence of danger; the lack of concern; and crossing the stone's throw distance. The origins and so forth are the same as the first Kathina training rule, but this is a kiriyākiriyā (offense by action or inaction) training rule.

## The Explanation of the First Senāsana Sikkhāpada is Finished.

## 5. The Explanation of the Second Senāsana Sikkhāpada

In the fifth (Second Senāsana) training rule, "vihāre" means in a room or any other fully covered lodging as described. "Seyyaṃ" (bedding) refers to a mattress, a coarse cloth, a coverlet, a floor mat,
203:
a reed mat, a piece of leather, a sitting cloth (nisīdana), an individual spread, a grass spread, or a leaf spread, as stated [in the Pali]. Among these ten types of bedding, a cimilikā (coarse cloth/rug) is a spread made to protect the color of a prepared floor. An uttarattharaṇa (coverlet) is a spread suitable for spreading over a bedstead, bench, etc. A bhūmattharaṇa (floor mat) is a special spread such as a reed mat or fine mat to be spread over a cimilikā if present, or on the bare ground if not. A taṭṭikā (reed mat) is a mat made of palm leaves and so forth. A cammakkhaṇḍa (leather mat) is any piece of leather; indeed, the prohibition applies only to the personal possession of lion skins and so forth, but for use as monastery equipment, there is no such thing as prohibited leather. A paccattharaṇa (individual spread) refers only to a cloak or a woolen rug; the rest are well-known.

Thus, if a monk who is about to go to another region takes even one of these ten types of bedding according to his seniority and spreads it or has it spread in a monastery of the described type, and then neither puts it away nor has it put away in such a manner that it will not be eaten by termites, and departs without asking permission as described in the previous training rule: for the first step as he crosses the boundary of a fenced monastery or the precinct (upacāra) of an unfenced one, he incurs a wrongdoing (dukkaṭa); for the second step, an expiation (pācittiya). However, if there is no suspicion of danger from termites in that monastery, it is allowable to go even without asking permission, though asking is the proper conduct for one who is departing (gamikavatta).

This training rule was laid down in Sāvatthī on account of the group of seventeen monks (sattarasavaggiya) who departed without putting away their bedding and without asking permission after spreading it in a communal monastery. It is a common regulation, anāṇattika, and involves a triad of expiation. In a personal (puggalika) monastery, it is a triad of wrongdoing. If he spreads it or has it spread in the dining hall near the precinct of a monastery of the described type, or in an unfenced pavilion, or in a fenced pavilion that is a gathering place for many people, or at the foot of a tree; or if he spreads or has spread a bedstead or bench in a monastery or its precinct as described, and departs without putting it away, he incurs only an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa). There is no offense: if it is his own property; if it is the property of a friend; if he puts it away; if he departs after leaving the obstruction as in the previous method; if he goes to the other side of a river or to another village with the concern that "I will return and look after it this very day," and then while staying there the thought of continuing his journey arises and he sends someone or asks permission from there; if he is unable to return because he is obstructed by a flooded river, danger from kings, or danger from thieves, etc.; if there is danger; or in the case of one who is insane, etc. If these seven factors are present—the bedding is of the described type, it is communal, it is spread or caused to be spread in a monastery of the described type, there is no obstruction, there is no danger, he departs without concern, and he crosses the precinct—[he incurs an expiation]. The fifth training rule is finished.

## 6. Anupakhajja Sikkhāpada

"Jānaṃ" (knowing) means knowing that "this monk should not be made to get up [from his place]." Therefore, in the word-analysis (padabhājanī) of that term "jānaṃ," the Blessed One said, "He knows he is senior, he knows he is one appointed by the Saṅgha," and so forth. To clarify the reason: a senior monk should not be made to get up because he is superior to oneself, and a sick monk should not be made to get up because he is unwell and deserves compassion.
204:
Departing to another place and transgressing the boundary of the precincts—these seven factors are present in this (Second Senāsana) training rule. The origination (samuṭṭhāna) and so forth are in the same manner as stated in the preceding training rule.

## The Commentary on the Second Senāsana Training Rule Ends.

## 6. Anupakhajja Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā

In the sixth training rule, "knowing" (jānaṃ) means knowing that "this monk is one who should not be made to rise (from his place)." For this reason, in the word-analysis (padabhājanī) of that term, it is stated: "He knows he is an elder; he knows he is sick; he knows he is one assigned by the Saṅgha." This is because an elder should not be made to rise due to his seniority; a sick monk should not be made to rise due to his illness; and the Saṅgha, having noted the great service and distinguished qualities of a storekeeper monk, a Dhamma-preacher, a Vinaya-expert, or a teacher of the texts, designates and gives a dwelling for their permanent residence. Therefore, one who has been given a place by the Saṅgha is also one who should not be made to rise.

"One who has arrived first" (pubbupagataṃ) refers to one who reached the place before oneself. "Intruding" (anupakhajja) means encroaching into the vicinity (upacāra) of the bed or chair, or into the vicinity of a monk who is entering or leaving that dwelling. Regarding that vicinity: in a large dwelling, the area of one and a half cubits (diyaḍḍha-hattha) around the bed or chair is the vicinity. In a small dwelling, the vicinity is as much as one and a half cubits can be obtained. For a monk who is entering, the vicinity is from the foot-washing stone to the bed or chair; for a monk who is leaving, it is from the bed or chair to the place of urination.

"Should lie down" (seyyaṃ kappeyya) means that if one spreads a bed or has it spread, out of a desire to crowd that monk within that vicinity, using any one of the ten types of bedding, one commits an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa). If one sits or lies down there, one commits an offense of expiation (pācittiya). If one does both, two pācittiyas are committed. If one does it repeatedly, a pācittiya is committed according to the number of efforts (payoga).

This training rule was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning the Chabbaggiya monks in the case of spreading bedding by intruding nearby. It is a common regulation (sādhāraṇa-paññatti), not requiring a command (anāṇattika). It involves the pācittiya triad (tika-pācittiya). In a personal dwelling, it is a dukkaṭa triad. Outside the stated vicinity, or in an assembly hall and so forth, or in the precincts of the monastery, a dukkaṭa is committed for spreading, having it spread, sitting, or lying down. There is no offense for spreading in one's own dwelling or in the dwelling of a close friend; for one who enters because he is sick or oppressed by cold or heat; in times of danger; or for those who are insane and so forth. There are four factors: it is a communal dwelling (saṅghika), knowing the person should not be made to rise, the desire to crowd them, and sitting or lying down in the vicinity.
205:
These are the four factors here. The origination (samuṭṭhāna) and so forth are the same as the first Pārājika training rule; however, this training rule involves only painful feeling (dukkha-vedanā).

## The Commentary on the Anupakhajja Training Rule Ends.

## 7. Nikkaḍḍhana Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā

In the seventh training rule, "angry" (kupito) means being enraged. "Displeased" (anattamano) means having a dissatisfied mind. In the phrase "if he should expel or cause to be expelled, there is a pācittiya," if there are stately mansions (pāsāda) with many floors or four-sided halls (catussālā) with many gates, and if one expels a monk from such lodgings by grabbing him and pushing him out in a single effort without stopping in between, one pācittiya is committed. If one makes him stop repeatedly and expels him through various efforts, pācittiyas are committed according to the number of doors. The same rule applies to a monk who expels another by speech, saying "Get out!" without touching him with the hand. For one who causes another to be expelled, a dukkaṭa is committed merely by giving the command; but if the person commanded passes through many doors after a single command, only one pācittiya is committed by the commander. However, if the command is specified as "Expel him through this many doors" or "Expel him as far as the main gate," then pācittiyas are committed according to the number of doors.

## It was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning the Chabbaggiya monks in the case of expelling a monk from a communal dwelling.

This training rule is a common regulation (sādhāraṇa-paññatti), involves a command (sāṇattika), and is a pācittiya triad. If one expels a monk from a personal dwelling, a dukkaṭa triad is committed. If one expels that monk's requisites (parikkhāra), or if one expels that monk or his requisites from the monastery precincts such as the assembly hall and so forth, (a dukkaṭa is committed). In expelling or causing to be expelled an unordained person (anupasampanna) or the requisites of an unordained person from a dwelling or its precincts, only a dukkaṭa is committed. That dukkaṭa should be understood as being according to the number of requisites when the requisites are not connected. 

There is no offense in expelling from one's own dwelling or a close friend's dwelling; in expelling or causing to be expelled a quarrelsome monk or his requisites from the entire monastery park (saṅghārāma); in expelling from one's own residence a shameless (alajjī) monk, an insane monk, or pupils (antevāsika) and shared-residents (saddhivihārika) who do not conduct themselves properly, or their requisites; or if one is oneself insane and so forth.
206:
The factors of this training rule are these three: it is a communal dwelling (saṅghika-vihāra); the ordained monk is free from being a quarrelsome person and so forth; and one expels him or causes him to be expelled out of anger. The origins and other aspects are similar to the training rule on taking what is not given (adinnādāna). This training rule involves painful feeling.

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on Expulsion is Finished.

## 8. Explanation of the Training Rule on the Upper-story Cell

In the eighth training rule on the upper-story cell, 'in an upper-story cell' (upari vehāsakuṭiyā) refers to a two-story or three-story dwelling where the upper floor is not yet covered. However, in the word-analysis (padabhājanī), to show the type of dwelling intended here, it is said, 'where the head of a medium-sized man does not hit [the beams].' 'With removable legs' (āhaccapādaka) means having legs that are inserted into holes carved in the frame. 'Should sit down upon' (abhinisīdeyya) means to sit down by overpowering or pressing down. Alternatively, the accusative case in 'a bed or a chair' (mañcaṃ vā pīṭhaṃ vā) is used in the sense of the locative case; the meaning is that one sits or lies down on a bed or a chair. The prefix 'abhi' is merely for the sake of word-ornamentation. Therefore, if a monk sits or lies down on a bed or chair with removable legs placed above the beams of an upper-story cell with the aforementioned characteristics—at the very least, having a height where a medium-sized man's head does not hit the lower beams in any way—he incurs an offense of expiation (pācittiya) according to the number of efforts, as described in the training rule on encroaching (anupakhajja).

This was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning a certain monk, due to the incident of suddenly sitting or lying down on a bed or chair with removable legs in an upper-story cell. It is a common regulation (sādhāraṇa-paññatti). It is a rule not requiring a command (anāṇattika). It is a pācittiya involving the triad (tika-pācittiya). In a private dwelling, there is a triad of wrong-doing (tika-dukkaṭa). There is no offense for one who sits on a bed with removable legs in his own dwelling, in the dwelling of a close friend, in a dwelling that is not an upper-story cell, in a dwelling where the head hits the beams, in a dwelling that is not in use because timber and other materials are stored below, or in a dwelling where the upper floor is covered with planks or finished with plaster and so forth; or if a monk, while standing on a bed with removable legs in such an upper-story cell, reaches for or hangs something; or if it is a bed where a pin (āṇi) has been driven in, where the pin is inserted above the tops of the legs; or for one who is insane and so forth. The factors are: it is a communal dwelling; it is an upper-story cell where the head does not hit the beams; below...
207:
...it is in use; and sitting or lying on a bed or chair with removable legs where no pin has been driven. These are the four factors here. The origins and other aspects are similar to the training rule on sheep’s wool (eḷakaloma).

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on the Upper-story Cell is Finished.

## 9. Explanation of the Training Rule on the Large Dwelling

In the ninth training rule, 'large' (mahallaka) means having an owner or donor. 'Dwelling' (vihāra) means a brick building plastered inside and out. In the phrase 'up to the door-frame' (yāva dvārakosā), the door-frame refers to the area around the door-casing, at most two and a half cubits in extent. 'For the sake of fixing the bolt' (aggaḷaṭṭhapanāya) means for the purpose of making the door-frame, along with the door-leaf, stable. Indeed, a door-leaf turns quickly and tends to strike the wall when opening and the door-frame when closing. Due to that striking, the wall shakes, and from that, the fine clay (plaster) moves; after moving, it becomes loose or falls off. Therefore, the Blessed One said, 'up to the door-frame, for the sake of fixing the bolt,' meaning to keep the door-leaf and door-frame from moving within two and a half cubits around the door-frame.

In that text, although it is not directly stated in the Matika or the word-analysis that 'this specific task must be done,' according to the authority of the origin story which says, 'he caused it to be roofed again and again, he caused it to be plastered again and again,' the meaning should be understood as: one should plaster it oneself or cause it to be plastered again and again up to two and a half cubits around the door-frame so that the door-leaf and door-frame do not move. In the phrase 'for the finishing of the light-aperture' (ālokasandhiparikammāya), 'light-aperture' refers to the small shutters of a window. When those shutters are opened, they strike the wall area for about a span or more. In this case, the surrounding area (upacāra) is available in all directions. Therefore, the intention here is that one should plaster or cause to be plastered an area the size of the door-leaf's width in all directions to ensure the window shutters are firm.

Having thus shown what is to be done in the plastering work, he now says 'of two or three layers of roofing' (dvatticchadanassa) and so forth to show what is to be done in the roofing. In that phrase, 'the sequence of two or three layers of roofing' (dvatticchadanassa pariyāyaṃ) means two or three layers around the roof. 'Pariyāya' refers to roofing in layers. The meaning is that one should arrange for two or three layers of roofing. 'Standing where there are no green crops' (appaharite ṭhitena) means standing where there is no green vegetation. Here, 'green' (harita) refers to the seven types of grain and so forth known as 'pre-grains' (pubbaṇṇa), and to 'post-grains' (aparaṇṇa) such as green gram, black gram, sesame, kulattha-beans, gourds, pumpkins, and so forth. Even a crop that has been planted in that field but is not yet mature is called 'harita' because it will thrive when it rains. Therefore, a monk who supervises while standing where there are such green crops incurs an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).

For a monk standing where there are no green crops, there is also this following measurement: a man sitting beside the ridge-pole or beside the pinnacle (thūpikā) of a dwelling topped with a pinnacle, when looking down from the edge of the roof-eaves, can see the monk standing on a certain piece of ground, and the monk standing in that place can also see the person sitting above...
208:
Crops such as sesame, beans, gourds, and pumpkins that have been planted, even if they are not yet complete (have not yet sprouted), are still called 'harita' (green crops) because they will become complete when it rains. Therefore, a monk who stands in a place where such green crops exist to supervise [construction] incurs an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa).

For a monk who stands in a place where there are no green crops to supervise, there is this limitation: if a man sitting beside the roof-beam or the pinnacle of a gabled house looks down through the edge of the eaves, at which ground area can he see the monk standing? And standing in which place can the monk look up and see the person sitting above through that same edge of the eaves? He should stand only in such a place where they can see each other. Even if there are no green crops within that boundary, he is not allowed to stand [outside it].

Beyond that, in roofing a dwelling, if it is a dwelling roofed in a straight manner, an offense of confession (pācittiya) is incurred for more than three layers of straight roofing. If it is a dwelling roofed in a circular manner, for more than three layers of circular roofing. When roofing with bricks, stones, or plaster, the offense is according to the number of bricks, stones, or pieces of plaster. When roofing with grass or leaves, it is according to the number of leaves or handfuls of grass.

This training rule was laid down on account of the Elder Channa in Kosambī, regarding the matter of repeatedly having [a dwelling] roofed and plastered. It is a common regulation (sādhāraṇa-paññatti). It is not an injunction (anāṇattika). It is a pācittiya of the triple-set (tika-pācittiya). If one perceives it as more than the limit when the roofing is less than two or three layers, or if one is in doubt, an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa) is incurred.

There is no offense: in applying white-wash and so on; in roofing two or three layers or less; in roofing a cave, a grotto, or a grass hut; in supervising for the sake of another; in building with one's own wealth; in supervising buildings other than the dwelling; and for those who are insane and so on. There are three factors here: it being a large dwelling, it being one's own dwelling, and supervising more than three layers. The origins (samuṭṭhāna) and so on are the same as those stated in the Sañcaritta training rule.

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on Large Dwellings is finished.

## 10. Explanation of the Training Rule on [Water containing] Living Beings

In the tenth training rule, 'knowing it contains living beings' (jānaṃ sappāṇakaṃ) means knowing by any means, such as seeing or hearing, that 'this water contains living beings.' 'Should sprinkle or cause to sprinkle' (siñceyya vā siñcāpeyya vā) means either sprinkling [grass or clay] oneself with that water containing living beings or commanding another to sprinkle it. In such sprinkling, if one pours it all at once without breaking the flow of water, there is only one offense for one pot of water. If one sprinkles by breaking (pausing) the flow of water, there are offenses according to the number of efforts (payoga).

If one directs a watercourse containing living beings toward one's desired direction and lets it flow, even if it flows all day, there is only one offense. If one blocks it here and there and leads it elsewhere, there are offenses according to the number of efforts. If one puts many grasses, leaves, branches, etc., into water containing living beings with a single effort, there is only one offense.
209:
For a monk who puts [grass, leaves, etc.] into water containing living beings with a single effort, there is only one offense. For a monk who puts them in one by one, there are offenses according to the number of efforts. This was said in reference to the kind of water that might be exhausted or become turbid such that the living beings would die by such putting in [of grass, etc.]; it was not said in reference to a large body of water. In causing another to sprinkle, an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa) is incurred by the command. Even if many [pots of] water are sprinkled by a single command, there is only one pācittiya for the one who gave the command.

This training rule was laid down on account of the Āḷavaka monks in Āḷavī, regarding the matter of sprinkling water. It is a common regulation (sādhāraṇa-paññatti) and is a training rule where an offense is incurred even if one commands (sāṇattika). For a monk who sprinkles water perceiving it to contain living beings when it does not, or who is in doubt about both [whether it contains them or not], an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa) is incurred. There is no offense for: a monk who sprinkles perceiving it to be without living beings; one who sprinkles unintentionally or through lack of mindfulness; one who does not know [there are living beings]; and for those who are insane and so on. There are four factors for this training rule: (1) the water containing living beings, (2) knowing that 'the living beings will die by sprinkling,' (3) the water being of that kind [where they would die], and (4) sprinkling grass and so on for some purpose without the intention to kill. The origins (samuṭṭhāna) and so on are similar to the training rule on taking what is not given (adinnādāna). This training rule is a 'breach of regulation' (paṇṇatti-vajja) and occurs with three types of consciousness and three types of feeling.

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on [Water containing] Living Beings is finished.

## The Second Chapter: On Vegetation (Bhūtagāma Vagga) [is finished].

## 3. The Chapter on Exhortation (Ovāda Vagga)

## 1. Explanation of the Training Rule on Exhortation

In the first training rule of the Exhortation Chapter, 'unauthorized' (asammato) refers to one who has not been authorized by the formal act consisting of a motion and three proclamations (ñatticatuttha-kamma) as an exhorter of nuns (bhikkhunovādaka-sammuti), which was allowed by the Blessed One for a monk endowed with eight factors. 'Should exhort' (ovadeyya) means exhorting the Community of Nuns, or several nuns, or a single nun by reciting the eight heavy rules (garudhamma) as a way of instruction, such as: 'A nun ordained for a hundred years must perform salutation, rising up, making the añjali gesture, and proper homage toward a monk ordained that very day.' 'Pācittiya' means that an offense of confession is incurred at the conclusion of the exhortation.

This training rule was laid down on account of the Chabbaggiya monks in Sāvatthī, regarding the matter of exhortation. It is an uncommon regulation (asādhāraṇa-paññatti) and is a training rule where an offense is not incurred by mere command (anāṇattika). An offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa) is incurred for a monk who exhorts nuns with a teaching other than the garudhammas, or who exhorts a nun who has only just been ordained [among the nuns]. Even if he is authorized, if that act of authorization is an illegal act (adhamma-kamma), and while perceiving that illegal act as an illegal act, in a group of the Community of Nuns...
210:
For the monk who exhorts, there is a triad of Pācittiya. Likewise, for one who has doubt and for one who perceives it as a legal act, there are nine Pācittiyas. Even if the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha is in concord, by way of an illegal act, there are eighteen Pācittiyas. However, if that act is a legal act, excluding this final clause: 'Perceiving a legal act as a legal act, he exhorts the concordant Bhikkhunī Saṅgha perceiving them as concordant' (Pāc. 151), in the same manner, there are seventeen Dukkaṭa offenses. For a monk who teaches another Dhamma even though they said, 'Venerable sir, all are assembled'; and for a monk who teaches the eight Garudhammas even though they said, 'Venerable sir, the group is incomplete'; and for a monk who teaches another Dhamma without concluding the exhortation, there is only a Dukkaṭa offense.

There is no offense for a monk who, perceiving a legal act as a legal act, exhorts the concordant Bhikkhunī Saṅgha perceiving them as concordant; who recites the text of the Garudhammas; who gives an explanation; who recites when requested, 'Venerable sir, please recite'; who answers a question asked; who speaks for the sake of another while the bhikkhunīs are listening; who speaks to a probationer (sikkhamānā) or a female novice (sāmaṇerī); and for those who are insane, etc. In this training rule, there are three factors: (1) being one who is not authorized, (2) the bhikkhunī being one who is fully ordained, (3) teaching the eight Garudhammas by way of exhortation. The origin, etc., are the same as the Padasodhamma training rule.

## The Commentary on the Ovāda Training Rule is finished.

## 2. Atthaṅgata Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā

In the second training rule, 'should exhort' means that even for an authorized monk who exhorts with the eight Garudhammas or with another Dhamma, a Pācittiya offense occurs.

This training rule was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning Venerable Cūḷapanthaka, on account of the matter of exhorting when the sun had set. This is an uncommon regulation (asādhāraṇa-paññatti), not involving an order (anāṇattika), and involves a triad of Pācittiya. There is a Dukkaṭa offense for one who perceives that the sun has set when it has not, or for one who has doubt, and for one who exhorts a bhikkhunī who is ordained only on one side. As in the previous training rule, there is no offense by way of recitation, etc. In this training rule, there are three factors: (1) the sun having set, (2) being one who is fully ordained, (3) exhorting. The origin, etc., are the same as the Padasodhamma training rule.

## The Commentary on the Atthaṅgata Training Rule is finished.
211:
## 3. Bhikkhunuပဿယ Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā

In the third training rule, 'Bhikkhunupassaya' refers even to a place where a bhikkhunī stays for a single night. Regarding 'should exhort' (ovadeyya), in this training rule, a Pācittiya offense occurs only for a monk who exhorts with the Garudhammas. If he is a monk who has not received authorization (sammuti), there are two Pācittiyas. If he exhorts after the sun has set, there are three. However, for an authorized monk who exhorts at night, there are only two. This is because, for an authorized monk, there is no Pācittiya rooted in the exhortation of Garudhammas. 'Sick' (gilānā) refers to a bhikkhunī who is unable to go either for exhortation or for the communal acts (uposatha, pavāraṇā).

This training rule was laid down among the Sakyans concerning the Chabbaggiya monks, on account of the matter of going to the bhikkhunīs' quarters to exhort. 'Except on the proper occasion' (aññatra samayā) is the supplementary regulation here. This is an uncommon regulation, not involving an order. It involves a triad of Pācittiya. There is a Dukkaṭa offense for one who perceives an unordained person (sikkhamānā, sāmaṇerī) as ordained, or has doubt; for one who exhorts a person ordained on one side with any Dhamma; or for one who exhorts another (fully ordained) bhikkhunī with a Dhamma other than the Garudhammas. There is no offense if it is on the proper occasion, for an unordained person, or by way of recitation, etc., as in the previous training rule. The four factors in this training rule are: going to the bhikkhunīs' quarters, the bhikkhunī being fully ordained, it not being the proper occasion, and exhorting with the Garudhammas. The origin, etc., are the same as the first Kathina training rule. This is an act of commission (kiriya).

## The Commentary on the Bhikkhunupassaya Training Rule is finished.

## 4. Āmisa Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā

In the fourth training rule, 'for the sake of material gain' (āmisahetu) means for the sake of any of the four requisites such as robes, etc. 'Monks' (bhikkhū) in this training rule refers to authorized monks. 'Pācittiya' means a Pācittiya offense occurs for a monk who speaks thus with the desire to cause a lack of reputation for such monks.

This was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning the Chabbaggiya monks, on account of the matter of saying, 'They exhort for the sake of material gain (āmisahetu).' This is an uncommon regulation, not involving an order. It involves a triad of Pācittiya in the case of a legal act, and a triad of Dukkaṭa in the case of an illegal act. There is only a Dukkaṭa offense for speaking thus about an unauthorized monk, or about a novice (sāmaṇera) whether authorized or not. Among them, if a person who received authorization while being a monk is now established in the stage of a novice, he is called an 'authorized unordained person' (sammata anupasampanna). If one speaks thus to a monk who truly exhorts for the sake of material gain...
212:
There is no offense for one who speaks thus, for the insane, and so forth. The four factors of this training rule are: being a monk, having a legally obtained authorization, having no desire for material gain, and speaking thus without seeking fame. The origin and so forth are similar to the rule on taking what is not given (adinnādāna); this training rule involves only painful feeling (dukkha-vedanā).

## The Commentary on the Āmisa Sikkhāpada is finished.

## 5. Cīvaradāna Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā

The fifth training rule was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning a certain monk regarding the giving of a robe. The rest of the explanation should be understood in the same way as stated in the Cīvarappaṭiggahena Sikkhāpada. In that rule, a monk is the recipient, whereas in this rule, a bhikkhunī is the recipient; this is the distinction, the rest is the same.

## The Commentary on the Cīvaradāna Sikkhāpada is finished.

## 6. Cīvarasibbana Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā

In the sixth training rule, 'robe' refers to a cloth suitable for wearing as an inner or outer garment. In the phrase 'whether he sews it himself or has it sewn,' for a monk sewing it himself, a pācittiya offense is incurred for every insertion and withdrawal of the needle. For one who pierces even a hundred times but withdraws it only once, there is only one pācittiya. If a monk who is commanded to sew completes the entire needlework, the commanding monk incurs only one pācittiya. However, if it is said, 'Whatever needs to be done to this robe is your responsibility,' and he completes it, the [commanding] monk incurs a pācittiya for every needle-path (every withdrawal of the needle). With a single command, many pācittiya offenses may be incurred by the commanding monk; it goes without saying that many offenses are incurred if he commands repeatedly.

It was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning the Elder Udāyi regarding the sewing of a robe. This is an uncommon regulation (asādhāraṇa-paññatti), involving a command (sāṇattika), and is a triad-pācittiya (tika-pācittiya). There is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for a monk who sews for a bhikkhunī who is a relative but whom he perceives as a non-relative, or if he is in doubt, or if he sews for one who is ordained on one side only (ekato-upasampannā). There is no offense for sewing other requisites such as a bag, or for sewing even a robe for a bhikkhunī who is a relative, or for a sikkhamānā or a sāmaṇerī, or for the insane and so forth. For a bhikkhunī who is not a relative...
213:
(The robe being sewn) belongs to a bhikkhunī, it is suitable for wearing, and sewing it oneself or having it sewn according to the stated characteristics—these are the three factors here. The origin and so forth are similar to the Sañcaritta Sikkhāpada.

## The Commentary on the Cīvarasibbana Sikkhāpada is finished.

## 7. Saṃvidhāna Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā

In the seventh training rule, the Saṃvidhāna Sikkhāpada, 'saṃvidhāya' means having consulted and arranged, making an appointment at the time of departure. 'Ekaddhānamagga' means a journey known as a single stretch, or a long journey traveled together. 'Satthagamanīya' means a journey that should be traveled with a caravan. The meaning of the remaining words is clear.

The decision in this rule is: for a monk who consults and arranges while standing on unsuitable ground, a dukkaṭa offense is first incurred due to the act of arranging. Unsuitable ground refers to any place except a bhikkhunī's quarters, a village monastery, a refectory, or a residence of non-Buddhists (titthiya). After arranging, if he goes with a bhikkhunī without breaking the appointed time (such as 'today' or 'tomorrow'), even if the appointment for the gate or the road is missed, there is no offense as long as he has not entered the village precinct (upacāra) designated by people as 'this is the precinct of this village' for another very near village. Upon entering that precinct, there is a dukkaṭa for the first step and a pācittiya for the second step. Thus, pācittiya offenses are counted according to the entry into village precincts. In a place where there is no village, a pācittiya is incurred for every half-league (yojana) crossed.

This training rule was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning the Chabbaggiya monks regarding traveling on a single long journey. 'Except on occasion' (aññatra samayā) is the supplementary regulation (anupaññatti) here. It is an uncommon regulation, not involving a command (anāṇattika), and a triad-pācittiya. A dukkaṭa offense is incurred for a monk who perceives an unarranged journey as arranged, or is in doubt, or for a monk who arranges by himself while the bhikkhunī does not arrange.

There is no offense for a monk who goes having arranged during a permitted occasion, for one who does not arrange himself, for one who goes when the appointment is broken, for one who goes during dangers, or for the insane and so forth. The five factors here are: (1) traveling by arrangement of both parties, (2) the appointment not being broken, (3) it not being a permitted occasion, (4) the absence of danger, and (5) entering another village precinct or crossing half a league. If traveling with one ordained on one side only (ekato-upasampannā) and so forth, an offense is incurred under the Mātugāma Sikkhāpada. This training rule has the origin of a journey (addhāna-samuṭṭhāna), is an act (kiriya), does not involve release by perception (no-saññā-vimokkha), is unintentional (acittaka), is a regulation-violation (paṇṇatti-vajja), involves bodily action, vocal action, three types of consciousness, and three types of feeling.

## The Commentary on the Saṃvidhāna Sikkhāpada is finished.
214:
## 8. Nāvābhiruhanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

In the eighth training rule, the word 'saṃvidhāya' means making an arrangement or appointment at the time of boarding the boat, with the intention of enjoying oneself. 'Uddhaṃgāminī' refers to a boat going upstream against the river's current for the purpose of pleasure. 'Adhogāminī' refers to a boat going downstream with the river's current for that same purpose of pleasure. If a boat is taken either upstream or downstream for the purpose of reaching a desired landing place (port), there is no offense in such travel. In the phrase 'aññatra tiriyaṃ taraṇāya', the word 'taraṇāya' is in the ablative case with the sense of the accusative case. It means 'except for a boat used for crossing across (the river)'. 'Pācittiyaṃ' means that a Pācittiya offense is incurred for every village passed when traveling along a bank where there are villages; or for every half-league when traveling along a bank where there are no villages, or when traveling through the middle of a river that is one league wide. In the ocean, however, it is allowable to travel as one pleases.

This training rule was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning the group-of-six monks in the case of boarding a boat. The phrase 'aññatra tiriyaṃ taraṇāya' is an additional regulation (anupaññatti) in this training rule. The remaining points should be understood in the same manner as stated in the preceding training rule.

## The Commentary on the Training Rule on Boarding a Boat is finished.

## 9. Paripācitasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

In the ninth training rule, 'bhikkhuniparipācitaṃ' means almsfood caused to be prepared by a bhikkhunī. It refers to almsfood obtained by a bhikkhunī praising the virtues of a monk to laypeople who are neither his relatives nor those who have invited him, nor her own relatives or invited persons, saying, "Give to the venerable one, prepare for the venerable one," and thus prompting them to provide it. In the phrase 'pubbe gihisamārambhā', 'samārambha' is a name for food that has been well-prepared (arranged). It means that except for food already prepared by laypeople for the sake of monks before the bhikkhunī's intervention, or food belonging to relatives or those who have invited them, a monk who eats other food knowing it was caused to be prepared by a bhikkhunī incurs a Pācittiya offense. That Pācittiya offense is incurred for every swallow. In the act of receiving it, however, he incurs a Dukkaṭa offense.

This training rule was laid down in Rājagaha concerning Devadatta in the case of eating almsfood caused to be prepared by a bhikkhunī. The phrase 'aññatra pubbe gihisamārambhā' is an additional regulation (anupaññatti) in this training rule. This is a specific regulation (asādhāraṇapaññatti) for monks, not involving a command (anāṇattika), regarding eating food caused to be prepared by a bhikkhunī ordained on one side...
215:
...for a monk who eats food caused to be prepared [by such a bhikkhunī], or for one who eats unprepared food with the perception that it is prepared, or for one who is in doubt in both cases, a Dukkaṭa offense is incurred. There is no offense for: one who perceives it as unprepared in both cases; food initiated by laypeople; food prepared by a sikkhamānā, a sāmaṇera, and so on; food other than the five types of meals; and for those who are insane, etc. In this training rule, there are five factors: 1. It is caused to be prepared by a bhikkhunī, 2. Knowing that it was caused to be prepared, 3. It was not initiated by laypeople beforehand, 4. It is one of the five types of meals, 5. The act of swallowing it. The origins (samuṭṭhāna) and other aspects are the same as the first Pārājika. This training rule involves a regulation-based fault (paṇṇattivajja), and involves three types of consciousness and three types of feelings.

## The Commentary on the Training Rule on Food Caused to be Prepared is finished.

## 10. Rahonisajjasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

In the tenth training rule, the entire sequence of explanation should be understood in the same manner as stated in the second Aniyata. This training rule has the same scope as the second Aniyata and the fourth training rule laid down concerning Upananda in the Acelaka Vagga above. However, it was laid down separately based on the specific occasion of its origin.

## The Commentary on the Training Rule on Sitting in Private is finished.

## The Third Chapter: The Chapter on Exhortation (Ovāda Vagga).

## 4. Bhojana Vagga

## 1. Āvasathasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

In the first training rule of the Food Chapter (Bhojana Vagga), 'agilānena' refers to a monk who is capable of walking even half a league. 'Eko' refers to almsfood for one day. 'Āvasathapiṇḍa' refers to almsfood provided by those desiring merit at places such as rest-houses, without specifically designating it for a particular sect by saying "for these people" or "for this many people," or without designating the amount by saying "only this much food." 'Bhuñjitabbo' means that almsfood provided by one family or by many families together, at one place or at various places, or at an unfixed location such as "today at one place, tomorrow at another," should be eaten at one place for only one day. From the second day onwards, if one receives their almsfood at that place or at another place, a Dukkaṭa is incurred; for every swallow, a Pācittiya offense is incurred.
216:
In Sāvatthī, it was laid down concerning the Chabbaggiya monks regarding the matter of eating food at a public rest house (āvasatha) after staying there. The phrase "by a monk who is not ill" is a supplementary regulation (anupaññatti) in this training rule. This training rule is a common regulation (သာဓာရဏပညတ်), not involving a command (anāṇattika), and is a Pācittiya in a triad (tikapācittiya). For a monk who is ill but perceives himself as not ill, or for one who is in doubt, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).

There is no offense for: a monk who is ill and perceives himself as ill; a monk who eats only once; a monk who eats one day on the way while traveling, one day at the destination, one day on the way while returning, and one day at the place of return; a monk who, intending to leave, eats and sets out but returns due to some danger and, knowing it is safe, eats for one more day when setting out again; a monk who eats when the owners invite and offer; a monk who eats food dedicated specifically for monks and not for all comers; a monk who eats other snacks, etc., excluding the five kinds of food; and for those who are insane, etc. The three factors here are: being food from a rest house, being not ill, and eating after staying. The origin (samuṭṭhāna), etc., are the same as the Eḷakaloma training rule.

## The Commentary on the Āvasatha Training Rule is finished.

## 2. Commentary on the Gaṇabhojana Training Rule

In the second training rule, Gaṇabhojana, "Gaṇabhojana" means eating a meal of a group. In this training rule, "gaṇa" (group) refers to four or more monks. It means eating any one of the five kinds of food, such as boiled rice, etc., obtained through invitation or request by those monks.

In this matter, this is the decision: If someone approaches four monks and invites them using any synonym or another language, mentioning the name of the five kinds of food, saying, "I invite you with boiled rice, please accept my boiled rice," etc., and if those monks, being thus invited together or separately, go together or separately and accept together, and later eat together or separately, it is a group meal (gaṇabhojana). Acceptance alone is the standard here. If they request by mentioning the name of boiled rice, etc., together or separately, and after going, they accept together, this is also a group meal. In both types of group meal, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) upon such acceptance, and a Pācittiya offense for every swallow. In the occasion of illness (gilānasamaya), etc., when one is unable to wander for alms because the soles of the feet are cracked...
217:
This time is called the occasion of illness (gilānasamaya). For monks who have spread the Kathina, it is five months; for others, the month of Kattika is called the occasion of robe-giving (cīvaradānasamaya). The time when a monk is making a robe and performing any necessary task for the robe is called the occasion of robe-making (cīvarakārasamaya). The time when a monk desires to travel, is traveling, or has traveled a distance of half a league (yojana) is called the occasion of a journey (addhānagamanasamaya). The same logic applies to the occasion of boarding a boat. The time when four monks wandering for alms in a resort village do not get enough food is called a great occasion (mahāsamaya). The time when any ascetic invites with a meal is called the occasion of an ascetic's meal (samaṇabhattasamaya). On these occasions, it is allowable to eat a group meal.

In Rājagaha, it was laid down concerning Devadatta regarding the matter of eating by requesting. The phrase "except on an occasion" is a sevenfold supplementary regulation in this training rule. This training rule is a common regulation, not involving a command, and is a Pācittiya in a triad. For one who perceives a non-group meal as a group meal or is in doubt, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). There is no offense for: one who perceives it as a non-group meal; two or three monks who accept together; many monks who wander for alms and eat together; in the case of permanent meals (niccabhatta), etc.; in the case of all congee, snacks, and large or small fruits, excluding the five kinds of food; and for those who are insane, etc. The three factors here are: being a group meal, the absence of an occasion, and the act of swallowing. The origin, etc., are the same as the Eḷakaloma training rule.

## The Commentary on the Gaṇabhojana Training Rule is finished.

## 3. Commentary on the Paramparabhojana Training Rule

In the third training rule, Paramparabhojana, "Paramparabhojana" (successive meal) means eating the meal of a subsequent donor out of order or without making an assignment (vikappanā), instead of eating the meal of the donor who first invited with the five kinds of food, following the method mentioned in the Gaṇabhojana training rule. Therefore, if a monk, without assigning the first invitation to any one of the five classes of co-religionists (sahadhammika), saying either in their presence, "I give my expectation of a meal to you," or "I assign it to you," or in their absence, "I give it to such-and-named person," or "I assign it," swallows even a single morsel from the meal obtained from a family that invited him later, he commits a Pācittiya offense. The occasions (samaya) are the same as the method already mentioned.
218:
In Vesālī, on account of many monks, the regulation was laid down regarding the matter of eating an invited meal (nimantitabhojana) at a house other than the one first invited. The phrase "except on occasion" (aññatra samayā) constitutes the three supplementary regulations (anupaññatti) in this training rule. However, in the Parivāra, including the act of assignment (vikappanā), it is stated by the Elders of the Council as "four supplementary regulations." This training rule is an unshared regulation (asādhāraṇapaññatti) [not shared with bhikkhunīs], it is not involving a command (anāṇattika), and it belongs to the Pācittiya triad (tikapācittiya). For one who perceives a meal that is not a subsequent meal (paramparabhojana) as a subsequent meal, or is doubtful, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).

There is no offense for one who perceives it as not being a subsequent meal; or for a monk who eats during the allowed occasion (samaya); or who eats after making an assignment (vikappanā); or who eats meals mixed as one; or who eats two or three invitations combined as one; or who eats according to the order of invitations; or who, being invited by an entire village or a group (pūga), eats at any one of those houses; or who, while being invited, says "I will take alms"; or in the case of constant meals (niccabhatta) and so forth; or in the case of all gruels, snacks, and large or small fruits, excluding the five types of meals; or for one who is insane and so forth. The three factors here are: being a subsequent meal, the absence of an occasion, and the act of swallowing. The origin (samuṭṭhāna) and so forth are the same as the first Kathina training rule; however, this is a rule of action and inaction (kiriyākiriyā).

## The Commentary on the Training Rule concerning Subsequent Meals (Paramparabhojana Sikkhāpada) is finished.

## 4. Commentary on the Kāṇamātā Training Rule

In the fourth training rule, "with cakes" (pūvehi) refers to any kind of snacks such as atirasaka, modaka, sakkhalikā, etc., prepared for the purpose of a gift. "With parched grain" (manthehi) refers to any kind of provisions such as sattu, sesame, rice, etc., prepared for the purpose of a journey. "Two or three bowlfuls" means two or three bowlfuls not exceeding the lower rim of the bowl's edge. "Beyond that" means if he takes even a third bowlful heaped up (thūpīkata); there is a Pācittiya offense according to the number of cakes situated above the lower rim of the bowl's edge.

In the phrase "having accepted two or three bowlfuls," if a monk has accepted two bowlfuls, upon seeing another monk outside the house, he should say, "I have accepted two bowlfuls here, venerable sir, please accept one bowlful." That second monk, upon seeing another monk, should say, "The monk who came first has accepted two bowlfuls, I have accepted one; do not you accept any." If a monk accepts one bowlful first, the same method applies when informing others in succession. If a monk himself has accepted three bowlfuls, upon seeing another monk, he should say, "Do not accept anything here"; if he does not say so, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). For the monk who accepts even after hearing that speech, there is also an offense of wrong-doing. Having taken them out from there, together with the monks...
219:
"Should be shared" (saṃvibhajitabbaṃ) means going from the place where they were received to the nearest dining hall, or the monastery, or the place where one regularly goes, and after setting aside one bowlful for oneself, the remainder should be given to the Saṅgha of monks. However, it is not permissible to give out of favoritism (yathāmittaṃ). The monk who has accepted only one bowlful need not give anything if he does not wish to; he may do as he pleases.

In Sāvatthī, on account of many monks, the regulation was laid down regarding the matter of accepting without knowing the limit. This training rule is a shared regulation (sādhāraṇapaññatti), it is not involving a command (anāṇattika), and it is a Pācittiya triad (tikapācittiya). For one who perceives cakes that are less than two or three bowlfuls as being more, or is doubtful, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). There is no offense for one who perceives it as less; or for one who accepts cakes not prepared as a gift or as provisions for a journey; or for one who accepts the leftovers of what was prepared for that purpose; or when the journey has been cancelled; or for one who accepts when relatives or those who have given an invitation are offering; or for one who takes them with his own property; or for the insane and so forth. The five factors here are: being cakes or parched grain of the described characteristics, not being leftovers, the journey not being cancelled, being non-relatives and so forth, and accepting more than two or three bowlfuls. The origin (samuṭṭhāna) and so forth are the same as the Sañcaritta training rule.

## The Commentary on the Kāṇamātā Training Rule is finished.

## 5. Commentary on the First Pavāraṇā Training Rule

In the fifth, "one who has eaten" (bhuttāvī) means a person who has eaten. A monk who has swallowed even as much as a mustard seed from the five types of meals is called "one who has eaten." "One who has refused" (pavārito) means one who has made a refusal by virtue of the five factors stated in the Pāḷi: "Eating is evident, the food is evident, standing within arm's length he offers, refusal is evident." Among those factors, by the factor "eating is evident," one whose meal is in progress (vippakatabhojana) is called "pavārita." For one whose meal is in progress, some has been eaten and some has not; in reference to what has been eaten, he also comes under the designation "one who has eaten" (bhuttāvī). Therefore, we do not see any distinct meaning achieved by the word "bhuttāvī" separately; however, it should be understood that this was stated as an accompaniment to the word "pavārito" and for linguistic smoothness, like the words "two nights, three nights" (diratta-tiratta) and so forth in the Pāḷi.

Among the factors of Pavāraṇā, "eating is evident" means the meal in progress is seen, and the meaning is that this person is currently eating that food. "The food is evident" means food suitable for refusal is seen, meaning it is any one of the five types of meals, such as alms-food, that is worthy of being refused.
220:
Food suitable for causing pavāraṇā is seen; it means it is one of the five types of food, such as odana (cooked rice), which ought to be refused. "Standing within a hatthapāsa" means the donor, holding food suitable for causing pavāraṇā, stands at a distance of two and a half cubits. "Brings forward" means that the donor personally brings that food toward the monk. "The refusal is evident" means the refusal is seen; it means the monk refuses that food brought forward either by body or by speech. Thus, by way of these five factors, one becomes a pavārita (one who has refused further food).

In these five factors, the decision is as follows: Among the terms beginning with "asana" (eating), it should be understood that the food being eaten and the food brought forward by one standing within a hatthapāsa which is refused must be one of the five types of food: cooked rice (odana), barley bread (kummāsa), parched meal (sattu), fish (maccha), or meat (maṃsa).

Among those five types of food, odana (cooked rice) refers to taking the grains of the seven types of grain—sāli rice, vīhi rice, barley, wheat, millet, varaka grass, and kudrūsaka grain—and cooking them with the intention of "we shall cook a meal" or "we shall cook gruel." Whether hot or cold, if at the time of eating, distinct marks or boundaries (finger or spoon marks) are evident at the place where it is taken, it is called odana and it causes pavāraṇā.

Milk-rice or sour gruel that has just been removed from the stove and is so hot that it can only be tilted and sipped, if no distinct boundary is evident even at the place where it is taken by hand, it does not cause pavāraṇā.

If, however, it becomes thick after the steam has dissipated and can show a boundary, it causes pavāraṇā again; the previous thin state does not protect from pavāraṇā. Even if many leaves, fruits, or sprouts are added and only a handful of rice is included, if a distinct boundary is evident at the time of eating, it causes pavāraṇā.

In an invitation without gruel, if they intend to offer gruel and pour water, fermented rice-water, or milk into the rice and offer it saying "Please accept the gruel," even if it is thin, it still causes pavāraṇā.

If, however, it is cooked by adding it to boiling water, etc., it falls under the category of actual gruel (yāgu) and does not cause pavāraṇā.

Even in gruel, if a piece of fish, meat, or tendon the size of a mustard seed is added, it causes pavāraṇā.

Except for the seven grains mentioned and their equivalents, rice made from other things like bamboo seeds, tubers, roots, or fruits does not cause pavāraṇā.

Kummāsa refers to food made from barley. Kummāsa made from other things like green gram does not cause pavāraṇā.

Sattu refers to food made by roasting the seven types of grain. At the very least, of the paddy roasted until well-cooked...
221:
Powder made by pounding paddy or broken rice also falls under the category of sattu (parched meal). However, broken rice roasted just enough or dried in the sun, any whole rice, popped rice, or meals and sattu made from popped rice do not cause pavāraṇā. The decision regarding fish and meat is as follows: If two pieces of fish or meat, each the size of a grain of rice in gruel, are offered in a single vessel or different vessels to a monk who is drinking gruel, and if he refuses any other food suitable for causing pavāraṇā without having eaten those pieces of fish or meat, pavāraṇā is not incurred. If he has eaten one of them and while the other is in his hand or bowl, he refuses another food, pavāraṇā is incurred. If both have been eaten and not even a mustard-seed-sized portion remains in the mouth, even if he refuses another food, pavāraṇā is not incurred.

If one refuses another allowable or unallowable food while eating unallowable meat, or unallowable food resulting from corrupting families (kuladūsana), medical practice, announcing superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma), or accepting gold and silver, pavāraṇā is not incurred. Thus, a monk who refuses food being eaten or food brought forward by one standing within a hatthapāsa causes pavāraṇā. Having understood that point, this decision should be known to understand how pavāraṇā is incurred now.

In the phrase "asanaṃ bhojanaṃ" (eating food), if a monk who has already swallowed even a single morsel refuses another food with the aforementioned characteristics while still having food in his bowl, mouth, or hand and still having the desire to eat that food, pavāraṇā is incurred. If, however, he has no desire and does not wish to swallow what remains in the bowl, etc., or wishes to give it to another, or wishes to go and eat it elsewhere, even if he refuses, pavāraṇā is not incurred.

In the phrase "hatthapāse ဌိတော" (standing within a hatthapāsa), if the monk is sitting, it starts from the back edge of the buttocks; if standing, from the edge of the heels; if lying down, from the edge of the side on which he lies. Excluding the outstretched hand of the donor who is sitting, standing, or lying down, the distance of two and a half cubits measured from the nearest part of the donor's body is to be known as the hatthapāsa. Pavāraṇā occurs only for a monk who refuses food brought forward while standing within that hatthapāsa, not beyond it. "Brings forward" means one standing within the hatthapāsa moves it close for acceptance. If, however, a monk sitting nearby says "Please take the meal" without bringing forward the bowl held in his hand or on a bowl-stand, there is no pavāraṇā for the one who refuses it. Even if a basket of rice is brought and placed on the ground in front of him and this is said, the same rule applies. But if it is said "Please take it" after lifting it slightly or tilting it, pavāraṇā is incurred for the monk who refuses that meal.
222:
It is pavāraṇā. For one who is serving food while holding a rice basket, if another person says, 'I will hold it,' and merely holds it while the server continues to carry the basket, that rice basket is considered as being brought forward by the server himself. Therefore, for a monk who refuses while [the server] is picking [food] with the intention to give, it is pavāraṇā. However, if the server merely touches it and the other person carries the rice basket, even if [the monk] refuses while [the server] is picking [food] with the intention to give, it is not pavāraṇā. In the case of food taken out with a spoon, it is pavāraṇā. Even in a load carried equally by two people, the one who refuses is indeed committing pavāraṇā. While giving to a monk who is immediately adjacent, if another monk closes his bowl, it is called refusing food brought forward for another monk. Therefore, it is not pavāraṇā. In this context, 'refusal' does not apply to food brought forward only by word. However, for a monk who refuses food brought forward physically, either by bodily gesture such as moving a finger or by verbal gesture such as saying 'Enough, do not give,' it is pavāraṇā.

A person brings forward liquid along with meat and says, 'Please accept the liquid.' For a monk who refuses after hearing those words, it is not pavāraṇā. However, if he says 'meat broth' and the monk refuses, it is pavāraṇā. It is also pavāraṇā when he says, 'Please accept this.' Even if the meat is separated and he says 'meat broth,' if there is still a piece of meat as small as a mustard seed, it is pavāraṇā for the one who refuses. If there is none, it is allowable to refuse. People cook fish and meat mixed with sprouts, jackfruit, etc. If they take that curry and say, 'Please accept the sprout broth' or 'Please accept the jackfruit curry,' it is not pavāraṇā even if refused. Why? Because it is spoken by the name of a curry that does not qualify for pavāraṇā. However, if they say 'fish and meat curry' or 'Please accept this,' it is pavāraṇā. This is the summary here; the detailed explanation is given in the Samantapāsādikā. Among postures such as walking, one should eat only without breaking the posture in which pavāraṇā occurred.

'Anatititta' means that which is not leftover, not in excess. That anatititta is either food not made [allowable] by the seven Vinaya procedures such as akappiyakata, or food that is not in excess for a sick person. Therefore, in the Padabhājana, 'akappiyakata' and so on are taught. In that context, if there are fruits, tubers, roots, etc., that have not been made allowable by the five methods of making allowable for monks (samaṇakappiya), or if there is unallowable meat or unallowable food, this is called akappiya (unallowable). Making such unallowable things into leftovers by saying 'All this is enough' is to be understood as akappiyakata. 'Appaṭiggahitakata' means making leftovers of food that has not yet been formally received by a monk, according to the previous method. 'Anuccāritakata' means when a monk who has come to make food allowable has not even slightly...
223:
...not lifted or not moved towards [the monk]. 'Hatthapāse kataṃ' means it is done by a Vinayadhara standing outside the hand-reach (hatthapāsa) of the person who has come to make it allowable. 'Abhuttāvinā kataṃ' means it is done by a Vinayadhara who makes the leftover, without having yet eaten food sufficient for pavāraṇā. The factor 'done by one who has eaten and is pavārita after rising from the seat' is quite clear. It is a case where one has not verbally said, 'All this is enough.' Thus, both the leftovers not made allowable by these seven Vinaya methods and those that are not leftovers of a sick person are called anatititta (not made allowable as leftovers). Atititta (leftover) should be understood by the opposite method of anatititta.

A slight distinction here: according to 'bhuttāvinā kataṃ hoti,' even if one has eaten just one grain of rice or a shred of meat from the bowl of a monk sitting nearby, it is considered 'done by one who has eaten.' A Vinayadhara who has thus eaten and is pavārita in the early morning can still make food brought by another monk allowable even near noon. However, if other food is poured in while eating that which has been made allowable, that Vinayadhara cannot make it allowable again. This is because it is stated that only food not yet made allowable should be made allowable, and only by one who has not yet [eaten to the point of pavāraṇā]. Therefore, when it is being done in that vessel, it is already considered done along with the first act, so it is not proper to do it again in that vessel. However, in another vessel, either he himself or another person can make it allowable. Food made allowable in this way can be eaten even after mixing it with the first food. Not only for him, but excluding the Vinayadhara who made it allowable, other monks who are pavārita can also eat it. To avoid mixing with food not yet made allowable, one should eat only after cleansing the mouth and hands. 'Gilānātititta' (leftovers for the sick) is not merely the scraps of a sick person; rather, anything brought for a sick person with the thought, 'He will eat it today, tomorrow, or whenever he wishes,' is to be understood as gilānātititta. 'Khādanīya' (hard food) or 'bhojanīya' (soft food) refers to any yāvakālika (temporary) substance. For a monk who is pavārita, if he receives any anatititta food for the purpose of swallowing, there is a dukkaṭa offense in receiving it, and a pācittiya offense for every swallow.

This was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning many monks in another case of eating. 'Anatititta' is a supplementary regulation (anupaññatti) here. It is an uncommon regulation (asādhāraṇapaññatti), not by command (anāṇattika), and involves a triad of pācittiya (tikapācittiya). There is a dukkaṭa offense for a monk who receives yāmakālika etc. for the sake of nutriment, and for one who swallows without food [substance]. Likewise, for one who perceives anatititta in what is atititta...
224:
For one who is in doubt; for one who, although perceiving it as leftover, takes it with the intention, "I will have it made into leftovers and then eat"; for one who takes it for the sake of another; for one who consumes non-material items such as yāmakālika (period-limited) according to the permitted use; and for the insane and so forth, there is no offense. In this training rule, there are three factors: (1) being one who has refused further food (pavārita), (2) the material food not being leftover (anatiritta), (3) swallowing during the [proper] mealtime. The origins and so forth are the same as the first Kathina training rule; however, this training rule is kiriyākiriya (action and non-action).

## The Commentary on the First Pavāraṇā Training Rule is Finished.

## 6. Dutiya Pavāraṇā Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā

In the sixth training rule, "abhihaṭṭhuṃ pavāreyya" means to bring [food] forward and invite by saying, "Here, monk, chew or eat." "Jānanti" means knowing that the monk has refused further food (pavārita), either by hearing or seeing. "Āsādanāpekkho" means one who is concerned with criticizing or causing embarrassment (manku). In the phrase "bhuttasmiṃ pācittiyaṃ," there is first an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa) due to the act of bringing [the food] forward. If that monk takes that food, there is again an offense of wrongdoing for the one who brought it. While that pavārita monk is eating, there is an offense of wrongdoing for the bringer for every swallow, and at the conclusion of the meal, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).

This was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning an unknown monk, due to the cause of inviting by bringing food that was not leftover. It is an uncommon regulation (asādhāraṇa-paññatti) and is anāṇattika (not by command). If one invites a pavārita monk, perceiving him as pavārita, there is an offense of expiation. For one who is in doubt; for one who brings yāmakālika and so forth for the sake of nutriment; for the receiving and swallowing of those items; for one who perceives a non-pavārita monk as pavārita; and for one who is in doubt, there is an offense of wrongdoing. For one who perceives a monk as non-pavārita; for one who gives after having made it leftover; for one who gives saying, "Eat after having it made [leftover]"; for one who gives with the instruction, "Take this for the sake of another"; for one who gives yāmakālika and so forth saying, "Consume it if there is a reason"; and for the insane and so forth, there is no offense. In this training rule, there are five factors: (1) being one who has refused further food (pavārita), (2) perceiving him as pavārita, (3) having the intention to annoy/criticize, (4) inviting by bringing food that is not leftover, (5) reaching the conclusion of the meal. The origins and so forth are similar to taking what is not given (adinnādāna); however, this training rule is dukkhavedanā (painful feeling).

## The Commentary on the Second Pavāraṇā Training Rule is Finished.
225:
## 7. Vikālabhojana Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā

In the seventh training rule, "vikāla" (the wrong time) means the period from the passing of noon until the rising of the dawn. Therefore, if any monk, during that interval, receives any forest root or fruit, whether raw or ripe, or any food or meal categorized as material food (āmisa), for the purpose of swallowing, there is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa) in receiving it, and an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for every swallow.

This was laid down in Rājagaha concerning the group of seventeen monks (sattarasavaggiya), due to the cause of eating at the wrong time. It is a common regulation (sādhāraṇa-paññatti), anāṇattika, and a tika-pācittiya (triad of expiation). For the receiving and swallowing of yāmakālika and so forth for the sake of nutriment; for one who perceives the right time as the wrong time; and for one who is in doubt, there is an offense of wrongdoing. For one who perceives the right time as the right time; for one who consumes yāmakālika and so forth because there is a reason; and for the insane and so forth, there is no offense. By the method of permission: "Monks, I allow the remastication (ruminating) of one who ruminates; but, monks, it should not be swallowed after having been taken out of the mouth-door," there is also no offense for a monk who ruminates. The three factors in this training rule are: (1) it being the wrong time, (2) it being morning-limited food (yāvakālika), (3) the act of swallowing. The origins and so forth are similar to the sheep's wool (eḷakaloma) training rule.

## The Commentary on the Vikālabhojana Training Rule is Finished.

## 8. Sannidhikāraka Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā

In the eighth training rule, "sannidhikāraka"—the words kāra, karaṇa, and kiriyā are the same in meaning. Sannidhikāra means the act of storing up; sannidhikāraka is the same as sannidhikāra. This is the name for food that has been received and kept past one night. Therefore, for a monk who takes any yāvakālika or yāmakālika thus stored, with the intention, "I will swallow it," there is an offense of wrongdoing in receiving it, and an offense of expiation for every swallow.

Even if a bowl is washed unclearly, such that a mark is visible when rubbed with a finger; or if oil remains in the crevices of a bowl that has joints, and that oil flows out when dried in the sun, or becomes visible when hot gruel is placed in it—for a monk who eats from such a bowl on the following day, there is an offense of expiation. However, if a monk, without expectation [of eating it himself], gives food to novices, and then receives and consumes what was stored by those novices, that food...
226:
It is allowable. (If a monk, without the intention of eating it later, gives food to novices, and then receives it back from where the novices stored it and eats it,) it is allowable. Indeed, for a monk who eats allowable food on the next day which he himself accepted and did not give away, there is an offense of Pācittiya. Among unallowable meats, if he eats human flesh, there is an offense of Pācittiya along with Thullaccaya. For other remaining meats, there is an offense of Pācittiya along with Dukkaṭa. For a monk who swallows stored Yāmakālika when there is a reason, there is an offense of Pācittiya; if he swallows it for the sake of nutriment, there is an offense of Pācittiya along with Dukkaṭa. If a monk who has already refused a further meal (pavārita) swallows [Yāmakālika] that has not been made leftover (anatirittakata), another Pācittiya offense is added in all cases of Vikappa. If he swallows it at the wrong time (vikāla), there is no offense in all cases of Vikappa due to the reason of it being anatiritta. If there is a reason, there is no offense for Yāmakālika etc. due to the reason of wrong time. For the remaining Yāvakālika items, however, the Pācittiya offense is always added due to the reason of wrong time. Stored food of a monk is allowable for a nun, and stored food of a nun is allowable for a monk. It is said to be allowable because it is permitted in the Bhikkhunī Khandhaka.

It was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning Venerable Belaṭṭhasīsa regarding the matter of eating food that has been stored (sannidhikāraka). This training rule is a common regulation (sādhāraṇa-paññatti), it is anāṇattika (not involving command), and it is a Tika-Pācittiya (involving three cases). There is an offense of Dukkaṭa in accepting and swallowing Sattāhakālika and Yāvajīvika for the sake of nutriment.
