Just as these are not allowable for the sake of nutriment, so too are Yāmakālika etc. that are mixed with Yāvakālika etc. not allowable. For it was said: "Monks, Yāmakālika mixed with Yāvakālika, if accepted on that day, is allowable in the morning, but not allowable at the wrong time (afternoon)," and so forth. Therefore, if one obtains various Kālikas mixed with one another, if the tastes are not blended, or if it is well-washed so that the mixture with the other taste is not apparent, it is allowable to consume it according to its own proper time.

However, if the tastes are blended, or if it is not cleanly washed, it is not allowable. Indeed, Yāvakālika brings all three types, such as Yāmakālika, which are blended in taste with it, into its own nature. Yāmakālika brings both Sattāhakālika and Yāvajīvika into its own nature. Sattāhakālika brings only Yāvajīvika into its own nature. Therefore, Yāvajīvika accepted on that day or on a previous day, along with Sattāhakālika accepted on that day, is allowable for seven days. Along with Sattāhakālika accepted two days ago, it is allowable for six days. Along with Sattāhakālika accepted three days ago, it is allowable for five days... along with Sattāhakālika accepted seven days ago, it should be known that it is allowable only on that day. For that very reason, it was said, "Yāvajīvika accepted is allowable for seven days," without saying "Yāvajīvika accepted on that day along with Sattāhakālika, O monks." In these cases of Yāvakālika, Yāmakālika, and Sattāhakālika, the offenses should be known by way of the training rules on eating at the wrong time (Vikālabhojana), storing food (Sannidhi), and medicines (Bhesajja), due to exceeding the morning time, the night watches, and the seven days. Among these four types of Kālika—
227:
Among the four types of Kālika, only these two—Yāvakālika and Yāmakālika—can be Antovuṭṭha (items kept indoors overnight) and Sannidhikāraka (stored items). As for Sattāhakālika and Yāvajīvika, it is allowable to keep them even in an Akappiyakuṭi (unallowable hut), and it does not produce the fault of Sannidhi. However, even if the other two, Sattāhakālika and Yāvajīvika, are accepted on that very day, it is not suitable to consume them if they are kept together with Yāvakālika or Yāmakālika that have become Antovuṭṭha in an Akappiyakuṭi. This is called Mukhasannidhi. In the Mahāpaccarī Commentary, however, it is said to be Antovuṭṭha. In this difference of opinion, only the name is different; the offense is only Dukkaṭa in either case.

In this context, an Akappiyakuṭi is a house (building) made for living, whether it belongs to the Saṅgha or to an individual ordained person. Yāvakālika and Yāmakālika belonging to the Saṅgha or to an individual ordained person, which are stored in a place in that Akappiyakuṭi sufficient for sleeping together, are called Antovuṭṭha. Yāvakālika cooked in that building is called Antopakka. Yāvakālika cooked by oneself in any other place is called Sāmaṃpakka. All these—Antovuṭṭha, Antopakka, and Sāmaṃpakka—are items that should not be swallowed.

Kālika mixed with such Antovuṭṭha etc. is also of the same nature as those Antovuṭṭha etc. For a monk who swallows any of these, there is an offense of Dukkaṭa. Therefore, to be free from Antovuṭṭha and Antopakka, the Blessed One permitted four types of Kappiyabhūmi (allowable grounds/huts). The decision regarding these Kappiyabhūmi has been stated in the Samantapāsādikā Commentary. In a monastery where these Kappiyakuṭis do not exist, it is allowable to consume items by making them the property of a layperson or a novice. It is also allowable to re-cook (reheat) items that were cooked by oneself. For one who perceives an item that is not Sannidhikāraka as being Sannidhikāraka, or for one who is in doubt, there is an offense of Dukkaṭa (if consumed).

There is no offense for: one who perceives it as not being Sannidhikāraka; one who consumes the three Kālikas such as Yāvakālika by storing them without exceeding their respective time limits; one who consumes Yāvajīvika at any time when there is a reason; and for those who are insane, etc. In this training rule, there are three factors: (1) being an item of food (āmisa) that is Yāvakālika or Yāmakālika, (2) being stored up (sannidhi), (3) the swallowing of that food. The originations (samuṭṭhāna) etc. are the same as the Eḷakaloma training rule.

## The Explanation of the Sannidhikāraka Training Rule is Finished.

## 9. Paṇītabhojana Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā

In the ninth training rule, the Paṇītabhojana Sikkhāpada, 'paṇītabhojanāni' refers to foods made from the seven types of grain mixed with superior nutriment. Just as a chariot joined with thoroughbred horses is called a 'thoroughbred chariot,' so in this training rule, foods mixed with superior nutriment are called 'superior foods' (paṇītabhojana). Those foods mixed with superior ingredients are called 'paṇītabhojana.' To show the different varieties of those superior nutriments, the Blessed One said, "seyyathidaṃ sappi navanီtaṃ" (namely: ghee, butter), and so forth. In that Pali text, ghee and so forth...
228:
In the Bhesajja Sikkhāpada (in the commentary on the Bhesajja Sikkhāpada in the Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī), it should be understood according to the characteristics already mentioned. Among fish and so forth, any fish that has the characteristic described as 'aquatic creature' is indeed a fish. In this training rule, the meat, milk, and curd of animals whose meat is allowable are intended. Such 'fine foods' (paṇītabhojana) are those foods called 'fine foods' because they are mixed with ghee and so forth. One who can live comfortably even without those fine foods is called 'not ill' (agilāna).

Regarding the phrase 'requesting for oneself'—if a monk who is not ill requests pure ghee and so forth, which is not mixed with other food, for the sake of medicine, it should be decided by the Mahānāma Sikkhāpada. If he requests the four items—fish, meat, milk, and curd—it should be decided by the Sūpodanavinnatti Sikkhāpada. If he requests foods mixed with ghee and so forth, it should be decided by this training rule.

Herein is the decision: For a monk who requests thus—'Give rice with ghee,' 'Give by pouring ghee,' 'Give by mixing with ghee,' 'Give together with ghee,' or 'Give both ghee and rice'—there is a dukkaṭa for the request, a dukkaṭa for the reception, and a pācittiya offense for every swallow. However, if he says 'Give ghee-rice (sappibhatta),' since there is no such thing as 'ghee-rice' distinct like 'sāli-rice,' there is only a dukkaṭa offense according to the Sūpodanavinnatti Sikkhāpada.

If, upon saying 'Give rice with ghee,' the donor gives rice and then says, 'Make this fresh butter or milk into ghee and eat it,' or gives an allowable object saying, 'Exchange this for ghee and eat it,' an offense occurs according to the nature of the object (pācittiya). If he says 'Give rice with cow-ghee,' and the donor gives cow-ghee, or if that is unavailable, gives fresh butter etc. as in the previous method, or gives a cow saying 'Make ghee from this cow and eat it,' it is also according to the nature of the object.

If he requests 'Give with cow-ghee' but the donor gives goat-ghee etc., it is a mismatch (visanketa). In such a case, since one thing was requested and another was given, there is no offense. This same method applies to requests such as 'Give with goat-ghee.' If he says 'Give with allowable ghee' but the donor gives unallowable ghee, it is also a mismatch. If he says 'Give with unallowable ghee' and the donor gives unallowable ghee, there is a dukkaṭa offense both in receiving and in consuming. In this way, the decision should be understood in all cases.

If he requests all nine types, such as ghee and so forth, either in one place or in various places, and mixes the obtained food together, and then swallows even a single drop of that mixed-flavor food even as much as the tip of a blade of kusa-grass, nine pācittiya offenses are incurred.

This training rule was laid down because of the reason of requesting fine foods. For a monk who is actually ill but requests and eats thinking he is not ill, or having doubt, a dukkaṭa offense is incurred. There is no offense if he eats what was requested while he was ill but he has since recovered (the illness is gone), or if he eats the leftovers of an ill monk, or if he requests and eats from relatives or those who have offered an invitation (pavāraṇā), or if he eats what was requested for the sake of another, or if he eats what was obtained with his own property, or if he is insane, etc.
229:
Regarding the phrase "Give rice mixed with ghee," if it is given with allowable ghee, only a dukkaṭa offense is incurred for both receiving and consuming. By this method, the decision should be understood for all terms such as fresh butter (navanīta) and so forth. If one requests food mixed with ghee etc., either in one place or in various places, and makes the obtained food into a single mixture of flavors, and if one swallows even a single drop of that food even as much as the tip of a blade of kusa-grass, nine pācittiya offenses are incurred.

This was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning the group of six monks, on the matter of requesting fine foods. The term "agilāno" (not ill) is a supplementary regulation (anupaññatti) here. This training rule is an uncommon regulation (asādhāraṇapaññatti), not by command (anāṇattika), and is a triad of pācittiya (tikapācittiya). For a monk who is ill but perceives himself as not ill, or for one who is in doubt, there is a dukkaṭa offense. There is no offense for: one who perceives himself as ill; one who requested while ill but eats when not ill (after recovery); the leftovers of an ill monk; from the place of relatives or those who have offered an invitation; food requested for the sake of another; food obtained with one's own wealth; and for those who are insane, etc. The four factors here are: being fine food, being not ill, receiving after making a request, and swallowing. It has the following technical qualities: addhāna-samuṭṭhāna, kiriyā, no-saññā-vimokkha, acittaka, paṇṇatti-vajja, bodily action, vocal action, three types of consciousness, and three types of feeling.

## The Explanation of the Paṇītabhojana Sikkhāpada is Finished.

## 10. Dantapona Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā

In the tenth training rule, "adinnaṃ" (not given) refers to nutriment that is not given by any of the three means—by body, by something connected to the body, or by releasing—to a monk who is receiving it while standing within arm's reach (hatthapāsa) by means of his body or something connected to his body. This is the name for what is not formally offered (appaṭiggahitaka). It is not allowable for a monk to swallow even his own property if it has not been formally offered. What has been formally offered is allowable to eat, even if it is the property of one with whom he is intimate (vissāsika); its characteristics should be understood as the opposite of what was said for "not given."

If anyone who is not ordained, even an animal, standing within arm's reach, gives to a monk or a nun by any of the means such as the body, etc., and if it is received by the monk with any part of his body, or with something connected to it, or with a movable object even a bed, or with something capable of carrying it even a leaf not currently growing on a tree, or even by just touching it with a needle, it is indeed formally received (paṭiggahita). Here, there is no such thing as "connected to the connected" (paṭibaddhappatibaddha). If nutriment given with a nose-cleaner is received with the nose, or if an unhealthy monk receives it with his mouth, it is all allowable; for in this matter of receiving, the mere intention (ābhoga) is the measure. If there was a prior intention to receive, even what is placed in the bowl of a monk who later falls asleep is considered formally received if he is within arm's reach. Even what falls into the hand of one who is sitting with the thought "I will receive with the bowl" is certainly allowable.
230:
Dust falling from a vessel brought forward is also allowable. In that act of formal acceptance, the forearm's length (hatthapāsa) of those standing, sitting, or lying down should be understood exactly as stated in the Pavāraṇā training rule.

If, between the donor and the recipient, one is in the air and the other is on the ground, the forearm's length should be determined from the near edge of the limb that is closest—either from the head of the one on the ground or from the outstretched hand of the one in the air intended for giving or receiving. If one is in a pit and the other is on the bank, or if one is in a tree and the other is on the ground, the forearm's length should be determined in the same manner as previously stated.

While stationed within that forearm's length, if two or three novices roll a load that an average man could lift and place it onto the monk's hand which is resting on the ground, or if they lift it and place it even on a portion of the monk's outstretched hand, that object is considered formally accepted.

However, dust that falls into the bowl of a monk walking for alms is considered not yet formally accepted; therefore, alms-food should be taken only after formal acceptance. For a monk who takes it without formal acceptance, there is an offense of wrongdoing (Vinaya-dukkaṭa); however, if he eats it after having it formally accepted again, there is no offense. If, despite being told "Please give after formal acceptance," the donors continue to offer the alms-food either because they did not hear or because they disregarded the words, the monk is free from the Vinaya-dukkaṭa, but he must formally accept other alms-food again.

If a strong wind blows dust from various directions such that it is impossible to receive the alms-food formally, it is allowable to take it by resolving with a pure mind, "I shall give this to an unordained person." After giving that food to an unordained person, it is allowable to eat it if that person gives it back or through one's trust (vissāsa) in that person. 

Regarding tears, saliva, snot, and the like, if they move from their place, such as the eye-socket, and fall onto the hand or into the bowl, they must be formally accepted; however, those that remain attached to the body are already considered accepted. If the falling tears or such are interrupted (the flow is broken), they must not be taken in between; this is called 'wrongly taken' (uggahitaka), and even if formally accepted later, it is not allowable.

When one goes after taking medicine, or roots and fruits for one's mother and others, or after lifting a fruiting branch for the sake of shade, it is allowable to eat what one desires from those objects after formally accepting them again. If a monk takes hold of and shakes a branch or a vine that is still producing fruit on that tree, the fruit obtained from that is not allowable for him, and he incurs an offense of wrongdoing due to improper conduct (durupaciṇṇa-dukkaṭa); however, it is allowable for another monk. Leaning against or holding onto a fruiting tree is allowable. If other sprouts and such emerge from an object that has already been formally accepted and kept, those sprouts are also considered already accepted.

As long as one has not yet become indifferent (nirapekkha) toward the nutriment released from the hand, or even if one is indifferent, as long as it is from the hand...
231:
...it is not released, the formal acceptance (paṭiggahana) is not relinquished until then. This is the summary here; the detailed explanation is stated in the Samantapāsādikā Commentary.

'Mouth-door' (mukhadvāra) refers to the throat (gullet). Whether it is entered through the mouth or the nose, since it must be swallowed through the throat, all of it is considered as having been introduced into the mouth-door. 'Nutriment' (āhāra) refers to any of the four types: yāvakālika, yāmakālika, sattāhakālika, or yāvajīvika. All these are called 'nutriment' because they are to be swallowed. Among these four, the seven kinds of grain and items similar to grain; the nine kinds of large fruits known as palmyra, coconut, jackfruit, breadfruit, gourd, pumpkin, bottle gourd, and various types of cucumbers and melons; and other roots, leaves, flowers, and fruits used for food—all these are called yāvakālika (temporary) because they are to be consumed only until the noon hour.

These eight kinds of juices—mango juice, rose-apple juice, wild plantain juice, cultivated banana juice, honey-tree (madhuka) juice, grape juice, water-lily root juice, and phaggula (fārusaka) juice—and all juices of small fruits similar to them, such as rattan fruit, tamarind, citron, wood-apple, kapiṭṭha, and karamanda, are called yāmakālika (watch-bound) because they may be stored and consumed until the last watch of the night, provided they are prepared by unordained persons by crushing them with cold water or by cooking them in the sun. The same rule applies to other permitted juices of fruits, leaves, and flowers. The five kinds of medicine, such as ghee and so on, are called sattāhakālika (seven-day-bound) because they may be stored and consumed for seven days.

Excluding these three types (yāvakālika, etc.) and water which is exempt from time (kālavimutta), other roots, large and small fruits, and so on, which serve neither as snacks (khādanīya) nor as main meals (bhojanīya), are called yāvajīvika (life-long) because they may be stored for life and consumed when there is a cause (such as illness).

'Should take' (āhareyya) means should introduce (swallow). The phrase 'except for water and tooth-wood' was spoken to dispel the doubts of monks who, out of apprehension, might perceive water as nutriment or think 'this tooth-wood has been introduced into the mouth-door.' It is allowable to drink water as one pleases and to use the tooth-wood (dantapona) as a utility. However, excluding these two, if one takes other things for the purpose of swallowing, one incurs a dukkaṭa offense in the act of taking, and a pācittiya offense for every swallow. Even if the juice of the tooth-wood enters inside unknowingly, it is still a pācittiya offense.

This training rule was laid down in Vesālī concerning an unnamed monk regarding the matter of introducing unoffered nutriment into the mouth. The phrase 'except for water and tooth-wood' is a supplementary regulation (anupaññatti) in this context.
232:
This training rule is a common regulation (sādhāraṇapaññatti); it is without command (anāṇattika) and is a threefold Pācittiya (tikapācittiya). For one who perceives an item that has been formally offered as not yet offered, or for one who is in doubt, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). There is no offense for one who perceives it as offered; for water and tooth-sticks; for a monk who, in the event of a cause such as a snake bite, takes and consumes the four great filth medicines (mahāvikaṭa) by himself when there is no lay attendant (kappiyakāraka) to make them allowable; and for one who is insane, etc. In this context, a lay attendant who is difficult to speak to or incapable is also considered as being in the group of those who are absent. If there are no ashes, it is allowable to burn dry wood; if there is no dry wood, it is allowable even to cut green wood from a tree to make ashes. It is also allowable to dig the earth for fine clay. However, these four great filth medicines are called 'kālodissa' (referring to the time of a snake bite). It is allowable to take them by oneself only at the moment of being bitten by a snake. At other times, they must be consumed only after being formally offered. The four factors are: not being formally offered, not being a specifically permitted item, not being a negligible substance like smoke (abbohārika), and swallowing. The origins, etc., are similar to the Eḷakaloma training rule.

## The Explanation of the Tooth-stick Training Rule is Finished.

## The Fourth Chapter on Food (Bhojana Vagga).

## 5. The Naked Ascetic Chapter (Acelaka Vagga)

## 1. The Explanation of the Naked Ascetic Training Rule

In the first training rule of the Naked Ascetic Chapter, for a monk who gives any material gift (āmisa) to those naked ascetics and other sectarians with a single effort, there is one Pācittiya. If he gives by repeatedly breaking the effort (stopping and starting), there is a Pācittiya for every effort.

It was laid down in Vesālī concerning the matter of the Venerable Ānanda giving two cakes to a female wanderer. It is an uncommon regulation (asādhāraṇapaññatti); it is without command (anāṇattika) and is a threefold Pācittiya. For a monk who gives water or a tooth-stick; for one who perceives a non-sectarian as a sectarian; and for one who is in doubt, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). There is no offense for one who perceives a non-sectarian as a non-sectarian; for one who causes an unordained person (anupasampanna) to give; for one who, having placed a vessel near those sectarians, says, 'Take this'; or for one who puts it into a vessel placed by them; for one who gives external ointments; and for one who is insane, etc. In this training rule, there are four factors: being another sectarian, not being a permitted item, being something to be swallowed, and giving into a vessel not placed by one's own hand for the purpose of swallowing. The origins, etc., are similar to the Eḷakaloma training rule.

## The Explanation of the Naked Ascetic Training Rule is Finished.
233:
## 2. The Explanation of the Dismissing Training Rule
In the second training rule, 'whether having caused it to be given or not' means whether having caused any material gift (āmisa) such as alms-food or congee to be given or not. 'Should dismiss' means to send away by saying 'Go' or similar words, because of wanting to laugh, play, or sit in private with a woman. 'Only for this reason' means making only such improper conduct the cause, and not for any other suitable reason. In 'Pācittiya', there is first an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) merely by dismissing. When the person dismissed moves away by one step from the range of sight (dassanūpacāra) or the range of hearing (savanūpacāra), there is another offense of wrong-doing. When they move away by the second step, there is a Pācittiya. In this context, the range of sight in an open space is twelve cubits; the range of hearing is the same. If there are walls, doors, or enclosures in between, being obscured by those things itself constitutes exceeding the range (upacāra).

It was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning the matter of dismissing, in relation to the Venerable Upananda. It is a common regulation. It is a rule involving a command (sāṇattika) because of the command to dismiss. It is a threefold Pācittiya. Regarding an unordained person (anupasampanna), there is a threefold Dukkaṭa. For speaking with the intent to oppress or revile both parties out of anger, there is only a Dukkaṭa. There is no offense for one who dismisses for suitable reasons such as 'We two cannot subsist together on alms-food,' or for one who is insane, etc. The three factors of this training rule are: the desire to engage in improper conduct, dismissing an ordained person for that purpose, and the person so dismissed exceeding the range. The origins, etc., are similar to the Taking what is not given (Adinnādāna).

## The Explanation of the Dismissing Training Rule is Finished.

## 3. The Explanation of the Sitting in a Bedroom Training Rule
In the third training rule, 'sabhojana' means being together with two people (a husband and wife). Alternatively, 'sabhojana' means 'sabhoaga' (with enjoyment). For a man overwhelmed by lust, a woman is an object of enjoyment (bhoga), and for a woman, a man is an object of enjoyment. Therefore, in the word-analysis (padabhājana), it was said: 'If there is a woman, and if there is a man,' etc. 'Having intruded, should sit' means to enter and sit nearby. If there is a sleeping chamber (sayanighara) in that house, if it is a large sleeping chamber made in a great four-sided hall, etc., it means sitting within the sleeping chamber near a spot after leaving the forearm's length (hatthapāsa) from the doorpost; if it is a small house, it means sitting after crossing the center. For a monk who sits in this way, there is a Pācittiya offense.
234:
In Sāvatthī, concerning Venerable Upananda, it was laid down regarding the matter of sitting close [to a woman]. It is a common regulation, not by command (anāṇattika), and involves a threefold Pācittiya (tika-pācittiya). If one perceives a place that is not a bedroom as a bedroom, or if one is in doubt, there is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa). There is no offense for one who does not perceive it as a bedroom, for one who sits without exceeding the area of the stated characteristics, when a second monk is present, when both [husband and wife] have left the room, for one who sits being free from passion [an Anāgāmī], or for those who are insane, etc. These are the four factors here: the presence of a husband and wife who are not free from passion, it being a bedroom, the absence of a second monk, and sitting close. The origins (samuṭṭhāna) and so forth are similar to the first Pārājika.

## The Commentary on the Sabhojana Sikkhāpada is finished.

## 4-5. Commentary on the Rahopaṭicchanna and Rahonisajja Sikkhāpadas

The fourth and fifth training rules were laid down in Sāvatthī concerning Venerable Upananda regarding the matters of sitting in a concealed seat and sitting in private. These are common regulations. The origins and so forth of these training rules are also just like the first Pārājika. The remaining explanation should be understood according to the method already stated in the two Aniyata training rules.

## The Commentary on the Rahopaṭicchanna and Rahonisajja Sikkhāpadas is finished.

## 6. Commentary on the Cāritta Sikkhāpada

In the sixth training rule, "invited" (nimantito) means invited with any of the five kinds of meals. "Being one who has a meal" (sabhatto samāno) means being one who has that very invited meal. "Without asking a monk who is present" (santaṃ bhikkhuṃ anāpucchā) means seeing a monk within the vicinity (upacāra-sīmā) and in sight, and without asking with a common expression such as "I am going to the house of such-and-such a person" or "I am going on a visit," which could be asked in normal speech. "Before the meal or after the meal" (purebhattaṃ vā pacchābhattaṃ vā) means whether that meal with which one was invited has been eaten or not. "Should go on a visit among families" (kulesu cārittaṃ āpajjeyya) means entering houses other than the one where one was invited. "Except on an occasion, there is a Pācittiya" (aññatra samayā pācittiyaṃ) means if that monk, excluding the two kinds of occasions with the stated characteristics...
235:
...enters another house before noon has passed (excluding the occasion), then there is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa) upon stepping into the house precinct. For a monk crossing the threshold with the first foot, there is another wrongdoing. Upon crossing with the second foot, there is a Pācittiya offense.

In Rājagaha, concerning Venerable Upananda, it was laid down because of the matter of going on a visit. In this rule, there is a fourfold supplementary regulation: "without asking a monk who is present, before the meal, after the meal, except on an occasion." It is a common regulation, not by command (anāṇattika), and involves a threefold Pācittiya. For one who is not invited but perceives himself as invited, or for one who is in doubt, there is an offense of wrongdoing. There is no offense for one who is not invited and perceives himself as not invited, for one who enters after asking a monk who is present during an occasion, for one who enters without asking when no monk is present, for one who goes by a path that is another's house or house precinct, for one who goes to a monastery within a village, a nunnery, a dwelling of titthiyas, a refectory, or a house where there is a meal, during times of danger, or for those who are insane, etc.

These are the five factors here: accepting an invitation for any of the five kinds of meals, not asking a monk who is present, entering another house from the house where the meal is, not exceeding the time of noon, and the absence of an occasion or dangers. The origins and so forth are just like the first Kathina training rule. This training rule, however, is [an offense of] action and non-action (kiriya-akiriya).

## The Commentary on the Cāritta Sikkhāpada is finished.

## 7. Commentary on the Mahānāma Sikkhāpada

In the seventh training rule, "an invitation for requisites for four months" (catumāsappaccayapavāraṇā) means an invitation for requisites for the sick for four months. All this was stated by way of the originating story. The meaning here is: whether it be a four-month invitation, a renewed invitation, or a permanent invitation, all should be accepted. One should not reject it thinking, "I have no illness now"; one should accept it thinking, "I will ask if there is an illness."

In the phrase "if he should accept beyond that," if a limit was made there by nights or by medicines, such as "only for this many nights" or "only these many medicines should be asked for," then if he asks beyond that limit of nights or limit of medicines—asking for medicine for a purpose not requiring medicine, or asking for another medicine for a purpose requiring a different medicine—there is a Pācittiya offense for that monk.
236:
It was laid down in the Sakyan country, concerning the group of six monks, on the matter of requesting medicinal requisites. This training rule is a common prescription (sādhāraṇa-paññatti), not by command (anāṇattika), and a pācittiya involving a triad (tika-pācittiya). There is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa) for a monk who, though not exceeding the invited limit, perceives it as exceeding, or for a monk who is in doubt. There is no offense for: a monk who does not exceed the limit and perceives it as not exceeding; a monk who, when there is a need for medicines other than those invited or for more than invited, requests them; a monk who, when there is a need after the invited nights have passed, requests them after explaining the actual situation; those who request from relatives, from those who have given a personal invitation, or from those who have given an unlimited invitation; those who request for the sake of another; those who request with their own property; and those who are insane, etc. The four factors here are: invitation by the Saṅgha, requesting medicine from that invitation, not being ill (agilāna), and exceeding the limit. The origins (samuṭṭhāna) and so forth are the same as the Sañcaritta training rule.

## The Commentary on the Mahānāma Training Rule is finished.

## 8. Uyyuttasenāsikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

In the eighth training rule, 'uyyutta' means prepared for battle, having departed from the village. 'Sena' refers to the fourfold army. For a monk who goes specifically to see the army without such a reason, there is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa) for every step. For a monk who stands and watches within the vicinity (upacāra) of the viewing area, there is a pācittiya offense. The vicinity of the viewing area means the place where one stands and can see the army; for a monk who leaves that place and watches repeatedly, there is a pācittiya for every effort (payoga).

It was laid down in Sāvatthī, concerning the group of six monks, on the matter of watching an army. "Except for a corresponding reason" (aññatra tathārūpappaccayā) is the supplementary regulation (anupaññatti) in this rule. This training rule is a common prescription, not by command, and a pācittiya involving a triad. In going to see any one of the army factors such as elephants, etc., there is an offense of wrongdoing as previously mentioned. Likewise, there is an offense of wrongdoing for a monk who perceives an army that is not marching as one that is marching, or for one who is in doubt. There is no offense for: a monk who perceives an army that is not marching as not marching; a monk who, while standing in the monastery (ārāma), watches an army that has come to his location or is passing by; a monk who goes because of such a reason; a monk who goes because of danger; and those who are insane, etc. The four factors here are: going for the purpose of seeing a marching army, seeing it elsewhere than in the permitted area, and the absence of such a reason or danger. The origins and so forth are the same as the Eḷakaloma training rule. This rule is a worldly fault (lokavajja), involves unwholesome consciousness, and is associated with the three feelings.

## The Commentary on the Uyyuttasena Training Rule is finished.
237:
## 9. Senāvāsasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

In the ninth training rule, the Senāvāsa training rule, 'beyond that' (tato ce uttari) means on the fourth day, exceeding three nights, when the sun sets, whether one is standing, sitting, or lying down within the army; even if one maintains any posture in the air by psychic power, it is a pācittiya. 

This training rule was laid down in Sāvatthī, concerning the group of six monks, on the matter of staying with an army for more than three nights. It is a common prescription and an anāṇattika training rule where the offense is incurred only by one's own action, not by command. There is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa) for one who perceives a stay of less than three nights as more, or for one who is in doubt. There is no offense for: one who perceives it as less than three nights; one who departs from the army before dawn on the third night and returns; one who is ill; one who stays for the sake of an ill person; one who is in an army besieged by an enemy army; one who is obstructed by someone; one who faces dangers; and those who are insane, etc. The three factors here are: (1) exceeding three nights, (2) sunset while with the army, (3) absence of reasons such as being ill. The origins and so forth are the same as the Eḷakaloma training rule.

## The Commentary on the Senāvāsa Training Rule is finished.

## 10. Uyyodhikasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

In the tenth training rule, the Uyyodhika training rule, 'uyyodhika' is the name of the battlefield, so called because it is the place where one goes up to fight. 'Balagga' is the place for counting troops, so called because it is where the strength of the forces is known. 'Senābyūha' is the name for the army encampment, referring to the specific arrangement of the army. 'Anīkadassana' means seeing the troops. 'Anīka' (a troop unit) is defined by the characteristic: 'an elephant with twelve men, a horse with three men, a chariot with four men'; thus, three elephants constitute the minimum elephant unit (hatthānīka). The same method applies to the horse and chariot units. Four armed infantrymen constitute the minimum infantry unit (pattānīka). For a monk who goes to see any of these, there is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa) for every step. For a monk who stands and watches within the vicinity (upacāra), there is a pācittiya offense. For a monk who, after leaving the vicinity, watches repeatedly, there is a pācittiya for every effort (payoga). The rest of the procedure should be understood as stated in the Uyyuttasena training rule. There is no further distinction of offenses here.

## The Commentary on the Uyyodhika Training Rule is finished.

## The Fifth Chapter, the Acelaka Vagga, is finished.
238:
## 6. Surāpāna Vagga
## 1. Commentary on the Surāpāna Training Rule
In the Surāmerayapāna training rule, which is the first training rule of the Surāpāna Vagga, liquor made from flour and so forth is called 'surā'. Fermented drink made from flowers and so forth is called 'meraya'. For a monk who drinks both these types of liquor and fermented drinks, even as much as a drop on the tip of a blade of kusa grass, starting from the seed, there is an offense of pācittiya for every effort.

It was laid down in Kausāmbī concerning the Elder Sāgata regarding the incident of drinking liquor. It is a common regulation (sādhāraṇa-paññatti), not involving an order (anaṇattika), and a triad of pācittiya (tika-pācittiya). For one who perceives what is not liquor as liquor, or is in doubt, there is an offense of dukkaṭa. There is no offense for: one who perceives what is not liquor as not liquor; one who drinks loṇasovīraka (salted sour gruel) or a drink called sutta which resembles liquor in color, smell, and taste; one who drinks soup and so forth cooked with a small amount of liquor added for the purpose of imparting a scent; one who drinks ariṭṭha medicine which, though resembling liquor, is made from the juice of emblic myrobalan (āmalaka) and so forth and is not intoxicating; and for one who is insane, etc. There are two factors in this training rule: it being liquor, and the drinking of that liquor. The origins (samuṭṭhāna) and so forth are the same as the Eḷakaloma training rule. This training rule is a worldly fault (lokavajja), involves unwholesome consciousness (akusala-citta), and has three types of feeling (ti-vedanā).

## The Commentary on the Surāpāna Training Rule Ends.
## 2. Commentary on the Aṅgulipatodaka Training Rule
In the second training rule, Aṅgulipatodaka, it means poking the armpits and so forth with the fingers. Furthermore, if one touches a monk with any part of the body with the intention of playing, there is an offense of pācittiya.

It was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning the group of six monks regarding the incident of laughing by poking with fingers. It is a common regulation, not involving an order, and a triad of pācittiya. For one who is not ordained (anupasampanna), there is a triad of dukkaṭa. In this training rule, a nun is considered unordained for a monk, and a monk is considered unordained for a nun. In all cases such as things connected to the body (kāyapaṭibaddha), there is only an offense of dukkaṭa. There is no offense for: one who touches when there is a duty to be done without the intention of playing; and for one who is insane, etc. There are two factors in this training rule: the intention of playing, and touching the body of an ordained monk with one's own body. The origins and so forth are the same as the first Pārājika.

## The Commentary on the Aṅgulipatodaka Training Rule Ends.
239:
## 3. Commentary on the Hasadhamma Training Rule

In the third training rule, 'sporting in the water' (hasadhamma) means playing in the water. Therefore, if a monk, while walking in water deeper than the ankles, dives or surfaces with the intention of playing, there is an offense of dukkaṭa for the hands and feet of that monk as he descends for the purpose of diving and so forth. For every effort in diving and surfacing, there is an offense of pācittiya. For a monk who goes under the water after diving, for every movement of the hands and feet, or for a monk who swims, for every effort of whichever limb he swims with, there is an offense of pācittiya.

It was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning the group of seventeen monks regarding the incident of playing in the water. It is a common regulation. It does not involve an order. It is a triad of pācittiya. If one perceives what is not water-sporting as water-sporting, or is in doubt, there is an offense of dukkaṭa. Similarly, for a monk who plays with a boat; or strikes the water with hands, feet, wood, or a potsherd; or throws water from a vessel, or fermented rice-scum (kañjika) and so forth, or mud, for the sake of playing, there is an offense of dukkaṭa. However, it is allowable to write letters on the water to clarify a meaning. There is no offense for: a monk who descends and dives etc. when there is a duty to be done without the intention of playing; a monk who is crossing to the other side; one who acts during dangers; and for one who is insane, etc. These are the two factors: the water being above the ankles, and playing with the intention of sporting. The origins and so forth are the same as the first Pārājika.

## The Commentary on the Hasadhamma Training Rule Ends.

## 4. Commentary on the Anādariya Training Rule

In the fourth training rule, 'disrespect' (anādariya) means showing disrespect towards either a person or the Dhamma. Therefore, if a monk, when being spoken to by another ordained monk regarding a regulation, shows disrespect because of not wanting to follow his words or not wanting to train in that Dhamma, there is an offense of pācittiya for that monk due to that disrespect.

It was laid down in Kausāmbī concerning the Elder Channa regarding the incident of showing disrespect. It is a common regulation. It does not involve an order. It is a triad of pācittiya. For one who is not ordained, there is a triad of dukkaṭa. If spoken to by an ordained or unordained person with words that are not the regulation, such as "This matter does not lead to the thinning out of defilements," there is only an offense of dukkaṭa for the monk's disrespect.
240:
If a monk shows disrespect to one speaking Sutta or Abhidhamma, which are not Vinaya regulations, saying "This matter does not lead to the reduction of defilements," etc., it is only an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). However, there is no offense for a monk who, holding onto the learning passed down through a lineage of teachers, says, "This is the learning and inquiry of our teachers," nor for those who are insane, etc. The two factors for this training rule are: speaking to a higher-ordained monk (upasampanna) regarding a Vinaya regulation, and the act of showing disrespect. The origin (samuṭṭhāna), etc., are similar to the training rule on taking what is not given (adinnādāna). This [offense] involves painful feeling (dukkha-vedanā).

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on Disrespect (Anādariya Sikkhāpada) is Finished.

## 5. Explanation of the Training Rule on Frightening (Bhiṃsāpana Sikkhāpada)

In the fifth training rule, "frighten" (bhiṃsāpeyya) means presenting frightening sights, etc., or speaking frightening words with the intention to cause fear. Whether the person being frightened actually becomes afraid or not, the monk who frightens commits an offense of expiation (pācittiya).

This was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning the group of six monks (chabbaggiya) in the case of frightening. It is a common regulation (sādhāraṇa-paññatti), not involving a command (anāṇattika), and involves the triad of expiation (tika-pācittiya). If one frightens a non-ordained person, it is a triad of wrong-doing (tika-dukkaṭa). There is no offense for a monk who does so without the intention to frighten, nor for those who are insane, etc. The two factors for this training rule are: the person being a higher-ordained monk, and the effort made with the intention to frighten within the range of that monk's sight or hearing. The origin, etc., are the same as the preceding training rule.

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on Frightening (Bhiṃsāpana Sikkhāpada) is Finished.

## 6. Explanation of the Training Rule on Fire (Joti Sikkhāpada)

In the sixth training rule, "desiring to warm oneself" (visibbanāpekkho) means having the wish to warm oneself. "Should kindle" (samādaheyya) means lighting a fire. "Except for a sufficient reason" (aññatra tathārūpappaccayā) means lighting a fire without a reason such as lighting a lamp or baking a bowl, etc. The decision here is: for a monk who kindles a fire himself, from the moment he sets up the fire-sticks until the flame arises, every effort constitutes an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). When the flame arises, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya). If he commands another, there is an offense of wrong-doing due to the command. Even if the person commanded kindles many fires based on a single command, there is only one offense of expiation.
241:
This was laid down in the Bhagga country concerning many monks in the case of warming oneself at a fire, stating "unless he is ill, or except for such a reason." In this training rule, there are two supplementary regulations (anupaññatti). It is a common regulation (sādhāraṇa-paññatti). It involves a command (sāṇattika). It is a triad of expiation (tika-pācittiya). For a monk who is ill but perceives himself as not ill, or for one who is in doubt, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). Similarly, there is an offense of wrong-doing for a monk who picks up a firebrand fallen from the hearth, or for one who picks up an unextinguished (flaming) firebrand and places it back in its original position. For a monk who makes an extinguished fire burn (by blowing), it is only an offense of expiation (pācittiya).

There is no offense for a monk who is ill and perceives himself as ill; for one who warms himself at a fire made by another or at glowing embers without flame; if there is a sufficient reason such as lighting a lamp, baking a bowl, or putting fire in a sauna (jantāghara); in times of danger; or for those who are insane, etc. The four factors for this training rule are: not being ill, the absence of a permitted reason, the desire to warm oneself, and kindling the fire. The origin, etc., should be understood in the same way as stated in the Sañcaritta training rule.

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on Fire (Joti Sikkhāpada) is Finished.

## 7. Explanation of the Training Rule on Bathing (Nahāna Sikkhāpada)

In the seventh training rule, "should bathe" (nahāyeyya) means: if a monk in the Middle Country (Majjhimadesa), before half a month (15 days) has passed since the day he bathed, except for the permitted occasions (samaya), prepares soap powder or clay with the thought "I will bathe," from the time of such preparation, every effort constitutes an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). At the conclusion of the bath, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya). Among the occasions (samaya), even the act of sweeping the monastery precinct is called "occasion of work" (kamma-samaya). The time for a monk who wishes to travel, is traveling, or has traveled half a league (yojana) is called "occasion of traveling" (addhāna-gamana-samaya). The time when a monk's body is covered with dust-laden wind and two or three drops of water fall on it is called "occasion of wind and rain" (vāta-vuṭṭhi-samaya). The remaining words are clear.

This was laid down in Rājagaha concerning many monks in the case of bathing without knowing the proper limit, stating "except for the occasion." In this training rule, there are these six supplementary regulations. It is a common regulation (sādhāraṇa-paññatti). It does not involve a command (anāṇattika). It is a triad of expiation (tika-pācittiya). For a monk who, although more than half a month has passed, perceives it as not yet full, or for one who is in doubt, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). There is no offense for a monk who perceives that more than half a month has passed; for one who bathes during a permitted occasion; for one who, while crossing to the other side of a river, bathes in pits made by digging sand; for all monks living in the border regions outside the Middle Country; in times of danger; or for those who are insane, etc. Being in the Middle Country, bathing before half a month is full, or the occasions, or going to the other side of a river...
242: Or the absence of dangers—these three factors are present in this training rule. The origin and other aspects are just like the Eጶakaloma training rule.## The Explanation of the Bathing Training Rule is finished.## 8. Dubbaፃፃakaraፃa Sikkhāpada VaፃፃanāIn the eighth training rule, in the word 'alabhi', 'labha' refers to the one who receives. Receiving itself is called 'lābha' (gain). What did he receive? A new robe. Thus, although it should be said as 'nava-cģvara-lābhena', it is spoken as 'navaፃ-cģvara-lābhena' without dropping the niggahģta. It means one who has obtained a new robe. Regarding the two words situated in the middle (pana, bhikkhunā), 'pana' is merely a particle. The word 'bhikkhunā' indicates the monk who obtained the robe. For one who perceives what has been marked as not marked, or who is in doubt, there is an offence of Dukka፡a. There is no offence for one who perceives it as marked, for one whose mark has disappeared, for one whose place where the mark was made has worn out, for one who sews together a marked robe and an unmarked robe, for one who uses it after later adding patches, borders, or binding, and for the insane, etc. The three factors in this training rule are: not making the mark on the aforementioned type of robe, the robe not being a lost one, and wearing or wrapping it. The origin and other aspects are like the Eጶakaloma training rule. This training rule is 'kiriya-akiriya' (action and non-action).## The Explanation of the Discolouring Training Rule is finished.## 9. Vikappana Sikkhāpada VaፃፃanāIn the ninth training rule, in the word 'vikappetvā', there are two types of assignment: Sammukhā-vikappanā (assignment in the presence) and Parammukhā-vikappanā (assignment in the absence). How does Sammukhā-vikappanā occur? Knowing whether the robes are single or many, and whether they are near or not near, one should say, 'I assign this robe' or 'these robes' or 'that robe' or 'those robes' to you. This is one type of Sammukhā-vikappanā. By this much assignment, it is allowable to store it. However, it is not yet allowable to use it, discard it, or determine it. 243: ...knowing whether the robe is single or many, and whether it is near or not near, and having said 'this robe' or 'these robes' or 'that robe' or 'those robes', one should say 'I assign it to you'. This is one type of Sammukhā-vikappanā (assignment in the presence). By this much assignment, it is allowable to store it. However, it is not yet allowable to use it, discard it, or determine it. When it is said, 'Use my property (or my properties) if you wish to use it, discard it if you wish to discard it, or do as you see fit,' this is called 'paccuddhāra' (withdrawal). From that time onwards, use and so forth are also allowable. Another way: Similarly, knowing whether the robes are single or many, and whether they are near or not near, and having said 'this robe' etc. in the presence of that monk, taking the name of any one of the five classes of co-religionists whom one desires, one should say, 'I assign it to the monk Tissa' or 'I assign it to the nun Tissā, to the trainee, to the novice, to the female novice Tissā'. This is another type of Sammukhā-vikappanā. By this much, it is allowable to store it; among use and so forth, not even one is allowable. When that monk says, 'Use the property of the monk Tissa... the property of the female novice Tissā, discard it, or do as you see fit,' it is called 'paccuddhāra'. From then on, use and so forth are allowable. How does Parammukhā-vikappanā (assignment in the absence) occur? Knowing such condition of the robes, and having said 'this robe' etc., one should say, 'I give this to you for the purpose of assignment.' That monk should ask, 'Who is your friend or acquaintance?' Then the other (the owner of the robe) should say, 'The monk Tissa' etc., in the same way as the previous method. Again, that monk should say, 'I give it to the monk Tissa' etc. This is Parammukhā-vikappanā. By this much, it is allowable to store it; among use and so forth, not even one is allowable. When that monk says, in the same way as mentioned in the second Sammukhā-vikappanā, 'Use the property of the one named so-and-so, discard it, or do as you see fit,' it is called 'paccuddhāra'. From then on, use and so forth are allowable. In the assignment of an alms-bowl, this is also the method. Thus, having assigned the robe to any one of the five classes of co-religionists by either of these two types of assignment...
244:
In the manner already stated, an offense of expiation (pācittiya) is incurred by a monk who uses a robe that has not yet been revoked (paccuddhara), or who uses it without the trust of the monk with whom the formal Vinaya act was performed.

It was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning Venerable Upananda on account of using [a robe] without revocation. It is a common regulation (sādhāraṇa-paññatti). It is an offense not involving a command (anāṇattika). There are three types of pācittiya (tika-pācittiya). An offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa) is incurred by one who determines (adhiṭṭhāna) or relinquishes that robe which has not yet been revoked. Similarly, a dukkaṭa offense is incurred by one who uses a robe that has been revoked but perceives it as not revoked, or is in doubt. No offense is incurred by one who uses it perceiving it as revoked, or uses it out of trust, or by those who are insane, etc. The three factors here are: non-revocation of a robe personally assigned (vikappita), the robe being suitable for assignment, and the act of using it. The origins (samuṭṭhāna), etc., are the same as the first Kathina training rule. This training rule is one of action and non-action (kiriyā-akiriyā).

## The Explanation of the Vikappana Training Rule is Finished.

## 10. Apanidhāna Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā

In the tenth training rule, 'bowl' refers to a bowl suitable for determination. 'Robe' refers to a robe suitable for assignment. 'Sitting cloth' (nisīdana) refers to one with a border. 'Needle case' (sūcighara) refers to one with or without needles. 'Waistband' (kāyabandhana) refers to either a flat band or one shaped like a pig's tail. 'Should hide' (apanidheyya) means to remove and conceal. 'Desiring to joke' (hasāpekkha) means having the intention to play or be humorous. 'An offense of expiation' (pācittiya) means a pācittiya is incurred by the monk who hides it himself. For one who commands another, a dukkaṭa offense is incurred due to the command; when the other person has hidden it, a pācittiya is incurred by the one who gave the command.

It was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning the group-of-six monks (chabbaggiya) on account of hiding [items]. It is a common regulation. It is an offense involving a command (sāṇattika). There are three types of pācittiya. In hiding the property of one not fully ordained (anupasampanna), there are three types of dukkaṭa (tika-dukkaṭa). Except for the aforementioned bowls, etc., a monk who hides other requisites belonging to a monk or one not fully ordained incurs only a dukkaṭa offense. No offense is incurred by one who puts away a poorly placed requisite, or by one who puts it away thinking, 'I will give it back after giving a Dhamma talk,' or by those who are insane, etc. The two factors here are: hiding bowls, etc., belonging to a fully ordained monk, and having the intention to annoy or the intention to joke. The origins, etc., are the same as for taking what is not given (adinnādāna).

## The Explanation of the Apanidhāna Training Rule is Finished.

## The Sixth Chapter: Surāpāna Vagga.
245:
## 7. Sappāṇaka Vagga

## 1. Sañcicca Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā

In the first training rule of the Sappāṇaka Vagga, 'pāṇa' refers to an animal. A monk who kills such an animal, whether small or large, incurs an offense of expiation (pācittiya). However, if the animal is large, the unwholesome merit (akusala) is greater because of the greater effort required.

It was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning Venerable Udāyi on account of depriving a living being of life. This is a common regulation. It involves a command (sāṇattika). A dukkaṭa offense is incurred by one who is in doubt about whether it is a living being, by one who perceives what is not a living being as a living being, or by one who is in doubt [about what is not a living being]. No offense is incurred by one who perceives it as not a living being, one who kills unintentionally, one who does not know it is a living being, one who has no intention to kill, or by those who are insane, etc. The remaining points are the same as stated in the training rule on human beings (manussaviggaha).

## The Explanation of the Sañcicca Training Rule is Finished.

## 2. Sappāṇaka Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā

In the second training rule, 'sappāṇaka' refers to water containing small insects that would die through use. For a monk who uses such water knowing it contains insects, a pācittiya offense is incurred for every effort.

It was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning the group-of-six monks on account of using water known to contain insects. The remaining points should be understood in the same manner as stated in the Siñcana training rule.

## The Explanation of the Sappāṇaka Training Rule is Finished.

## 3. Ukkoṭana Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā

In the third training rule, 'yathādhamma' (according to the rule) means according to the very Vinaya rule taught for the settling of a particular legal issue (adhikaraṇa). 'Nihatādhikaraṇa' (a settled legal issue) refers to a legal issue that has been settled by the Dhamma taught by the Teacher in the Samathakkhandhaka. The method of settling such legal issues will be shown in the Adhikaraṇasamatha section.

'Should reopen for a repeat action' (punakammāya ukkoṭeyya) means going to various monks and saying things such as 'The act was not [properly] performed,' thereby agitating for the act to be performed again. A pācittiya offense is incurred by one who acts in this way, not allowing the matter to remain as it was settled. Regarding a legal issue that [was settled] in accordance with the Dhamma...
246:
That legal issue which has been settled is indeed well-settled. If one objects while the formal act is being performed (before completion), it should be performed after convincing that objecting monk. Otherwise (if performed while the objection persists), the formal act is invalid, and the performing monks incur an offense.

It was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning the group of six monks in the case of reopening (ukkoṭana) a legal issue. It is a common regulation (sādhāraṇa-paññatti). It is a training rule that does not involve command (anāṇattika). For one who is doubtful about a formal act performed according to the Dhamma; for one who perceives a formal act not according to the Dhamma as being according to the Dhamma; or for one who is doubtful, there is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa). For one who perceives it as not according to the Dhamma, or for one who reopens it knowing that "it was performed not according to the Dhamma, or by an incomplete group, or for a person not entitled to the formal act," or for those who are insane, etc., there is no offense. The three factors here are: the state of being settled according to the Dhamma, knowledge, and reopening. The originations (samuṭṭhāna), etc., are similar to the training rule on taking what is not given (adinnādāna). This training rule involves painful feeling (dukkha-vedanā).

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on Reopening (Ukkoṭana) is finished.

## 4. Explanation of the Training Rule on Grave Offenses (Duṭṭhullā)

In the fourth training rule, "grave offense" (duṭṭhullā) refers to a saṅghādisesa offense. For a monk who knows of such an offense by any means and conceals it, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya). Even if he gives up the responsibility, thinking, "I will not tell any monk about this offense now," and tells it later, it is considered telling only after having incurred the pācittiya offense. If he gives up the responsibility and tells another person only for the purpose of concealing it, and that person tells another, in this way, even if there are a hundred monks, they all incur an offense as long as the chain is not broken. How is the chain broken? If the monk who incurred the offense tells one monk, and that monk tells another, and that third person turns back and tells the second monk who told him, when the third person tells the second person in this way, the chain is broken.

It was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning a certain monk in the case of concealing a grave offense. It is an uncommon regulation (asādhāraṇa-paññatti). It is an anāṇattika rule. Regarding a grave offense, for the first case (concealing while knowing it is grave), there is a pācittiya offense. For the remaining two cases, there is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa). Regarding a non-grave offense, there is a dukkaṭa of the triple-set (tika-dukkaṭa). For the transgression of an unordained person, whether grave or non-grave, there is only a dukkaṭa. For one who does not tell, thinking, "There will be quarrels, etc., for the Saṅgha," or thinking, "This monk is harsh and rough; he will cause danger to my life or danger to my holy life (brahmacariya)," or for one who does not see a suitable monk to tell,
247:
for one who does not see a suitable monk to tell, for one who has no intention to conceal, for one who does not tell thinking, "He will be known by his own deed," and for those who are insane, etc., there is no offense. The two factors here are: knowing the grave offense of a monk, and giving up the responsibility with the desire to conceal, thinking, "I will not tell." The originations, etc., are the same as the training rule on formal rebuke (samanubhāsana).

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on Grave Offenses (Duṭṭhullā) is finished.

## 5. Explanation of the Training Rule on One Under Twenty Years (Ūnavīsativassa)

In the fifth training rule, "one under twenty years" (ūnavīsativassa) refers to a person who has not completed twenty years of age, starting from the time of conception. "Should ordain" (upasampādeyya) means acting as a preceptor (upajjhāya) and conferring higher ordination (upasampadā). Whether the preceptor knows or does not know that the person is under-age, if he confers ordination, that person is not a true monk but remains unordained (anupasampanna). However, if that pseudo-monk confers ordination on another after ten years, and if the group (gaṇa) is complete excluding him, then that person is well-ordained. As long as that pseudo-monk does not know he is not a monk, there is no obstacle to heaven or obstacle to liberation for him. But once he knows, he must be ordained again. "Those monks are blameworthy" (te ca bhikkhū gārayhā) means that excluding the preceptor, the remaining monks are blameworthy; all of them incur an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa). "This is a pācittiya for him" (idaṃ tasmiṃ pācittiyaṃ) means this pācittiya offense should be understood as applying only to the person who acts as the preceptor and confers ordination. Therefore, for one who intends, "I will confer ordination in this way," and searches for a group, a teacher, a bowl, or a robe, or consecrates a boundary (sīmā), or demarcates a water-boundary, for all such preliminary duties, for the motion (ñatti), and for the two proclamations (kammavācā), he incurs offenses of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa), and at the conclusion of the proclamation, he incurs a pācittiya offense.

It was laid down in Rājagaha concerning many monks in the case of conferring higher ordination on one under twenty years of age. It is an uncommon regulation (asādhāraṇa-paññatti) and an anāṇattika rule. For one who is doubtful about a person under twenty years; for one who perceives a person who has completed twenty years as being under-age; or for one who is doubtful, there is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa). For one who perceives both types of persons as having completed twenty years, and for those who are insane, etc., there is no offense. The three factors here are: being under twenty years of age, perceiving the person as under-age, and conferring higher ordination. The originations, etc., are similar to the training rule on taking what is not given (adinnādāna). This training rule is an offense by regulation (paññattivajja) and is associated with three types of mind and three types of feeling.

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on One Under Twenty Years (Ūnavīsativassa) is finished.
248:
## 6. Theyyasatthasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā
In the commentary on the sixth training rule regarding a caravan of thieves: There are thieves traveling on a journey, either wishing to deceive the king or to evade taxes, who have either already committed a theft or have not yet committed one. Among those thieves, in this training rule, for a monk who, perceiving them as a 'theyya-sattha' (a caravan of thieves) and knowing their status as such, makes an agreement and travels with them, the judgment of the offense regarding the agreement and the traveling should be understood according to the method stated in the Ovādavagga.

It was prescribed in Sāvatthī concerning a certain monk who made an agreement and traveled along the same path with a caravan of thieves. It is a common prescription (sādhāraṇa-paññatti). It is a non-command rule (anāṇattika—the offense is incurred only if committed by oneself). For a monk who travels by making an agreement himself even when the people do not make an agreement, for one who is in doubt about the caravan being a caravan of thieves, and for one who perceives a non-thief caravan as a caravan of thieves, or for one who is in doubt, an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa) is incurred. There is no offense for one who perceives it as not a caravan of thieves, for one who travels without making an agreement, for one who travels at a different time than the appointed time, for one who travels during dangers, or for the insane and so forth. In this training rule, there are four factors: being a caravan of thieves, knowing it, making an agreement, and traveling according to the agreement. The origin of the theyyasattha rule is: action, release by perception, with intention, worldly fault (paṇṇatti-vajja), bodily action, vocal action, three thoughts, and three feelings.

## Theyyasatthasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā Niṭṭhitā.

## 7. Saṃvidhānasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā
In the commentary on the seventh training rule regarding making an agreement: It was prescribed in Sāvatthī concerning a certain monk who traveled along the same path with a woman by making an agreement. The rest of the details here should be understood in the same manner as stated in the training rule regarding making an agreement with a bhikkhunī.

## Saṃvidhānasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā Niṭṭhitā.

## 8. Ariṭṭhasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā
In the commentary on the eighth training rule regarding Ariṭṭha: They are called 'antarāyika' (obstructive things) because they cause obstacles to heaven and liberation. These obstructive things are of five kinds: kamma (action), kilesa (defilement), vipāka (result), upavāda (reproach), and paṇṇatti-vītikkhama (transgression of prescriptions). Among those five...
249:
Just as the touch of soft rugs and so forth is permissible, the touch of women is also permissible—thus (the monk Ariṭṭha) spoke with the intention that, not seeing any fault in the transgression of sexual intercourse, those obstructive things taught by the Blessed One are not capable of causing an obstacle for one who indulges in them. 'Aneka-pariyāyena' (in many ways) means by many reasons, such as 'sensual pleasures are like a skeleton' and so forth. That monk should be addressed three times by the monks who see or hear him, thus: 'Venerable, do not say this... indeed, these things are capable of causing an obstacle for one who indulges in them.' If he does not give it up when thus addressed, he incurs an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa); for those who hear but do not speak, there is also an offense of wrongdoing. Again, having brought him into the midst of the Saṅgha, he should be addressed in the same manner; there too, if he does not give it up, and if the other monks do not speak, it is an offense of wrongdoing. If he still does not give it up, he should be formally admonished up to three times by a formal act consisting of a motion and three proclamations (ñatti-catuttha-kamma). Then, for that monk who does not give it up, there is an offense of wrongdoing for the motion and for each of the two proclamations; at the conclusion of the third proclamation, an offense of expiation (pācittiya) is incurred.

It was prescribed in Sāvatthī concerning the monk Ariṭṭha in the matter of not giving up a harmful view. It is a common prescription. It is a non-command rule. It is a pācittiya involving three cases (tika-pācittiya). In a non-dhamma act, there is a triple wrongdoing (tika-dukkaṭa). There is no offense for one who has not yet been formally admonished, for one who gives up the view, or for the insane and so forth. In this training rule, there are three factors: being a legal act (dhamma-kamma), formal admonition, and not giving up. The origins and so forth are the same as the Samanubhāsana training rule.

## Ariṭṭhasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā Niṭṭhitā.

## 9. Ukkhittasambhogasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā
In the ninth training rule, 'tathāvādinā' means with one who is in the habit of saying, 'As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One...' and so forth. In 'akatanudhammena', 'anudhamma' refers to the reinstatement (osāraṇā) performed after seeing the proper conduct (anuloma-vatta) of a monk who has been expelled (ukkhittaka) by a legal Vinaya act for not seeing an offense, or for not making amends, or for not giving up a harmful view. One for whom that anudhamma known as reinstatement has not been performed is called 'akatanudhammena'; it means 'together with such a person'. 'Sambhuñjeyya vā' means if one should engage in material association (āmisa-sambhoga) or Dhamma association (dhamma-sambhoga). 'Saṃvaseyya vā' means if one should perform a Saṅgha act such as the Uposatha and so forth.
250:
...should do. "He may share a sleeping place" (Saha vā seyyaṃ kappeyya) means sleeping in a monastery under the same roof, even if there are different precincts. In doing so, regarding the shared use of material things (āmisa), whether giving or taking many material things with a single effort, one Pācittiya offense is committed. If the act of giving or taking is interrupted, a Pācittiya offense is committed for each effort. Regarding the shared use of the Dhamma, the determination of offenses should be understood according to the method stated in the Padasodhamma Sikkhāpada for the teacher or the student using phrases and so on. In communion (saṃvāsa), it is determined by the completion of the formal act (kamma); in sharing a sleeping place (sahaseyya), it is determined by the effort of sleeping by the other person after one has already lain down.

This training rule was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning the group of six monks (chabbaggiya) in the case of communion with the monk Ariṭṭha. This is a common regulation (sādhāraṇa-paññatti) and an anāṇattika training rule (where an offense is not committed through ordering another). A Dukkaṭa offense is committed for one who has doubt about an expelled (ukkhittaka) monk, and for one who perceives a non-expelled monk as expelled or has doubt about him. There is no offense for one who perceives both as not expelled, for one who knows "he has been reinstated" or "he has given up that wrong view," or for those who are insane, etc. There are three factors here: (1) being one who has not yet performed the proper duty (reinstatement into the Saṅgha), (2) knowing that it has not been performed, (3) engaging in communion and so on. The origins (samuṭṭhāna) and so forth are similar to those of taking what is not given (adinnādāna). This training rule is a regulation-breach (paṇṇatti-vajja) because it violates a decree, and it is associated with three types of consciousness and three types of feeling.

## The Commentary on the Ukkhittasambhoga Sikkhāpada is finished.

## 10. Kaṇṭaka Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā

In the tenth training rule, "samaṇuddesa" means a novice (sāmaṇera). "Cara" means "go." "Pire" is a term used to address a profane outsider who does not cherish the Triple Gem. "Vinassā" means "perish" or "go to a place where we cannot see you." In this context, "tathānāsitaṃ" refers to three types of expulsion (nāsanā): expulsion from communion (saṃvāsa-nāsanā), expulsion from the outward form (liṅga-nāsanā), and expulsion by punishment (daṇḍakamma-nāsanā). Among these, expulsion due to not seeing an offense and so forth is called saṃvāsa-nāsanā. "A corrupt novice should be expelled" and "Expel the bhikkhunī Mettiya" are called liṅga-nāsanā (destruction of the outward form). "From this day forth, friend novice, that Blessed One is not to be referred to as your teacher" is called daṇḍakamma-nāsanā (expulsion by punishment). In this training rule, only this daṇḍakamma-nāsanā is intended. Therefore, it is said "tathānāsitaṃ." "Upalāpeyya" means to entice or win over by saying, "I will give you a bowl, a robe, instruction, or interrogation." "Upaṭṭhāpeyya" means accepting bathing powder, clay, and so on...
251:
...and making that novice perform services for oneself. The rules for communion and sharing a sleeping place are exactly as stated in the preceding training rule; therefore, the determination of offenses here should also be understood by the method stated in that preceding training rule.

This was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning the group of six monks in the case of enticing the novice named Kaṇṭaka; the rest is similar to what was stated in the Ariṭṭha Sikkhāpada.

## The Commentary on the Kaṇṭaka Sikkhāpada is finished.

## The Seventh Chapter: Sappāṇaka Vagga.

## 8. Sahadhammika Vagga

## 1. Sahadhammika Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā

In the first training rule of the Sahadhammika Vagga, the meaning of the phrase "sahadhammikaṃ vuccamāno" (being spoken to according to the Dhamma) has been stated in the Dubbaca Sikkhāpada. "Etasmiṃ sikkhāpade" means "I will not yet train in that practice which has been spoken of in this training rule." In this text, "pācittiyaṃ" means that for a monk who speaks in this way through a pretext (lesa) out of fear of the offense due to disrespect, a Pācittiya offense is to be understood for every word spoken. "Sikkhamānena" means being one who truly desires to train, having accepted the advice with the head (respectfully). "Aññātabbaṃ" means it should be made known. "Paripucchitabbaṃ" means it should be asked repeatedly, "What is the meaning of this word?" "Paripañhitabbaṃ" means it should be reflected upon and weighed.

This was laid down in Kosambī concerning the Elder Channa for speaking in this manner. It is a common regulation (sādhāraṇa-paññatti), an anāṇattika rule, and involves a triad of Pācittiya offenses (tika-pācittiya). In speaking to one not fully ordained (a layperson or novice), it is a triad of Dukkaṭa offenses (tika-dukkaṭa). Even if both the fully ordained and the not fully ordained are spoken to with words that are not part of the Vinaya regulations, such as "This is not for the sake of effacement," a monk who speaks in this way commits only a Dukkaṭa offense. There is no offense for a monk who replies, "I will find out, I will train," or for those who are insane, etc. Speaking to one fully ordained with the Vinaya regulations and speaking in this way because of not wanting to train—these two are the factors of this training rule. The origins and so forth are similar to those of taking what is not given (adinnādāna). This training rule involves painful feeling (dukkha-vedanā).

## The Commentary on the Sahadhammika Sikkhāpada is finished.
252:
## 2. Commentary on the Vilekhana Training Rule

In the second training rule, the phrase "when it is being recited" (uddissamanne) means while a teacher is teaching a student, or while one is reciting it by oneself for the purpose of memorization. "With minor and lesser [rules]" (khuddānukhuddakehi) means with both minor (khuddaka) and lesser (anukhuddaka) training rules. The phrase "only to this extent" (yāvadeva) is a term defining the limit of the arising of remorse and so on. This is what is meant: for those who recite, cause to recite, or study these minor and lesser training rules, it only results in the arising of remorse (vippaṭisāra) through worrying "is this allowable or not?", weariness (vihesā), doubt (vicikicchā), and mental confusion (manovilekha).

Alternatively, "only to this extent" (yāvadeva) defines an excess. This term should be connected with the word "results in" (saṃvattanti); it means it results excessively in remorse, weariness, and confusion. "Sikkhāpadavivaṇṇake" means that an offense of pācittiya is incurred for thus disparaging or criticizing the training rules.

This training rule was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning the group of six monks (chabbaggiya) in the case of disparaging the Vinaya. It is a common regulation (sādhāraṇa-paññatti), not by command (anāṇattika), and involves a threefold pācittiya (tika-pācittiya). If one disparages it to a non-ordained person (anupasampanna), a threefold dukkaṭa (tika-dukkaṭa) is incurred. If one disparages teachings other than the Vinaya (Sutta or Abhidhamma) to both [ordained and non-ordained], it is only a dukkaṭa. There is no offense for one who has no intention to disparage, such as one saying, "Venerable, please first learn the Suttanta, the verses, or the Abhidhamma; you will learn the Vinaya later," nor for the insane and so on. The two factors for this training rule are: the intention to disparage and disparaging the training rule in the presence of an ordained monk. The origins (samuṭṭhāna) and so on are similar to the adinnādāna training rule. This rule involves painful feeling (dukkha-vedanā).

## The Commentary on the Vilekhana Training Rule Ends.

## 3. Commentary on the Mohana Training Rule

In the third training rule, "every half-month" (anvaḍḍhamāsaṃ) means successively every half-month. "When it is being recited" (uddissamanne) means being recited by way of the Uposatha. "Whatever offense he falls into in that training rule" means the offense incurred through improper conduct which that monk, having committed it, wishes to let others know he committed unknowingly. "He should be dealt with according to the Dhamma" means that although he committed the offense unknowingly, there is no exemption from it; he must be cured of that offense according to how the Dhamma and Vinaya are established. If it is an offense remediable by confession (desanāgāminī), he must be made to confess; if it is an offense remediable by rehabilitation (vuṭṭhānagāminī)...
253:
...he must be rehabilitated. This is the meaning. "Furthermore, the act of delusion should be imposed on him" means that beyond dealing with him according to the Dhamma, he should be rebuked with words such as "Friend, for you who..." and then the act of delusion (moha-kamma) should be imposed on that person by a formal act consisting of a motion and a second announcement (ñatti-dutiya-kamma). "In this mohanaka, there is a pācittiya" means that if, after the act of delusion has been thus imposed, he causes confusion again, this pācittiya should be understood to apply to that person who causes confusion (mohanaka). It means it is not a pācittiya if the act of delusion has not yet been imposed.

This was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning the group of six monks in the case of delusion (mohana). It is a common regulation, not by command, and involves a threefold pācittiya. In an invalid formal act (adhamma-kamma), it is a threefold dukkaṭa. If one causes confusion before the act of delusion is imposed, it is only a dukkaṭa. There is no offense for one who has not heard the Pātimokkha in detail, or who has heard it in detail less than two or three times, or for those who have no intention to cause confusion, or for the insane and so on. The four factors for this training rule are: the imposition of the act of delusion, the intention to cause confusion, having heard it as mentioned, and the act of causing confusion. The origins and so on are similar to the adinnādāna training rule. This rule involves painful feeling.
