## The Commentary on the Mohana Training Rule Ends.

## 4. Commentary on the Pahāra Training Rule

In the fourth training rule, regarding "should give a blow" (pahāraṃ dadeyya), if a blow is given with the intention to strike, even if the victim dies, it is only a pācittiya.

This was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning the group of six monks in the case of giving a blow. It is a common regulation, not by command, and involves a threefold pācittiya. If one strikes a non-ordained person (anupasampanna), it is a threefold dukkaṭa. Even for an ordained monk, if one cuts off an ear or similar part with the intention to disfigure, it is only a dukkaṭa. There is no offense for one who, being harassed by someone, strikes with the intention to escape, nor for the insane and so on. The three factors for this training rule are: being angry, not having the intention to escape, and giving a blow to an ordained monk. The origins and so on are similar to the first Pārājika. This rule involves painful feeling.

## The Commentary on the Pahāra Training Rule Ends.

## 5. Commentary on the Talasattika Training Rule

In the fifth training rule, "should raise a palm-weapon" (talasattikaṃ uggireyya) means raising the body or a weapon connected to the body, showing the manner of giving a blow. In this rule, a pācittiya is incurred due to the act of raising [the hand or weapon]. If...
254:
However, if one raises [a weapon] and, missing [the target], happens to strike, a dukkhaṭa offense is incurred because it was done without the intention to strike. Even if something like a hand is broken or destroyed by that strike, it is still only a dukkhaṭa offense. Everything else in this training rule should be understood in the same manner as stated in the previous training rule.

## The Explanation of the Talasattika Training Rule is Finished.

## 6. Amūlaka Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā
In the sixth, the Amūlaka training rule: "Amūlakena" means being without grounds or basis such as seeing [the offense] (with a saṅghādisesa offense). "Anuddhaṃseyya" means to accuse oneself or to cause another to accuse. "Pācittiya" means if the accused person understands at that very moment of accusation, "He is accusing me," a pācittiya offense is incurred by the accusing monk.

It was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning the group of six monks regarding the matter of accusing with a groundless saṅghādisesa offense. It is a common regulation (sādhāraṇapaññatti). It is a training rule involving a command (sāṇattika). A triad of pācittiya (tikapācittiya) applies. If one accuses regarding a failure in conduct (ācāravipatti) or a failure in view (diṭṭhivipatti), a dukkhaṭa offense is incurred. If one accuses a non-ordained person (a layperson or a novice), a triad of dukkhaṭa (tikadukkaṭa) applies. There is no offense for a monk who perceives it as such [i.e., that a saṅghādisesa was committed], or for those who are insane, etc. In this training rule, there are four factors: (1) being a monk, (2) the saṅghādisesa offense being groundless, (3) the act of accusing, and (4) the understanding at that moment. The origins (samuṭṭhāna), etc., are similar to the Adinnādāna training rule. This training rule involves painful feeling (dukkhavedanā).

## The Explanation of the Amūlaka Training Rule is Finished.

## 7. Sañcicca Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā
In the seventh, the Sañcicca training rule: "Kukkuccaṃ upadaheyya" means to cause remorse (kukkucca) by saying things such as, "I think you were less than twenty years old [when ordained]," and so forth. For a monk who intentionally causes remorse in this way when there is no other reason for remorse to arise, a pācittiya offense is incurred for every word spoken.

It was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning the group of six monks regarding the matter of causing remorse. It is a common regulation. It is a training rule not involving a command (anāṇattika). A triad of pācittiya applies. If one causes remorse in a non-ordained person, a triad of dukkhaṭa applies. There is no offense for a monk who speaks thus without the intention to cause remorse but out of a desire for [the other's] welfare, or for those who are insane, etc. In this training rule, there are three factors: (1) being a monk, (2) the intention to cause discomfort (aphāsukāmatā), and (3) the causing of remorse. The origins, etc., are the same as the previous training rule.

## The Explanation of the Sañcicca Training Rule is Finished.
255:
## 8. Upassuti Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā
In the eighth training rule: "Vivādāpannānaṃ" refers to those [monks] who have reached a state of dispute (vivādādhikaraṇa) that has escalated through quarreling and contention. "Upassutiṃ" means near the range of hearing; it means standing in a place where it is possible to hear their words. For a monk who goes with the intention to accuse, thinking "I will listen there," a dukkhaṭa offense is incurred for every step. The same applies whether going quickly or lagging behind. If he hears while standing in a certain place, a pācittiya offense is incurred for the monk standing there. Even if those monks come to the place where he is standing and consult together, he should make himself known by clearing his throat or saying, "I am here." For a monk who does not make himself known in this way, a pācittiya offense is incurred simply by hearing.

It was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning the group of six monks regarding the matter of eavesdropping (upassutiṭṭhāna). It is a common regulation, not involving a command (anāṇattika), and a triad of pācittiya applies. For non-ordained persons (laypeople, novices), a triad of dukkhaṭa applies. There is no offense for a monk who goes thinking, "Having heard these [monks], I will desist, refrain, be at peace, or free myself," nor for those who are insane, etc. The three factors are: being a monk, the intention to accuse, and hearing. This training rule has the same origin as the theft-caravan (theyyasattha). It may arise through an act (kiriya) or through an omission (akiriya). It is associated with perception as a means of release (saññāvimokkha), is intentional (sacittaka), is a worldly fault (lokavajja), and involves bodily action, vocal action, unwholesome consciousness, and painful feeling.

## The Explanation of the Upassuti Training Rule is Finished.

## 9. Kammap paṭibāhana Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā
In the ninth training rule: "Dhammikānaṃ kammānaṃ" refers to these four types of legal acts performed according to the Dhamma, the Vinaya, and the Teacher's Dispensation: apalokana-kamma, ñatti-kamma, ñattidutiya-kamma, and ñatticatuttha-kamma. Regarding these acts, the summary decision is as follows: Among these four, the apalokana-kamma is an act performed by announcing the specific matter with the consent of a harmonious Saṅgha and proclaiming three times, "Is it pleasing to the Saṅgha?" An act performed with a single motion (ñatti) with the consent of a harmonious Saṅgha is called ñatti-kamma. An act performed with a single motion and a single proclamation (anussāvana or kammavācā) is called ñattidutiya-kamma.
256:
An act performed with one motion and three proclamations is called a ñatticatutthakamma. Among these acts, the apalokanakamma (act of announcement) reaches five categories: osāraṇā (reinstatement), nissāraṇā (exclusion), bhaṇḍukamma (shaving), brahmadanda (the Brahma-punishment), and kammalakkhaṇa (characteristic of the act). Among these five, an act such as the expulsion of the novice Kaṇṭaka is called nissāraṇā. Seeing that such an expelled novice is practicing well and bringing him back into the Saṅgha is to be known as 'osāraṇā'. Asking for permission to shave the hair of a candidate for ordination is called bhaṇḍukamma. For a monk who is foul-mouthed and harasses other monks with harsh words, the act performed by saying, 'This monk named so-and-so is foul-mouthed and lives harassing monks with harsh words; let that monk say whatever he wishes; the monks should not speak to this monk named so-and-so, nor should they give him advice or instruction, nor should they admonish him,' and then asking, 'Venerable sirs, I ask the Saṅgha: does the Saṅgha approve of the giving of the Brahma-punishment to this monk named so-and-so?' for a second and third time, is called brahmadanda. The Blessed One, due to reasons such as a monk exposing his thigh to the bhikkhunīs, allowed the act of 'not to be saluted' (avandiya), saying, 'Monks, that monk should be made one who is not to be saluted by the Bhikkhunī-saṅgha.' When the bhikkhunīs, while staying in their own convent, perform an act saying, 'Ladies, this venerable one named so-and-so performs what is displeasing to the bhikkhunīs; does the Bhikkhunī-saṅgha approve of making this venerable one not to be saluted?'—such an act is called kammalakkhaṇa because it does not fall under osāraṇā etc., but is merely the characteristic of the act itself. Although this kammalakkhaṇa was prescribed on account of the bhikkhunīs, it is also applicable to the monks. Therefore, when monks wish to give robes to those whose robes have been snatched away, or wish to use or remove objects that should be used or removed, or wish to make a similar lawful agreement, they should perform the apalokanakamma by announcing it three times. All of this falls under kammalakkhaṇa. Thus, the apalokanakamma reaches five categories.

The ñattikamma (act with a motion) reaches nine categories: osāraṇā, nissāraṇā, uposatha, pavāraṇā, sammuti, dāna, paṭiggaha, paccukkaḍḍhana, and kammalakkhaṇa. Among these nine categories, 'Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me. This person named so-and-so is the candidate for ordination of the Venerable so-and-so. He has been instructed by me. If it is suitable for the Saṅgha, let this person named so-and-so...'
257:
...come; he should be told, 'Come.' In this way, bringing a person who seeks the state of a monk (a candidate for ordination) into the Saṅgha is called osāraṇā.

'Venerable sirs, let the venerable ones hear my words. This monk named so-and-so is a dhammakathika (Dhamma-preacher). Neither the Sutta (the Matika) nor the Sutta Vibhaṅga comes to his mind (he has not mastered them). Without considering the meaning, he obstructs the meaning with the shadow of the words. When it is time for the venerable ones to perform the act, let us settle this legal issue by having this monk named so-and-so leave the Saṅgha, and the rest of us shall settle it.' In this way, in the ubbāhika-vinicchaya (referral to a committee), the exclusion of a dhammakathika monk from the Saṅgha is called nissāraṇā.

'Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear my words. Today is the Uposatha day... let the Uposatha be performed.' In this way, a motion set forth by the power of the uposatha act is called uposatha.

'Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear my words. Today is the fifteenth day, the pavāraṇā day. If it is suitable for the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha perform the pavāraṇā.' In this way, a motion set forth by the power of the pavāraṇā act is called pavāraṇā.

'Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear my words. This person named so-and-so is the candidate for ordination of the venerable one named so-and-so. If it is suitable for the Saṅgha, I shall instruct this person named so-and-so,' or 'If it is suitable for the Saṅgha, let the monk named so-and-so instruct this person named so-and-so.' In this way, a motion set forth to designate oneself or another is called sammuti.

'Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear my words. This robe of the monk named so-and-so is to be forfeited and has been surrendered to the Saṅgha. If it is suitable for the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha give this robe to the monk named so-and-so.' In this way, the giving of surrendered robes, bowls, and so forth is called dāna.

'Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear my words. This monk named so-and-so remembers an offense, reveals it, makes it clear, and confesses it. If it is suitable for the Saṅgha, I shall accept the offense of this monk named so-and-so.' That monk should be asked, 'Do you see it?' and he should reply, 'Yes, I see it,' and he should be told, 'Restrain yourself in the future.' In this way, the acceptance of an offense is called paṭiggaha.

'Venerable sirs, residents of this monastery, let the venerable ones hear my words. If it is suitable for the venerable ones, let us now perform the uposatha, let us recite the Pātimokkha, and let us perform the pavāraṇā at a later time.' In this way, the pulling up (postponing) of a pavāraṇā that has been performed is called paccukkaḍḍhana.

In the tiṇavatthāraka-samatha (covering with grass settlement), the motion that includes everything (sabbasaṅgāhika-ñatti) and the single motion for each side—these three kinds of motions are also called kammalakkhaṇa. Thus, the ñattikamma reaches nine categories.
258:
A formal act with a motion and one proclamation (ñattidutiya-kamma) pertains to seven instances: reinstatement (osāraṇa), expulsion (nissāraṇa), authorization (sammuti), giving (dāna), removal (uddhāra), designation (desana), and the nature of the act (kammalakkhaṇa). Among these seven instances, 'expulsion' refers to the act of turning down the bowl (pattanikkujjana) by the Saṅgha to cease association with a lay follower who possesses the eight factors, such as striving for the loss of the monks. 'Reinstatement' should be understood as the act of turning the bowl upright (pattukkujjana) for that same lay follower when he conducts himself properly. These two, expulsion and reinstatement, are taught in the Khuddakakkhandhaka in the story of Vaḍḍha the Licchavi. 

'Authorization' should be understood by way of these authorizations: authorization of a boundary (sīmā), authorization to be not away from the three robes, authorization of a mat, authorization of a meal-allocator, authorization of a lodging-assigner, authorization of a storekeeper, authorization of a receiver of robes, authorization of a distributor of rice-gruel, authorization of a distributor of fruit, authorization of a distributor of snacks, authorization of a disposer of trifles, authorization of a distributor of rain-robes, authorization of a distributor of bowls, authorization of a sender of monastery-attendants, and authorization of a sender of novices. 

'Giving' should be understood by way of giving Kathina robes and giving the robes of the deceased. 'Removal' should be understood by way of the removal of the Kathina. 'Designation' should be understood by way of designating the site for a hut and the site for a monastery. 'The nature of the act' should be understood by way of the two formal acts with a motion and one proclamation taught in the settlement by covering with grass (tiṇavatthāraka-samatha), one for each side, as well as the formal acts taught in the act of charging with delusion (mohāropana-kamma) and so forth. Thus, a formal act with a motion and one proclamation pertains to seven instances.

A formal act with a motion and three proclamations (ñatticatuttha-kamma) also pertains to only seven instances: reinstatement, expulsion, authorization, giving, punishment (nigga-ha), formal admonition (samanubhāsana), and the nature of the act. Among these seven instances, 'expulsion' should be understood by way of the seven acts such as the act of censure (tajjaniya-kamma), and 'reinstatement' by way of the revocation of those same acts. 'Authorization' is by way of the authorization of an exhorter of nuns. 'Giving' is by way of giving probation (parivāsa) and giving penance (mānatta). 'Punishment' is by way of sending back to the beginning (mūlāyapaṭikassana). 'Formal admonition' should be understood by way of the formal admonitions of these eleven persons: the nun who follows one who is suspended (ukkittānuvattikā), the eight monks who are subject to formal admonition up to the third time (yāvatatiyaka), the monk Ariṭṭha, and the nun Caṇḍakāḷī. 'The nature of the act' should be understood by way of the act of higher ordination (upasampadā-kamma) and the act of rehabilitation (abbhāna-kamma). Thus, a formal act with a motion and three proclamations pertains to seven instances.

Among these four types of acts, an act by announcement (apalokana-kamma) should be performed only by announcement; it should not be performed by way of a formal act with a motion, etc. A formal act with a motion (ñatti-kamma) should be performed only by making a motion once; it should not be performed by way of an act by announcement, etc. As for a formal act with a motion and one proclamation...
259:
There are acts that should be performed by announcement and those that should not. Among those acts, these six acts—authorization of a boundary, removal of a boundary, giving Kathina robes, removal of the Kathina, designation of a site for a hut, and designation of a site for a monastery—are heavy acts (garuka-kamma); therefore, it is not proper to perform them merely by announcement. They must be performed only after proclaiming the formal act with a motion and one proclamation. The remaining thirteen authorizations, along with the authorization of a lodging-assigner and the authorization of giving the robes of the deceased, are light acts (lahuka-kamma); therefore, it is proper to perform them even by announcement, but they should certainly not be performed by way of a formal act with a motion, etc. A formal act with a motion and three proclamations must also be performed only with its own full characteristics, not by way of other acts. Thus, these acts performed with their respective characteristics and with the fulfillment of the basis (vatthu), the motion (ñatti), the proclamation (kammavācā), the boundary (sīmā), and the assembly (parisā), are called 'lawful' (dhammika) because they are performed in accordance with the truth, the Vinaya, and the Teacher's Dispensation. For a monk who, having given his consent (chanda) to such lawful acts, later engages in criticism, there is a pācittiya offense for every word spoken.

It was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning the case of engaging in criticism, with reference to the group of six monks. It is a common regulation (sādhāraṇa-paññatti). It is not by command (anāṇattika). There is a dukkaṭa offense for one who is in doubt about a lawful act, and for one who perceives an unlawful act as a lawful act, or is in doubt about it. There is no offense: for one who perceives it as an unlawful act; for one who criticizes while knowing, "They are performing the act unlawfully, or as a separate group, or for one not worthy of the act"; and for one who is insane, etc. The three factors here are: it is a lawful act, the perception of it as a lawful act, and criticizing after having given consent. The origin (samuṭṭhāna) and so forth are the same as for taking what is not given (adinnādāna). This training rule involves painful feeling.

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on Obstructing Legal Acts is Finished.

## 10. Chandaṃ-adattāgamana-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā

In the tenth training rule on leaving without giving consent, the phrase 'discussion for a decision' (vinicchayakathāyāti) means: as long as the matter has been reported but not yet decided, or as long as the motion has been made but the proclamation has not been finished, it is called an ongoing 'discussion for a decision'. If a monk, desiring to disrupt the act during this interval, leaves the reach of the hand (hatthapāsa) of the assembly, there is a dukkaṭa offense in the act of leaving, and a pācittiya offense when he has left.

It was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning the case of leaving without giving consent, with reference to a certain monk. It is a common regulation. It is not by command. For one who is in doubt about a lawful act...
260:
For one who perceives a legal act (kamma) that is in accordance with the Dhamma as such, or for one who is doubtful, [if they leave,] they incur an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa). However, for one who perceives it as an illegal act—if a monk knows that 'quarrels and so forth will arise in the Saṅgha,' or 'they will perform the act through an illegal or a fragmented assembly, or for one not entitled to the act,' or if he himself is ill, or due to the business of a sick person, or if he is pressed by the need to defecate or urinate, and he goes away with the intention 'I will return again' without the desire to spoil the act, there is no offense for him, nor for those who are insane and so forth.

In this context, the six factors [for the offense] are: the discussion for decision is ongoing, it is a legal act (dhamma-kamma), perceiving it as a legal act, being within the same boundary (sīmā), being of the same communion (samānavāsaka), and leaving the reach of the hand (hatthapāsa) with the desire to spoil the act. This training rule has the same origin as the formal rebuke (samanubhāsana-samuṭṭhāna); it is an offense of action and non-action (kiriyākirya); it is released by perception (saññā-vimokkha); it is intentional (sacittaka); it is a worldly fault (lokavajja); it is produced by bodily and vocal actions; it is produced by unwholesome consciousness; and it has painful feeling.

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on Leaving Without Giving Consent is Finished.

## 11. Dubbala-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā

In the eleventh [explanation], the Dubbala-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā: "Together with a harmonious Saṅgha" means having given a robe together with the Saṅgha that is of the same communion and situated within the same boundary. "According to one's acquaintance" means according to whoever is an acquaintance by way of being a friend, a familiar person, or a devoted attendant; it refers to those specific persons. "Pācittiya" means that for a monk who, after having given a robe to a monk who was himself authorized by the Saṅgha as an assigner of lodgings and so forth, later reviles him, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for every word spoken.

It was laid down in Rājagaha concerning the group of six monks (chabbaggiya) in the case of reviling after giving a robe. It is a common regulation (sādhāraṇa-paññatti) and is non-commandable (anāṇattika) [an offense incurred only by one's own action]. In a legal act, there are three types of pācittiya (tika-pācittiya). If one reviles after giving other distributable and divisible requisites, excluding robes, one incurs an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa). "Distributable and divisible requisites" refers to the remaining requisites excluding the five types of heavy articles (garubhaṇḍa). The Blessed One has taught the five types of heavy articles by way of groups. Among those five: (1) a park (ārāma) and the ground of a park; (2) a monastery (vihāra) and the ground of a monastery; (3) a couch, a chair, a mattress, and a pillow; (4) an iron pot, an iron jar, an iron water-pot, an iron basin, an adze, an axe, a hatchet, a hoe, and a chisel; (5) creepers, bamboo, muñja grass, babbaja grass, grass...
261:
Fine clay, wooden articles, and clayware are the fifth group of heavy articles. Indeed, these five types of property belonging to the Saṅgha should not be given away or divided by the Saṅgha or by a group or an individual. Even if they are given away or divided, they remain the property of the Saṅgha. However, it is allowable to exchange a permanent heavy article for another permanent one, or to exchange an unallowable heavy article or a valuable allowable one for another item beneficial to the Saṅgha, after considering the benefit to the Saṅgha. It is also allowable to dispose of inferior items in order to protect noble monasteries and so forth, and to use [the proceeds].

Among these groups of heavy articles, in the first three groups, there is nothing that is not a heavy article. In the fourth group, these three—iron/bronze pots, iron jars shaped like large water-vessels, and iron basins—are heavy articles even if they hold only a handful of water. As for the iron water-pot (loha-vāraka), if it is made of iron, copper, bronze, lead, or an alloy, and if it holds one pāda (about 5 nāḷi in Magadhan measure) as used in the island of Sīhaḷa, it is divisible. If it holds more than that, it is a heavy article. These are the iron vessels mentioned in the Pali.

Although not directly mentioned in the Pali, small items such as water pitchers, spittoons, ladles, spoons, bowls, saucers, drinking cups, boxes, charcoal pans, and smoking ladles are also heavy articles. Iron bowls, iron plates, and copper plates are, however, divisible. Special vessels made of bronze or lead are allowable if used as Saṅgha property or if they have been altered by laypeople (gihi-vikaṭa); they are not allowable for personal use. Excluding those special vessels, other allowable iron/bronze articles such as collyrium sticks, collyrium pins, nose-tubes, ear-picks, needles, small knives, awls for piercing needle-eyes, hooks, bolts, walking-stick ferrules, forks, solid iron/bronze, and unfinished iron/bronze articles are all divisible.

Smoking pipes, plowshares, lampstands, charcoal pans, hanging lamps, statues of women, men, or animals, or items attached to walls, roofs, and doors—all iron articles down to at least an iron nail—are heavy articles. Even if one has obtained them oneself, they should not be used for personal use; they are allowable as Saṅgha property or if altered by laypeople. The same rule applies to lead (tipu) articles. Bowls, drinking cups, and so forth made of milk-colored stone are also heavy articles.
262:
## 

A pot for lotuses or an oil pot is considered communal property (garubhaṇḍa) only if it exceeds one pāda (approximately one salay) in capacity. Vessels made of gold, silver, brass, or crystal, specially crafted by laypeople, are not allowable (whether communal or personal). However, all items for use as monastery furniture (senāsanaparibhoga) are allowable, whether they are of a type that may be handled or not.

Among billhooks (knives) and similar tools, a small billhook that can only be used for cutting tooth-sticks or peeling sugarcane, and cannot perform other major tasks, is distributable (bhājanīya). Other large billhooks made in various forms are communal property. An axe, even a small one used by physicians for bloodletting, is communal property; likewise, a hatchet is communal property. A knife made in the form of a weapon is an item not to be handled (anāmāsa). There is no such thing as a spade or a handled chisel that is not communal property. However, a chisel without a handle used only for carving broom handles, which can be carried in a small bag, is distributable. An awl is also included in the category of chisels. If laypeople who have donated billhooks and such to a monastery experience a fire or robbery at their home and request, "Venerable sirs, please lend us our utensils for a while; we will return them later," they should be given. If they return them, it should not be forbidden; if they do not return them, they should not be asked for.

All iron or bronze tools of blacksmiths, bronze-smiths, turners, reed-workers, gem-cutters, and bowl-menders, such as anvils, hammers, pincers, and scales, are communal property from the time they are given to the Saṅgha. The same applies to the tools of tin-smiths, goldsmiths, and leather-workers. However, there is this distinction: a small tin-cutting knife of a tin-smith, a small gold-cutting knife of a goldsmith, and a small leather-cutting knife of a leather-worker are distributable. Among the tools of barbers and tailors, except for large scissors, large pincers, and large needles, all other tools are allowable; those large items are communal property.

Among vines and such, any vine like a rattan vine measuring half an arm's length (about a span and four finger-breadths) is communal property, whether it was donated to the Saṅgha or grew on communal land, provided it is guarded and protected. If such vines remain after the work of the Saṅgha and the Cetiya is completed, it is allowable to use them for personal matters as well. Small ropes or leather thongs made of cotton, hemp, coconut fiber, or leather, or communal ropes made by twisting hemp or coconut fiber into single or double strands, are communal property. However, untwisted cotton, hemp, and coconut fiber that have been donated are distributable. Those donors who have donated these small ropes...
263:
## 

...if these small ropes and such were donated by donors, it is not forbidden for those donors to take them for their own necessary tasks.

A piece of bamboo at least eight finger-breadths in length and about the thickness of a stylus, whether donated to the Saṅgha or grown on communal land, is communal property if it is guarded and secured. If such bamboo remains after the work of the Saṅgha and the Cetiya is completed, it is allowable to give it for personal matters. An oil tube holding one pāda of oil, a walking stick, a shoe-hook stick, an umbrella handle, and umbrella ribs are distributable property (bhājanīya) in this context. If people whose houses have burned down take them, it should not be forbidden.

Muñja grass, pabbaja grass, and other roofing grasses, even a handful of roofing grass, or any single leaf among those used for roofing and screening such as palmyra leaves, is communal property if it was donated to the Saṅgha, grew on communal land, or grew in a communal meadow outside the monastery and is guarded. This too, if it remains after the work of the Saṅgha and the Cetiya is completed, it is allowable to be given for personal matters. If people whose houses have burned down take them, it should not be forbidden. A blank palm leaf about eight finger-breadths long is also communal property.

Whether it is ordinary fine earth, five-colored fine earth, plaster, or any substance like resin, wood-oil, or lacquer, if it is brought from a difficult-to-reach place and donated, or if it is produced there and guarded, even an amount the size of a ripe palmyra fruit is communal property. This too, if it remains after the work of the Saṅgha and the Cetiya is completed, it is allowable to be given for personal matters. However, substances like asafoetida, cinnabar, orpiment, realgar, and antimony are distributable property.

Among wooden items, any piece of wood of the size mentioned for bamboo, whether donated to the Saṅgha or grown there and guarded, is communal property. Furthermore, all things made of wood, bamboo, leather, stone, etc., are included under wooden items. Among those wooden items, all seats—starting from rectangular benches and such that are not included among couches and chairs, down to benches made of cloth, straw, or leaves—are communal property.

A curved plank, a long plank, a plank for washing robes, a plank for beating robes, a wooden mallet, a small block for cutting tooth-sticks, a handled mallet, a boat, a water storage trough, a dye trough, a trough for catching robe-wringing water, a casket (with or without legs) made of wood, ivory, or bamboo, a chest, a small box holding more than one pāda, a water trough, a water jar, a water dipper, a ladle, and a drinking cup...
264:
Among these items such as drinking conch shells, any item offered to the Saṅgha is Garubhaṇḍa (heavy property). However, a small conch-shell cup is Bhājanīya (distributable property); likewise, a wooden water bottle is also Bhājanīya.

A circular object similar to a foot-scrubbing pot, whether made of wood, cloth, leaves, etc., is all Garubhaṇḍa. Among items called bowl stands, bowl lids, palm-leaf fans, square fans, flower baskets, baskets, brooms with handles, and hand-brooms—whether small or large, and whether made of wood, bamboo, leaves, leather, etc.—any such item is only Garubhaṇḍa.

Among pillars, beams, stair-planks, etc., whether made of wood or stone, any item that is a component of a monastery building, any mat, any floor covering, any unallowable leather rug—all such Saṅghika property is Garubhaṇḍa; it is allowable to use them as floor coverings. Sheepskin, however, is treated like an upper cover/rug; that sheepskin is also only Garubhaṇḍa. Allowable skins are Bhājanīya items. In the Kurundī Commentary, however, it is stated that all skins the size of a couch are Garubhaṇḍa.

Mortars, pestles, winnowing baskets, grindstones, grindstone rollers, stone troughs, stone pots, and all farming tools are also Garubhaṇḍa. All wheeled vehicles are also only Garubhaṇḍa. Among items called the legs and frames of couches and chairs, and the handles of billhooks, axes, etc., any unfinished item is Bhājanīya; however, an item that has been planed and smoothed is Garubhaṇḍa. The handle of an allowable billhook, umbrellas, hand-held palm leaves, walking sticks, sandals, sets of lathe-turning blocks and pins, water strainers, myrobalan bottles worth not more than one pāda, myrobalan pots, gourd bottles, gourd pots, and horn bottles—all these items are Bhājanīya; if they exceed that [value/size], they are Garubhaṇḍa.

Ivory or any horn, if unplaned and in its natural state, is Bhājanīya. Regarding couch and chair legs, etc., made from those ivory or horns, the decision should be understood as previously stated. Even if planed and finished, items called asafoetida boxes, collyrium boxes, buttons, belt-fasteners, collyrium pots, collyrium sticks, and water-wiping towels—all these are only Bhājanīya.

Among earthenware, all items for human use, both internal and external, such as pots and lids made by potters, bowl-baking pots, charcoal pans, pipes, lampstands, lamp bowls, grooved bricks, roofing tiles, and pinnacles—all are Garubhaṇḍa. Among these aforementioned Garubhaṇḍa items, a monk who wishes to take something like bamboo for himself should take it only after performing phātikamma (replacement/exchange) with an item of equal or greater value.
265:
A small pot (ghaṭaka) with a capacity not exceeding one pāda, bowls, cups, water basins (or bowls), and water pitchers (or ewers)—these are Bhājanīya items among earthenware. Just as with earthenware, among metalware, the water pitcher also belongs only to the Bhājanīya category. Thus, for a monk who gives away such requisites other than robes—known as vissajjīya (disposable) and vebhaṅgiya (distributable)—and then criticizes [the distribution], there is an offense of dukkaṭa. As for avissajjīya (non-disposable) and avebhaṅgiya (non-distributable) requisites other than the vissajjīya vebhaṅgiya ones, it is not even proper to give them away. A monk who gives them away by assuming authority commits a thullaccaya offense. A monk who takes them with the intention to steal should be dealt with by having the property appraised.

Just as there is a dukkaṭa offense for one who gives away requisites other than robes and then criticizes, there is also a dukkaṭa offense for one who gives robes or other requisites to a person not authorized by the Saṅgha and then criticizes. In giving to unordained persons (laypeople or novices), there is a triple dukkaṭa offense in all circumstances. There is no offense for one who criticizes upon seeing a monk acting out of natural favoritism, etc., saying, "What is the use of giving to him? Even if he receives it, he will scatter it about; he will not use it properly," nor is there an offense for those who are insane, etc. The four factors here are: being ordained, being one who has received authorization according to the Dhamma, giving a robe that is suitable for formal transfer (vikappanā) together with the Saṅgha, and criticizing with the desire to disparage later. The originations (samuṭṭhāna), etc., are similar to those of taking what is not given (adinnādāna). This training rule involves painful feeling (dukkha-vedanā).

## The Explanation of the Dubbala Sikkhāpada is Finished.

## 12. Pariṇāmana Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā

In this twelfth training rule, the entire discussion follows the method already stated in the Pariṇāmana Sikkhāpada of the Tiṃsaka Kaṇḍa (Nissaggiya Pācittiya). The distinction is this: in that Tiṃsaka Kaṇḍa Pariṇāmana Sikkhāpada, because one diverts [property] to oneself, it is a Nissaggiya Pācittiya offense. In this training rule, because one diverts it to another person, it is a Suddhika Pācittiya offense.

## The Explanation of the Pariṇāmana Sikkhāpada is Finished.

## The Eighth Chapter: Sahadhammika Vagga.

## 9. Ratana Vagga

## 1. Antepura Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā

In the first training rule of the Ratana Vagga, "khattiyassa" means a king of the Khattiya (warrior) caste. "Muddhābhisittassa" means a king who has been anointed on the head with the Khattiya consecration. It is called "anikkhantarajaka" because the king has not yet departed from the royal bedchamber. It means "in the royal bedchamber where the king has not yet departed." A queen is called "ratana" (gem). "Niggataṃ" means a "gem" that has departed. It is called "aniggataratanaka" because the queen-gem has not yet departed from the royal bedchamber. In that [bedchamber] where the queen-gem has not yet departed...
266:
Because the king has not yet departed from this bedchamber, it is called 'anikkhantarājaka'. It means in that bedchamber from which the king has not yet departed. The chief queen is called 'ratana' (treasure). To have gone out is called 'nikkhanta'; because the queen-treasure has not yet departed from this bedchamber, it is called 'aniggataratanaka'. It means in that bedchamber from which the queen-treasure has not yet departed. Regarding the phrase 'indakhīlaṃ atikkameyya' (should cross the threshold), here, for a monk who crosses the threshold of the bedchamber without making his arrival known, a dukkaṭa offense is incurred at the first step, and a pācittiya offense at the second step.

This was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning the Venerable Ānanda, regarding the incident of entering the king's inner palace. This training rule is an asādhāraṇapaññatti (uncommon regulation), anāṇattika (not involving command), and a tikapācittiya (pācittiya involving a triad). For one who has been announced but perceives himself as not announced, or is in doubt, there is a dukkaṭa offense. There is no offense for: one who perceives himself as announced; one who is not of the kshatriya (warrior-noble) class; a king who has not yet been consecrated; when both the king and queen have departed, or when either of the two has departed and one enters the bedchamber; in a place that is not a bedchamber; and for those who are insane, etc. These are the five factors here: being a kshatriya, being consecrated, both not having departed from the bedchamber, not being announced, and crossing the threshold. The origins (samuṭṭhāna) and so forth are similar to the first Kathina training rule. This training rule, however, is kiriya-akiriya (involving both action and inaction).

## The Commentary on the Antepura Training Rule Ends.

## 2. Ratanasikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā

In the second training rule, 'ratana' (gem/treasure) refers to the ten kinds of gems such as pearls, etc. 'Ratanasammata' (regarded as a treasure) refers to any kind of internal or external utility used by humans. 'Ajjhārāme vā' (or in the monastery) means within the enclosure if the monastery is fenced; if it is not fenced, it means within the range of two stone-throws. 'Ajjhāvasathe' (in the dwelling) means within the enclosure if the house is fenced; if it is not fenced, it means within the range of a pestle-fall. Here is the decision: if one picks up or causes someone to pick up gold or silver for oneself, a nissaggiya pācittiya offense is incurred. If it is for the sake of the Saṅgha, a group, an individual, a stupa, or construction work (navakamma), a dukkaṭa offense is incurred. Regarding the remaining gems such as pearls, etc., a dukkaṭa offense is incurred regardless of whom they are for. Even if it is the property of one's own mother, if a monk stores it as a storekeeper, whether it is a kapiya (allowable) or akapiya (unallowable) object, he incurs a pācittiya offense. However, it is allowable to store such property of one's mother by treating it as one's own. When requested, 'Please store this,' one should refuse, saying, 'It is not allowable.'
267:
One should refuse, saying, 'It is not allowable.' If the owners, being angry, drop the item and leave, it becomes what is called a 'palibodha' (a responsibility/impediment); in that case, it must be stored. If carpenters and others working in the monastery, or those close to the king, say, 'Please store some utility or bedding for us,' one must not do so out of affection or fear; however, it is allowable to show them a secure place.

In the monastery or in the dwelling, only in such places where there is a suspicion that 'it might have been picked up by monks or novices,' should one pick it up oneself or cause another to pick it up, mark it, and store it. One should also announce, 'Whoever has lost an item, let that person come.' Then, the person who comes should be asked, 'What kind of marks does your item have?' If they can describe it according to the marks, it should be given. If not, they should be told, 'Look for it further.' A monk departing from that monastery should entrust it into the hands of suitable monks; if such monks are not present, he should entrust it into the hands of suitable lay devotees before departing. If he does not depart and does not see the owner, he should use that property to build a permanent dwelling, a stupa, or a pond. If the owner arrives after a long time, one should show the structure and say, 'Please rejoice (in this merit).' If the owner does not rejoice and demands, 'Give me my wealth,' one must collect and compensate them.

This was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning an unnamed monk regarding the incident of picking up a treasure. The phrase 'except in a monastery or in a dwelling' is the twofold anupaññatti (supplementary regulation), a sādhāraṇapaññatti (common regulation), and a sāṇattika (involving command) in this training rule. For a monk who picks up an item in an allowed place but out of disrespect fails to store it, there is a dukkaṭa offense. There is no offense for: one who picks up and stores it in an allowed place; one who picks up a valuable object (ratanasammata) that is touchable out of trust (vissāsa) or for temporary use; one who takes it perceiving it as ownerless (paṃsukūla); and for those who are insane, etc. These are the four factors here: performing an unallowed act, the object belonging to another, the absence of trust or paṃsukūla perception, and picking it up or causing it to be picked up. The origins (samuṭṭhāna) and so forth are similar to the Sañcaritta training rule.

## The Commentary on the Ratana Training Rule Ends.
268:
## 3. Vikālagāmappavesanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

In the third training rule, the phrase 'santāṃ bhikkhuṃ anāpucchā' (without asking a monk who is present) is to be understood in the same manner as explained in the Cāritta training rule. 'Vikāla' (improper time) refers to the period from the time past noon until before dawn. Within that interval, if a monk—without asking permission by saying 'I ask permission to enter the village at an improper time' or 'I will enter the village', and in the absence of such urgent business—crosses the boundary of a fenced village or enters the precinct of an unfenced village, he incurs an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa) at the first step, and an offense of expiation (pācittiya) at the second step. If many monks enter a village for some business, they must all ask permission of one another. For monks who go to another village because 'that business is not completed in that village', there is no need to ask permission again. However, if they have quelled their effort to enter a village and are returning to the monastery, but wish to enter another village on the way before reaching the monastery, they must indeed ask permission. A monk who has finished his meal duties at a family house or a refectory and wishes to wander for alms of oil or ghee must ask permission if there is a monk nearby; if there is none, he may go, thinking 'there is no one'. Even if he sees a monk after having descended onto the street, there is no further duty to ask permission.

For a monk traveling on a road through the middle of a village, if the thought arises, 'I will wander for the sake of oil and so on', he must ask permission if he sees a monk nearby. For one who wanders without deviating from the road, there is no duty to ask permission; for one who deviates, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) as previously stated.

This training rule was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning the group of six monks (chabbaggiya) in the case of entering a village at an improper time. The phrases 'santāṃ bhikkhuṃ', 'anāpucchā', and 'aññatra tathārūpā accāyikā karaṇīyā' are the three additional regulations (anupaññatti) in this training rule. This training rule is an unshared regulation (asādhāraṇapaññatti), it is not by command (anāṇattika), and it involves a triad of expiation (tika-pācittiya). For a monk who perceives the improper time as the proper time, or who is in doubt, there is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa). There is no offense for: a monk who enters perceiving the time as the proper time; a monk who enters when there is urgent business; a monk who enters after asking a monk who is present; a monk who enters without asking when no monk is present; a monk who goes to any of the following within a village: a monastery, a nunnery, a place of titthiyas, or a refectory; a monk traveling on a road that passes through a village; a monk entering during times of danger; and for insane monks, etc. The three factors here are: not asking a monk who is present, the absence of an authorized reason, and entering a village at an improper time. The origins (samuṭṭhāna) and so on are similar to the Kathina training rule; however, this is an action and non-action (kiriyākiriyā).

## The Commentary on the Training Rule on Entering a Village at an Improper Time is finished.
269:
## 4. Sūcigharasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

In the fourth training rule, breaking itself is called 'bhedanaka'; because it has this factor of breaking, the expiation offense is called 'bhedanaka'. Therefore, there is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa) in making or having such needle cases made. Upon receiving it, however, one must break that needle case and then confess the offense of expiation (pācittiya).

This was laid down in the Sakyan country concerning many monks in the case of requesting many needle cases. This is a shared regulation (sādhāraṇapaññatti). It is by command (sāṇattika). There is a fourfold expiation (catukka-pācittiya) for one who obtains it after finishing what was unfinished by himself, either by himself or by others, or after finishing what was unfinished by others, either by himself or by others. There is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa) in making or having it made for another, and in using what was made by another after receiving it.

There is no offense for a monk who makes any of the following out of bone and so on: a button (ganṭhika), a spindle (araṇika), a belt buckle (vidha), a collyrium box (añjanī), a collyrium stick (añjanisalākā), a hatchet handle (vāsijaṭa), or a water-wiper (udakapuñchanī); and for insane monks, etc. The three factors here are: it being a needle case, it being made of bone etc., and the receiving of it after making it or having it made for oneself. The origins (samuṭṭhāna) and so on are similar to the Sañcaritta training rule.

## The Commentary on the Training Rule on Needle Cases is finished.

## 5. Mañcapīṭhasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

In the fifth, 'mañca' (couch) refers to any of the four types of couches such as masāraka. 'Pīṭha' (chair/stool) is similar, but it is not very long like a couch, nor is it level and square like an āsandika (high chair). 'Chedanaka' (cutting) is just like bhedanaka.

This was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning Venerable Upananda in the case of sleeping on a high couch. There is no offense for: a monk who makes it according to the measure; a monk who, having obtained one that exceeds the measure, uses it after cutting it so that only the proper measure is visible above, either by burying it in the ground, or by turning it over, or by constructing a scaffold; and for insane monks, etc. The two factors here are: it being a couch or chair exceeding the measure, and the receiving of it after making it or having it made for oneself. All the rest is just like the Sūcighara training rule.

## The Commentary on the Training Rule on Couches and Chairs is finished.
270:
## 6. Tūlonaddha-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā

In the sixth training rule, it is called 'tūlonaddha' (stuffed with cotton) because cotton is stuffed into the bed or chair. It refers to a bed or chair made by spreading a coarse cloth, putting cotton inside, and covering it with another coarse cloth on top. 'Uddālanaka' (tearing out) is the same as 'bhedanaka' (destroying).

This was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning the group of six monks (chabbaggiya) who had beds and chairs stuffed with cotton made. There is no offense for an āyoga-patta (binding strap), a kāyabandhana (waistband), an aṃsabaddhaka (shoulder strap), a bowl-bag (pattatthavikā), a water-filter (parissāvana), or a pillow (bimbohana); nor for a monk who, having obtained a bed or chair stuffed with cotton made by another, uses it after tearing out the cotton; nor for one who is insane, etc. In this context, a pillow is allowable only if it is the size of a head. The 'size of a head' means that in terms of width, the distance between two of the three corners is one span and four finger-breadths; in the middle, it is one cubit and a fist; and in length, it is one and a half or two cubits. The two factors for this offense are: it being a bed or chair stuffed with cotton, and making it for oneself or having it made and then obtaining it. The rest is to be understood as previously explained.

## The Commentary on the Tūlonaddha Training Rule Ends.

## 7. Nisīdana-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā

In the seventh training rule, 'nisīdana' (sitting cloth) is the name of a requisite similar to a rug (santhata), which is spread out and has three fringes made by splitting a section the size of one Sugata-span at one end in two places.

This was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning the group of six monks who wore oversized sitting cloths. The supplementary regulation (anupaññatti) here is: "The fringe shall be one span." This is an uncommon regulation (asādhāraṇa-paññatti). There is no offense for a monk who makes a sitting cloth of the correct size or smaller; for one who, having obtained an oversized one made by another, uses it after cutting it down; for one who makes anything such as a canopy (vitāna); or for one who is insane, etc. The two factors for this offense are: the sitting cloth exceeding the prescribed size, and making it for oneself or having it made and then obtaining it. The rest is to be understood as previously explained.

## The Commentary on the Nisīdana Training Rule Ends.
271:
## 8. Kaṇḍuppaṭicchādi-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā

In the eighth training rule, 'kaṇḍuppaṭicchādi' (itch-covering cloth) is a robe allowed for the purpose of covering itches, boils, discharging sores, or thick scabs (scabies) from below the navel to above the knee. This rule was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning the group of six monks who wore oversized itch-covering cloths. It is a common regulation (sādhāraṇa-paññatti). The rest is to be understood as explained in the Nisīdana training rule. ## The Commentary on the Kaṇḍuppaṭicchādi Training Rule Ends. ## 9. Vassikasāṭika-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā In the ninth training rule, this was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning the group of six monks who wore oversized rain-bathing cloths. The remaining points to be mentioned here are exactly as explained in the Nisīdana training rule. ## The Commentary on the Vassikasāṭika Training Rule Ends. ## 10. Nanda-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā In the tenth training rule, this was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning the Venerable Nanda, who wore a robe the size of the Buddha's robe. It is a common regulation. The remaining points are exactly as explained in the Nisīdana training rule. ## The Commentary on the Nanda Training Rule Ends. ## The Ninth Chapter on Jewels (Ratana-vagga). ## In the Commentary on the Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī Pātimokkha, ## The Commentary on the Pure Pācittiya (Suddha-pācittiya) Ends.
272:
## Pāṭidesanīya Section
## 1. Commentary on the First Pāṭidesanīya Training Rule
In the first training rule among the Pāṭidesanīyas, according to the words "antara-gharaṃ paviṭṭhāya" (having entered the village), if that nun gives while standing in a village monastery compound etc., and the monk himself receives it while standing in any of the places such as a street, an alley, a crossroads, or a house, there is no offense. However, if that nun gives while standing in a main road etc., or if she gives while standing in a main road or a village monastery compound etc., for a monk who receives any kind of nutriment for the purpose of swallowing, there is a dukkaṭa offense upon receiving, and a pāṭidesanīya offense for every swallow. The manner in which that offense is to be confessed has already been shown in the training rule by the method starting with "Gārayhaṃ āvuso" (It is blameworthy, friend).

It was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning a certain monk, in the case of receiving nutriment from the hand of an unrelated nun who had entered the village. This training rule is an uncommon regulation (asādhāraṇa-paññatti) and is not by command (anāṇattika). Just like this training rule, the remaining ones are also the same. It is a triad of pāṭidesanīya (tika-pāṭidesanīya). In receiving or swallowing yāmakālika (watch-period) etc., a dukkaṭa offense is incurred. In receiving yāvakālika (until-noon food) from a nun ordained by only one side of the Saṅgha, it is likewise a dukkaṭa. The same method applies to those who perceive an unrelated nun as related or who are in doubt. For a monk who perceives her as related, or if a related nun has someone else give it, or if she gives it after placing it down, or if any nun standing in a village monastery, a nunnery, a titthiya monastery, or a rest house gives it after taking it outside the village, or if she gives yāmakālika etc. saying, "Please use it if there is a cause," or for a monk who uses it after receiving it from the hands of that nun, a sikkhamānā (probationer), or a sāmaṇerī (novice), or for insane persons etc., there is no offense. The five factors here are: being a fully ordained nun, being unrelated, receiving with one's own hand from the hand of a nun standing in the village, being yāvakālika, and swallowing. The origins (samuṭṭhāna) etc. are the same as the Eḷakaloma training rule.

## End of the Commentary on the First Pāṭidesanīya Training Rule.
## 2. Commentary on the Second Pāṭidesanīya Training Rule
In the second training rule, the words "Idha sūpaṃ" (Here, curry) etc. show the manner of giving instructions. The words "Apasakka tāva bhaginī" (Step aside for a moment, sister) etc. show the manner of rebuking. The decision therein is: If even another monk does not rebuke, for monks who receive nutriment for the purpose of swallowing, there is a dukkaṭa upon receiving, and a pāṭidesanīya offense for every swallow. This training rule is laid down because of the reason of not rebuking when a nun gives instructions. It is a tika-pāṭidesanīya. If a monk does not rebuke when a nun ordained by only one side of the Saṅgha gives instructions, he incurs a dukkaṭa offense. For a monk who does not rebuke an unordained person, perceiving them as a nun or being in doubt, it is likewise a dukkaṭa offense. However, for a monk who receives and uses it while perceiving an unordained person as unordained, or if a monk has his own alms given or gives the alms of others, there is no offense.
273:
Even if it is a single monk, for those monks who, without preventing [the nun giving directions], accept food or edibles for the purpose of swallowing, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) in the act of accepting, and an offense to be confessed (pāṭidesanīya) for every swallow.

This training rule was laid down in Rājagaha concerning the Group-of-Six monks in the matter of not preventing a nun who was giving directions. It is a Triad-Pāṭidesanīya (tika-pāṭidesanīya). For a monk who does not prevent a nun who has been ordained by both sides [the Saṅghas] while she is giving directions, there is an offense of wrong-doing. Similarly, for a monk who perceives one who is not a nun (a sikkhamānā or a sāmaṇerī) as a nun, or who is in doubt, there is an offense of wrong-doing. For a monk who perceives one who is not a nun as not a nun; or if a nun causes his own food to be given; or if she gives others' food herself; or if she causes food that has not yet been offered to be given; or if she causes food to be given to one to whom it has not been offered; or if she causes food to be given equally to all monks; or for a monk who eats after accepting from a sikkhamānā or a sāmaṇerī who is giving directions; or in the case of food other than the five types of meals, such as gruel, hard food, fruit, etc.; and for one who is insane, etc., there is no offense. The five factors here are: (1) being a fully ordained nun, (2) the five types of meals, (3) giving directions in a manner other than what is permitted in a village, (4) not preventing her, (5) swallowing. The origin (samuṭṭhāna) etc., are the same as the Kathina training rule.

## The Commentary on the Second Pāṭidesanīya Training Rule is Finished.

## 3. Commentary on the Third Pāṭidesanīya Training Rule

In the third training rule, "sekhasammatāni" means those [families] who have received the designation of Sekha (trainee). "Pubbe animantito" means not being invited beforehand, prior to entering the precincts of the house. The name "agilāno" refers to a monk who is able to go on almsround. "Pāṭidesanīyaṃ" means: for a monk who enters the precincts of the house and accepts food or edibles, there is an offense of wrong-doing in the act of accepting; when he takes that food and eats it anywhere, there is an offense to be confessed for every swallow.

This training rule was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning many monks in the matter of accepting without knowing the proper measure. These two supplementary regulations (anupaññatti)—"not invited beforehand" and "not ill"—exist in this training rule. It is a Triad-Pāṭidesanīya. There is an offense of wrong-doing in accepting and swallowing in the case of yāmakālika (to be taken within a watch), etc. Similarly, for a monk who perceives a family not designated as Sekha as one that is designated, or who is in doubt, there is an offense of wrong-doing. For a monk who perceives a family not designated as Sekha as not designated; or if he was invited beforehand; or if he is ill; or if he accepts food belonging to another, or food placed in the house of those Sekha-designated families (there is no offense). For a monk to whom they give food brought out from the house to a dining hall, etc.; or if they give food brought out from the house and placed near the door before seeing the monk; for a monk who eats that food; in the case of a constant meal (niccabhatta), a meal by tickets (salākabhatta), a meal on a fortnight (pakkhikabhatta), a meal on an Uposatha day (uposathikabhatta), a meal on the first day of the fortnight (pāṭipadikabhatta); for a monk who consumes yāmakālika etc., after being told "Consume it if there is a reason"; and for one who is insane, etc., there is no offense.
274:
Whether it be a monk who is ill, or for the sake of another, if he accepts food prepared in the house of those [Sekha-designated] families; or if food is brought out from the house and given in a dining hall etc., or placed at the door before seeing the monk, for a monk who eats that food; for a monk who eats constant meals, ticket-meals, fortnightly meals, Uposatha-meals, first-day meals; for a monk who consumes yāmakālika etc. when offered with the words "Consume if there is a reason"; and for one who is insane, etc., there is no offense.

There are five factors in this training rule: being a family designated as Sekha, not being invited beforehand, not being ill (agilāna), entering the precincts of the house, and accepting and eating food other than constant meals, etc. The origin etc., are the same as the Eḷakaloma training rule.

## The Commentary on the Third Pāṭidesanīya Training Rule is Finished.

## 4. Commentary on the Fourth Pāṭidesanīya Training Rule

In the fourth training rule, the meaning of the words "yāni kho pana tāni āraññakāni" etc., should be understood in the same way as stated in the Cīvaravippavāsa training rule. In the phrase "pubbe appaṭisaṃviditaṃ": if a woman, a man, a layperson, or a [non-Buddhist] renunciant enters a monastery or its precincts and informs: "Venerable sir, such-and-such a family will bring hard food or soft food," and then it is brought as informed; or if many other items of hard or soft food are brought along with it as accompaniments; or if other families, hearing that "such-and-such a family has notified beforehand and is coming with hard or soft food," also bring [food] with them—all this is called "paṭisaṃvidita" (notified beforehand). That which is not informed and not brought in this way is called "appaṭisaṃvidita" (not notified beforehand). One who is able to go for alms is called "agilāna".

"Pāṭidesanīyaṃ" means: for a monk who accepts such hard or soft food—even if given by travelers passing through the middle of the monastery—within the monastery or its precincts and swallows it, there is an offense of wrong-doing in the act of accepting, and an offense to be confessed (pāṭidesanīya) for every swallow.

This training rule was laid down in the Sakyan country concerning many monks because of the matter of not informing about thieves (robbers) living in the monastery. The word "agilāno" is a supplementary regulation in this training rule.
275:
It is a threefold Pāṭidesanīya. In the case of yāmakālika (time-limited) medicines and such, there is only an offense of dukkaṭa (wrongdoing) in both receiving and swallowing them for the purpose of nutriment. Similarly, for a monk who perceives food that has been informed beforehand as not informed, or for one who is in doubt, there is also an offense of dukkaṭa.

However, there is no offense for: a monk who perceives it as informed; a monk who is sick; food that is the remainder of what was informed or the remainder of a sick monk's food; food received outside the monastery; roots, fruits, etc., that grow within that very monastery; a monk who consumes whatever among yāmakālika etc. is obtained after being told, "Consume it if there is a cause"; and those who are insane, etc.

The seven factors here are: being a forest dwelling with the aforementioned dangers, the yāvakālika (temporary) food not growing in that forest dwelling, not being sick, not being the remainder of a sick monk's food, not being informed beforehand, receiving it within the monastery, and swallowing it. The origins (samuṭṭhāna) and so forth are the same as the Kathina training rule. This training rule is of the kiriyākirya (action or omission) type.

## The Explanation of the Fourth Pāṭidesanīya Training Rule is Finished.
## In the Explanation of the Pātimokkha in the Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī,
## the Explanation of the Pāṭidesanīya is Finished.
276:
## Sekhiya Section
## 1. Explanation of the Parimaṇḍala Training Rule
In the Parimaṇḍala training rule, which is the first among the Sekhiya training rules, "parimaṇḍala" means wearing [the robe] in a circular manner all around. The training should be practiced in all places, whether in the monastery or in the village, with the thought, "I will wear [the robe] in a circular manner." In these Sekhiya training rules, the duties taught in the Vattakkhandhaka are also Sekhiyas because they must be practiced; therefore, they are not categorized by number as in the Pārājika and other rules. For the purpose of showing the discipline of conduct (cāritta-vinaya), the Pāḷi text was established for all training rules as "The training is to be done," rather than stating the name of the offense as "If a monk wears it hanging down, there is an offense of dukkaṭa." However, in the Padabhājanīya, it is stated, "There is an offense of dukkaṭa"; thus, it should be understood that in all Sekhiya training rules, a dukkaṭa offense occurs due to disregard (anādariya).

Now, regarding "parimaṇḍala" here: a monk who wears the lower robe (nivāsana) by covering the circle of the navel and letting it down to a length of about eight finger-breadths from the shin bone below the kneecap is said to be wearing it in a circular manner all around. For a monk who does not wear it thus but, out of disregard, wears it hanging down in the front or in the back, there is an offense of dukkaṭa. Not only for that monk, but also for a monk who wears it according to the faults of wearing mentioned in the Khandhaka: "At that time, the group of six monks wore [the robe] like laypeople; they wore it in the elephant's trunk style (hatthisoṇḍaka), the fish-tail style (macchavālaka), the four-cornered style (catukkaṇṇaka), the palmyra-fan style (tālavaṇṭaka), the style with many folds (satavalika), and the tucked-up style (saṃvalliye)," there is also an offense of dukkaṭa.

Among those styles of wearing: hatthisoṇḍaka means wearing it hanging down from the base of the navel in the shape of an elephant's trunk, like the way women of the Coḷa country wear it. macchavālaka means wearing it with the hem hanging down on one side and the inner corner hanging down on the other. catukkaṇṇaka means wearing it showing four corners—two at the top and two at the bottom. tālavaṇṭaka means wearing the robe hanging down in the shape of a palmyra-leaf fan. satavalika means wearing a long robe by coiling it many times into a roll, or wearing it showing folds continuously on the left and right sides. However, if one or two folds are visible from the knee downwards, it is allowable.
277:
"Saṃvalli" refers to wearing the robe by tucking it up or like a loincloth, as boxers or laborers do. This manner of dress is not permissible even for a sick monk or a monk traveling on a road. For monks traveling on a road, it is not permissible to lift one or two corners and hook or tuck them above the lower robe (antaravāsaka), nor is it permissible to wear one lower robe inside with the corners tucked up and another robe over it; all such ways of wearing are not permissible.

A sick monk, however, is allowed to show the roll (ovaṭṭika) of the inner lower robe and wear another one over it. A monk who is not sick, if wearing two robes, must wear them together as a double layer. Thus, avoiding all prohibited ways of wearing mentioned in the Khandhaka and the "hanging down" style, one should wear the robe "all around" (parimaṇḍala), without distortion and endowed with the prescribed characteristics. For one who does not wear it thus and creates any distortion, there is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa).

In the decision starting with "Nidānaṃ puggalaṃ vatthu," the surusuru training rule was laid down in the city of Kosambī. The two rules concerning hands with food (sāmisa) and rinsing the water-pot and bowl with grains of rice were laid down in the Bhagga country on account of many monks. All the remaining Sekhiya rules were laid down in Sāvatthī on account of the group of six monks (chabbaggiya), regarding matters such as wearing the robe hanging down. In the rule on requesting bean-curd and rice (sūpodana-viññatti) and in rules concerning teaching the Dhamma, there is one supplementary regulation (anupaññatti) regarding the sick. All the Sekhiya rules are common regulations (sādhāraṇa-paññatti) shared with bhikkhunīs. They are rules without command (anāṇattika). In all of them, there is only an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa); there is no other variety of offense. The investigation of the failure (vipatti) has already been mentioned. We shall show the origin (samuṭṭhāna) and so forth at the end of all the Sekhiya rules. The non-offense and the factors should be stated for all. They are stated as follows: In this training rule, there is no offense for one who is unintentional, for one who is unmindful, for one who does not know, for one who is sick, in times of danger, and for those who are insane, etc.

Among those, "unintentional" (asañcicca) means there is no offense for one who, without the intention "I will wear it not all around," but rather with the thought "I will wear it all around," wears it not all around due to a mistake. "Unmindful" (assatiyā) means there is no offense for one who wears it thus while the mind is elsewhere. "Unknowing" (ajānantassa) means there is no offense for one who does not know how to wear it all around; however, the duty of wearing the robe should be learned. If a monk has thin calves or large calf muscles, it is permissible to wear it lowered more than eight finger-breadths for the sake of suitability. "Sick" (gilānassa) means if a monk has a sore on his calf or foot, it is permissible for him to wear it either lifted or lowered. "In times of danger" (āpadāsu) means when wild beasts or robbers are pursuing...
278:
...there is no offense. For the insane and so forth, the method is as already stated. Herein, there are three factors: (1) disrespect, (2) absence of a reason for non-offense, (3) wearing it not all around. Just as in this rule, in all the rules, there are only three factors: the first two factors and the doing of the opposite of what is stated in each rule. Therefore, after this, we shall state only the non-offense (anāpatti) without mentioning those factors.

## 2. Commentary on the Second Parimaṇḍala Training Rule

In the second training rule, "Monks, the layperson's way of covering should not be used," thus it was prohibited. Covering by making both corners even, without covering in the layperson's way, is called "covering all around" (parimaṇḍala-pāruta). Among those lay styles: covering like those who wear white cloth, covering like wanderers (paribbājaka), covering with a single cloth, covering like drunkards, covering like those in the inner palace, covering like head carpenters, covering like those entering a field hut, covering like Brahmins, and covering like a monk who arranges the line—all these ways of covering other than the "all around" characteristic are called "layperson's covering" (gihīpāruta).

Therefore, one should not cover like the half-clad (aḍḍhapālaka) Nigaṇṭhas who wear white cloth; or like some wanderers who leave the chest open and place the covering on both shoulder-points; or like people with a single cloth who cover the back with one end of the worn cloth and place both corners on both shoulder-points; or like drunkards and others who wrap the cloth around the neck and let both ends hang on the chest or throw them over the back; or like palace women who cover themselves veiled, showing only the eyes; or like head carpenters who wear a long cloth and cover the whole body with one end of it; or like farmers who, when entering a field hut, wrap the cloth, tuck it into the armpits, and cover the body with one end of it; or like Brahmins who insert the cloth between both armpits and place it on the shoulder-points; or like a monk who arranges the line, who, while covering with one shoulder, leaves the left arm open and places the robe on the shoulder-point. Avoiding all these faults of covering and other similar faults, one should cover "all around" without distortion.

For one who does not cover thus and, out of disrespect, creates any distortion either in the monastery or in an inhabited area, there is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa). The non-offense (anāpatti) is the same as the previous one. Just as in this rule, it is the same in all rules. Where there is a distinction, we shall state it in that place.
279:
## 3-4. Commentary on the Suppaṭicchanna Training Rules
In the third training rule, 'suppaṭicchanna' means being well-covered. It means fastening the button in the loop, covering the neck with the edge of the hem, keeping both edges even, rolling them, and covering down to the wrists, with the intention, 'I will go into the village.' For a monk who goes without doing so, exposing either the knees or the chest, there is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa).

In the fourth training rule, a monk who sits covering the rest of the body while exposing the head from the hollow of the throat upwards, the outer hands from the wrists onwards, and the lower feet from the calf muscles onwards, is called 'suppaṭicchanna.' In this training rule, there is no offense for a monk who has arrived in the village for the purpose of staying.

## 5-6. Commentary on the Susaṃvuta Training Rules
In the fifth training rule, 'susaṃvuta' means one who is well-disciplined, not playing with the hands or feet. The same method applies to the sixth training rule.

## 7-8. Commentary on the Okkhittacakkhu Training Rules
In the seventh training rule, 'okkhittacakkhu' means having downcast eyes, looking at the ground about a yoke's length (four cubits) ahead while walking. However, it is permissible to stop in one place and look around to see if there are dangers such as elephants or horses. The same method applies to the eighth training rule.

## 9-10. Commentary on the Ukkhittaka Training Rules
In the ninth training rule, 'ikkhittakāya' refers to the act of lifting. It means having the robe lifted on one side or both sides. One must not go in this manner (with the robe lifted) starting from inside the village threshold (indakhīla).

In the tenth training rule, even a monk who is taking out a water filter (dhamakaraṇa) while sitting must take it out without lifting the robe. There is no offense for a monk who is staying [in a house].

## 11-12. Commentary on the Ujjagghika Training Rules
In the eleventh training rule, 'ujjagghikāya' means laughing loudly. Here too, the instrumental case is used in the sense of 'characterized by such a state' (itthambhūtalakkhaṇa).

The same method applies to the twelfth training rule. In both rules, there is no offense for a monk who merely smiles when there is a reason for laughter.
280:
## 13-14. Commentary on the Uccasadda Training Rules
In the thirteenth training rule, 'appasadda' means not having a high-pitched or loud, spreading voice. The same method applies to the fourteenth training rule. The definition of being low-voiced (appasadda) in these rules is as follows: If, in a house twelve cubits long, the senior monk (Saṅghatthera) sits at the beginning, the second elder in the middle, and the third elder at the end; when the senior monk consults with the second elder, if the second elder hears the sound and can distinguish the words, but the third elder only hears the sound and cannot distinguish the words, then it is considered a low voice (appasadda) to this extent. If the third elder can also distinguish the words, it is called a loud voice (mahāsadda).

## 15-20. Commentary on the Kāyappacālakādi Training Rules
In the next six training rules, 'kāyappacālaka' means walking while repeatedly swaying the body; this method applies to all [these rules]. Therefore, one should walk and sit while keeping the body and so forth firmly controlled, motionless, and upright. In the three training rules related to sitting, there is no offense for a monk staying inside a monastery.

## 21-22. Commentary on the Khambhakata Training Rules
In the twenty-first and twenty-second training rules, 'khambhakata' means placing the hands on the waist and standing with arms akimbo.

## 23-24. Commentary on the Oguṇṭhita Training Rules
In the twenty-third and twenty-fourth training rules, 'oguṇṭhita' means being wrapped up including the head.

## 25. Commentary on the Ukkuṭika Training Rules
In the twenty-fifth training rule, 'ukkuṭikā' refers to walking while touching the ground only with the toes while lifting the heels, or only with the heels while lifting the toes. Here, the instrumental case has the same characteristic as previously mentioned.
281:
## 26. Commentary on the Pallatthika Training Rules
In the twenty-sixth training rule, 'na pallatthikāya,' one must not sit clasping the knees with the hands or with a cloth (āyogapaṭṭa). For a monk who sits disrespectfully, there is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa). However, upon reaching the place of residence (monastery), there is no offense in this rule, nor in the previously mentioned twenty-second to twenty-fourth rules.

## The Commentary on the Twenty-Six Sāruppiya Training Rules is Finished.

## 27. Commentary on the Sakkaccapaṭiggahaṇa Training Rule
Among the training rules related to food, in the first rule, 'sakkaccaṃ' means establishing mindfulness (receiving with respect).

## 28. Commentary on the Pattasaññīpaṭiggahaṇa Training Rule
In the second training rule, the perception (saññā) regarding the bowl is called 'pattasaññā.' One who has that perception is 'pattasaññī.' It means one should receive [food] with the mind focused on one's own bowl.

## 29. Commentary on the Samasūpakapaṭiggahaṇa Training Rule
In the third training rule, 'samasūpaka' means that the bean curry made from mung beans, black grams, or horse grams, etc., which can be taken by hand, is in a quantity equal to one-fourth of the rice. For a monk who takes more than that, there is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa). Excluding the bean curry, all other various side dishes are called 'rasarasa' (savory dishes). Regarding these savory dishes, or when relatives or those who have invited [the monk] offer them, or when receiving for the sake of another, or when purchasing with one's own funds, there is no offense in this training rule.

## 30-32. Commentary on the Samatittika Training Rule
In the fourth training rule, 'samatittikaṃ' means being evenly full, filled up to the inner rim-line of a prescribed bowl (adhiṭṭhānupaga) without exceeding it. 'Piṇḍapātaṃ' refers to any yāvakālika (food allowed from dawn to noon). In a bowl that is not prescribed, it is permissible to receive yāvakālika food, yāmakālika (drinks), etc., even if they are heaped up in some vessel. Receiving with two bowls and filling one to carry to the monastery; cakes, sugarcane pieces, or fruits falling down while being poured; offering items like bay leaves in the shape of a crest on top; or placing items in a leaf or a small dish on top of the bowl—these are not called 'heaped up' (thūpīkata), and therefore all such are permissible. In this training rule, there is no exception even for a sick monk, therefore even he...
282:
(A sick monk) should also receive alms-food only up to the level of the rim of the bowl. In all cases of heaped-up food (thūpīkata), it is only improper to receive it in that manner; however, once received, it is proper to consume it if it has been received correctly. The fifth and sixth training rules are to be understood in the same manner as previously mentioned.

## 33-34. Commentary on the Sapadāna Training Rules
In the seventh (Sapadāna training rule), 'sapadāna' means eating in order/sequence without skipping any part [of the food in the bowl]. If a monk, while giving to others or pouring into another vessel, touches the food here and there, or if he takes side-dishes (uttarabhanga) out of sequence, there is no offense in this training rule. The eighth training rule is also in the same manner as previously mentioned.

## 35. Commentary on the Thūpakata Training Rule
In the ninth (Thūpakata training rule), 'thūpakata' means [eating by digging] from the top or from the middle. If a monk gathers the small amount of remaining food together, presses it down, and eats it, there is no offense.

## 36. Commentary on the Odanappaṭicchādana Training Rule
