In the tenth (Odanappaṭicchādana training rule), if the donors of the food cover the side-dishes with rice during slaughter-free times (māghāta) and so on, and if the monk does not cover it himself with the desire to get more, there is no offense for such monks. For a sick monk, however, since he is not mentioned in the section on non-offense (anāpattivāra), it is indeed an offense.

## 37. Commentary on the Sūpodanavinnatti Training Rule
In the eleventh (Sūpodanavinnatti training rule), the point regarding [requesting] from relatives, from those who have invited him, for the sake of another, or with one's own property, is an additional detail included in the section on non-offense.

## 38. Commentary on the Ujjhānasannī Training Rule
In the twelfth (Ujjhānasannī training rule), the perception (sannā) with the intent to criticize is called 'ujjhānasannā'; one who has such perception is called 'ujjhānasannī'. In this training rule as well, a sick monk is not exempt from the offense. However, there is no offense for a monk who looks with the thought "I will give" or "I will cause to be given," nor for one who looks without the intent to criticize.

## 39. Commentary on the Kabaḷa Training Rule
In the thirteenth (Kabaḷa training rule), regarding 'not making the morsel too large,' a peacock's egg is too large and a hen's egg is too small; the size in between the two is the proper measure. There is no offense in the case of all kinds of snacks such as roots and the like, nor in the case of large or small fruits.
283:
## 40. Commentary on the Ālopa Training Rule
In the fourteenth training rule, the Parimaṇḍala-ālopa rule, "parimaṇḍala" means a morsel of food that is not elongated (i.e., it is round). In this training rule, there is no offense in the case of snacks, large or small fruits, and side-dishes (uttarabhanga).

## 41-42. Commentary on the Anāhaṭa Training Rules
In the fifteenth training rule, the Anāhaṭa rule, "anāhaṭa" means before the morsel has been brought to or reached the opening of the mouth. In the sixteenth training rule (Na bhuñjamāna), "sabbahattha" means all the fingers.

## 43. Commentary on the Sakabaḷa Training Rule
In the seventeenth training rule, the Sakabaḷa rule, if a morsel of food is so large that it causes the words to be indistinct or incomplete, it is an offense for a monk who speaks while such a morsel is in his mouth. If a monk, while preaching the Dhamma, holds a myrobalan fruit (harīṭaka) or similar items in his mouth, and if those items do not cause the words to be indistinct, it is proper to preach while holding such an amount in the mouth.

## 44. Commentary on the Piṇḍukkhepaka Training Rule
In the eighteenth training rule, the Piṇḍukkhepaka rule, "piṇḍukkhepaka" means eating by repeatedly tossing the morsels of food. In this training rule as well, there is no offense in the case of snacks and large or small fruits.

## 45. Commentary on the Kabaḷāvacchedaka Training Rule
In the nineteenth training rule, the Kabaḷāvacchedaka rule, "kabaḷāvacchedaka" means eating by repeatedly biting off pieces from the morsel. In this training rule, there is no offense in the case of snacks, large or small fruits, and side-dishes.

## 46. Commentary on the Avagaṇḍakāraka Training Rule
In the twentieth training rule, the Avagaṇḍakāraka rule, "avagaṇḍakāraka" means eating by stuffing the morsels into the cheeks like a monkey. In this training rule, there is no offense in the case of merely large or small fruits.

## 47. Commentary on the Hattaniddhunaka Training Rule
In the twenty-first training rule, the Hattaniddhunaka rule, "hattaniddhunaka" means eating by repeatedly shaking the hand. In the section on non-offense for this rule, the phrase "shaking the hand while discarding rubbish" is an additional detail included.
284:
## 48. Commentary on the Sitthāvakaraka Training Rule
In the twenty-second training rule, the Sitthāvakaraka rule, "sitthāvakaraka" means eating by scattering rice grains here and there. In this training rule as well, the phrase "discarding a rice grain while discarding rubbish" is an additional detail in the section on non-offense.

## 49. Commentary on the Jivhānicchāraka Training Rule
In the twenty-third training rule, the Jivhānicchāraka rule, "jivhānicchāraka" means eating by repeatedly sticking out the tongue.

## 50-51. Commentary on the Capucapukāraka Training Rules
In the twenty-fourth training rule, the Capucapukāraka rule, "capucapukāraka" means eating by repeatedly making a sound like "capu capu." The twenty-fifth training rule (Surusurukāraka) is also in the same manner.

## 52-54. Commentary on the Hattanillehaka and Other Training Rules
In the twenty-sixth training rule, the Hattanillehaka rule, "hattanillehaka" means eating by repeatedly licking the hand. Indeed, a monk who is eating should not lick even a single finger. However, it is proper to pick up thick rice gruel (yāgu), molasses, milk-rice (pāyāsa), and the like with the fingers and eat by putting the fingers into the mouth. The twenty-seventh (Pattanillehaka) and twenty-eighth (Oṭṭhanillehaka) training rules are also in the same manner. Therefore, one should not scrape the bowl even with a single finger, nor should one lick even one side of the lips with the tongue; however, it is proper to take [the food] with the lips themselves and bring it inside.

## 55. Commentary on the Sāmisa Training Rule
In the twenty-ninth training rule (Pānīyatthālaka), the rule "one should not hold [the vessel] with a hand soiled with food (sāmisa)" was prohibited because holding with a soiled hand is repulsive. Therefore, whether it is the property of the Saṅgha, an individual, a layperson, or one's own, one should not hold a drinking conch, a drinking cup, or a drinking vessel (thālaka) [with a soiled hand]; for a monk who does so, there is a dukkaṭa offense. If, however, a part of the hand is not soiled with food, it is proper to hold it with that part. In this training rule, the phrase "holding with the intent to wash it oneself or to have another wash it" is an additional detail in the section on non-offense.

## 56. Commentary on the Sasitthaka Training Rule
In the thirtieth training rule (Sasitthaka), the phrase "discarding by picking out, or by breaking, or into a receptacle, or by taking outside" is an additional detail in the section on non-offense. In that phrase, "by picking out" means the rice grains...
285:
Having removed the rice grains from the water and made a pile in one place, he discards the water alone. "Bhinditvā vā" (or having broken) means breaking (or crushing) the rice grains and making them like water, then discarding them. "Paṭiggahe vā" (or in a receptacle) means discarding into the waste-water basin of those who receive it with a basin. "Nīharitvā" (having taken out) means taking it outside the village and discarding it; for a monk who discards in this way, there is no offense.

## End of the Commentary on the Thirty Training Rules Connected with Food.
## 57. Commentary on the Chattapāṇi Training Rule
Among the training rules connected with teaching Dhamma, in the first training rule, one who has any kind of umbrella in hand is called "chattapāṇi" (one with an umbrella in hand). Even if he places that umbrella on any part of the body such as the shoulder or thigh, as long as he does not release it from his hand, it is not proper to teach him Dhamma. However, if another person holds the umbrella for him, or if it is placed by his side, as soon as it is away from his hand, he is no longer called "chattapāṇi"; it is proper to teach him Dhamma. The definition of Dhamma in these rules should be understood in the same way as stated in the Padasodhamma training rule.

## 58-59. Commentary on the Daṇḍapāṇi Training Rules
In the second training rule, "daṇḍa" (staff) refers to a staff four cubits in length for an average man; his state of being "daṇḍapāṇi" (one with a staff in hand) should be understood in the same way as stated for "chattapāṇi". In the third training rule, the method is the same. Indeed, even one who stands with a sword fastened (or slung) does not fall into the category of "satthapāṇi" (one with a weapon in hand).

## 60. Commentary on the Āvudhapāṇi Training Rule
In the fourth training rule, all varieties of bows along with varieties of arrows should be understood as "āvudha" (weapon). Therefore, it is not proper to teach Dhamma to one who is standing or sitting while holding a bow with an arrow, or just a bow without an arrow, or just an arrow without a bow, or a strung bow, or an unstrung bow. However, if the bow is slung (or hung) on his shoulder, as long as he does not hold it with his hand, it is proper to teach Dhamma.

## 61-62. Commentary on the Pādukā Training Rules
In the fifth training rule, "pādukāruḷhassa" (for one mounted on footwear) refers to one who merely steps on it without inserting the toe-peg (which is like an umbrella handle) between the toes, or to one who has it fastened by way of standing after inserting it between the toes. In the sixth training rule also...
286:
In this (Upāhanāruḷhasikkhāpada) also, the method is the same. Specifically, in this training rule, one who stands with the heel-strap (heel-binding) fastened is called "one wearing shoes"; it is also not proper to preach the Dhamma to him.

## 63. Yānasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā
In the seventh (Yānagatasikkhāpada), even if he is one who is carried by two people with hands joined, or one who is carried on a pole after being placed in a cloth, or one who is sitting even on just a wheel of a vehicle such as a covered cart that is not hitched to oxen or horses, or one that has been dismantled, he is still designated as "one who has gone into a vehicle" (yānagata). If both the preacher and the listener are sitting in the same vehicle, it is proper (to preach). Even when sitting separately, it is proper for a monk sitting in a higher vehicle to preach to one sitting in a lower vehicle; it is also proper in vehicles of equal height. Likewise, it is proper for one sitting in a front vehicle to preach to one sitting in a rear vehicle. However, it is not proper for one sitting in a rear vehicle to preach, even if he is sitting in a vehicle that is higher (than the one in front).

## 64. Sayanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā
In the eighth (Sayanagatasikkhāpada), "to one who has gone to a bed" means it is not proper for one who is standing or sitting on a high couch, stool, or ground area to preach the Dhamma to one who is lying down, at the very least, on a mat, a rug, or even on the natural ground. A monk who has gone to a bed (who is lying down), however, may preach while lying down to one who has gone to a bed (who is lying down), whether his own bed is higher or of equal height. A monk who is lying down may preach to one who is standing, sitting, or lying down. A monk who is sitting may preach to one who is standing or sitting. A monk who is standing, however, may preach only to one who is standing.

## 65. Pallatthikasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā
In the ninth (Pallatthikasikkhāpada), it is not proper to preach the Dhamma to one who is sitting with any kind of binding, such as binding the knees with the hands (hatthapallatthika) and so forth.

## 66. Veṭhitasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā
In the tenth (Veṭhitasīsasikkhāpada), "to one with a wrapped head" refers to one whose head is wrapped with a cloth (turban) or with a diadem and so forth such that the hairline is not visible. For this reason, it is stated in the section on non-offense (anāpattivāra) of this training rule: "He preaches after having him reveal the hairline."

## 67. Oguṇṭhitasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā
In the eleventh (Oguṇṭhitasīsasikkhāpada), "to one with a covered head" refers to one who is covered (clothed) including the head. In the section on non-offense of this training rule, however, the statement "He preaches after having him reveal the head" is additional (distinctive).
287:
## 68. Chamāsikkhāpadavaṇṇanā
In the twelfth training rule, the Chamā training rule, "chamāyaṃ nisīditvā" means sitting on the ground. "Āsane" means for one who is sitting on a seat, even if it is at the very least a cloth or grass spread out (meaning one should not teach Dhamma to such a person).

## 69. Nīcāsanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā
In the thirteenth training rule, the Nīcāsana training rule, "ucce āsane" means for one who is sitting on a high seat, even if it is at the very least a high spot on the ground (meaning one should not teach Dhamma to such a person).

## 70. Ṭhitasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā
In the fourteenth training rule, the Ṭhita training rule, "na ṭhito nisinnassa" means if a Mahāthera, while sitting on a seat, asks a question to a junior monk who has come to attend to him and is standing, it should not be answered. However, out of respect, it is not proper to say to that Elder, "Ask after standing up." Therefore, it is allowable to answer while thinking, "I will answer the monk standing at my side."

## 71. Pacchatogamanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā
In the fifteenth training rule, the Pacchatogamana training rule, if someone walking in front asks a question, one should not answer him but should answer after saying, "I will answer the monk following behind." However, it is allowable to recite the Dhamma learned together or to answer one who is walking side-by-side.

## 72. Uppathenagamanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā
In the sixteenth training rule, the Uppathenagamana training rule, in the phrase "na uppathena," if both the teacher and the listener walk side-by-side on a cart track, either on separate wheel tracks or off the path, it is allowable (to teach).

## 73. Ṭhito-uccārasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā
In the seventeenth training rule, the Ṭhito-uccāra training rule, in the section on non-offense for "asañcicca" (unintentionally), if excrement or urine comes out suddenly while going to a secluded place, it is considered to be done without intention.

## 74. Harite-uccārasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā
In the eighteenth training rule, the Harite-uccāra training rule, whether it is the root of a living tree visible on the ground or a branch touching the ground, all such things are called "harita" (greenery). But as for sitting on the trunk of a tree...
288:
It is allowable to discharge [excrement or urine] in a place where there is no green vegetation (appaharita). If, while looking for a place without green vegetation, it comes out suddenly, it is considered a case of illness (and thus no offense). The statement, "Even if done in a place without green vegetation, it might spread over the green vegetation," is an additional point in the section on non-offenses (anāpatti) for this training rule. In such a discharge, if one cannot find a place without green vegetation and places a coil of grass or a coil of straw [to discharge upon], even if the feces, urine, or mucus subsequently spreads over the green vegetation, it is indeed allowable. In this training rule, mucus is also included along with saliva.

## 75. Commentary on the Training Rule Regarding Excrement in Water

This statement, "not in water," which is the nineteenth [in this group], is spoken with reference only to usable water. There is no offense for discharging in water that is not for use, such as water in a cesspool or the ocean. When it rains and floods occur all around, if one cannot find a dry place, it is allowable to discharge in the water. In this training rule also, the statement "Even if done on dry land, it might spread over the water" is an additional point in the section on non-offenses. The remaining words are clear in all the training rules.

For the purpose of showing the origins (samuṭṭhāna) and so forth, I shall state this miscellaneous decision: The four training rules related to loud laughter (ujjagghika) and loud noise (uccāsadda); the one rule on speaking with a mouthful of food; and the five rules related to sitting on the ground, sitting on a low seat, standing, following from behind, and going on a wrong path—these ten training rules have the origin of samanubhāsana. Each of these is characterized by action (kiriya), release by perception (saññāvimokkha), being intentional (sacittaka), being a worldly fault (lokavajja), bodily action (kāyakamma), verbal action (vacīkamma), unwholesome mind (akusalacitta), and painful feeling (dukkhavedanā). The training rule on requesting curry and rice (sūpodanaviññatti) has the origin of theyyasattha, and is characterized by action, release by perception, being intentional, being a worldly fault, bodily action, verbal action, unwholesome mind, and painful feeling. The eleven training rules regarding holding an umbrella, a staff, a knife, or a weapon; and wearing sandals, shoes, using a vehicle, a bed, clasping the knees (pallatthika), wearing a turban, or muffling the head—these have the origin of dhammadesanā, and are characterized by action and non-action, release by perception, being intentional, being a worldly fault, verbal action, unwholesome mind, and painful feeling. The remaining fifty-three training rules have various origins, such as that of the first pārājika.

## The Commentary on the Nineteen Training Rules Related to Teaching the Dhamma is Finished.

## Within the Commentary on the Pātimokkha in the Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī,

## The Commentary on the Sekhiya Rules is Finished.

## Explanation of the Settlement of Legal Processes

Among the settlements of legal processes, the word "seven" is the delimitation of their number. They are called "settlements of legal processes" (adhikaraṇasamatha) because they settle or appease legal processes. "They come to the recitation" means that for the sake of inquiring into the state of purity regarding the offenses known as the legal process concerning offenses (āpattādhikaraṇa), as well as regarding the offenses which are the causes of the remaining three legal processes, they come to the state of being recited. "Arising and arising" means whatever (legal processes) have arisen. "Of legal processes" means for the sake of these four legal processes: the legal process concerning disputes (vivādādhikaraṇa), the legal process concerning accusations (anuvādādhikaraṇa), the legal process concerning offenses (āpattādhikaraṇa), and the legal process concerning business (kiccādhikaraṇa). "For the sake of settling and appeasing" means for the purpose of settling and for the purpose of appeasing, the verdict in the presence (sammukhāvinaya) should be given... and so on, up to the settlement by covering with grass (tiṇavatthāraka); these seven settlements should be given. Herein, the decision is as follows: First, among the legal processes, the dispute of monks who are disputing over the eighteen grounds, such as "it is Dhamma" or "it is not Dhamma," is called the legal process concerning disputes. The accusation, disparagement, and charging of monks who are accusing [others] of a failure in virtue (sīlavipatti), or a failure in conduct (ācāravipatti), views (diṭṭhivipatti), or livelihood (ājīvavipatti), is called the legal process concerning accusations. The seven groups of offenses—the five groups mentioned in the Matika and the two groups mentioned in the Vibhanga—are called the legal process concerning offenses. The performance of the four types of formal acts of the Sangha, such as the act of notification (apalokana), is called the legal process concerning business.

Among those legal processes, the legal process concerning disputes is settled by two settlements: the verdict in the presence and the majority decision (yebhuyyasikā). When it is settled by the verdict in the presence alone, it is settled either in the very monastery where it arose, or on the way for those going to another place to settle it, or in the monastery where they have arrived and handed it over to the Sangha, by the Sangha settling it there, or if the Sangha there is unable to settle it, by the decision of persons appointed by a committee (ubbāhikā) in that very monastery. When it is thus being settled, the four kinds of presence in that legal process—presence of the Sangha (saṅghasammukhatā), presence of the Dhamma (dhammasammukhatā), presence of the Vinaya (vinayasammukhatā), and presence of the persons (puggalasammukhatā)—is called the verdict in the presence. Among these four, the presence through the power of the concord of the Sangha involved in the act is "presence of the Sangha." The factual nature of the matter to be settled is "presence of the Dhamma." The settling of it in the exact manner that it should be settled is "presence of the Vinaya." The presence of both parties, the one who disputes and the one with whom he disputes, is "presence of the persons." However, in settling by a committee, the presence of the Sangha is reduced. In this way, first, it is settled by the verdict in the presence alone.
290:
If it cannot be settled even in this way, the monks appointed by the committee (ubbāhikā) return it to the Sangha, saying, "We are not able to settle it." Because of this handing over, the Sangha appoints a monk endowed with five qualities as a ballot-taker (salākaggāhāpaka). That monk must have the ballots taken by one of the three methods of ballot-taking: the secret (guḷhaka), the open (vivaṭṭaka), or the whispering (sakaṇṇajappaka) method. In the assembly thus gathered, according to the majority of those who speak according to the Dhamma (dhammavādī), the legal process settled in the way those Dhamma-speakers say is settled by both the verdict in the presence and the majority decision. Among those two, the verdict in the presence is just as already described. The performance of the formal act of majority decision is called "majority decision." Thus, the legal process concerning disputes is settled by two settlements.

The legal process concerning accusations is settled by four settlements: the verdict in the presence, the verdict of mindfulness (sativinaya), the verdict of past insanity (amūḷhavinaya), and the act of further punishment (tassapāpiyasikā). In the legal process concerning accusations that is settled by the verdict in the presence alone, after listening to the words of the accusing monk and the accused monk, if there is no offense, both are made to ask for forgiveness; if there is an offense, it is settled by deciding, "In this matter, there is such-and-such an offense." In settling it thus, the characteristic of the verdict in the presence is just as already described. When an Arahant monk is accused of a groundless failure in virtue and requests a verdict of mindfulness, the Sangha gives the verdict of mindfulness by a formal act consisting of a motion and three proclamations (ñatticatuttha kamma). Then, it is settled by both the verdict in the presence and the verdict of mindfulness. Once the verdict of mindfulness has been given, no further accusation by any monk against that Arahant person can proceed. When a monk who was insane has committed an improper act not becoming of a monk through the power of insanity, and is charged by monks saying, "Venerable, remember such an offense," even though he says, "Friends, I did this while I was insane, I do not remember that offense," he is still being charged by the monks; so, in order not to be charged further, he requests a verdict of past insanity. The Sangha gives that monk the verdict of past insanity by a formal act consisting of a motion and three proclamations. Then, it is settled by both the verdict in the presence and the verdict of past insanity. Once the verdict of past insanity has been given, no further accusation by any monk against that person on that account can proceed.

When a person of evil nature, who prevaricates when being charged with a pārājika offense or an offense close to a pārājika, and who has an abundance of evil, the Sangha, thinking, "If this monk's root is not yet cut, he will receive restoration after practicing properly; if his root is cut, his destruction will occur naturally,"...
291:
By the motion and fourfold proclamation (ñatticatutthakamma), one performs the tassapāpiyasika act for that person; at that time, the legal issue is settled by both sammukhāvinaya and tassapāpiyasika. Thus, anuvādādhikaraṇa (legal issues arising from accusations) is settled by four samathas. Āpattādhikaraṇa (legal issues arising from offenses) (Cūḷavagga 239) is settled by three samathas: sammukhāvinaya, paṭiññātakaraṇa, and tiṇavatthāraka. In that āpattādhikaraṇa, there is no settlement by sammukhāvinaya alone. However, when a monk confesses a light offense (lahukāpatti) in the presence of another monk, or in the midst of a group or the Saṅgha according to the method mentioned in the explanation of nissaggiya, then the āpattādhikaraṇa is settled by sammukhāvinaya and paṭiññātakaraṇa.

Among those two samathas, in sammukhāvinaya, the presence of the monk who confesses and the monk who receives the confession is called puggalasammukhatā (presence of the person); the rest (such as dhammasammukhatā) are just as previously mentioned. When confessing in the presence of a person or a group, saṅghasammukhatā (presence of the Saṅgha) is absent. In this āpattādhikaraṇa, the confession such as "Venerable sir, I have fallen into such-and-such an offense," and when asked "Do you see it?" replying "Yes, I see it," is called paṭiññā (acknowledgment). The resolution "Restrain yourself in the future" based on that acknowledgment is called paṭiññātakaraṇa. In the case of a saṅghādisesa offense, the request for parivāsa etc. is paṭiññā; the granting of parivāsa etc. is called paṭiññātakaraṇa.

Monks who are divided into two factions and are quarrelsome, having committed many improper acts unsuitable for recluses, when the sense of shame (lajjī) arises again, they see the fault in making each other settle those offenses individually, thinking: "If we settle these offenses with each other, that legal issue might lead to harshness and violence." When they perform the tiṇavatthāraka act, then the āpattādhikaraṇa is settled by sammukhāvinaya and tiṇavatthāraka. In that tiṇavatthāraka-samatha, even if the monks within the forearm's length (hatthapāsa) are asleep without expressing their own view like "I do not approve of this act," they are cleared from all offenses, except for grave faults (pārājika and saṅghādisesa) and those connected with the laity. Thus, āpattādhikaraṇa is settled by three samathas.

Kiccādhikaraṇa (legal issues arising from duties) (Cūḷavagga 242) is settled by only one samatha, namely sammukhāvinaya. Thus, these four legal issues are settled by these seven samathas as appropriate. Therefore, it was said: "For the settlement and stilling of legal issues that have arisen... tiṇavatthāraka."
292:
"The Settlement in the Presence should be given... (and so on) the Settlement by Covering Over with Grass" is stated. (In saying so, when they perform the act of Covering Over with Grass, seeing the fault in making each other confess offences or in making decisions, thinking that harshness or boldness might arise, the legal issue of offences is settled. In such settlement, they are rehabilitated from all offences, except for the grave offences of Pārājika and Saṅghādisesa, and those involving laypeople.) This is the brief method of decision in this (Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī) commentary. The detailed method has already appeared in the Samathakkhandhaka, and the decision of that detail has also been stated in the Samantapāsādikā (the Vinaya commentary).

In that (recitation of the Pātimokkha), I ask the venerable ones: "Are you pure in this (settlement of legal issues)?" In this statement, it is asking: "How is it, among these seven ways of settling legal issues, are you pure? Do you, venerable ones, have any legal issue that should be settled by these ways of settlement?" By asking this, the state of being pure from all offences is asked.

"Venerable ones, the Introduction has been recited" and so forth are the concluding words. In those concluding words, "ettakaṃ" means training rules of this extent. "Suttāgataṃ" means (training rules) that have come in the Pātimokkha Pāḷi called the Sutta. "Suttapariyāpannaṃ" means (training rules) included in that very Pātimokkha. "Anvaddhamāsaṃ uddesaṃ āgacchati" means it comes to be recited every half-month by way of performing the Uposatha. "Samaggehi" means those who are in harmony by way of physical harmony (kāyasamaggī). "Sammodamānehi" means those who greatly rejoice by having a common inclination through mental harmony (cittasamaggī). "Avivadamānehi" means those who do not dispute even for any single reason among the eighteen grounds for dispute. "Sikkhitabbaṃ" means the training in higher virtue (adhisīlasikkhā) should be fulfilled without transgressing those various training rules. If any word is not mentioned in between, it should be understood that all such words are not mentioned because they have already been stated in the preceding training rules and because their meaning is clear.

293:
## Commentary on the Bhikkhunī Pātimokkha
## Homage to Him, the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Fully Enlightened One
## The Chapter on Defeats

For the benefit of the bhikkhunīs, the Protector (the Buddha) has clearly taught the Pātimokkha; the sequence of the commentary for that [Bhikkhunī Pātimokkha] has now duly arrived.

## Shared Defeats
## 1-4. Commentary on the Training Rule regarding Sexual Intercourse

In that [Bhikkhunī Pātimokkha], the meaning of the words beginning with "Suṇātu me" (Let [the Saṅgha] listen to me) should be understood in the same manner as stated in the commentary on the Bhikkhu Pātimokkha. Indeed, the only difference between that [Bhikkhu Pātimokkha] and this [Bhikkhunī Pātimokkha] is the mere mode of address, such as "Bhante" (Venerable Sir) and "Ayye" (Noble Lady), and the mere difference in gender. Furthermore, since there is no such thing as "renouncing the training" (sikkhāpaccakkhāna) for a bhikkhunī, it is not said for bhikkhunīs, "having attained the training and livelihood, without renouncing the training and without declaring weakness," but rather it is said, "Whatever bhikkhunī should indulge in sexual intercourse with lustful intent."

In that context, "with lustful intent" (chandaso) means with the desire and liking associated with sexual lust. If there is no desire and she is violated by force, there is no offense. Therefore, if a bhikkhunī who has received the full ordination (upasampadā), with lustful intent, inserts even an area as small as a sesame seed into any of her three tracts—the anus (vaccamagga), the urinary tract (passāvamagga), or the mouth (mukhamagga)—the male organ of any living or dead human, non-human, or animal, whether a male, a hermaphrodite (ubhatobyañjanaka), or a eunuch (paṇḍaka), whether it is covered or uncovered, whether it is not eaten by dogs or jackals or mostly not eaten by them, whether [her tract] is covered or uncovered, in a moist place not touched by natural wind; or if she consents to any of the stages of insertion, being inserted, staying within, or withdrawing while being inserted by another, this bhikkhunī becomes one who is defeated (pārājikā). The remaining terms in this rule and in the subsequent shared training rules should be understood according to the method already stated.
294:
## Unshared Defeats
## 5. Commentary on the Training Rule regarding [Touching] Above the Knees

Among the unshared training rules, in the first of the four defeats, "avassutā" (oozing) means being wet or stained with lust for physical contact. The same method applies to the second term. "Purisapuggalassa" (of a male person) refers to a person designated as a male, of the human species, possessing intelligence, and capable of engaging in physical contact. "Adhakkakaṃ" means below one's own collarbones. "Ubbhajāṇumaṇḍalaṃ" means above the kneecaps; and in this training rule, the area above the elbows is also included within the term "ubbhajāṇumaṇḍala." "Āmasanaṃ" (rubbing) means vigorous rubbing, or striking forcefully in the same spot without moving beyond the point of contact. "Parāmasanaṃ" (stroking) means moving or shifting the touch from here to there. "Gahaṇaṃ" (grasping) means the mere act of holding. "Chupanaṃ" (touching) means mere contact without forceful striking. "Paṭipīḷanaṃ" (squeezing) means grasping and pressing the limbs. "Sādiyeyya" (should consent) means if a bhikkhunī consents to such stroking, etc., by a man on her body within the defined limits, or if she herself, while consenting, touches any part of the man's body with her body within those defined limits, this bhikkhunī is one who is defeated, known as "ubbhajāṇumaṇḍalikā" (one who [consents to contact] above the knees); this is the summary of the meaning here.

In the detailed decision beginning with "Nidānaṃ puggalaṃ vatthuṃ" (The origin, the person, the object), since all these are unshared regulations (asādhāraṇapaññatti), from this training rule onwards, after stating the existing secondary regulation (anupaññatti), we will not distinguish by saying "shared regulation" or "unshared regulation." In the analysis of command (āṇatti), where there is no command, we will say nothing; where there is, we will state it there. The investigation of failure (vipatti) has already been mentioned.

The remaining concluding remarks should be stated for all training rules. This is what is said: This training rule was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning Sundarīnandā on account of the matter of engaging in physical contact. If only the bhikkhunī on one side is "oozing" (with lust) and touches the man's body with her body within the defined limits; or even if both sides are "oozing," if she touches an object connected to the body with her body, or touches his body with an object connected to her body within the defined limits or with the rest of her body, there is a thullaccaya (grave) offense for the bhikkhunī. Even in the case of non-human males, ghosts, eunuchs, or animals in human form, if both sides are "oozing" and she touches the body with her body within the defined limits, there is also a thullaccaya offense. However, if the man has no lust for physical contact, even in a situation that could lead to a defeat, there is only a thullaccaya offense. In the remaining cases, such as touching an object connected to the body with another object connected to the body, and in all instances of sexual lust or household-based affection, there is a dukkaṭa (wrongdoing) offense. For one who is unintentional, unmindful, unknowing...
295: There is no offense for a nun who does not consent (to a man's touch), for an insane nun, and so forth. The factors, origins, and so on should be understood in the same manner as stated in the Kāyasaṃsagga Sikkhāpada of the Bhikkhu Pātimokkha. ## The Explanation of the Ubbhajāṇumaṇḍalika Sikkhāpada is finished. ## 6. Vajjappaṭicchādika Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā In the second training rule, "gaṇassa" means (not informing) other nuns. "Ṭhitā" means remaining in her own status as a nun. "Cutā" means passed away (deceased). "Nāsitā" means the destruction of the status as a nun, either by herself or by others. "Avassaṭā" means having gone over to the fold of the heretics. "Lady, I knew this even before" — this statement shows the time when that nun who concealed the fault speaks. In fact, as soon as she knows that a nun remaining in her status has committed a pārājika offense and gives up the effort, thinking, "Now I will not tell this to anyone," this nun incurs the pārājika offense called vajjappaṭicchādika. This training rule was laid down on account of the nun Thullanandā in Sāvatthī, because she neither reproved (the offender) herself nor informed the group. The remaining procedure here should be understood in the same manner as stated in the Duṭṭhullāpattipaṭicchādana Sikkhāpada in the Sappāṇaka Vagga. The only difference is that in that training rule, it is a pācittiya offense, whereas in this training rule, it is a pārājika offense; the rest is the same. ## The Explanation of the Vajjappaṭicchādika Sikkhāpada is finished. ## 7. Ukkhittānuvattika Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā In the third training rule, "ukkhitta" refers to a monk who has been expelled due to not seeing an offense, and so forth. "Dhammena" means by way of a factual matter. "Vinayena" means by way of reproving and reminding (of the fault). "Satthusāsanena" means that in this training rule also, the act of reproving and reminding is indeed called the Teacher's Instruction (satthusāsana). "Anādaraṃ" means a lack of respect or not practicing properly towards the Saṅgha that performed the ukkhepaniya-kamma, or towards the group included in that Saṅgha, or towards an individual, or towards that ukkhepaniya-kamma. "Appaṭikāraṃ" means without remedy, not yet reinstated into the Saṅgha. "Akatasahāyaṃ" means that monks who share the same communion (saṃvāsa) due to being together in acts like the ekakamma (single legal act) are called "sahāya" (companions). If a nun does not have that communion with them, she is said to have not made them her companions.
296:
Because of the state of being together, monks of the same communion are called companions. If a monk does not have communion with them, he is called 'akatasahāya' because he has not made them his companions. 'Taṃ akatasahāyaṃ' means that monk who has not entered the state of being of the same communion. "Tam anuvatteyya" means that a nun follows that expelled (ukkhittaka) monk, who remains in the state of being expelled, by adopting the same view that he holds. If that nun, although being admonished individually and in the midst of the Saṅgha according to the method stated in the Saṅghabhedasikkhāpada and so forth, does not relinquish that view, she incurs the pārājika offense called ukkhittānuvattikā at the conclusion of the formal act of admonishment (samanubhāsana).

This training rule was laid down on account of the nun Thullanandā in Sāvatthī, for the reason of following the view of an expelled monk. There is a dukkaṭa offense due to the motion (ñatti). There are two thullaccaya offenses due to the two formal announcements (kammavācā). At the end of the third formal announcement, which reaches the syllable 'yya' in "yassā nakkhamati, sā bhāseyya," a pārājika offense is incurred. If it is an unlawful act (adhammakamma), three kinds of dukkaṭa are incurred. The rest of the procedure should be understood in the same manner as stated in the Saṅghabhedasikkhāpada and so forth.

## The Commentary on the Ukkhittānuvattika Training Rule is finished.

## 8. Commentary on the Aṭṭhavatthuka Training Rule

In the fourth training rule of the eighth pārājika, "avassutā" means being moistened with the passion of physical contact through the power of forming friendships that are enjoyed by worldly people. This very meaning is stated in the Sinhalese Mātikāṭṭhakathā. In the Samantapāsādikā, however, this meaning has been scrutinized. The same method applies to the second word, "avassutassa." In the phrases such as "purisapuggalassa hatthaggahanaṃ vā," the grabbing of the hand performed by a male person is called "purisapuggalassa hatthaggahanaṃ." The same method applies to saṅghāṭikaṇṇaggahana (grabbing the edge of the robe).

In this term "hatthaggahanaṃ," grabbing any part of the body that is not the grounds for a pārājika is called hatthaggahana. Grabbing any part of the undergarment worn or the upper robe draped is called saṅghāṭikaṇṇaggahana. In the phrases such as "santiṭṭheyya vā," it means standing together within arm's reach (hatthapāsa) of a man for the sake of indulging in the misconduct known as physical contact, or conversing while standing there, or going to a designated place when told by a man, "Come to such and such a place," or consenting to the approach of that man, or being concealed by some object...
297:
One should understand the meaning as: 'entering a secluded place, and while standing within arm's length (hatthapāsa) of a man, bringing the body close.' 'This nun also is defeated (pārājika)' means that, like the nuns mentioned previously, this nun, for the purpose of practicing this ignoble conduct (asaddhamma) known as physical contact, fulfills these eight grounds (vatthu) either in order or out of order, and thus reaches the Pārājika known as the 'Eight Grounds' (Aṭṭhavatthuka).

It was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning the group-of-six nuns, on account of the fulfillment of the eighth ground. In going to the rendezvous, for every step, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). As soon as she enters within arm's length (hatthapāsa) of the man, there is a grave offense (thullaccaya). If she consents to the man's approach, there is also an offense of wrong-doing. For entering within arm's length, there is a grave offense. For each of the remaining grounds, there is only a grave offense. Upon the completion of the eighth ground, there is an offense of defeat (pārājika). Even if she transgresses each ground a hundred times, she is released from those offenses by confessing them. A small distinction to be noted here is regarding 'countable' (gaṇanūpikā) offenses. An offense confessed after making an effort to give up the burden, saying 'I will not commit this again from now on,' is countable; it enters the count of confessed offenses and does not become a factor for Pārājika. Therefore, if a nun commits one offense, gives up the burden and confesses, but then commits it again through the power of defilement and confesses again, she does not become one who has committed Pārājika even if she fulfills the eighth ground in this way. But if a nun, having committed an offense, confesses with the effort of thinking 'I will commit another ground again,' her offense is 'uncountable' (agaṇanūpikā); even if confessed, it is as if unconfessed, and it becomes a factor for Pārājika. There is no offense for one who acts unintentionally, unmindfully, unknowingly, without consenting, or for one who is insane, etc. There are three factors here: lust for physical contact, effort, and the completion of the eighth ground. The origination is like the Samanubhāsana (formal admonition), it is an action and non-action, with perception and release, with intention, a worldly fault, bodily action, vocal action, unwholesome mind, and two feelings.

## The Commentary on the Aṭṭhavatthuka Sikkhāpada is finished.

'Ladies, the eight Pārājika rules have been recited' means that the four shared (sādhāraṇa) Pārājikas laid down concerning monks and these four unshared ones have been recited in the order of the Pātimokkha recitation; this is how the meaning should be understood. The rest is the same as the method stated in the commentary on the Bhikkhu Pātimokkha.

## in the Bhikkhunī Pātimokkha,
## the Commentary on the Pārājika is finished.
298:
## Section on Saṅghādisesa
## 1. Commentary on the Ussayavādikā Sikkhāpada
Among the Saṅghādisesa rules, in the first rule, 'Ussayavādikā' refers to one who disputes in the presence of high officials (judges) for the purpose of litigation, through the power of haughty pride or through the power of haughty anger. By the words 'or with a householder' (gahapatina vā), etc., laypeople and ascetics/wanderers are included, excluding the five classes of co-religionists (sahadhammika). In the phrase 'This nun is a first-offender' (paṭhamāpattika), it means she has an offense that is first reached at the beginning; it is an offense to be incurred at the very moment of transgression. She reaches that first offense. 'She has incurred' (āpannā) means she has reached the conclusion of the litigation. It is called 'leading to expulsion' (nissāraṇīya) because it causes the nun to be expelled from the Saṅgha. She reaches that offense named Saṅghādisesa which is thus 'leading to expulsion.'

It was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning the nun Thullanandā in the matter of litigation (Ussayavādika). This rule is a Sāṇattika rule, laid down by command. For a nun who, intending 'I will litigate,' searches for any companion, witness, or associate, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for the searching. From the place where the thought 'I will go to litigate' arises in the nun, for every step she takes from there, there is an offense of wrong-doing. If she sees judges who have come to the nunnery at any place and reports her case to them, there is an offense of wrong-doing. If her case has been reported by the other party (the opponent), there is a grave offense (thullaccaya) for the nun. Even if the other party speaks first and the nun speaks later, the method is the same.

If the nun says to that person, 'You yourself report both my case and your case,' and that person reports either his own case or the nun's case first, there is an offense of wrong-doing for the nun for the first reporting. For the second reporting, there is a grave offense. If the nun speaks after being told thus by that person, the method is the same. If the nun has someone else speak, the method is also the same. In whatever way it is reported, for the first reporting, there is an offense of wrong-doing for the nun, and for the second reporting, there is a grave offense. After hearing the words of both parties, when the judges make a decision, it is called the conclusion of the litigation (aḍḍapariyosāna). At that conclusion of the litigation, whether the nun wins or loses, there is an offense of Saṅghādisesa.

There is no offense for a nun who goes because she is forcibly dragged by enemies who either sent a messenger or came themselves saying, 'Come, Lady'; or for a nun who, without specifying who, reports and asks for protection regarding improper conduct committed by others in the nunnery; or if the judges, having heard from others without the nun saying anything, conclude the litigation themselves; or for a nun who is insane, etc. (The offense is incurred) in cases such as litigating without being dragged by others, or the conclusion of the litigation. Specifically, this rule is a Kiriya (action) rule involving the act of improper litigation. The first rule is finished.
299:
If the judges hear from others and conclude the lawsuit themselves without [the nun] saying anything, there is no offense for that nun, nor for those who are insane, etc. The two factors here are: initiating the lawsuit without being forced by others, and the conclusion of the lawsuit. The origins and other aspects are similar to the first Kathina training rule; however, this is an offense of action (kiriya) only.

## The Explanation of the Ussayavādikā Sikkhāpada is Finished.

## 2. Corivuṭṭhāpikā Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā

In the second training rule, a woman who has stolen someone else's property, starting from an object worth five māsakas, is called a thief (corī). [There is an offense if one ordains] that thief. "Known to be worthy of death" (vajjhaṃ viditaṃ) means she is well-known as "this woman deserves death" because of that crime. "Without asking permission" (anapaloketvā) means without requesting. "Group" (gaṇa) refers to the Malla group, the Bhaṭiputta group, and so on. "Association" (pūga) refers to a Dhamma group (devotees of the Sasana). "Guild" (seṇi) refers to the perfume merchants' guild, the cloth merchants' guild, and so on.

In whatever place the kings delegate authority to groups and so on, saying, "You alone shall govern this village or town," in those places, those groups and so on are the rulers. Therefore, this was said in reference to them. In this context, even if permission is obtained from the king or the group, etc., the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha must also be asked.

"Except for one who is allowable" (aññatra kappā) refers to one who has been previously ordained among sectarians or other nuns; such a person is called "kappā" (allowable for ordination). For a nun who ordains another (unallowable) woman excluding such a person, an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa) is incurred for seeking a group, seeking a teacher, seeking a bowl and robes, establishing the boundary, and the motion (ñatti). Due to the two formal proclamations (kammavācā), a grave offense (thullaccaya) is incurred. At the conclusion of the formal proclamation, an offense entailing a formal meeting of the Saṅgha (saṅghādisesa) is incurred.

This was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning the case of Thullanandā ordaining a thief. If there is doubt regarding the woman being a thief, an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa) is incurred. Likewise, if one perceives a non-thief as a thief, or if there is doubt, an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa) is incurred. There is no offense if one perceives her as a non-thief, if one ordains her without knowing, if one ordains after asking permission, if one ordains an allowable person, or for those who are insane, etc. The three factors here are: being a thief, perceiving her as a thief, and ordaining her without an authorized reason. It has the origin of ordaining a thief (corivuṭṭhāpana-samuṭṭhāna), it is an offense of action or non-action (kiriya-akiriya), it is dependent on perception (saññā-vimokkha), it is intentional (sacittaka), it is a breach of a conventional precept (paṇṇatti-vajja), it involves bodily action and vocal action, and it involves three types of consciousness and three types of feeling.

## The Explanation of the Corivuṭṭhāpikā Sikkhāpada is Finished.
300:
## 3. Ekagāmantaragamana Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā

In the third training rule beginning with "between villages" (gāmantara), there is no offense yet for a nun who is first departing from her own village. For a nun who, after departing, goes to another village, there is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa) for every step. When she crosses the enclosure or the precinct (upacāra) of another village with one foot, there is a grave offense (thullaccaya). As soon as she crosses with the second foot, there is an offense entailing a formal meeting of the Saṅgha (saṅghādisesa). The same method applies to a nun who leaves that other village and re-enters her own village. If, however, she can enter only the nunnery grounds through a broken wall or a gap in the fence, she is said to have entered allowable ground (kappiya-bhūmi), and thus it is permissible. In brief, an offense is incurred for a nun who, standing outside a village, enters unallowable ground on foot, whether it be her own village or another village.

Regarding crossing to the other side of a river (nadipāragamana), for a nun who goes to the other bank without a companion in a river having the characteristics described, or for a nun who, after quarreling with a companion in the middle of the river, returns alone to this bank: a grave offense (thullaccaya) is incurred at the moment the first foot is lifted and placed on the bank. When the second foot is lifted, an offense entailing a formal meeting of the Saṅgha (saṅghādisesa) is incurred. However, it is permissible to descend to the other bank by psychic power, bridge, vehicle, or boat; and for a nun who has descended for a reason such as bathing, it is permissible to return to this bank even on foot.

Regarding spending the night away from a companion (rattivippavāsa), an offense is incurred for a nun who stays until dawn in a place beyond the reach of a companion's hand (hatthapāsa), even in the same room, without the intention of "I will return within the reach of my companion's hand before dawn."

In the phrase "alone from a group" (ekā vā gaṇamhā), even a single nun is considered a "group" (gaṇa). "Should be left behind" (ohīyeyya) means being separated, or abandoning the range of sight (dassanūpacāra) or the range of hearing (savanūpacāra). Therefore, from the moment of crossing the village threshold (indakhīla), if she is separated from the companion's range of sight due to being obstructed by trees, pillars, curtains, walls, etc., outside the village, an offense is incurred even if the range of hearing still exists. In an open space, however, the range of sight can extend far. In such an open space, if she exceeds the range of hearing when being called "Lady!"—similar to the voice of one who has lost the way or the voice announcing the hearing of Dhamma—an offense is incurred. If, however, while traveling, she is left behind but follows with the effort of "I will catch up now," it is permissible.
301:
In Sāvatthī, concerning a certain bhikkhunī, in the case of going to another village (gāmantaragamanan), three additional regulations (anupaññatti) were laid down, beginning with "whether alone or across a river." For a bhikkhunī who leaves her own village before dawn and, at the time of sunrise, reaches the other side of a river belonging to another village, all four offenses occur simultaneously. It is also said:

"The four Saṅghādisesa rules were proclaimed by the Excellent Buddha;
One may fall into all of them with a single effort;
This problem has been considered by the wise who are skilled in the Vinaya."

In this way, the occurrence of three or two offenses together should also be understood. There is no offense for a bhikkhunī who goes to another village if her companion bhikkhunī has left, disrobed, died, or joined another sect, or if there are dangers; nor is there an offense for an insane bhikkhunī, etc. The three factors here are: being alone without danger, reaching one of the destinations such as another village, and the absence of danger. The origins and so forth are similar to the first Pārājika. This training rule is an offense by regulation (paṇṇattivajja) and involves three minds and three feelings.

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on Going to Another Village Alone is finished.

## 4. Explanation of the Training Rule on Restoring an Expelled Bhikkhunī

In the fourth training rule, 'ukkhittakaṃ' refers to a bhikkhunī who has been expelled for not seeing an offense (adassana), etc. 'Anaññāya gaṇassa chandaṃ' means without knowing the consent of the performing Saṅgha. 'Osāreyya' means performing the act of restoration (osāraṇakamma). For a bhikkhunī who does so, there is a dukkaṭa offense in seeking a group, in the boundary, and in the motion (ñatti); a thullaccaya offense for the two proclamations (kammavācā); and a saṅghādisesa offense at the conclusion of the proclamation.

In Sāvatthī, concerning Thullanandā, this was laid down in the case of restoration. This training rule is a Tika-saṅghādisesa (Saṅghādisesa with three variations). In an illegal act, there is a Tika-dukkaṭa. There is no offense for a bhikkhunī who restores after asking the performing Saṅgha, or knowing the consent of the group, or restoring one who is abiding by the rules, or restoring when the performing Saṅgha is absent, or for an insane bhikkhunī, etc. Being one who was expelled by a legal act, other...
302:
...restoration for a reason other than those permitted—these two factors are present here. The origins and so forth are as stated in the Saṅghabheda training rule. This training rule, however, is one of commission and omission (kiriyākirya).

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on Restoring an Expelled Bhikkhunī is finished.

## 5. Explanation of the First Training Rule on Receiving Food

In the fifth training rule, 'avassutā' means one who is wet with desire and lust. 'Avassutassa' means to such a man (one wet with desire). In the phrase 'should eat or consume,' there is a thullaccaya offense for receiving, and a saṅghādisesa offense for every swallow.

In Sāvatthī, concerning Sundarīnandā, this was laid down in the case of a lustful bhikkhunī receiving material things (āmisa) from the hand of a lustful man. If only one side is lustful, there is a dukkaṭa offense for receiving and a thullaccaya offense for every swallow. Even if both sides are lustful, the same rule applies when receiving from the hand of a yakkha, a peta, a paṇḍaka, or an animal in human form. In those cases (yakkha, etc.), if only one side is lustful, there is a dukkaṭa offense. In all cases, there is only a dukkaṭa offense for receiving or using water and tooth-sticks. There is no offense if both are not lustful, or if she receives knowing 'the man is not lustful,' or for an insane bhikkhunī, etc. The four factors here are: the item being an edible other than water or a tooth-stick, both being lustful, receiving with one's own hand, and swallowing. The origins and so forth are similar to the first Pārājika.

## The Explanation of the First Training Rule on Receiving Food is finished.

## 6. Explanation of the Second Training Rule on Receiving Food

In the sixth training rule, 'yato tvaṃ' means 'because you.' 'Ingha' is an indeclinable (nipāta) used in the sense of exhortation. In the word 'ayampi,' the bhikkhunī who thus exhorts—by that exhortation, by that speech, and by the other's receiving—falls into dukkaṭa offenses, and into thullaccaya offenses according to the number of swallows, and reaches a saṅghādisesa offense at the end of the meal.

In Sāvatthī, concerning a certain bhikkhunī, this was laid down in the case of such exhortation. It is a training rule involving an instruction (sāṇattika). There is a dukkaṭa offense in exhorting to receive water or tooth-sticks from the hand of a man or a yakkha, etc., and in the use of that water or tooth-stick. The same rule applies to exhorting, receiving, and swallowing other food from the hand of a yakkha, etc. However, at the end of the meal, there is a thullaccaya offense. Knowing 'the man is not lustful'...
303:
There is no offense for a nun who urges [another nun to accept food], knowing that "He is a man not moistened by lustful desire," or knowing that "He does not accept because he is angry," or knowing that "He does not accept out of compassion for the family (fearing they would suffer if they gave to her)"; nor is there an offense for an insane nun and others. The three factors of this training rule are: being a human male; urging [the nun] to "take and eat the food and edibles" for a reason other than the permitted ones; and the completion of eating by the other nun who took [the food] because of those words. The origination (samuṭṭhāna) and other aspects are the same as the Adinnādāna training rule.

## The Explanation of the Second Training Rule on Accepting Food is Finished.

## 7-8-9. Explanation of the Training Rules on Sañcaritta and Others

The decision regarding the seventh, eighth, and ninth training rules should be understood in the same manner as stated in the three training rules beginning with Sañcaritta.

## The Explanation of the Training Rules on Sañcaritta and Others is Finished.

## 10. Explanation of the Training Rule on Renouncing the Training

In the tenth training rule, "Kiṃnumāva samaṇiyo" means "Are only these [daughters of the Sakyans] recluses?" "Tāsāhaṃ" means "I [in the presence] of those [nuns]." The meaning of the term 'up to the third time' (yāvatatiyaka) should be understood as stated in the explanation of the Bhikkhu Pātimokkha, and the remaining decision should be understood in the same manner as stated in the explanation of the Saṅghabheda training rule in that same Bhikkhu Pātimokkha. Specifically, this training rule was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning the nun Caṇḍakāḷī, due to the incident of her saying words such as "I renounce the Buddha." The fact that such speaking is the first of the four factors of this training rule is the distinction. The rest is the same as in that Saṅghabheda training rule.

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on Renouncing the Training is Finished.

## 11. Explanation of the Training Rule on Being Angry over Legal Issues

In the eleventh training rule, "Kismiñcideva adhikaraṇe" means in any one of the four types of legal questions (adhikaraṇa) without specification. "Paccākatā" means being defeated. This training rule was also laid down in Sāvatthī concerning Caṇḍakāḷī, due to the incident of her saying words such as "The nuns follow the path of favoritism (chandāgati)." The rest should be understood in the same manner as stated in the tenth training rule.

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on Being Angry over Legal Issues is Finished.
304:
## 12. Explanation of the First Training Rule on Evil Conduct

In the twelfth training rule, "Saṃsaṭṭhā" means living in association with laypeople in a manner unsuitable for recluses, through bodily and verbal actions such as pounding grain, cooking, and carrying messages. They are called "Pāpācārā" because they have evil bodily and verbal conduct. They are called "Pāpasaddā" because they have an evil reputation. They are called "Pāpasilokā" because they have evil fame regarding their livelihood. "Bhikkhunisaṃghassa vihethikā" means being harassers by way of protesting when the Community of Nuns performs formal acts (kamma) for one another. "Vajjappaṭicchādikā" means being a concealer of even minor faults.

This training rule was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning many nuns, due to the incident of their living in association with laypeople. The rest here should also be understood in the same manner as stated in the tenth training rule. However, specifically, when performing the act of formal admonition (samanubhāsana), two or three nuns should be admonished together.

## The Explanation of the First Training Rule on Evil Conduct is Finished.

## 13. Explanation of the Second Training Rule on Evil Conduct

In the thirteenth training rule, "Evaṃ vadeyya" means those nuns who have been formally admonished would speak in this way. "Evācārā" means "What kind of conduct is your conduct? You are people of such conduct"; this is the meaning. This method is the same in all places. "Uññāyā" means through knowing [them] by regarding them as low-class. "Paribhavena" means through knowing [them] with disdain, thinking "What can these nuns do?" "Akkhantiyā" means through intolerance, which means anger. "Vebhassiyā" means through intimidation, wishing to show one's power as a strong person. "Dubbalyā" means through your weakness. In all places, the meaning should be understood as a combination of "uññāyā" and "paribhavena." "Viviccatha" means live apart; it means give up the unsuitable bodily and verbal association.

This training rule was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning the nun Thullanandā, due to the incident of her urging, "Ladies, you should live only in association; do not live separately." The rest here should also be understood in the same manner as stated in the tenth training rule.

## The Explanation of the Second Training Rule on Evil Conduct is Finished.
305:
## 14. Saṅghabhedakādisikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

Regarding the four training rules beginning with Schism in the Saṅgha (Saṅghabheda), the decision should be understood according to the method already stated in the commentary on the Bhikkhu Pātimokkha. In truth, a bhikkhunī cannot split the Saṅgha independently; however, she can strive for a split and follow those who cause a split. In the statement, "Ladies, the seventeen Saṅghādisesa rules have been recited," there are 7 common (sādhāraṇa) training rules shared with the bhikkhus and 10 uncommon (asādhāraṇa) training rules not shared with the bhikkhus, thus making seventeen. Regarding the phrase, "The Pakkhamānatta (fortnightly penance) must be practiced in both Saṅghas," even if a bhikkhunī conceals an offense, there is no such thing as practicing Parivāsa (probation), nor does she incur a Dukkaṭa offense due to concealment. Therefore, whether she conceals it or not, she must practice only the single Pakkhamānatta.

Bhikkhunīs must grant that Pakkhamānatta by cleansing their own boundary (sīmā) and convening a group of at least four bhikkhunīs, either in the monastery boundary or, if unable to cleanse the monastery boundary, in a small boundary (khaṇḍasīmā). If there is one offense, it should be granted based on that one; if there are two, three, or many, whether of the same nature or different natures, one should take what is desired from the objects, lineages, names, and types of offenses mentioned in the commentary on the Bhikkhu Pātimokkha and apply them in the formal act (kammavācā).

In such application, this is a brief illustration based on the first offense: That bhikkhunī who has committed the offense should approach the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha, arrange her upper robe over one shoulder, pay homage at the feet of the senior bhikkhunīs, sit on her heels, join her hands in reverence, and speak thus: "Ladies, I have committed one offense of Ussayavāda (inciting a dispute). Ladies, I request the Saṅgha for Pakkhamānatta for that one offense of Ussayavāda." After having her request thus three times, a competent and capable bhikkhunī should inform the Saṅgha:

"Let the Saṅgha, ladies, hear me. This bhikkhunī named so-and-so has committed one offense of Ussayavāda. She requests the Saṅgha for Pakkhamānatta for that one offense of Ussayavāda. If the Saṅgha is ready, let the Saṅgha give Pakkhamānatta to the bhikkhunī named so-and-so for one offense of Ussayavāda. This is the motion (ñatti).

Let the Saṅgha, ladies, hear me. This bhikkhunī named so-and-so... (as above) For the second time... (as above) For the third time I speak this matter. Let the Saṅgha, ladies, hear me... (and so on)" she should recite. "The Saṅgha has given Pakkhamānatta to the bhikkhunī named so-and-so for one offense of Ussayavāda..."
306:
"...for the offense of Ussayavāda. It is acceptable to the Saṅgha, therefore it is silent. Thus I record this."

At the end of the formal act (kammavācā), she should undertake the duties, saying, "I undertake the duties, I undertake the penance (mānatta)." Having informed the Saṅgha, if the bhikkhunī wishes to stay having set aside the duties, she should set them aside either in the midst of the Saṅgha in that same boundary, or if the bhikkhunīs have departed, in the presence of a single bhikkhunī who is not her companion, saying, "I set aside the duties, I set aside the penance." She may also set them aside by informing a visiting bhikkhunī. From the time the duties are set aside, she remains in the status of one of normal standing (pakatatta). After that, before dawn, four bhikkhunīs should take that bhikkhunī and, having gone beyond two stone-throws from the precincts of the village and the precincts of the bhikkhus' monastery, and having turned off the main road, she should sit in a place concealed by bushes, fences, and so on. Four bhikkhus should also go there and sit separately not far from the bhikkhunīs. Then, that bhikkhunī, having undertaken the duties in the manner already mentioned, should first inform the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha thus:

"Ladies, I committed one offense of Ussayavāda. I requested the Saṅgha for Pakkhamānatta for that offense of Ussayavāda. The Saṅgha gave me Pakkhamānatta for that one offense of Ussayavāda. I am practicing the penance. Ladies, I inform you that I am practicing the penance. Let the Saṅgha record me as one practicing the penance."

After that, she should go to the Bhikkhu Saṅgha and inform them thus: "Venerable Sirs, I committed one offense of Ussayavāda... (as above)... I inform you that I am practicing the penance. Let the Saṅgha record me as one practicing the penance." Having informed them, she should stay only in the presence of the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha. From that time on, even if the bhikkhus depart, or if the bhikkhunīs depart leaving one companion behind, the penance is considered practiced in both Saṅghas. As long as dawn has not yet risen, she must inform the first bhikkhu or bhikkhunī she sees. When dawn rises, she should set aside the duties and go to the bhikkhunī residence. In this manner, fifteen dawns must be observed.

If a bhikkhunī does not set aside the duties, she should inform the four bhikkhus and four bhikkhunīs daily when there are no visitors, and inform all visitors when they are present, practicing properly for fifteen days according to the method taught in the Parivāsikakkhandhaka. This is the summary in this commentary. As for the details...
307:
A bhikkhunī who reports [her practice of penance] for fifteen days should conduct herself properly according to the method stated in the Pārivāsikakkhandhaka (Cūḷavagga, 75 onwards); this is the summary in this Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī Commentary. The detailed explanation has already been stated in the Samantapāsādikā Commentary. (In detail: After that, the bhikkhunī, having undertaken the duties, should first report to the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha: "Venerable ladies, I have fallen into an offense through the training rule on provoking a dispute (ussayavāda). I have requested fifteen days of penance (mānatta) because of that offense. The Saṅgha has granted it to me. I am practicing that penance. Venerable ladies, I inform you that I am practicing penance; may the Saṅgha recognize me as one practicing penance." Then, she must go to the Bhikkhu Saṅgha and report in the same manner. After reporting, she must reside only with the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha. From that time on, even if the bhikkhus depart, or if the bhikkhunīs depart leaving one companion, the penance is considered practiced in the dual Saṅgha (ubhato-saṅgha). Until the dawn has not yet risen, whichever bhikkhu or bhikkhunī she sees first, she must report to that bhikkhu or bhikkhunī. When dawn rises, she should relinquish the duty and go to the bhikkhunī nunnery. In this way, fifteen days (fifteen dawns) are taken. A bhikkhunī who has not yet relinquished the duty must report daily to four bhikkhus and four bhikkhunīs if there are no visitors; if there are visitors, she must report to all visitors and practice for the full fifteen days.)

Regarding the phrase "ciṇṇamānattāya bhikkhuniyā" (for a bhikkhunī who has practiced penance): when a bhikkhunī has thus completed the practiced penance, the act of rehabilitation (abbhāna-kamma) should be performed for her according to the method stated: "wherever there may be a group of twenty bhikkhunīs." The rest of the text is clear.

## In the explanation of the Pātimokkha of the Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī Commentary
## In the Bhikkhunī Pātimokkha
## The explanation of the Saṅghādisesa is finished.

Nissaggiya Pācittiya Section (Patta-vagga). 1. Among the Nissaggiya training rules, in the first training rule of the first group (varga), before the second group etc., regarding the phrase "patta-sannicayaṃ kareyya": if one should make an accumulation of bowls, it means keeping a bowl worthy of determination for even a single day without determining (adhiṭṭhāna) it or without assigning (vikappanā) it. This training rule was laid down because of the accumulation of bowls. The rest of the text should be understood according to the method stated in the explanation of the Bhikkhu Pātimokkha. Indeed, the slight difference is that in that Bhikkhu Pātimokkha training rule, an offense is committed after ten days have passed; however, in this training rule, an offense is committed even after one day has passed. This is the only difference between that training rule and this one. The rest of the procedure is exactly the same as that training rule.

The first training rule is finished.
308:
## Nissaggiya Section
## 1. Explanation of the Training Rule on Accumulation of Bowls
Among the Nissaggiya training rules, in the first training rule of the first group, the phrase "should one make an accumulation of bowls" means one should make a hoard of bowls; it means keeping a bowl worthy of determination for even a single day without determining it or without assigning it.

This was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning the group-of-six bhikkhunīs on the occasion of accumulating bowls. The rest of the explanation should be understood according to the method stated in the explanation of the Bhikkhu Pātimokkha. Indeed, while in that Bhikkhu Pātimokkha training rule an offense is committed after ten days have passed, here it is after one day has passed; this much is the difference between that and this. The rest is exactly the same.

## The explanation of the training rule on accumulation of bowls is finished.

## 2. Explanation of the Training Rule on Out-of-season Robes
In the second training rule, "out-of-season robe" (akāla-cīvara) refers to a robe that arises at a time other than the robe-months if the Kaṭhina has not been spread, or other than the Kaṭhina months if the Kaṭhina has been spread; or it refers to a robe given by designation even during the [proper] time. A robe given by designation means a robe given after saying, "Let whoever arrives distribute it," or after saying, "I give this to the group, I give this to you," or a robe given by placing it at the feet with the intention to give. For a bhikkhunī who, having determined such an out-of-season robe as a "season-robe" (kāla-cīvara), causes it to be distributed, there is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa) due to the effort; that which she receives herself becomes a Nissaggiya (to be forfeited). Even after forfeiting and receiving it back, it must be applied only according to the original gift; this same method applies to other training rules of this nature.

This was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning the bhikkhunī Thullanandā on the occasion of distributing an out-of-season robe by determining it as a "season-robe." There is a wrongdoing (dukkaṭa) if there is doubt regarding an out-of-season robe, and also if there is the perception of it being an out-of-season robe or doubt regarding a season-robe. There is no offense if there is the perception of it being a season-robe in both cases, or for one who is insane, etc. The four factors here are: it being an out-of-season robe, having such a perception, causing it to be distributed by a pretext (lesena) after determining it as a "season-robe," and the acquisition. The origins (samuṭṭhāna) etc. are similar to the training rule on taking what is not given (adinnādāna).

## The explanation of the training rule on out-of-season robes is finished.
309:
## 3. Cīvaraparivattanasikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā

In the third training rule, 'handa' means 'take'. 'Acchindeyya' means that for a nun who herself snatches back many robes that have been tied in a bundle, there is only a single offense. However, for other robes that are not bundled, there are offenses according to the number of items. In the case of causing someone else to snatch (commanding), even if many robes are snatched through a single command, there is only a single offense.

This training rule was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning the nun Thullanandā, on account of her snatching back a robe after having exchanged it. This training rule involves a command. A tika-pācittiya (Pācittiya in three ways) is incurred. For requisites other than robes, a tika-dukkaṭa is incurred. For the robes of those not fully ordained (sikkhamānās and sāmaṇerīs), only a tika-dukkaṭa is incurred. There is no offense for a nun who takes a robe given by the owner, or takes it out of trust in the owner, nor for those who are insane, etc. The three factors here are: being fully ordained, the exchanged robe being one that is suitable for formal assignment (vikappanā), and snatching it back or causing it to be snatched with the perception that it is one's own. The origins (samuṭṭhāna), etc., are similar to those of stealing (adinnādāna). This training rule involves painful feeling.

## The Commentary on the Training Rule on Exchanging Robes is finished.

## 4. Aññaviññāpanasikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā

In the fourth training rule, 'viññāpetvā' means making known, or asking, "Bring such and such a thing." 'Aññaṃ viññāpeyya' means rejecting the item that was previously asked for—after being asked, "Noble Lady, what is your discomfort? What should be brought?"—and asking for something else other than that original item, with the desire to take either that item or another. For that nun, there is a dukkaṭa offense for the act of asking, and it becomes a nissaggiya [pācittiya] upon acquisition.

This training rule was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning the nun Thullanandā, on account of her asking for something else after having already asked for one thing. A tika-pācittiya is incurred. If it is not something else, a dvika-dukkaṭa is incurred. However, there is no offense for asking for something that is not different with the perception that it is not different; for asking for the same thing again if it was insufficient; for asking for something else along with the original item if there is a need for it; for asking for something else entirely after showing the benefit that the other item is of better value than the one requested; nor for those who are insane, etc. The three factors here are: the desire to take by means of a pretext, asking for something else, and acquisition. The origins, etc., are similar to those of the sañcaritta (acting as a go-between) rule.

## The Commentary on the Training Rule on Asking for Something Else is finished.
310:
## 5. Aññacetāpanasikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā

In the fifth training rule, 'aññaṃ cetāpetvā' means causing something else to be bartered by saying, "Bring such and such a thing," using one's own allowable goods. 'Aññaṃ cetāpeyya' means thinking, "After giving me this item, they will bring another as well," and then saying, "I have no need for this; bring me such and such a thing for my sake," thus causing something else to be bartered instead of the item originally intended for exchange. For that nun, there is a dukkaṭa offense for the effort to have it bartered. When it is obtained, whether it was brought with the original allowable goods or with another price, it is a nissaggiya. The rest of the procedure is exactly the same as the fourth training rule.

## The Commentary on the Training Rule on Having Something Else Bartered is finished.

## 6. Paṭhamasaṅghikacetāpanasikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā

In the sixth training rule, 'aññadatthikena' refers to requisites given for the sake of another thing. 'Aññuddisikena' refers to requisites given by designating another thing. 'Saṅghikena' refers to requisites dedicated to the Sangha. 'Parikkhārena' refers to allowable goods. 'Aññaṃ cetāpeyya' means causing something else to be bartered from the requisites that the donor had designated and specified by saying, "Please use such and such a thing." For that nun, there is a dukkaṭa offense for the effort, and it becomes a nissaggiya upon acquisition.

This training rule was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning many nuns, on account of their causing something else to be bartered with such requisites. A tika-pācittiya is incurred. For a requisite that is not for another purpose, a dvika-dukkaṭa is incurred. However, there is no offense for a nun who applies it [to another purpose] with the perception that it is not for another purpose; for a nun who applies the remainder; for a nun who applies it after informing the donors, saying, "You have given this for this purpose, but we have a need for such and such a thing"; for nuns who apply it in such times of danger as when they must even abandon the monastery and depart; nor for those who are insane, etc. The rest of the procedure is exactly the same as the fourth training rule.

## The Commentary on the First Training Rule on Bartering Sangha Property is finished.

## 7. Dutiyasaṅghikacetāpanasikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā

In the seventh training rule, 'saññācikena' means with requisites that were asked for by oneself. This term 'saññācikena' is the only difference here. The rest of the procedure is exactly the same as the sixth training rule.

## The Commentary on the Second Training Rule on Bartering Sangha Property is finished.
311:
## 8. Commentary on the First Training Rule on Bartering with a Group
In the eighth training rule, 'mahājanikena' means with requisites renounced to a group of bhikkhunīs. The inclusion of this term in this training rule is the difference from the sixth training rule.
## Conclusion of the Commentary on the First Training Rule on Bartering with a Group.
## 9. Commentary on the Second Training Rule on Bartering with a Group
