In the ninth training rule, the term 'saññācikena' is an addition compared to the eighth training rule. The remaining meanings in both training rules are the same as the sixth training rule.
## Conclusion of the Commentary on the Second Training Rule on Bartering with a Group.
## 10. Commentary on the Training Rule on Bartering with an Individual
In the tenth training rule, 'puggalikena' means with requisites renounced to a single nun. 'Saññācikena' means with requisites requested by oneself. 'Aññaṃ cetāpeyya' means she barters for something else; for a nun who barters for something other than the object intended for donation, there is a dukkaṭa offense for the effort and a nissaggiya offense upon acquisition.
In Sāvatthī, it was laid down concerning the case of the nun Thullanandā bartering for another object with such requisites. The rest is the same as the sixth rule.
## Conclusion of the Commentary on the Training Rule on Bartering with an Individual.
## First Chapter: Alms-bowl Chapter (Patta-vagga).
## 11. Commentary on the Training Rule on Heavy Cloaks
In the first training rule of the second chapter, 'garupāvuraṇaṃ' refers to a cloak worn in the cold season. In the term 'catukkaṃsaparamam', a kaṃsa is a kahāpaṇa worth four units, therefore it means a cloak worth sixteen kahāpaṇas. 'Cetāpetabbaṃ' means that, excluding fellow practitioners, relatives, and those who have invited her, she may request it when another person, pleased by some quality, says, "Lady, tell me what you need." 'Tato ce uttarī' means that for a nun who requests more than that value of sixteen kahāpaṇas, there is a dukkaṭa offense, and a nissaggiya offense when it is obtained.
312:
In Sāvatthī, it was laid down concerning the case of the nun Thullanandā requesting a blanket from the King of Kosala. A tika-pācittiya (threefold pācittiya) is incurred. For a cloak worth less than four kaṃsas, a dvika-dukkaṭa (twofold dukkaṭa) is incurred. However, there is no offense: for a nun who, perceiving it to be less than four kaṃsas, requests a cloak not exceeding four kaṃsas; from relatives or those who have invited her; for the sake of another; with her own money; for a nun who requests a cheap cloak when the donor intended to have her request an expensive one; and for those who are insane, etc. Being a heavy cloak, having a value exceeding four kaṃsas, requesting in an unpermitted place, and acquisition—these four are the factors of this training rule. The origin (samuṭṭhāna) and so forth are the same as the Sañcaritta training rule.
## Conclusion of the Commentary on the Training Rule on Heavy Cloaks.
## 12. Commentary on the Training Rule on Light Cloaks
In the second training rule, 'lahupāvuraṇaṃ' refers to a cloak worn in the hot season. 'Aḍḍhateyyakaṃsaparamam' means a cloak worth ten kahāpaṇas. The rest is the same as the first rule.
## Conclusion of the Commentary on the Training Rule on Light Cloaks.
The eighteen training rules following this—eight in this chapter and ten in the third chapter—should be understood in the same manner as explained in the commentary on the Bhikkhu Pātimokkha.
## Third Chapter: Gold and Silver Chapter (Jātarūpa-vagga).
"Ladies, the thirty Nissaggiya Pācittiya rules have been recited." In this statement, there are eighteen shared (sādhāraṇa) training rules laid down concerning monks and twelve unshared (asādhāraṇa) training rules, thus making thirty. In all other places, the meaning is quite clear.
## In the Commentary on the Bhikkhunī Pātimokkha of the Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī,
## The Commentary on the Nissaggiya Pācittiya is Finished.
313:
## Pācittiya Section
## 1. Garlic Chapter (Lasuṇa-vagga)
## 1. Commentary on the Garlic Training Rule
Among the Pācittiya offenses, in the first training rule of the Garlic Chapter, 'lasuṇa' refers only to raw garlic with many cloves grown in the Magadha country; it does not refer to garlic with one, two, or three cloves. For a nun who receives such garlic with the thought "I will eat it," there is a dukkaṭa offense. For every swallow, there is a pācittiya offense.
In Sāvatthī, this training rule was laid down concerning the case of the nun Thullanandā having garlic brought. A tika-pācittiya is incurred. In the case of non-garlic, a dvika-dukkaṭa is incurred. However, there is no offense: if she perceives it as not being garlic; for yellow onion (palaṇḍuka), red onion (bhañjanaka), green onion (haritaka), spring onion (cāpalasuṇa), onion added in cooking soup, onion added in cooking meat, onion added in cooking oil, jujube jam (sāḷava), side dishes (uttaribhaṅga), and for those who are insane, etc. There are two factors here: being raw garlic and the act of swallowing. The origin (samuṭṭhāna) and so forth are the same as the Eḷakaloma training rule.
## Conclusion of the Commentary on the Garlic Training Rule.
## 2. Commentary on the Training Rule on Hair in the Private Area
In the second training rule, 'sambādha' refers to concealed places, meaning the armpits and the urinary area. 'Saṃharāpeyya' means that for a nun who has the hair removed by any means such as a razor, tweezers, or scissors, there is a pācittiya offense according to the number of efforts (payoga), not according to the number of hairs.
In Sāvatthī, this training rule was laid down concerning the case of the group-of-six nuns having hair removed from the private area. If she commands another for her own benefit, it is a training rule involving a command (sāṇattika). There is no variety of offenses. There is no offense if it is removed due to illness, or for those who are insane, etc. There are two factors here: the absence of illness and the removal of hair in the private area. The origin (samuṭṭhāna) and so forth are the same as the training rule on traveling on a journey with a nun.
## Conclusion of the Commentary on the Training Rule on Hair in the Private Area.
314:
## 3. Talaghātaka Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā
In the third Talaghātaka training rule, "talaghātaka" means striking the exterior of the urinary passage (passāvamagga), even with a lotus filament; it means a Pācittiya offense is committed by striking the urinary passage.

This training rule was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning two nuns on the grounds of striking the exterior of the urinary passage. It is a training rule involving a command (sāṇattika), just as in the previous method. There is no distinction in the offense. Indeed, from this training rule onwards, where there is no distinction in the offense, I shall proceed without mentioning it. There is no offense for a nun who strikes a boil or a wound due to illness, nor for insane nuns and so forth. The offense is committed if these three factors are present: the absence of illness, striking the urinary passage, and enjoying the sensation of the strike. The origins (samuṭṭhāna) and so forth are the same as the first Pārājika.

## The Commentary on the Talaghātaka Training Rule Ends.

## 4. Jatumuṭṭhaka Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā
In the fourth Jatumuṭṭhaka training rule, "jatumuṭṭhaka" refers to a smooth stick made of lacquer. This was stated by way of the original story. In fact, an offense is committed even by a nun who inserts a lotus filament out of lust.

This was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning a certain nun on the grounds of enjoying the use of a smooth lacquer stick. The rest of the explanation is exactly the same as the third training rule.

## The Commentary on the Jatumuṭṭhaka Training Rule Ends.

## 5. Udakasuddhika Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā
In the fifth Udakasuddhika training rule, "udakasuddhika" refers to the washing of the urinary passage. "Ādiyamānāya" refers to the nun who is performing it. "Dvaṅgulapabbaparamaṃ ādātabbaṃ" means that one may wash up to the length of two finger-joints, measuring one joint on each of two fingers. "Taṃ atikkāmentiyā" means that if, while washing, she inserts the tip of a third finger breadth-wise, or up to the third joint of a single finger depth-wise out of lust, she commits a Pācittiya offense.

This was laid down in the Sakyan country concerning a certain nun on the grounds of washing with water too deeply. There are three types of Pācittiya (tika-pācittiya). For insertion less than two finger-joints, two types of Dukkaṭa are committed. In that...
315:
Furthermore, there is no offense for a nun who, thinking it is less than two finger-joints, takes the measure of two finger-joints; for a nun who takes more than two finger-joints due to illness; or for insane nuns and so forth. The rest is the same as the third training rule.

## The Commentary on the Udakasuddhika Training Rule Ends.

## 6. Upatiṭṭhana Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā
In the sixth training rule, "bhuñjantassa" means (near) a monk who is eating one of the five kinds of meals. "Pānīyena" means with pure water or with one of the liquids such as buttermilk (to serve him). "Vidhūpanena" means (fanning) with any kind of fan. "Upatiṭṭheyya" means if she stands within the reach of a hand (hatthapāsa) holding either of these two, she commits a Pācittiya offense.

This was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning a certain nun on the grounds of standing thus near a monk who is eating. It is a Tika-pācittiya. A Dukkaṭa offense is committed by a nun who stands near a monk who is eating snacks outside the reach of a hand. Regarding unordained persons (anupasampanna), it is a Tika-dukkaṭa. There is no offense for a nun who gives it herself saying, "Drink this," or "Fan with this," or for one who causes another to give it, or for one who commands an unordained person to stand near, or for insane nuns and so forth. Standing within the reach of a hand of a monk who is eating, and holding either drinking water or a fan—these two are the factors of this training rule. The origins (samuṭṭhāna) and so forth are the same as the Eḷakaloma training rule.

## The Commentary on the Upatiṭṭhana Training Rule Ends.

## 7. Āmakadhañña Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā
In the seventh training rule, "viññatvā" means having asked, even from one's own mother. "Bhuñjeyya" means if she swallows. In this training rule, asking and eating are the essential factors. Therefore, from the moment of receiving—whether she asks for it herself and has another perform the roasting etc., or she has another ask for it and performs the roasting etc. herself—until the chewing with the teeth, Dukkaṭa offenses are committed for the preliminary actions. For every swallow, she commits a Pācittiya offense.

This was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning many nuns on the grounds of asking for raw grain. For raw grain obtained without asking, either by herself or by another, the roasting etc...
316:
Whether she prepares it herself or has someone else prepare it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for the nun who eats it. However, regarding raw grain obtained through another's request, there is also an offense of wrong-doing for the nun who eats it, even after roasting it herself or having it roasted. There is no offense for: a nun who requests it for the purpose of inducing perspiration, etc., when ill; a nun who accepts raw grain obtained without requesting it for the purpose of new construction (navakamma); a nun who requests beans such as mung beans or black grams from relatives or those who have offered an invitation; and those who are insane, etc. In this training rule, there are three factors: (1) requesting or having someone else request any of the seven types of grain; (2) obtaining it; (3) swallowing it after roasting it oneself or having it roasted. The origins (samuṭṭhāna), etc., are the same as the Addhānamagga-sikkhāpada.

## The Explanation of the Āmakadhañña Training Rule is finished.

## 8. The Explanation of the First Uccārachadḍana Training Rule

In the eighth training rule, 'saṅkāra' means rubbish. 'Vighāsa' means any leftover food; mouth-wash water and used tooth-sticks are also called vighāsa. Regarding bones and scraps spat out from the mouth, there is no need to specifically call them vighāsa. 'Tirokuṭṭe vā tiropākāre vā' means outside of any wall or enclosure. 'Chaḍḍeyya vā chaḍḍāpeyya vā' means if she throws these things (excrement, etc.) together with a single effort, there is only one offense. Even if she has many items thrown by a single command, there is only one offense.

It was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning a certain nun in the matter of throwing excrement over a wall. This training rule involves a command (āṇattika). For monks, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). There is no offense for a nun who throws it after looking down, or throws it in an unusable place, or for those who are insane, etc. The five factors in this training rule are: (1) being excrement, etc.; (2) not looking; (3) being a place used by people; (4) being outside a wall or enclosure; (5) throwing it oneself or having it thrown. The origins, etc., are the same as the Sañcaritta-sikkhāpada. This training rule is both action and non-action (kiriyā-akiriyā).

## The Explanation of the First Uccārachadḍana Training Rule is finished.

## 9. The Explanation of the Second Uccārachadḍana Training Rule

In the ninth training rule, 'harite' means in a field or in a garden such as a coconut grove, or in any place where green crops are planted. For a nun who throws those things (excrement, etc.) in such a green place herself, or has someone else throw them...
317:
The offense is incurred just as in the previous method. Even for a nun who, sitting in such a (green) place, drinks at least some water and then throws away a coconut shell with its top cut off, there is indeed an offense.

It was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning many nuns in the matter of throwing excrement, etc., on green crops. This training rule involves a command. There is an offense of pācittiya involving three cases (tika-pācittiya). For a monk, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). For a nun, there is an offense of wrong-doing as long as the sprouts have not yet emerged in a field where seeds have been sown. In a non-green place, there are two offenses of wrong-doing (dvika-dukkaṭa). There is no offense for throwing in such a green place while perceiving it as non-green, or throwing in a harvested field, or throwing after asking the owners for permission, or for those who are insane, etc. The remaining explanation is just the same as the eighth training rule.

## The Explanation of the Second Uccārachadḍana Training Rule is finished.

## 10. The Explanation of the Naccagīta Training Rule

In the tenth training rule, 'dancing' (nacca) includes even a peacock's dance. 'Singing' (gīta) includes even the long chanting of Dhamma-preachers. 'Music' (vādita) includes even the sound of a water-drum. 'For the purpose of seeing' (dassanāya) means for a nun who goes to see or hear any of these—dancing, singing, or music—there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for every step. If she stands and watches or listens in a certain place, there is one offense for a single effort. For a nun who looks in various directions, there is an offense for every effort.

It was laid down in Rājagaha concerning the group of six nuns in the matter of going to see dancing, etc. Whether she performs those things herself, or commands another, or speaks with a pretext such as 'Make an offering to the shrine,' or accepts by saying 'Very well' when told 'We shall make an offering to the shrine,' there is only an offense of pācittiya, as stated in all the commentaries. For monks, there is an offense of wrong-doing in all cases. However, there is no offense for: a nun who speaks with a pretext such as 'Attending to the shrine is good' when told 'We shall attend to your shrine'; a nun who watches or listens while standing within the monastery; similarly, one who encounters dancing, etc., that comes to where she is standing; one who sees it while going on a journey and encountering it on the way; one who sees it while going for a duty such as receiving food by tickets (salāka-bhatta); one who watches or listens after entering a festival area due to danger; and those who are insane, etc. The factors are: being one of the types of dancing, etc.; going or seeing for a reason other than those permitted...
318:
These three factors, including listening, are present in this training rule. The origin and so forth are the same as in the Eḷakaloma training rule. This training rule is a worldly fault (lokavajja), associated with unwholesome consciousness and the three feelings.

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on Dancing and Singing is finished.

## The First Chapter: Garlic (Lasuṇavagga).

## 2. The Chapter on the Darkness of Night (Rattandhakāravagga).

## 1. Explanation of the Training Rule on the Darkness of Night

In the first training rule of the Andhakāra Chapter, "rattandhakāre" means in the darkness of night. "Appadīpe" means in a place not illuminated by even one of these four kinds of light: a lamp, the moon, the sun, or the fire from a hearth. "Purisena" means with a human male who is capable of understanding, for the purpose of standing together or conversing together. "Santiṭṭheyya vā" means that by merely standing within a forearm's length (hatthapāsa), a pācittiya offense is committed. "Sallapeyyā" means that for a bhikkhunī who stands within that forearm's length and speaks words related to the household life, a pācittiya offense is also committed.

This was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning a certain bhikkhunī on the occasion of standing near [a man]. For a bhikkhunī who stands or speaks while leaving the forearm's length of a man, or without leaving the forearm's length of a yakkha and so forth, a dukkaṭa offense is committed. There is no offense for a bhikkhunī who does so after taking a wise companion, for one who does so without regard for seclusion, for one who is distracted, or for one who is insane, etc. These four factors are present in this training rule: it being the darkness of night, standing or speaking within the forearm's length of a man, the absence of a companion, and the regard for seclusion. It is associated with the origin of the theft-caravan (theyyasattha-samuṭṭhāna), action (kiriya), liberation by perception (saññāvimokkha), having intention (sacittaka), worldly fault (lokavajja), bodily action, vocal action, unwholesome consciousness, and the three feelings.

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on the Darkness of Night is finished.

## 2. Explanation of the Training Rule on a Concealed Place

In the second training rule, "paṭicchanne okāse" means in a place concealed by any kind of screen such as a wall. This term alone is the distinction in this training rule.

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on a Concealed Place is finished.
319:
## 3. Explanation of the Training Rule on Conversing in an Open Space

In the third training rule, only the term "ajjhokāse" (in an open space) is distinct. In both types of training rules, the rest of the explanation is the same as the first training rule.

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on Conversing in an Open Space is finished.

## 4. Explanation of the Training Rule on Sending Away the Companion

In the fourth training rule, "rathikāya" means on a carriage road. "Byūhe" means in a cul-de-sac (a short street that does not go through). "Siṅghāṭake" means at a crossroads. "Nikaṇṇikaṃ vā jappeyya" means to whisper something near the ear. "Uyyojeyya" means to send away the companion bhikkhunī, saying "You go," because of the desire to engage in improper conduct. "Pācittiyaṃ" means that, as in the previous method, there are three pācittiya offenses for standing and so forth. For the bhikkhunī who sends away the companion, a dukkaṭa offense is committed both for the act of sending away and for leaving the forearm's length (hatthapāsa). Once the forearm's length is left, a pācittiya offense is committed.

This was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning the bhikkhunī Thullanandā on the occasion of standing [near a man]. The rest of the explanation is the same as the previous three training rules. However, in the section on non-offense (anāpatti-vāra), the phrase "not desiring to engage in improper conduct, she sends away the companion bhikkhunī because there is a duty to be performed" is the additional distinction.

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on Sending Away the Companion is finished.

## 5. Explanation of the Training Rule on Leaving Without Asking Permission

In the fifth training rule, "purebhattaṃ" means from the time of dawn until noon. "Āsane" means in a place where one sits cross-legged. "Sāmike anāpucchā" means without asking any wise person in that family. In the term "pakkameyya," a dukkaṭa offense is committed at the first step and a pācittiya offense at the second step when, having sat inside a shelter, she passes beyond the area not reached by rain, or when she passes beyond the twelve-cubit precinct (upacāra) in an open space.

This was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning a certain bhikkhunī on the occasion of leaving without asking permission. There are three pācittiya offenses (tika-pācittiya). A dukkaṭa offense is committed in a place that is not for sitting cross-legged. Similarly...
320:
If she has asked permission but perceives that she has not, or if she is in doubt, [a dukkaṭa offense is committed]. There is no offense if she has asked permission and perceives that she has asked, or if she [sits and leaves without asking] in an immovable seat, or if she is ill, or if there are dangers, or for one who is insane, etc. These five factors are present in this training rule: it being before noon, sitting inside a house, the seat being suitable for sitting cross-legged, leaving without asking permission except for an allowed reason, and exceeding the stated limit. The origin and so forth are the same as in the Kaṭhina training rule; however, this training rule is one of action and non-action (kiriya-akiriya).

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on Leaving Without Asking Permission is finished.

## 6. Explanation of the Training Rule on Sitting Without Asking Permission

In the sixth training rule, "pacchābhatta" (after the meal) means from the time noon has passed until sunset. In the phrase "abhinisīdeyya vā" and so forth, one offense is committed for a bhikkhunī who leaves after sitting; one offense is also committed for one who leaves after lying down without sitting; and two offenses are committed for one who leaves after both sitting and lying down.

This training rule was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning the bhikkhunī Thullanandā on the occasion of sitting on a seat. The rest is the same as the fifth training rule. Just as there is no offense for an immovable seat in that fifth rule, here there is no offense for a seat that is permanently prepared (dhuvapaññatta).

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on Sitting Without Asking Permission is finished.

## 7. Explanation of the Training Rule on Spreading a Bed Without Asking Permission

In the seventh training rule, "vikāla" (wrong time) means after the sun has set. "Seyya" (bed) means even a spread of leaves. The rest is the same as the sixth training rule.

This training rule was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning many bhikkhunīs on the occasion of approaching families at the wrong time and spreading a bed and sitting without asking the owners. In the non-offense section of this training rule, there is no such thing as a "permanently prepared seat."

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on Spreading a Bed Without Asking Permission is finished.
321:
## 8. Paraujjhāpanaka Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā
In the eighth training rule, "duggahitena dūpadhāritena" means by words taken or remembered in a manner other than how they were spoken (implying causing blame). "Paraṃ" means a nun who causes another nun to be blamed in such a way as, "Lady, I heard that the senior nun does not serve [you] respectfully," etc., commits an offense of Pācittiya.

This training rule was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning a certain nun in the case of causing blame to others. There is a triad of Pācittiya (tika-pācittiya). If the person is unordained (a sikkhamānā or a sāmaṇerī), there is a triad of Dukkaṭa (tika-dukkaṭa). There is no offense only for an insane nun and others. The three factors here are: misunderstanding, causing blame, and the person being blamed being an ordained nun. The origins (samuṭṭhāna) and so forth are similar to the Adinnādāna Sikkhāpada. This [offense], however, involves painful feeling (dukkha-vedanā).

## The Commentary on the Paraujjhāpanaka Sikkhāpada is finished.

## 9. Para-abhisapana Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā
In the ninth training rule, "abhisapeyya" means she should make a curse. In making such a curse, a nun who says such things as, "May I be reborn in hell, may she be reborn in hell," etc., is said to curse by hell, meaning she abuses. A nun who says such things as, "May I become a laywoman, may she become a laywoman," etc., is said to curse by the holy life (brahmacariya). For every word spoken, she commits an offense of Pācittiya.

This training rule was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning the nun Caṇḍakāḷī in the case of cursing. There is a triad of Pācittiya. In cursing an unordained person (a layperson or a sāmaṇerī), there is a triad of Dukkaṭa. There is an offense of Dukkaṭa for cursing by means of animal birth, the realm of hungry ghosts (peta), or human misfortune (deformity). There is no offense for nuns who speak aiming at the meaning, the Dhamma, and instruction, nor for an insane nun and others. The three factors here are: cursing by hell or by the holy life, the person being ordained, and the absence of aiming for the meaning and the Dhamma. The origins and so forth are the same as the eighth training rule.

## The Commentary on the Para-abhisapana Sikkhāpada is finished.

## 10. Rodana Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā
In the tenth training rule, "vadhitvā" means having struck with the hands and so forth (implying crying). For a nun who performs both striking and crying, there is an offense of Pācittiya.
322:
This training rule was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning the nun Caṇḍakāḷī in the case of striking herself and crying. For a nun who only strikes or only cries, there is only an offense of Dukkaṭa. There is no offense for a nun who only cries without striking when affected by the loss of relatives, the affliction of disease, or the loss of wealth, nor for an insane nun and others. In this training rule, there are these two factors: striking oneself and crying. The origins and so forth are similar to the Samanubhāsana Sikkhāpada. This training rule, however, is a mere action (kiriya).

## The Commentary on the Rodana Sikkhāpada is finished.

## The Second Chapter, the Rattanandhakāra Vagga, is finished.

## 3. Nagga Vagga

## 1. Nagga Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā
In the first training rule of the Nagga Vagga, "naggā" means one who has neither a lower garment nor an upper garment. For a nun who bathes naked in this way, there is an offense of Dukkaṭa for every effort, and an offense of Pācittiya at the end of the bath.

This training rule was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning many nuns in the case of bathing naked. There is no offense for a nun who bathes in such dangers as when the water-cloth (udakasāṭika) has been snatched away or lost, or thinking, "This water-cloth is very valuable; if they see it, even thieves might take it away," nor for an insane nun and others. In this training rule, there are these three factors: nakedness, the absence of an allowed reason, and the completion of the bath. The origins and so forth are similar to the Eḷakaloma Sikkhāpada.

## The Commentary on the Nagga Sikkhāpada is finished.

## 2. Udakasāṭika Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā
In the second training rule, it was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning the group-of-six nuns in the case of wearing outsized water-cloths. Everything else in this rule should be understood in the same manner as stated in the Nisīdana Sikkhāpada of the Ratana Vagga.

## The Commentary on the Udakasāṭika Sikkhāpada is finished.

## 3. Cīvarasibbana Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā
In the third training rule, "visibbetvā" means having unpicked (or undone) a poorly sewn robe in order to sew it again. "Anantarāyikinī" means the absence of even one of the ten obstacles. Except...
323:
"Four or five days" means after five days have passed from the day the robe was unsewn, if she gives up the responsibility, thinking, "I will not sew it myself, nor will I make an effort to have others sew it," she commits a Pācittiya offense.

This training rule was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning the Bhikkhunī Thullanandā, on the grounds of unsewing a robe and not resewing it. It is a Pācittiya with three cases (tika-pācittiya). If it is a robe of an unordained person (sikkhamānā or sāmaṇerī), she commits a Dukkaṭa with three cases. The same applies to other requisites besides robes. There is no offense for a bhikkhunī who faces danger, who cannot find anything despite searching, who is still in the process of sewing even after five days have passed, who is ill, during times of emergency, or for one who is insane, etc. In this training rule, there are five factors: (1) it is a robe suitable for wearing or dressing, (2) it belongs to an ordained bhikkhunī, (3) unsewing or having it unsewn for the purpose of sewing, (4) exceeding five days without a permitted reason, and (5) giving up the responsibility. The origin (samuṭṭhāna), etc., are the same as the Samanubhāsana training rule.

## The Commentary on the Cīvarasibbana Training Rule is finished.

## 4. Saṅghāṭicāra Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā

In the fourth training rule, "five days" means within the period of five days. "Saṅghāṭicāra" means the rotation or use of the saṅghāṭi and other robes. It refers to the alternating use of the five robes—the three robes (ti-cīvara) named "saṅghāṭi" because they are joined by sewing, whether through use or through sunning, plus the water-strainer cloth (udakasāṭikā) and the bodice (saṅkaccikā). "If five days are exceeded, she commits a Pācittiya offense" means that at dawn on the sixth day, if even one robe has not been rotated as described, she commits one offense; if all five, she commits five offenses.

This training rule was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning many bhikkhunīs who left their robes behind and went on a walking tour in the countryside with only their inner and upper robes. It is a Pācittiya with three cases. If she rotates them thinking five days have passed when they have not, she commits two Dukkaṭa offenses. There is no offense for one who thinks five days have not passed when they have, for one who wears, dresses in, or suns the five robes on the fifth day, for one who is ill, in times of danger such as thinking, "This robe of mine is very valuable; it is not possible to carry it in a place with such danger of thieves," or for one who is insane, etc. In this training rule, there are four factors: (1) being one of the five robes, (2) exceeding five days, (3) absence of a permitted reason, and (4) not rotating them. The origin, etc., are the same as the Kathina training rule.

## The Commentary on the Saṅghāṭicāra Training Rule is finished.
324:
## 5. Cīvarasaṅkamanīya Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā

In the fifth training rule, the Cīvarasaṅkamanīya Sikkhāpada, "cīvarasaṅkamanīya" refers to a robe that ought to be transferred (returned). It means any of the five robes belonging to another bhikkhunī that was taken without asking and should be returned. "Dhāreyya" means if she wears or dresses in that robe which should be transferred, she commits a Pācittiya offense.

This was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning a certain bhikkhunī who took another bhikkhunī's robe and wore it without asking. It is a Pācittiya with three cases (tika-pācittiya). In taking and wearing the robe of an unordained person (sikkhamānā or sāmaṇerī), she commits a Dukkaṭa with three cases. There is no offense for a bhikkhunī who wears it if it was given by the owner, or if she asked the owner, or if her own robes were snatched away or lost, or if she wears it due to dangers such as thinking, "This robe of mine is very valuable; it is not possible to carry it in a place with such danger of thieves," or for one who is insane, etc. The four factors of this training rule are: (1) it is a robe to be transferred, (2) it belongs to an ordained bhikkhunī, (3) absence of a permitted reason, and (4) wearing it. The origin, etc., are the same as the first Kathina training rule. This training rule is "kiri-yākiriya" (action and non-action).

## The Commentary on the Cīvarasaṅkamanīya Training Rule is finished.

## 6. Gaṇacīvara Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā

In the sixth training rule, "gaṇassa" means of the community of bhikkhunīs. "Cīvaralābha" refers to the last robe to be received that is suitable for formal assignment (vikappanā). "Antarāyaṃ kareyya" means to make an effort in such a way that donors who wish to give do not give. "Pācittiya" means if those donors do not give because of that bhikkhunī's words, she commits a Pācittiya offense.

This was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning the Bhikkhunī Thullanandā on the grounds of obstructing a gain of robes for the community. In obstructing requisites other than robes, she commits a Dukkaṭa offense. In obstructing a gain of robes for many bhikkhunīs or for a single bhikkhunī, she also commits only a Dukkaṭa. There is no offense for a bhikkhunī who prevents it by showing a benefit, such as saying, "Give when the price is low," or for one who is insane, etc. The three factors of this training rule are: (1) it is the last robe suitable for formal assignment, (2) it is a gain already directed toward the Saṅgha, and (3) obstructing it without showing a benefit. The origin, etc., are the same as the taking of what is not given (adinnādāna).

## The Commentary on the Gaṇacīvara Training Rule is finished.
325:
## 7. Commentary on the Training Rule on Obstructing (Paṭibāhanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā)

In the seventh training rule, "lawful distribution of robes" (dhammikaṃ cīvaravibhaṅgaṃ) refers to the distribution of robes carried out by the unified Saṅgha in assembly according to the Dhamma. "Should obstruct" (paṭibāheyya) means to prohibit; for a bhikkhunī who thus prohibits, there is an offence of expiation (pācittiya).

It was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning Bhikkhunī Thullanandā in the matter of obstructing the lawful distribution of robes. If she obstructs with doubt regarding a lawful distribution, or with the perception of lawfulness or doubt regarding an unlawful distribution, there is an offence of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). There is no offence: if she obstructs with the perception of it being unlawful in both cases; if she obstructs by showing a benefit, saying, "If distributed now, there will not be enough for one robe per person; in three or four days more will be received, let us distribute then"; or if she is insane, etc. There are three factors here: (1) the distribution of robes is lawful, (2) the perception of it being lawful, (3) obstructing without showing a benefit. The origins (samuṭṭhāna), etc., are the same as for taking what is not given (adinnādāna).

## Commentary on the Training Rule on Obstructing is finished.

## 8. Commentary on the Training Rule on Giving Robes (Cīvaradānasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā)

In the eighth training rule, "a recluse's robe" (samaṇacīvaraṃ) refers to a robe that has been marked with a kappa-bindu and is suitable for wearing or covering. For a bhikkhunī who gives such a robe, having relinquished ownership, to any layperson or wanderer, excluding the five classes of co-religionists and her parents, there is an offence of expiation (pācittiya).

It was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning Bhikkhunī Thullanandā in the matter of giving a recluse's robe to a householder. For a bhikkhu, there is an offence of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). There is no offence: if she gives it to her parents having relinquished ownership; if she gives it to others only as a temporary loan; or if she is insane, etc. There are three factors here: (1) it is a recluse's robe, (2) giving it to others besides co-religionists and parents, (3) giving it by relinquishing ownership. The origins, etc., are the same as for matchmaking (sañcaritta).

## Commentary on the Training Rule on Giving Robes is finished.

## 9. Commentary on the Training Rule on Exceeding the Time (Kāla-atikkamanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā)

In the ninth training rule, "expectation of a weak robe" (dubbalacīvarapaccāsāyā) refers to an expectation that arises upon hearing a mere statement such as, "If we are able, we will give."
326:
The meaning is: "should exceed the robe-season" (cīvarakālasamayaṃ atikkāmeyya) means that while the bhikkhunīs who have completed the rains-residence are distributing the season-robes (kālacīvara), she says, "Wait, ladies, there is still an expectation of robes for the Saṅgha," and thus causes that robe-distribution period to be exceeded. For a bhikkhunī who has not spread the kaṭhina, if she exceeds the last month of the rainy season, or for a bhikkhunī who has spread the kaṭhina, if she exceeds the day of the removal of the kaṭhina, there is an offence of expiation (pācittiya).

This was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning Bhikkhunī Thullanandā because of exceeding the robe-season with the expectation of a weak robe. If she exceeds it with doubt regarding a weak robe, or with the perception of it being a weak robe or with doubt regarding what is not a weak robe, there is an offence of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). There is no offence: if she has the perception of it not being a weak robe in both cases; if she prevents it by showing a benefit, saying, "Even though they say 'we cannot [give],' now their cotton will be produced, or a faithful man will come; when he comes, he will certainly give"; or if she is an insane bhikkhunī, etc. There are three factors here: (1) it is a weak robe, (2) the perception of it being a weak robe, (3) preventing it without showing a benefit. The origins are the same as for taking what is not given (adinnādāna).

## Commentary on the Training Rule on Exceeding the Time is finished.

## 10. Commentary on the Training Rule on Removing the Kaṭhina (Kaṭhinuddhārasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā)

In the tenth training rule, "lawful removal of the kaṭhina" (dhammikaṃ kaṭhinuddhāraṃ) means that when a lay follower, wishing to give out-of-season robes to all the bhikkhunīs, gives an amount equal to or greater than the benefit derived from the kaṭhina spreading and makes a request, the unified Bhikkhunī Saṅgha removes the kaṭhina in the interim by a ñattidutiya-kammavācā. That removal is called "lawful." It refers to such a removal of the kaṭhina. "Should obstruct" (paṭibāheyya) means to prevent. For a bhikkhunī who prevents such a removal of the kaṭhina, there is an offence of expiation (pācittiya).

This was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning Bhikkhunī Thullanandā because of obstructing the removal of the kaṭhina. The rest of the procedure should be understood in the same way as stated in the seventh training rule.

## Commentary on the Training Rule on Removing the Kaṭhina is finished.

## The Third Chapter: On Nakedness (Naggavaggo Tatiyo).
327:
## 4. Tuvaṭṭa Vagga

## 1. Commentary on the Training Rule of Sleeping on One Bed

In the first training rule of the Tuvaṭṭa Vagga, the word 'tuvaṭṭeyyuṃ' means they should sleep (lie down). Among those two nuns, whether one is already asleep and the other lies down later, or both lie down at the same time, a pācittiya offense is incurred by both.

This training rule was laid down in Sāvatthī on account of many bhikkhunīs, regarding the incident of two nuns sleeping on a single bed. If one is sleeping while the other is sitting, or if both are sitting, there is no offense for those nuns, nor for those who are insane, and so forth. In this training rule, there are two factors: (1) being on a single bed, and (2) two people sleeping. The origins (samuṭṭhāna) and other details are the same as the Elakaloma training rule.

## The Commentary on the Training Rule of Sleeping on One Bed ends.

## 2. Commentary on the Training Rule of Sleeping with One Covering

In the second training rule, those who have a single spread and a single covering are called 'ekattharaṇapāvuraṇā'. This is a designation for nuns who sleep by spreading one end of a portable robe, spread, mat, or rug, and covering themselves with the other end. It means that a pācittiya offense is incurred by nuns who sleep by spreading and covering themselves with that same item.

This was laid down in Sāvatthī on account of many bhikkhunīs, regarding the incident of sleeping in such a manner. There is a triad of pācittiya (tika-pācittiya). If they use either a single spread or a single covering together, a dukkaṭa offense is incurred. When the spread and covering are different, but they perceive them as the same, two dukkaṭa offenses are incurred. However, if the spread and covering are different and they perceive them as different, and they sleep after showing the boundary, there is no offense for such a nun, nor for those who are insane, and so forth. The rest is the same as the first training rule.

## The Commentary on the Training Rule of Sleeping with One Covering ends.

## 3. Commentary on the Training Rule of Causing Discomfort

In the third training rule, 'aphāsu' (discomfort) means performing actions such as walking, standing, or sitting in front of another nun without asking permission, with the thought, "By doing this, this nun will be uncomfortable," or personally reciting the Pali, making others recite, questioning the meaning, or chanting. In walking, an offense is incurred for every turn; in standing and so forth, for every effort; and in reciting and so forth, a pācittiya offense is incurred for every word.
328:
This training rule was laid down in Sāvatthī on account of the bhikkhunī Thullanandā, regarding the incident of intentionally causing discomfort. It is a tika-pācittiya (triad of pācittiya). For causing discomfort to one who is not ordained (anupasampanna), it is a tika-dukkaṭa (triad of dukkaṭa). There is no offense if there is no desire to cause discomfort, if one performs walking, standing, or sitting in front after asking permission, or if one recites the Pali, makes others recite, questions the meaning, or chants, or for those who are insane, and so forth. In this training rule, there are four factors: (1) being ordained (upasampanna), (2) the desire to cause discomfort, (3) the act of causing discomfort, and (4) not asking permission. The origins (samuṭṭhāna) and other details are the same as the Adinnādāna training rule. This training rule is of the nature of action and inaction (kiriya-akiriya) and involves painful feeling (dukkha-vedanā).

## The Commentary on the Training Rule of Causing Discomfort ends.

## 4. Commentary on the Training Rule of Not Attending to the Sick

In the fourth training rule, 'dukkhita' means one who is ill (gilāna). 'Sahajīvinī' means a co-resident pupil (saddhivihārinī). 'Neva upaṭṭhaheyya' means that if she does not attend to that pupil herself, nor has others attend to her, a pācittiya offense is incurred as soon as the responsibility is abandoned.

This was laid down in Sāvatthī on account of the bhikkhunī Thullanandā, regarding the incident of not attending to a sick co-resident pupil. If she does not attend to a student (antevāsinī) or one who is not ordained (anupasampanna, such as a sikkhamānā or a sāmaṇerī), a dukkaṭa offense is incurred. There is no offense if, when one of the ten dangers exists, she searches for someone to attend but does not find anyone, if she is ill herself, in times of peril, or if she is insane, and so forth. In this training rule, there are four factors: (1) being ill, (2) being a co-resident pupil, (3) the absence of an allowed reason, and (4) the abandonment of the duty of attendance. The origins and other details are the same as the Samanubhāsana training rule.

## The Commentary on the Training Rule of Not Attending to the Sick ends.

## 5. Commentary on the Training Rule of Evicting

In the fifth training rule, 'upassayaṃ datvā' means having given one's own personal dwelling (vihāra) that has a door-leaf attached. 'Nikkaḍḍheyya' means that even if there are many doors, if she evicts with a single effort, one offense is incurred. If she evicts with multiple efforts, offenses are incurred according to the number of efforts. The same principle applies to commanding others. However, if she commands, "Drag her out past this door and that door," even with a single command, offenses are incurred according to the number of doors.
329:
In Sāvatthī, concerning the Bhikkhunī Thullanandā, this training rule was laid down regarding such a matter (of expelling). A Pācittiya of the triad is incurred. If one expels [a nun] from a dwelling that is not fitted with a door, a Dukkaṭa offense is incurred. If one expels a non-ordained person (such as a female novice), a Dukkaṭa of the triad is incurred. Whether the dwelling is fitted with a door or not, if one pulls out the requisites of both the ordained and the non-ordained, only a Dukkaṭa offense is incurred. The remaining points are as stated in the training rule on expelling from a communal dwelling (Saṃghika-vihāra-nikkaḍḍhana Sikkhāpada).

## Nikkaḍḍhana Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā Niṭṭhitā.

## 6. Saṃsaṭṭha Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā
The sixth training rule has a meaning that is clear and obvious. In Sāvatthī, concerning the Bhikkhunī Caṇḍakāḷī, it was laid down regarding the matter of associating with laypeople. The remaining decisions in this training rule are similar to the decisions stated in the first Ariṭṭha training rule.

## Saṃsaṭṭha Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā Niṭṭhitā.

## 7. Antoraṭṭha Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā
In the seventh training rule, "Antoraṭṭhe" means within the kingdom of the king where one resides. "Asatthikā cārikaṃ" means for a nun traveling without a caravan (or escort), a Pācittiya offense is incurred for every village-to-village interval, or for every half-yojana distance in a wilderness where there are no villages.

In Sāvatthī, concerning many Bhikkhunīs, it was laid down in the same manner as previously stated regarding the matter of setting out on a tour. There is no offense for one who goes with a caravan, in a safe and secure area, in times of danger, or for one who is insane, etc. There are four factors here: being within the kingdom, being unsafe, the absence of an allowed reason, and setting out on a tour. The origin (samuṭṭhāna), etc., are similar to the Sheep’s Wool training rule (Eḷakaloma Sikkhāpada).

## Antoraṭṭha Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā Niṭṭhitā.

## 8. Tiroraṭṭha Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā
In the eighth training rule, "Tiroraṭṭhe" means in the kingdom of another king, excluding the kingdom of the king where one resides. The remaining points should be understood in the same manner as stated in the seventh training rule. However, the city where this was laid down is Rājagaha.

## Tiroraṭṭha Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā Niṭṭhitā.
330:
## 9. Antovassa Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā
In the ninth training rule, "Antovassa" means within that very Rains, without having completed either the first three months or the latter three months of the Rains (referring to setting out on tour). In this training rule, there is no offense for a nun who goes for a seven-day business (sattāhakaraṇīya), for one who goes because of being harassed by someone, in times of danger, or for one who is insane, etc. The rest is similar to the eighth training rule.

## Antovassa Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā Niṭṭhitā.

## 10. Cārikanapakkamana Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā
In the tenth training rule, "Vassaṃvuṭṭhā" means having completed either the first three months or the latter three months of the Rains. In the phrase "Chappañcayojanāni," it is permissible to go up to five yojanas after performing the Pavāraṇā; as for six yojanas, it goes without saying (it is certainly permissible). However, if one goes for three yojanas and returns by the same path, it is not permissible; it is permissible to return by another path. A Pācittiya offense is incurred as soon as one gives up the effort, thinking, "I will not go the distance of the stated measure."

In Rājagaha, concerning many Bhikkhunīs, it was laid down because of the matter of not setting out on a tour after completing the Rains. There is no offense when there is an obstacle, for one who cannot find a companion nun despite searching, for one who is ill, in times of danger, or for one who is insane, etc. There are three factors here: having completed the Rains, the absence of an allowed reason, and not exceeding five yojanas. The origin (samuṭṭhāna), etc., are similar to the first Pārājika. This training rule is an "akiriya" (non-action) and involves painful feeling (dukkha-vedanā).

## Cārikanapakkamana Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā Niṭṭhitā.

## Tuvaṭṭavaggo Catuttho.

## 5. Cittāgāravaggo

## 1. Rājāgāra Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā
In the first training rule of the Cittāgāra Chapter, "Rājāgāra" means the king's pleasure house (or royal pavilion). "Cittāgāra" means a house built elaborately for the pleasure of the public (such as a painted gallery). "Ārāma" means a pleasure grove within the city for the public. "Uyyāna" means a pleasure garden outside the city for the public. "Pokkharaṇī" means a pleasure pond for the public. "Dassanāya" means (going with the intention) "I will see one of these, such as the Rājāgāra."
331:
For a bhikkhunī who goes with the intention, "I will look," there is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa) for every step. If she stands in a certain place and looks, and if she looks at all five types (such as the royal palace, etc.) without lifting her feet, there is only one offense. However, if she looks around at various places, there are as many offenses as there are efforts in turning the neck, but there is no offense for the number of times she opens her eyes.

This training rule was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning the Chabbaggiya bhikkhunīs who went to see a picture gallery (cittāgāra). For a bhikkhu, there is an offense of wrongdoing in all instances. The rest of the decision should be understood in the same manner as stated in the training rule on watching dancing (naccadassana).

## The Commentary on the Training Rule concerning the Royal Palace (Rājāgāra) is finished.

## 2. Commentary on the Training Rule concerning the Use of a High Couch (Āsandipari-bhuñjana)

In the second training rule, 'āsandī' refers to a high couch that exceeds the prescribed measurements. 'Pallaṅka' refers to a couch made with immovable figures of beasts of prey. In the phrase "should use," it should be understood that an offense of expiation (pācittiya) is incurred according to the number of efforts in sitting or lying down.

This training rule was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning many bhikkhunīs who used high couches and thrones (pallaṅka). There is no offense for a bhikkhunī who uses them after cutting the legs of the high couch (to less than eight finger-breadths) or after destroying the animal figures of the throne, nor for one who is insane, etc. The two factors here are: it being a high couch or a throne, and the act of sitting or lying down. The origins and other details are similar to the training rule on sheep’s wool (eḷakaloma).

## The Commentary on the Training Rule concerning the Use of a High Couch is finished.

## 3. Commentary on the Training Rule concerning Spinning Yarn (Suttakantana)

In the third training rule, 'yarn' (sutta) refers to any one of the six kinds, such as linen, etc. In the phrase "should spin," there is one offense for every time the yarn pulled by the hand is wound around the spindle. With reference to this winding on the spindle, it is stated in the word-analysis (padabhājanīya), "for every winding."

This training rule was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning the Chabbaggiya bhikkhunīs who were spinning yarn. Regarding all the preliminary efforts, such as picking cotton before spinning...
332:
...there is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa) according to the number of hand movements. There is no offense for a bhikkhunī who spins yarn that has already been spun, nor for one who is insane, etc. In this training rule, there are two factors: the state of the cotton not yet being spun, and the act of spinning. The origins and other details are similar to the training rule on sheep’s wool (eḷakaloma).

## The Commentary on the Training Rule concerning Spinning Yarn is finished.

## 4. Commentary on the Training Rule concerning Domestic Service for Laypeople (Gihi-veyyāvacca)

In the fourth training rule, 'domestic service for laypeople' (gihi-veyyāvacca) means service for householders. Even if it is for one's own parents, if a bhikkhunī performs tasks such as cooking rice gruel (yāgu) for them without being asked to do a specific task, she incurs offenses of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa) for the preliminary efforts according to the number of efforts; and she incurs an offense of expiation (pācittiya) according to the number of pots for the rice gruel, etc., or according to the number of cakes for the snacks, etc.

This was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning many bhikkhunīs who performed domestic service for laypeople. There is no offense for a bhikkhunī who, while people are preparing an offering of rice gruel, a meal, or a shrine-offering (cetiya-pūjā) for the Saṅgha, assists them by cooking rice gruel, etc., as their companion; nor for a bhikkhunī who performs those same tasks for someone who performs domestic service for her; nor for one who is insane, etc. The two factors here are: performing domestic service for laypeople, and the absence of a permitted reason. The origins and other details are similar to the training rule on sheep’s wool (eḷakaloma).

## The Commentary on the Training Rule concerning Domestic Service for Laypeople is finished.

## 5. Commentary on the Training Rule concerning Legal Issues (Adhikaraṇa)

In the fifth training rule, 'legal issue' (adhikaraṇa) refers to any one of the four kinds of legal issues. 'Pācittiya' means that in this training rule, just as in the training rule on robe-sewing (cīvarasibbana), an offense of expiation is incurred as soon as the effort is abandoned; there is no exemption from the offense even for a single day.

This was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning the bhikkhunī Thullanandā who did not settle a legal issue. The rest of the procedure here should be understood in the same manner as stated in the training rule on robe-sewing.

## The Commentary on the Training Rule concerning Legal Issues is finished.
333: ## 6. Bhojanadāna Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā In the sixth training rule, "with one's own hand" means (giving) by way of the body, or by an object connected to the body, or by throwing. Excluding the five classes of co-religionists, a nun who gives any kind of consumable food, except for water and tooth-wood, with her own hand to other persons incurs a pācittiya offense. This training rule was laid down on account of the nun Thullanandā in Sāvatthī, due to the incident of giving food and snacks to a householder. In giving water and tooth-wood, there is a dukkaṭa offense. There is no offense for a nun who does not give it herself but causes another to give it, or gives it by placing it nearby, or gives oil etc. for external application, nor for an insane nun and so forth. In this training rule, there are two factors: it being consumable food other than water and tooth-wood, and giving it with one's own hand to another person while excluding the five classes of co-religionists. The origins and so forth are similar to the Eḷakaloma Sikkhāpada. ## The Explanation of the Bhojanadāna Sikkhāpada is finished. ## 7. Āvasathacīvara Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā In the seventh training rule, "āvasathacīvara" refers to a robe (menstrual cloth) donated with the intention, "Let nuns who have their period use it." "Without relinquishing" means after washing it on the fourth day, not giving it to another, even to a sāmaṇerī who has her period. A nun who uses it without relinquishing it in this way incurs a pācittiya offense. This training rule was laid down on account of the nun Thullanandā in Sāvatthī, due to the incident of using an āvasathacīvara without relinquishing it. There are three types of pācittiya (tika-pācittiya). In the case of a robe that has been relinquished, there are two types of dukkaṭa (dvika-dukkaṭa). There is no offense for a nun who uses it with the perception that it has been relinquished, or uses it in another turn, or uses it because there are no other nuns with their period, or uses it because her own robe was stolen or lost, or uses it during dangers, nor for an insane nun and so forth. In this training rule, there are four factors: it being an āvasathacīvara, it being the fourth day, not relinquishing it after washing, and the absence of authorized reasons. The origins and so forth are similar to the Kathina Sikkhāpada. This training rule is an offense of kiriyākiriyā (action and non-action). ## The Explanation of the Āvasathacīvara Sikkhāpada is finished.
334:
## 8. Āvasathavihāra Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā

In the eighth training rule, *āvasatha* refers to a dwelling fitted with a door. *Anissajjitvā* means without handing it over for the purpose of protection, without asking, "Please look after this dwelling."

In the phrase "should she set out on a journey, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya)," for a nun who departs from her own village to another village even for a single night's stay, there is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa) upon merely crossing the enclosure of a fenced dwelling, or the precinct of an unfenced dwelling, with the first step; with the second step, there is an offense of expiation.

It was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning the nun Thullanandā in the case of setting out on a journey without handing over the dwelling. There are three types of pācittiya. There is an offense of wrongdoing for a dwelling not fitted with a door, and two offenses of wrongdoing for a dwelling that has been handed over. However, there is no offense if she perceives it as handed over, if there is danger, if she cannot find a caretaker after searching, if she is ill, in times of emergency, or if she is insane, etc. The three factors here are: it being a dwelling fitted with a door, departing in the manner described, and the absence of a permitted reason. The origins (samuṭṭhāna) and so forth are similar to the Kathina training rule. This is a training rule of action and non-action (kiriyākiriva).

## The Commentary on the Āvasathavihāra Training Rule is Finished.

## 9. Tiracchānavijjā-pariyāpuṇana Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā

In the ninth training rule, *tiracchānavijjā* (lowly arts) refers to any external knowledge not connected with the goal, such as the arts of elephants, horses, chariots, archery, and swordsmanship; Atharva spells, spells for making one stuck, spells for subjugation, spells for causing a ghost to appear, the application of poisonous medicines, and other such arts that cause harm to others. In the phrase "should she learn," for a nun who learns such an art from anyone by way of words and so forth, there is an offense of expiation according to the count of words and the count of syllables.

## The Commentary on the Tiracchānavijjā-pariyāpuṇana Training Rule is Finished.

## 10. Tiracchānavijjā-vācana Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā

In the tenth training rule, the word "vāceyya" (should she teach) is the distinction. Both of these training rules were laid down in Sāvatthī concerning the group-of-six nuns and many other nuns in the case of learning and teaching lowly arts. There is no offense in the art of writing, in the art of memorizing (dhāraṇa), in all protective spells (paritta) for the purpose of self-protection such as warding off spirits (yakkha) or drawing a boundary circle to prevent the entry of snakes (nāga), or in the case of one who is insane, etc. The three factors in both these training rules are: it being a lowly art, learning or teaching it, and the absence of a permitted reason. The origins and so forth are similar to the Padasodhamma training rule.
335:
There is no offense in all protective spells (paritta) such as those for warding off spirits (yakkha) or spells for drawing a boundary circle to prevent the entry of snakes (nāga); or in the case of one who is insane, etc. In both these training rules, there are three factors: it being a lowly art, learning or teaching it, and the absence of a permitted reason. The origins and so forth are similar to the Padasodhamma training rule.

## The Commentary on the Tiracchānavijjā-vācana Training Rule is Finished.

## The Fifth Chapter, the Cittāgāra Chapter, is Finished.

## 6. Ārāma Vagga

## 1. Ārāmapavisana Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā

In the first training rule of the Ārāma Chapter, "a monastery with monks" (sabhikkhukaṃ ārāmaṃ) refers to a place where monks reside, even at the foot of a tree. In the phrase "without asking," for a nun who, without asking any of the monks, novices, or monastery attendants, crosses the enclosure of a fenced monastery or enters the precinct of an unfenced monastery, there is an offense of wrongdoing with the first step and an offense of expiation with the second step.

This was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning many nuns in the case of entering a monastery without asking. There are two subsequent rulings (anupaññatti) in this training rule: "without asking a monk who is present" and "knowing it is a monastery with monks." There is an offense of wrongdoing for one who is in doubt about a monastery with monks, and for one who perceives a monastery without monks as having monks, or is in doubt about it.

There is no offense for one who enters perceiving both types of monasteries as having no monks; for one who enters after asking a monk who is present; for one who follows behind nuns who have already entered (looking up at them); for one who enters with the thought, "I will go to the presence of those nuns," where nuns have assembled; for one who goes along a path that lies within the monastery; for one who enters due to danger; or for one who is insane, etc. The four factors in this training rule are: it being a monastery with monks, the perception of it having monks, crossing the described boundary, and the absence of a permitted reason. The origin is the same as the Samanubhāsana training rule. It has action, non-action, release through perception (saññāvimokkha), intentionality (sacittaka), being a breach of a regulation (paṇṇattivajja), bodily action, vocal action, three types of consciousness, and three types of feeling.

## The Commentary on the Ārāmapavisana Training Rule is Finished.

## 2. Bhikkhu-akkosana Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā

In the second training rule, "should she revile" means she should revile with any of the ten grounds for reviling, whether face-to-face or behind the back. "Should she threaten" means she should show him danger (threaten him). "Pācittiya" means an offense of expiation for the nun who acts in such a way.
336:
In Vesālī, this training rule was laid down concerning the Chabbaggiya bhikkhunīs regarding the case of insulting the Venerable Upāli. It is a Pācittiya involving a triad (such as perceiving a monk as a monk). In insulting a non-monk (a layperson or a novice), an offense of Dukkaṭa involving a triad is committed. There is no offense for one who speaks with the intention of instructing for the sake of benefit and the Dhamma, nor for one who is insane, etc. In this training rule, there are three factors: (1) being a monk, (2) insulting or threatening, and (3) not having the benefit in view. The origins (samuṭṭhāna) and so forth are similar to the training rule on taking what is not given (adinnādāna). This offense occurs in painful feeling (dukkha-vedanā).

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on Insulting a Monk is Finished.

## 3. Gaṇa-paribhāsana-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā

In the third training rule, 'caṇḍikatā' means being angry. 'Gaṇa' refers to the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha. Regarding 'paribhāseyya' (should revile), if a bhikkhunī reviles in any place, whether in their presence or absence, saying, "These bhikkhunīs are fools, they are ignorant; they do not know kamma, the faults of kamma, the success of kamma, or the failure of kamma," she commits an offense of Pācittiya.

In Sāvatthī, it was laid down concerning the bhikkhunī Thullanandā regarding the case of reviling the group. If she reviles many bhikkhunīs, or one bhikkhunī, or a non-ordained person, she commits an offense of Dukkaṭa. The remaining points are the same as the second training rule. There is no offense if she speaks from the standpoint of instruction with the intention of teaching for the sake of benefit and the Dhamma, saying, "Even now you are not yet skillful; have loving-kindness so that this does not happen in future lives," etc.

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on Reviling the Group is Finished.

## 4. Pavārita-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā

In the fourth training rule, 'one who is invited' (nimantita) should be understood according to the method stated in the training rule on group-meal (gaṇa-bhojana), and 'one who has finished eating' (pavārita) should be understood according to the method stated in the Pavāraṇā training rule. 'Pācittiya' means that if that bhikkhunī, excluding the morning gruel and the other three period-limited (kālika) items, accepts any other food (āmisa) for the purpose of swallowing, there is a Dukkaṭa in the act of accepting, and for every swallow, she commits an offense of Pācittiya.

In Sāvatthī, it was laid down concerning many bhikkhunīs regarding the case of eating in another place (after being invited). If she accepts or swallows the three period-limited items for the sake of nutriment, she commits an offense of Dukkaṭa. If a bhikkhunī who is invited but has not yet finished her meal (apavārita) drinks gruel, or if she eats after asking permission from the owners...
337:
...eats after asking permission from the owners, or consumes the three period-limited items such as the yāmakālika when there is a reason, there is no offense for her, nor for one who is insane, etc. The three factors in this training rule are: being one who is invited, or one who has finished eating, or both; swallowing food (āmisa) having the stated characteristics in the morning; and not asking permission from the owners. The origin (samuṭṭhāna) is due to traveling (addhāna-samuṭṭhāna). Since an offense can occur for a bhikkhunī who is invited and eats without asking permission, it is sometimes an action-non-action (kiriyā-akiriyā). Since an offense can occur for a bhikkhunī who has finished eating and consumes food whether she has had the allowable remainder-rite (atirikta-vinaya-kamma) performed or not, it is sometimes an action (kiriyā). It is not a release through perception (saññā-vimokkha); it is without conscious intent (acittaka). It is a transgression of a regulation (paṇṇatti-vajja). It is bodily action and vocal action. It involves three types of consciousness and three types of feeling.

## The Explanation of the Pavārita Training Rule is Finished.

## 5. Kulamacchariṇī-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā

In the fifth training rule, stinginess regarding a family is 'kula-macchara'. A bhikkhunī who has stinginess regarding a family, or who is stingy about a family, is called 'kula-macchariṇī'. 'Assā' means if there were such a person who is stingy regarding a family. 'Pācittiya' means that if she thinks, "A certain family wishes to give requisites to the bhikkhunīs; how can the bhikkhunīs be made not to go there?" and speaks of the faults of the family in the presence of the bhikkhunīs; or if she thinks, "How can these donors be made not to give anything to those bhikkhunīs?" and speaks of the faults of the bhikkhunīs in the presence of the family, she commits an offense of Pācittiya.

In Sāvatthī, it was laid down concerning a certain bhikkhunī because of the case of being stingy regarding a family. There is no offense for a bhikkhunī who, without being stingy, points out an existing fault, nor for one who is insane, etc. The two factors in this training rule are: the desire for the bhikkhunīs not to receive gains, and speaking of the faults of the bhikkhunīs in the presence of the family or speaking of the faults of the family in the presence of the bhikkhunīs. The origins (samuṭṭhāna) and so forth are similar to the training rule on taking what is not given (adinnādāna). This training rule involves painful feeling (dukkha-vedanā).

## The Explanation of the Kulamacchariṇī Training Rule is Finished.

## 6. Abhikkhukāvāsa-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā

In the sixth training rule, if monks who are to give exhortation (ovāda) do not reside within half a league (yojana) from the bhikkhunīs' residence, or if the road is unsafe and it is not possible to go without danger...
338:
If [one is unable] to go, this residence is called 'without monks' (abhikkhuka). In that residence, a nun who, intending to 'spend the Rains retreat,' performs acts such as preparing bedding or setting out drinking water, commits an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa); at the moment of dawn, she commits an offense of expiation (pācittiya). This is the summary of this training rule; the detailed explanation is stated in the Samantapāsādikā (Pācittiya Commentary 144, etc.).

This training rule was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning the case of many nuns spending the Rains retreat in a residence without monks. There is no offense for a nun who stays in that residence (or a place near it) if the monks who had entered the Rains have left, disrobed, passed away, or moved to a heretical sect; nor is there an offense in times of danger, or for an insane nun, etc. In this training rule, there are three factors: being a residence without monks, entering the Rains retreat, and the rising of the dawn. The origins (samuṭṭhāna), etc., are the same as the sheep's wool training rule (eḷakalomasi-sikkhāpada).

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on Residence Without Monks is Finished.

## 7. The Explanation of the Training Rule on Invitation (Apavāraṇā)

In the seventh training rule, 'having completed the Rains retreat' means having stayed for either the first three months or the second three months. 'In both Saṅghas' means in both the Saṅgha of Bhikkhunīs and the Saṅgha of Bhikkhus. Here is the decision: Nuns should assemble only on the 14th day and set forth either an all-inclusive motion (sabbasaṅgāhika-ñatti), saying: 'Venerable ladies, let the Saṅgha listen to me. Today is the fourteenth-day Pavāraṇā. If it is the right time for the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha perform Pavāraṇā'; or a three-fold motion (tevācika-ñatti), saying: 'Let [the Saṅgha] perform Pavāraṇā with a three-fold speech'; or if there is danger, a two-fold motion (dvevācika-ñatti), a one-fold motion (ekavācika-ñatti), or a motion for those of equal seniority (samānavassika-ñatti). If an all-inclusive motion is set forth, Pavāraṇā should be performed in order, saying once: 'Venerable ladies, I invite the Saṅgha based on what is seen, heard, or suspected. May the venerable ladies speak to me out of compassion; seeing [the fault], I shall make amends'; or saying it twice or thrice: 'For the second time... For the third time... I shall make amends.' In a three-fold motion, the words of invitation must not be reduced; in two-fold motions, etc., it is permissible to increase [up to three times] but not to decrease. Having thus performed Pavāraṇā in the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha, a single nun should be authorized in that same precinct (sīmā) by a motion and a second proclamation (ñattidutiya-kamma) as stated in the Bhikkhunī Khandhaka to invite the Bhikkhu Saṅgha on behalf of the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha. That authorized nun...
339:
On the 15th day, having taken the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha and approached the Bhikkhu Saṅgha, having arranged the upper robe over one shoulder and raising the joined palms (añjali), she should speak thus: 'Venerable sirs, the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha invites the Saṅgha of the venerable sirs based on what is seen, heard, or suspected. May the Saṅgha of the venerable sirs speak to the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha out of compassion; seeing [the fault], it will make amends. For the second time, venerable sirs... [etc.]... For the third time, venerable sirs... [etc.]... seeing [the fault], it will make amends.' Thus should the Pavāraṇā be performed.

If the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha of a group of five is not complete, the Pavāraṇā should be performed by setting a group motion (gaṇa-ñatti) for four or three [nuns]. Two nuns should perform Pavāraṇā with each other without a motion (ñatti). A single nun should make a determination (adhiṭṭhāna): 'Today is my Pavāraṇā.'

Having gone to the monastery, she should say three times: 'Venerable sir, the nuns invite the Bhikkhu Saṅgha based on what is seen, heard, or suspected. May the Saṅgha of the venerable sirs speak to the nuns out of compassion; seeing [the fault], they will make amends'; and: 'Venerable sir, I invite the Bhikkhu Saṅgha based on what is seen, heard, or suspected. May the Saṅgha of the venerable sirs speak to me out of compassion; seeing [the fault], I shall make amends.'

If the Bhikkhu Saṅgha is not complete, she should say three times: 'Venerable sirs, the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha invites you based on what is seen, heard, or suspected. May you speak to the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha out of compassion; seeing [the fault], it will make amends'; and: 'Venerable sir, the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha invites you based on what is seen, heard, or suspected. May you speak to the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha out of compassion; seeing [the fault], it will make amends.'

When both Saṅghas are incomplete, she should say three times: 'Venerable sirs, the nuns invite you based on what is seen, heard, or suspected. May you speak to the nuns out of compassion; seeing [the fault], they will make amends'; and: 'Venerable sir, the nuns invite you based on what is seen, heard, or suspected. May you speak to the nuns out of compassion; seeing [the fault], they will make amends'; and: 'Venerable sirs, I invite you based on what is seen, heard, or suspected... [etc.]... May you speak to me out of compassion; seeing [the fault], I shall make amends'; and: 'Venerable sir, I invite you based on what is seen, heard, or suspected... [etc.]... May you speak to me out of compassion; seeing [the fault], I shall make amends.' Indeed, all nuns [should do so] in this manner...
340:
In this way, all the nuns have invited (performed Pavāraṇā) in the Saṅgha of both sides. If a nun who has completed the rains retreat (vassa) thinks, "I will not invite in the Saṅgha of both sides in this way," and gives up the effort (relinquishes the duty), she incurs a pācittiya offense simultaneously with giving up the effort.

It was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning many nuns who, having completed the rains retreat, did not perform Pavāraṇā. There is no offense if there is an obstacle, if she searches for monks but does not find them, if she is ill, in times of danger, or if she is insane, etc. There are three factors here: having completed the rains retreat, not performing Pavāraṇā in the Saṅgha of both sides, and the absence of an allowed reason. The origin (samuṭṭhāna) etc., are the same as the Samanubhāsana training rule.

## Commentary on the Apavāraṇā Training Rule is finished.

## 8. Commentary on the Ovāda Training Rule

In the eighth training rule, "ovādāya" means for the purpose of hearing the Garudhamma exhortation. "Saṃvāsāya" means for the purpose of asking about the Uposatha and for the purpose of Pavāraṇā. "Pācittiya" means a pācittiya offense is incurred merely by giving up the effort, thinking, "I will not go for the sake of these [exhortation and communion]."

It was laid down in the Sakyan country concerning the group-of-six nuns who did not go to receive exhortation. There is no offense if there is an obstacle, if she searches for a companion but does not find one, if she is ill, in times of danger, or if she is insane, etc. There are two factors here: not going for the sake of exhortation and communion, and the absence of an allowed reason. The origin etc., are the same as the first Pārājika; this training rule is of non-action (akiriya) and involves painful feeling.

## Commentary on the Ovāda Training Rule is finished.

## 9. Commentary on the Ovādūpasaṅkamana Training Rule

In the ninth training rule, "anvaddhamāsaṃ" means every half-month. "Uposathapucchakaṃ" means asking about the Uposatha. "Ovādūpasaṅkamanaṃ" means approaching for the sake of exhortation. In the phrase "taṃ atikkāmentiyā", the nuns should go to the monastery on the 13th or 14th day and ask, "Is this Uposatha on the 14th or 15th day?"
341:
On the Uposatha day, one should ask for permission to approach for exhortation according to the method stated in the Nidānavannaṇā. If a nun does not do both (asking about Uposatha and requesting exhortation) at the stated time and lets the time pass, she incurs a pācittiya offense merely by giving up the effort, thinking, "I will not ask about the Uposatha day, nor will I request exhortation."

It was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning many nuns who did not ask about the Uposatha or request exhortation. The non-offense is the same as the eighth training rule. The factors here are: giving up the effort in asking about the Uposatha and requesting exhortation, and the absence of an allowed special reason. The origin etc., are the same as the Samanubhāsana training rule.

## Commentary on the Ovādūpasaṅkamana Training Rule is finished.

## 10. Commentary on the Pasākhejāta Training Rule

In the tenth training rule, "pasākha" refers to the area below the navel and above the knee-caps. Because the two thighs branch out from that place like the main branches of a tree, it is called "pasākha" (the fork). In that pasākha, "gaṇḍa" means any kind of boil or abscess. "Rudhita" means a wound. In the phrases beginning with "bhedāpeyya vā", if she commands all actions saying, "Pierce it, cut it open," and the person commanded does so, there are 6 dukkaṭas and 6 pācittiyas. If she commands, "Do whatever needs to be done to this abscess," and that person performs all actions such as piercing, etc., there are 6 dukkaṭas and 6 pācittiyas for that single statement. However, if she commands only one action among piercing etc., saying, "Do such-and-such," but that person does everything, a pācittiya offense is incurred only for the performance of the commanded action.

It was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning a certain nun who had an abscess in the groin area pierced by a man. There is no offense for a nun who does so after having informed [the Saṅgha] or having taken a wise companion, nor for an insane nun, etc. There are four factors here: the abscess being in the groin, not informing, the absence of a companion, and having a man perform the piercing, etc. The origin etc., are the same as the Kathina training rule; this training rule is of action and non-action (kiriyākiriya).

## Commentary on the Pasākhejāta Training Rule is finished.

## The Sixth Chapter: The Monastery Chapter (Ārāmavagga).
342:
## 7. Gabbhinīvagga

## 1. Gabbhinīsikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

In the first training rule of the Gabbhinīvagga, for a bhikkhunī who, knowing a woman is pregnant, acts as a preceptor and ordains her (raises her from the status of a trainee), an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa) is incurred during the search for the group of officiating bhikkhunīs, and during the two motions consisting of the announcement (ñatti) and the formal act (kammavācā). At the conclusion of the formal act, an offense of expiation (pācittiya) is incurred.

This training rule was laid down in Sāvatthī on account of many bhikkhunīs ordaining a pregnant woman.
