If there is doubt regarding a pregnant woman, or if one perceives a non-pregnant woman as pregnant, or if there is doubt (regarding a non-pregnant woman), an offense of wrongdoing is incurred. There is no offense if one perceives a non-pregnant woman as non-pregnant, nor for those who are insane, etc. The three factors of this training rule are: being pregnant, knowing she is pregnant, and ordaining her. The origin (samuṭṭhāna) and other aspects are similar to the training rule on taking what is not given (adinnādāna). This training rule is prohibited by regulation (paṇṇattivajja), and is associated with three types of consciousness and three types of feeling.

## The Commentary on the Gabbhinī Training Rule ends.

## 2. Pāyantīsikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

In the second training rule, "Pāyantī" refers to a woman who is nursing. Whether it is the mother of the child being nursed or a wet-nurse (she is called pāyantī). In this training rule, only the subject matter (vatthu) is different. The rest is exactly the same as the first training rule.

## The Commentary on the Pāyantī Training Rule ends.

## 3. Paṭhamasikkhamānasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

In the third training rule, "for two years" means for two years by way of the pavāraṇā ceremony. "In the six rules" refers to the six training rules starting from abstaining from taking life and ending with abstaining from eating at the wrong time. "One whose training is not practiced" refers to one who has not been given the training (the six rules) or one whose training has been broken even though it was given, according to the method stated in the word-by-word commentary (padabhājanī). "Should ordain a trainee" means one should ordain an unordained one (anupasampanna) who has received this name either because of practicing those six rules or because of cherishing those rules known as training. "An offense of expiation is incurred" means an offense of expiation is incurred at the conclusion of the formal act, just as stated in the first training rule.
343:
This training rule was laid down in Sāvatthī on account of many bhikkhunīs ordaining such a trainee. In a legal act (dhammakamma), there is a triad of expiation (tika-pācittiya). In an illegal act (adhammakamma), there is a triad of wrongdoing (tika-dukkaṭa). There is no offense for a bhikkhunī who ordains a trainee who has practiced the six training rules for two years, nor for those who are insane, etc. The three factors in this training rule are: being one whose training is not practiced (according to the stated method), the performance of a legal act, and the conclusion of the formal act. The origin and other aspects are just as stated in the first training rule.

## The Commentary on the First Sikkhamāna Training Rule ends.

## 4. Dutiyasikkhamānasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

In the fourth training rule, "not authorized by the Saṅgha" (saṅghena asammataṃ) refers to a trainee to whom the Saṅgha has not given the agreement for ordination (upasampadā-sammuti) as described in the word-by-word commentary, even at the minimum in the ordination hall (māḷaka). These two types of trainees are also called "great trainees" (mahāsikkhamānā). In this training rule, there is no offense for a bhikkhunī who ordains a trainee who has been authorized by the Saṅgha, nor for those who are insane, etc. The rest of the procedure is the same as stated in the third training rule. This training rule, however, involves both action and non-action (kiriyā-akiriya).

## The Commentary on the Second Sikkhamāna Training Rule ends.

## 5. Paṭhamဂိဟိဂတသိက္ခာပဒဝဏ္ဏနာ (Paṭhamagihigatasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā)

In the fifth training rule, "Gihigata" refers to a woman who has gone to a man (one who has been married). In this training rule also, only this subject matter is the difference from the first training rule. If a bhikkhunī ordains a woman who is under twelve years of age, perceiving her as having completed twelve years, although there may be no offense, that trainee does not become a bhikkhunī (she remains unordained). The rest of the procedure is the same as the first training rule.

## The Commentary on the First Gihigata Training Rule ends.

## 6-7. Dutiyatatiyagihigatasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

In the sixth training rule, the entire procedure should be understood according to the method stated in the third training rule. In the seventh training rule also, everything should be understood only according to the method stated in the fourth training rule.

## The Commentary on the Second and Third Gihigata Training Rules ends.
344:
## 8. Paṭhamasahajīvinīsikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

In the eighth training rule, "sahajīvinī" means a female co-resident (saddhivihārinī). "Should not herself support" means she should not support her by herself through teaching the Pāḷi (uddesa) and so on. "Should not cause others to support" means she should not command another nun, saying, "Lady, please provide the teaching of Pāḷi and so on to this nun." "Pācittiya" means an offence of Pācittiya is incurred as soon as the responsibility for such support is abandoned.

This training rule was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning the nun Thullanandā in such a case. The remaining details are just as stated in the training rule on a sick female companion in the Tuvaṭṭa Chapter.

## Paṭhamasahajīvinīsikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

## 9. Nānubandhanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

In the ninth training rule, "the female preceptor who has given ordination" means the female preceptor who has performed the act of making one reach the state of a nun. "Should not follow (should not attend to)" means she should not attend to or serve her with various duties such as bathing powder, clay, tooth-wood, and water for washing the face. "Pācittiya" means an offence of Pācittiya is incurred as soon as the responsibility is abandoned, thinking, "I will no longer follow her."

This training rule was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning many nuns in the case of not following the female preceptor. However, there is no offence for a nun who does not follow a female preceptor who is ignorant of the Vinaya or is shameless (alajjī), or for a nun who is ill, or in times of danger, or for a nun who is insane, and so on. In this training rule, there are three factors: being the female preceptor who ordained her, abandoning the duty of not following for two years, and the absence of any allowed reason. The origins (samuṭṭhāna) and so on are similar to the first Pārājika. This training rule is an offence of omission (akiriya) and has painful feeling (dukkhavedanā).

## Nānubandhanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

## 10. Dutiyasahajīvinīsikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

In the tenth training rule, "should not herself take away" means she should not take her and go. "Should not cause others to take away" means she should not command another, saying, "Lady, please take this nun and go." "Pācittiya" means an offence of Pācittiya is incurred as soon as the responsibility is abandoned.

This training rule was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning the nun Thullanandā in the case of not taking away a female co-resident. However, in times of danger, or when a companion cannot be found despite searching, ...
345:
...there is no offense for a bhikkhunī who is ill, in times of danger, or for one who is insane, etc. In this training rule, there are three factors: being a co-resident, abandoning effort in taking her away or having her taken away, and the absence of any allowed reason. The origin (*samuṭṭhāna*) and other aspects are similar to the *Samanubhāsana* training rule.

## Dutiyasahajīvinisikkhāpadavaṇṇanā is finished.

## The Seventh Chapter, Gabbhinīvagga, is finished.

## 8. Kumāribhūtavagga

## 1-2-3. Paṭhamakumāribhūtādisikkhāpadavaṇṇanā
The first, second, and third training rules of the *Kumāribhūtavagga* are identical to the three *Gihigata* training rules. It should be understood that the very first two *Mahāsikkhamānās* were those over twenty years of age. Whether those *Mahāsikkhamānās* were formerly married (*gihigata*) or unmarried (*agihigata*), they should only be called "Sikkhamānā" in formal acts (*sammutikamma*) and so forth. They should not be called "Gihigata" or "Kumāribhūta." For a woman who was formerly married (*gihigata*), the agreement for training (*sikkhāsammuti*) is given at the age of ten, and she is ordained at the age of twelve. If given at eleven, she is ordained at thirteen. If the agreement for training is given at the ages of twelve, thirteen, fourteen, fifteen, sixteen, seventeen, or eighteen, she is ordained only when she reaches twenty years of age. From the age of eighteen onwards, it is appropriate to call such a person either "Gihigata" or "Kumāribhūta." As for a novice (*sāmaṇerī*) who is called "Kumāribhūta," she should not be called "Gihigata," but only "Kumāribhūta." However, by virtue of being given the agreement for training, it is appropriate to call all of them "Sikkhamānā."

## Paṭhamakumāribhūtādisikkhāpadavaṇṇanā is finished.

## 4. Ūnadvādasavassasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā
In the fourth training rule, "one who is less than twelve years" (*ūnadvādasavassa*) refers to a nun who has not completed twelve years since her ordination. *Pācittiya* means that for a nun who acts as a preceptor and ordains others, as previously explained, offenses of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) are incurred during the process, and an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) is incurred at the conclusion of the formal act (*kammavācā*).

## Ūnadvādasavassasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā is finished.
346:
## 5. Commentary on the Paripuṇṇadvādasavassa Training Rule

In the fifth training rule, 'not authorized by the Saṅgha' (saṅghena asammatā) refers to a nun who has not yet been granted the authorization for ordaining others (vuṭṭhāpanasammuti) by the Saṅgha, as stated in the Word-for-word Analysis (Padabhājana). The rest of the procedure is identical to the two Mahāsikkhamānā training rules in both cases.

## The Commentary on the Paripuṇṇadvādasavassa Training Rule Ends.

## 6. Commentary on the Khīyanadhamma Training Rule

In the sixth training rule, the phrase beginning with 'Enough for now, lady, with your ordaining' (alaṃ tāva te ayye vuṭṭhāpitena) refers to a nun who, when requesting the authorization for ordaining others, is investigated by the Saṅgha and prohibited thus: 'Because you are foolish, incompetent, and shameless, it is not yet suitable for you to ordain others.' 'Subsequent complaining' (pacchā khīyanadhamma) means that later, upon seeing the authorization for ordaining others being given to other competent and modest nuns, she complains in some place, saying things like, 'Am I really the only foolish one?' 'An offense of expiation' (pācittiyaṃ) means a pācittiya offense is incurred by a nun who falls into such complaining.

This training rule was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning the nun Caṇḍakāḷī, in the case of her falling into such complaining. There is no offense for nuns who naturally complain due to favoritism, etc. (in the granting of authorization), nor for those who are insane, etc. There are three factors here: requesting the authorization for ordaining others; the acceptance ('Very well') of the nun who was rejected after investigation, not due to favoritism, etc.; and subsequent complaining. The origin (samuṭṭhāna), etc., are the same as for taking what is not given (adinnādāna); however, this training rule involves painful feeling (dukkhavedanā).

## The Commentary on the Khīyanadhamma Training Rule Ends.

## 7-8. Commentary on the First and Second Training Rules Regarding the Ordination of a Sikkhamānā

In the seventh training rule, 'she afterwards' (sā pacchā) means that when a trainee (sikkhamānā) requests higher ordination (upasampadā), that bhikkhunī says, 'If you give me a robe, I will act as your preceptor and ordain you.' After receiving the robe, if she gives up her effort, saying, 'I will not ordain you, nor will I make any effort for your ordination,' even though there is no obstacle, she incurs a pācittiya offense simultaneously with the giving up of effort. The same method applies to the eighth training rule.

Both of these training rules were laid down in Sāvatthī concerning the nun Thullanandā in these cases. In both training rules, if there is an obstacle, if she cannot find [the necessary items] after searching, if she is ill, or if there are dangers...
347:
There is no offense for those who are insane and so forth. In both of these training rules, there are these four factors: 1. Making a promise, "I will ordain you in this way (if you give me a robe or if you follow me)," 2. The fulfillment of the desired benefit (obtaining the robe or following), 3. Subsequently slackening one's effort, and 4. The absence of an allowed reason. The origin (samuṭṭhāna) and so forth are the same as in the Samanubhāsana training rule.

## The Commentary on the First and Second Training Rules regarding the Ordination of a Sikkhamānā is finished.

## 9. Commentary on the Sokāvāsa Training Rule
In the ninth training rule, "Sokāvāsa" refers to one who causes grief (soka) to enter the hearts of men by making an appointment and then not coming; thus she is called a sokāvāsa. It refers to such a sikkhamānā. Alternatively, just as householders enter a house, this sikkhamānā, not obtaining the opportunity to meet a man, enters into grief; that grief which she enters is her dwelling (āvāsa), and thus she is called a sokāvāsa. Therefore, in the word-by-word analysis (padabhājanī) of that term, two meanings are stated: "Sokāvāsa means causing suffering to others, and entering into grief."

"Pācittiya" means that for the preceptor (upajjhāyā) who ordains such a sikkhamānā, a pācittiya offense is incurred at the conclusion of the formal act (kammavācā), according to the method already mentioned.

This was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning the bhikkhunī Thullanandā, on account of the matter of ordaining such a sikkhamānā. There is no offense for one who does not know that she is a sokāvāsa, or for those who are insane and so forth. There are these three factors: being a sokāvāsa, knowing that she is so, and ordaining her. The origin and so forth are the same as in the Gabbhinīvuṭṭhāpana training rule.

## The Commentary on the Sokāvāsa Training Rule is finished.

## 10. Commentary on the Ananuññāta Training Rule
In the tenth training rule, "by parents" means by the biological mother and the biological father. "By a husband" means by the husband who has taken her (as a wife). "Not permitted" means not permitted for the purpose of higher ordination (upasampadā). Indeed, bhikkhunīs must ask for permission twice: at the time of going forth (pabbajjā) and at the time of higher ordination. For bhikkhus, however, asking for permission once is sufficient. Therefore, if a preceptor ordains someone without asking for permission at the time of higher ordination, she incurs a pācittiya offense according to the method already mentioned.
348:
In Sāvatthī, the rule was laid down regarding the nun Thullanandā in the case of ordaining a probationer without permission (ananuññāta-vuṭṭhāpana). There is no offense for a nun who ordains a probationer after asking permission from the parents or husband, for a nun who does not know of their existence, or for one who is insane, and so on. In this training rule, there are three factors: (1) not asking for permission, (2) knowing that the parents or husband exist, and (3) ordaining. It has the origination of ananuññāta; it is an act of both commission and omission; there is no release from the offense due to perception (no saññā-vimokkha); it is an offense regardless of intention (acittaka); it is a proscribed fault (paṇṇatti-vajja); it is committed by bodily action and verbal action; it is associated with three types of consciousness and three types of feeling.

## The Commentary on the Ananuññāta Training Rule Ends.

## 11. Commentary on the Pārivāsika Training Rule

In the eleventh training rule, the Pārivāsika Training Rule, the phrase "pārivāsika-chandadānena" means by giving a consent that has been used (or has expired). In this context, there are four types of pārivāsiya: parisa-pārivāsiya, ratti-pārivāsiya, chanda-pārivāsiya, and ajjhāsaya-pārivāsiya.

Among these four, parisa-pārivāsiya is as follows: Monks are assembled for some business, and then it rains, or a commotion is made to clear the crowd, or people come and overwhelm the area. The monks, thinking, "We have no space here, let us go elsewhere," get up and leave without relinquishing their consent (chanda). This is called parisa-pārivāsiya. Although it is parisa-pārivāsiya, because the consent was not relinquished, it is proper to perform the formal act (kamma) in another place.

Furthermore, monks assemble at night, saying, "We shall perform the Uposatha and so on," and they urge one monk to preach the Dhamma, saying, "We shall listen to the Dhamma until everyone has assembled." While that monk is preaching the Dhamma, dawn rises. If they were sitting with the intention, "We shall perform the fourteenth-day Uposatha," it is proper to perform it as the "fifteenth-day Uposatha." If they were sitting to perform the fifteenth-day Uposatha, it is not proper to perform the Uposatha on the first day of the next fortnight (a non-Uposatha day). However, it is proper to perform other Sangha business. This is called ratti-pārivāsiya.

Furthermore, monks are sitting together, saying, "We shall perform some Sangha act such as Abbhāna." Among them, a monk who is an expert in astrology says, "Today the constellation is harsh; do not perform this act." Based on his words, they relinquish their consent and remain sitting right there. Then another monk arrives and says:
"For one who waits for the stars..." ... This is called chanda-pārivāsiya and ajjhāsaya-pārivāsiya. In this case...
349:
"Benefit has passed the fool by (Jātaka 1.1.49), what will you do with the stars?" he says. This is both chandapārivāsiya (stale consent) and ajjhāsayapārivāsiya (stale intention). In such a case of stale consent, it is not proper to perform a formal act without bringing fresh consent (chandapārisuddhi) again. With reference to this meaning, it was said, "by giving stale consent (pārivāsiya-chanda-dānena)."

"Pācittiya" means that for the bhikkhunī who ordains with such consent, a pācittiya offense is incurred at the conclusion of the formal act, according to the method already mentioned. This was laid down in Rājagaha concerning the bhikkhunī Thullanandā, on account of the matter of ordination (vuṭṭhāpana). There is no offense for a bhikkhunī who ordains someone without relinquishing the consent before the assembly has risen, nor for those who are insane and so forth. There are two factors in this training rule: being a giver of stale consent and the act of ordaining. The origin and so forth are the same as in the Gabbhinī training rule.

## The Commentary on the Pārivāsika Training Rule is finished.

## 12. Commentary on the Anuvassa Training Rule
In the twelfth training rule, "anuvassaṃ" means annually (every year). For a bhikkhunī who ordains in this way every year, a pācittiya offense is incurred according to the method already mentioned.

This was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning many bhikkhunīs, on account of the matter of ordaining annually. There is no offense for a bhikkhunī who ordains every other year, nor for those who are insane and so forth. There are two factors in this training rule: being annual and the act of ordaining. The origin and so forth are according to the method stated in the eleventh training rule.

## The Commentary on the Anuvassa Training Rule is finished.

## 13. Commentary on the Ekavassa Training Rule
In the thirteenth training rule, there is no offense for a bhikkhunī who ordains one person every other year, nor for those who are insane and so forth. The remaining points are the same as in the twelfth training rule.

## The Commentary on the Ekavassa Training Rule is finished.

## The Kumāribhūta Vagga, the Eighth.
350:
## 9. Chattupāhanavagga
## 1. Commentary on the Training Rule on Parasols and Sandals
In the first training rule of the Chattuvagga, 'chattupāhanaṃ' refers to a parasol and sandals with the characteristics already described in the Word Analysis (Padabhājanī). 'Dhāreyya' (should wear/carry) means that for a bhikkhunī who carries them throughout the day with a single effort while traveling, there is one offense. However, if she reaches a place where it is appropriate to fold the parasol and take off the sandals, and she repeatedly carries them by putting them on and taking them off, there is a pācittiya offense according to the number of efforts (payoga).

This training rule was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning the group of six bhikkhunīs regarding the wearing of parasols and sandals. 'Agilānā' (not ill) is the supplementary regulation in this rule. There is a dukkaṭa offense for wearing only a parasol or only sandals. For a bhikkhunī who is not ill, there is a pācittiya of the triple-set (tikapācittiya). For an ill bhikkhunī, there is a dukkaṭa of the double-set (dvikadukkaṭa). There is no offense for a bhikkhunī who is ill and wears them with the perception of being ill, or for one who wears them within the monastery or in the vicinity of the monastery, or in times of danger, or for one who is insane, etc. The two factors here are: wearing both [parasol and sandals], and the absence of an allowed reason. The origin and other aspects are similar to the Eḷakaloma training rule.

## The Commentary on the Training Rule on Parasols and Sandals is finished.
## 2. Commentary on the Training Rule on Vehicles
In the second training rule, 'yānena' refers to a vehicle such as a covered cart. In this rule also, for a bhikkhunī who repeatedly gets down and mounts again, there is a pācittiya offense according to the number of efforts. In the section on 'no offense', the permission "within the monastery or in the vicinity of the monastery" does not exist. The remaining points should be understood in the same way as stated in the first training rule.

## The Commentary on the Training Rule on Vehicles is finished.
## 3. Commentary on the Training Rule on Waist-strings
In the third training rule, 'saṅghāṇiṃ' refers to any ornament worn around the waist. 'Dhāreyya' means to fasten it around the waist. In this rule also, for a bhikkhunī who repeatedly takes it off and puts it on, there is a pācittiya offense according to the number of efforts.

This training rule was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning a certain bhikkhunī regarding the wearing of a waist-string. There is no offense for a bhikkhunī who wears a waist-string due to illness, or for one who is insane, etc. The remaining points should be understood in the same way as previously stated. This training rule arises from an unwholesome mind.

## The Commentary on the Training Rule on Waist-strings is finished.
351:
## 4. Commentary on the Training Rule on Women's Ornaments
In the fourth training rule, 'itthālaṅkāra' refers to any kind of ornament among those worn on the head, etc., which are not specifically named. In this training rule, the offense should be understood according to the number of objects (vatthu) based on each particular ornament.

This training rule was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning the group of six bhikkhunīs regarding the wearing of women's ornaments. There is no offense for a bhikkhunī who wears some ornament due to illness, or for one who is insane, etc. The rest of the procedure is exactly as previously stated.

## The Commentary on the Training Rule on Women's Ornaments is finished.
## 5. Commentary on the Training Rule on Scents and Cosmetics
In the fifth training rule, 'gandhavaṇṇaka' refers to any kind of scent and coloring (cosmetic). In this training rule, from the time of mixing the scents, etc., there is a dukkaṭa offense for the preliminary effort before the bathing is finished; at the conclusion of the bathing, there is a pācittiya offense. There is no offense for bathing due to illness, or for one who is insane, etc. The remaining meaning is exactly the same as the fourth training rule.

## The Commentary on the Training Rule on Scents and Cosmetics is finished.
## 6. Commentary on the Training Rule on Scented Water
In the sixth training rule, 'vāsitaka' refers to water scented with perfume. 'Piññāka' refers to sesame powder/paste made by grinding sesame. The remaining meaning is exactly the same as the fifth training rule.

## The Commentary on the Training Rule on Scented Water is finished.
## 7. Commentary on the Training Rule on Having a Bhikkhunī Rub
In the seventh training rule, 'ummaddāpeyya' means to have someone rub/scrub. 'Parimaddāpeyya' means to have someone massage. In this training rule, if one rubs without releasing the hand, there is only one offense. If one rubs by repeatedly releasing and reapplying the hand, there are many offenses according to the number of efforts. The same method applies to massaging.
352:
In Sāvatthī, on account of many bhikkhunīs, this training rule was laid down regarding the matter of causing a bhikkhunī to be rubbed and massaged. There is no offense for a bhikkhunī who is ill, in times of danger, or for one who is insane, etc. In this training rule, fatigue from traveling on a journey is also called 'illness' (gelañña). Shaking of the body due to fear of thieves, etc., are also 'dangers' (āpadā). The remaining meaning should be understood in the same way as stated in the fourth training rule.

## The Explanation of the Bhikkhunī-ummaddāpana Training Rule is finished.

## 8-9-10. The Explanation of the Training Rules on Causing a Sikkhamānā to be Rubbed, etc.

In the eighth, ninth, and tenth training rules, only the words 'a sikkhamānā, a sāmaṇerī, a laywoman' are different. The remaining meaning is just the same as the seventh training rule.

## The Explanation of the Training Rules on Causing a Sikkhamānā to be Rubbed, etc., is finished.

## 11. The Explanation of the Anāpucchā Training Rule

In the eleventh training rule, 'in front of a bhikkhu' does not mean only directly facing him; it should be understood that this is said referring to the precinct (upacāra) of 12 cubits. Therefore, for a bhikkhunī who sits within the precinct of a bhikkhu, even on the ground, without asking, 'Venerable sir, may I sit?', there is an offense of pācittiya.

In Sāvatthī, on account of many bhikkhunīs, this training rule was laid down regarding the matter of sitting without asking permission. It is a triple pācittiya. In the case of a bhikkhu who has been asked, there are two dukkhaṭas. There is no offense for one who sits with the perception that permission has been asked from that bhikkhu, for one who is ill, in times of danger, or for one who is insane, etc. Not asking the bhikkhu, sitting within the precinct, and the absence of an authorized reason—these three are the factors of this training rule. The origins (samuṭṭhāna), etc., are the same as the Kathina training rule. This training rule, however, is an offense of action and non-action (kiriyākiriya).

## The Explanation of the Anāpucchā Training Rule is finished.

## 12. The Explanation of the Pañhāpucchana Training Rule

In the twelfth training rule, 'without having asked for permission' means not having made an opportunity such as, 'I will ask in such and such a passage of the Pali.' Therefore, for a bhikkhunī who, having asked for permission regarding Suttanta, asks about Vinaya or Abhidhamma, there is an offense of pācittiya. In the remaining cases (Vinaya and Abhidhamma) also, the method is the same. If permission is not asked at all, there is no need to say (it is a pācittiya).
353:
In Sāvatthī, on account of many bhikkhunīs, this training rule was laid down regarding the matter of asking a bhikkhu a question without having asked for permission. There is no offense for a bhikkhunī who asks after having requested permission for that specific passage of the Pali, or for one who asks anywhere after having requested permission without specifying a passage, or for one who is insane, etc. Not requesting permission from the bhikkhu and asking a question—these two are the factors here. The origins (samuṭṭhāna), etc., are the same as the Padasodhamma training rule. This training rule is an offense of action and non-action (kiriyākiriya).

## The Explanation of the Pañhāpucchana Training Rule is finished.

## 13. The Explanation of the Asaṃkaccika Training Rule

In the thirteenth training rule, 'asaṃkaccikā' refers to one who is without the bodice (saṃkaccika) authorized for the purpose of covering the body, specifically from below the collarbones to above the navel. In the phrase 'if she should enter a village,' for a bhikkhunī who crosses the enclosure of a fenced village or enters the precinct of an unfenced village, there is a dukkhaṭa at the first step and a pācittiya at the second step.

In Sāvatthī, on account of a certain bhikkhunī, this was laid down regarding the matter of entering a village without a bodice. There is no offense for a bhikkhunī whose bodice-robe has been snatched away or lost, for one who is ill, in times of danger, or for one who is insane, etc. Being without a bodice, crossing the stated limit, and the absence of an authorized reason—these three are the factors here. The origins (samuṭṭhāna), etc., are the same as the Eḷakaloma training rule.

## The Explanation of the Asaṃkaccika Training Rule is finished.

## The Ninth Chapter, the Chattupāhana Vagga.

## 10-16. The Musāvāda Vagga, etc.

## The Explanation of the Musāvāda Training Rules, etc.

In the seven chapters starting from the Musāvāda Vagga, which follow this Chatta Vagga, the decision should be understood in the same way as stated in the explanation of the Bhikkhu Pātimokkha.

## The Sixteenth Chapter.

The 70 shared (sādhāraṇa) training rules laid down on account of bhikkhus and the 96 unique (asādhāraṇa) training rules not shared with bhikkhus—thus, 166 offenses have been recited in detail. In all training rules, the remaining collection of words is clear.

The explanation of the Suddha-pācittiya in the Bhikkhunī Pātimokkha, within the commentary on the Pātimokkha called Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī, is finished.

In that Suddha-pācittiya, I shall briefly state the decision on the origins (samuṭṭhāna) among the unique training rules. The Giraggasamajja training rule, the Cittāgāra training rule, the Saṅghāṇī training rule, the Itthālaṅkāra training rule, the Gandhavannaka training rule, the Vāsitakapinyāka training rule, and the training rules on causing a bhikkhunī, a sikkhamānā, a sāmaṇerī, or a laywoman to be rubbed or massaged—these are training rules that are acittaka (unintentional). They are also lokavajja (worldly faults).

'Acittaka' means that while there are two types of consciousness—consciousness of the object and consciousness of the regulation—the Giraggasamajja training rule is acittaka because an offense is incurred even if there is no consciousness of the object, such as dancing. In the subsequent training rules, it should be understood in the same way.
354:
Sisters, the one hundred and sixty-six Pācittiya offenses have been recited in detail: seventy that are shared, being prescribed in connection with the monks, and ninety-six that are unique [to nuns]. In all these training rules, the remaining words are clear.

## In the Explanation of the Pātimokkha called Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī
## In the Bhikkhunī Pātimokkha
## The Explanation of the Suddha-pācittiya is finished.

Regarding these Suddha-pācittiya rules, the decision on the origins (samuṭṭhāna) among the unique training rules is briefly as follows: The Giraggasamajja rule, the Cittāgāra rule, the Saṅghāṇī rule, the Itthālaṅkāra rule, the Gandhavannaka rule, the Vāsitakapiññāka rule, and the rules concerning having oneself rubbed or massaged by bhikkhunīs and so on—these ten training rules are acittaka (without intention), lokavajja (worldly faults), and involve unwholesome minds (akusala-citta).

The meaning here is: they are acittaka because they can be committed even without a mind aware of the object; however, when there is awareness, they are lokavajja and involve unwholesome minds because they are committed only with an unwholesome mind. The remaining rules are sacittaka (with intention) and are paṇṇattivajja (faults by regulation) only.

The Corivuṭṭhāpana rule, the Gāmantara rule, the Ārāma rule, the seven rules starting from the first in the Gabbhinivagga, the five rules starting from the first in the Kumāribhūtavagga, the Purisādisaṃsaṭṭha rule, the Pārivāsikachandadāna rule, the Anuvassavuṭṭhāpana rule, and the Ekantarikavuṭṭhāpana rule—these nineteen training rules are sacittaka and paṇṇattivajja. The remaining rules are sacittaka and lokavajja.
355:
## Pāṭidesanīya Section
## 1. Explanation of the Sappiviññāpana Training Rule
Among the Pāṭidesanīya rules, in the first, the Sappiviññāpana rule: "Ghee" (sappi) refers to cow's ghee and so on, as decided previously [in the Bhesajja rule] and as stated in the Pali. Regarding "should she request and eat": there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) in the act of accepting with the thought, "I will eat what is obtained by request." For every swallow of the ghee thus accepted, there is an offense to be confessed (pāṭidesanīya).

This rule was prescribed in Sāvatthī concerning the group-of-six nuns (chabbaggiya) in the case of requesting and eating ghee. "A nun who is not sick" is the supplementary regulation here. There are three types of pāṭidesanīya (tika-pāṭidesanīya). For a sick nun, there are two types of dukkaṭa (dvika-dukkaṭa).

There is no offense for a nun who is sick and eats with the perception of being sick; or if she requests while sick and eats later after recovering; or if she eats the leftovers of a sick nun; or if she eats what is requested from relatives or those who have given an invitation; or if she requests for the sake of another; or if she eats what is obtained with her own property; and there is no offense for one who is insane and so on. In this rule, there are four factors: ghee of the described characteristics, absence of an allowed reason, requesting, and swallowing. The origins and so on are similar to the Addhāna training rule.

## The Explanation of the Sappiviññāpana Training Rule is finished.
## 2. Explanation of the Telaviññāpana and other Training Rules
In the second rule and others, "oil" (tela) and so on are as decided previously and as stated in the Pali. However, regarding the eight items not explicitly mentioned in the Pali, there is only an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). All other procedures are the same as those stated in the first training rule.

## The Explanation of the Telaviññāpana and other Training Rules is finished.
## In the Explanation of the Pātimokkha called Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī
## In the Bhikkhunī Pātimokkha
## The Explanation of the Pāṭidesanīya is finished.
356:
## 1. Explanation of the Parimaṇḍala and other Training Rules
After these Pāṭidesanīya rules, the Sekhiya rules and the Adhikaraṇasamatha rules should be understood in every way according to the method already stated in the explanation of the Bhikkhu Pātimokkha.

## In the Explanation of the Pātimokkha called Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī
## The Explanation of the Bhikkhunī Pātimokkha is finished.

## Concluding Words
By this much sequence of words—
Requested by the Elder Soṇa, I, desiring the crossing of doubts for those who have developed doubts regarding the Vinaya,
Have undertaken this entire explanation of the Pātimokkha, following the method of the Sīhala (Sinhalese) Commentaries, based on the tradition of the residents of the Mahāvihāra.

Relying on that, this [work] has reached completion, having fully incorporated the essence of all commentaries and the entire meaning of the Pali.

In this [work], there is no such term that would contradict the Pali or the ancient commentaries of the residents of the Mahāvihāra.

Therefore, one who seeks his own benefit should not harbor doubt here, but should respectfully learn this Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī.

Just as this Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī has reached completion, with its Pali text measuring twenty-two bhāṇavāras,

So may all the mental desires of all beings, which are based on merit, be fulfilled soon and without obstacle.
357:
This commentary on the Pātimokkha named Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī—composed by the Elder who was given the name Buddhaghosa by his teachers; who is endowed with vast and pure wisdom; who is an ornament to the lineage of great elders such as Tipiṭaka Cūḷanāga, who resided at the Mahāvihāra, who were like torches in the lineage of elders, whose wisdom was well-established in the superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma)—namely, the absorptions (jhāna), paths (magga), and fruits (phala)—and who were adorned with qualities such as the six higher powers (abhiññā) and the retinue of the analytical insights (paṭisambhidā); who is a great poet renowned for composition and style; who is foremost among speakers; who is accustomed to speaking appropriate and pleasing words; who is endowed with the beauty of sweet and noble speech that flows easily and is produced by the perfection of the places and instruments of articulation; who is a great teacher who has mastered all the texts of grammar; who possesses the power of unimpeded knowledge in the Buddha's Dispensation, which consists of the various aspects of the Tipiṭaka scriptures together with the commentaries; who is endowed with sharpness of wisdom; who is capable of penetrating with wisdom into the dense forest of one's own doctrines and the doctrines of others; who is an accumulation of a collection of virtues such as conduct (consisting of vāritta-sīla and cāritta-sīla), uprightness, and gentleness; and who is adorned with extremely pure faith, wisdom, and energy—

May this commentary remain in the world, showing the way of purification of virtue (sīlavisuddhi) to sons of good family who seek liberation from the cycle of existence.

May it remain as long as the name "Buddha" of that Blessed One—who is of pure mind, the foremost in the world, and the seeker of the great virtue—endures in the world.

## The Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī Commentary is finished.
